Cymon.who: Cimone, the boorish youth of Cyprus whom love for Efigenia makes civilised, in Boccaccio's *Decameron* (5.1).

Cynics.who: The Cynics, the Greek philosophical sect of Antisthenes and Diogenes, who scorned wealth, convention and honours.

Cyniras.who: Cinyras, legendary king of Cyprus, whose daughter Myrrha loved him incestuously and bore Adonis (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 10).

Cynocephalus.who: Anubis, the dog-headed Egyptian god who in the myth helped Isis in her mourning search for Osiris.

Cynops.who: Cynops, a sorcerer of Patmos who contends with St John in the apocryphal Acts of John ascribed to Prochorus.

Cynosure.who: Cynosura, the Little Bear and its pole star, by which sailors steered; so, a guiding star.

Cynthia.who: In Martial's line, Cynthia, the mistress celebrated in Propertius' elegies; elsewhere simply a poetic or Italian girl's name.

Cyparissae.basis: The citation of Constantine's agriculture book 10 (the *Geoponica*, on trees) fits the cypress myth.
Cyparissae.who: The daughters of Eteocles (in legend, king of Orchomenus) who were turned into cypress trees, as told in the Byzantine *Geoponica*.

Cyprian Eichovius.who: Cyprianus Eichovius, German compiler of the *Deliciae Hispaniae* (Cologne, 1604), a collection of descriptions of Spain.

Cyprus.who: Cyprus, the eastern Mediterranean island, in antiquity sacred to Venus.

Cyril.who: St Cyril of Alexandria (d. 444), patriarch and theologian, who wrote a refutation of the emperor Julian's attack on Christianity.

Cyropaed.who: Xenophon's *Cyropaedia*, an idealised account of the education and reign of Cyrus the Great.

Cyrus.who: In the Xenophon passages, Cyrus the Great (d. 530 BC), founder of the Persian empire; in Plutarch's *Artaxerxes*, Cyrus the Younger, killed at Cunaxa in 401 BC.

Cyzeni.who: The people of Cyzicus, a Greek city on the Sea of Marmara, where Pliny places a spring of Cupid that cures love.

Cyzicum.who: Cyzicus, Greek city on the Sea of Marmara (Kapıdağ peninsula, Turkey), unsuccessfully besieged by Mithridates VI in 73 BC.

Cyzicus.who: Cyzicus, an ancient Greek city on the southern shore of the Sea of Marmara, now in ruins in Turkey.

D. Claudius.who: 'Divus Claudius', the emperor Claudius (r. AD 41–54), deified after his death.

D. Hadrianus.who: 'Divus Hadrianus', the emperor Hadrian (r. AD 117–138), deified after his death.

Daedalian.who: An adjective from Daedalus, the mythical master craftsman: so, intricately ingenious.

Daedalus.who: Daedalus, the legendary Athenian craftsman and sculptor, builder of the Cretan labyrinth.

Dagobert.who: Dagobert I (d. 639), Merovingian king of the Franks and patron of the abbey of Saint-Denis; father of Clovis II.

Dagon.who: Dagon, the chief god of the Philistines in the Old Testament (Judges 16; 1 Samuel 5).

Dalecampius.who: Jacques Daléchamps (1513–1588), French physician and botanist of Lyon, compiler of the *Historia generalis plantarum* (1586–87).

Dalliance.who: An allegorical figure, personified pleasure-making, in a symbolic picture of Opulentia (Wealth).

Damagetus.who: Damagetus, the addressee of the spurious Hippocratic letters describing Hippocrates' visit to Democritus at Abdera.

Damascen.basis: The cited works separate three different Damasceni; the medical one is the least certain.
Damascen.who: In *De orthodoxa fide*, St John of Damascus (d. c. 750), Greek theologian; on the Celts, Nicolaus of Damascus; 'Damascen the Arabian' is the Arabic medical author Johannes Damascenus.

Damascus.who: Damascus, the ancient city of Syria, famous for its gardens and waters.

Damasippus.who: Damasippus, a bankrupt art-dealer turned Stoic who, in Horace's *Satires* 2.3, argues that all fools are mad.

Damian.who: St Damian, with his twin St Cosmas a physician martyred in Syria (c. 300), patron saint of physicians; the two are always paired.

Damianus à Goes.who: Damião de Góis (1502–1574), Portuguese humanist and chronicler, who wrote a Latin account of the Lapps.

Damiata.who: Damietta, a port on the eastern mouth of the Nile in the delta of Egypt.

Damon.who: Damon, the Pythagorean of Syracuse who offered his life as surety for his friend Pythias (Phintias) before the tyrant Dionysius.

Danae.who: Danaë, Argive princess whom Zeus visited as a shower of gold in her prison; she became the mother of Perseus.

Danaeus.who: Lambert Daneau (c.1530–1595), French Calvinist theologian who wrote a dialogue on witches, a treatise against games of chance, and a catalogue of heresies.

Danaus.basis: The first passage is clearly the mythical Danaus. The second probably is too: Pausanias tells of Danaus finding husbands for his daughters by a race, and 'Lacedaemon' looks like Burton's slip.
Danaus.who: Danaus, mythical king of Argos and son of Belus, father of the fifty Danaids.

Dandinus.who: Girolamo Dandini (1554–1634), Italian Jesuit philosopher, author of a commentary on Aristotle's De anima.

Dane.who: A native of Denmark; here describing the Danish physician Petrus Severinus.

Daniel Federer.basis: a patient known only from a case recorded by Schenck

Daniel Gare.basis: a subject of a horoscope in Camerarius; nothing further known

Daniel Sennertus.who: Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), German physician and professor of medicine at Wittenberg, author of a widely used medical textbook.

Dante.who: Dante Alighieri (1265–1321), Florentine poet, author of the Divine Comedy.

Dantes.who: Dante Alighieri (1265–1321), Florentine poet whose Inferno describes hell.

Danubius.who: The Danube, the great river of central and south-eastern Europe.

Danvers.who: Henry Danvers, Earl of Danby (1573–1644), English soldier who founded the Oxford Physic Garden, now the Botanic Garden, in 1621.

Danzig.who: Danzig, now Gdańsk in Poland, a Baltic port in what was then Prussia ('Spruce').

Daphnaeus.who: Daphnaeus, a speaker in Plutarch's dialogue on love (Amatorius), where he praises marriage.

Daphne.who: Daphne, the nymph who fled from Apollo and was turned into a laurel (bay) tree.

Daphnis.basis: different figures: a girl in Aristaenetus' letters, a courtesan in Lucian's dialogues, and Theocritus' pastoral herdsman

Dares Phrygius.who: Dares Phrygius, the Trojan priest in Homer said to have written a history of Troy's fall; the surviving Latin prose version is late antique.

Darii.who: The Persian kings named Darius, used as a type of great wealth.

Darius.who: Darius III of Persia (r. 336–330 BC), defeated by Alexander, in the first two passages; Darius I (r. 522–486 BC) in the 1 Esdras story.

Darrell.who: John Darrell (b. c.1562), English Puritan exorcist whose claims to dispossess demoniacs set off a pamphlet war around 1599–1602.

Dasamonquepeuc.who: Dasamonquepeuc, an Algonquian village on the mainland facing Roanoke Island, North Carolina, described in the accounts of Raleigh's Virginia voyages.

Dathan.who: Dathan, an Israelite who rebelled with Korah against Moses and was swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16).

Daulis.who: Daulis, an ancient town in Phocis, central Greece, where the myth of Procne and Philomela was set (hence no swallows).

Dauphine.who: The Dauphiné, a former province of south-eastern France bordering Savoy.

David.who: David, king of Israel, traditionally the author of the Psalms.

David George.who: David Joris (c.1501–1556), Dutch glass-painter and Anabaptist leader from Delft, who claimed a messianic role.

David Helde.basis: a patient known only from Ruland's case

Dea Syria.who: The Syrian Goddess (Atargatis), whose inspiration Eunus claimed when he led the Sicilian slave revolt (c. 135 BC).

Deacon.who: John Deacon, co-author with John Walker of the Dialogicall Discourses of Spirits and Divels (1601) against Darrell; in the second passage 'the Deacon' is Philip the Evangelist.

Death.basis: common noun, personified in the Cupid fable

Deborah.who: Deborah, the nurse of Rebekah, buried under the oak Allon Bachuth near Bethel (Genesis 35:8); not the judge Deborah.

Deccan.who: The Deccan, the plateau of south-central India, then ruled by several sultanates.

Decii.who: The Decii Mures, Roman consuls (father 340 BC, son 295 BC) who each devoted themselves to death in battle to win victory for Rome.

Decius.who: Decius (r. 249–251), Roman emperor who led the first empire-wide persecution of Christians.

Declamat.basis: abbreviation of 'Declamatio', a reference to a work by Beroaldus

Deianira.who: Deianira, wife of Hercules, who unknowingly killed him with the shirt poisoned with Nessus' blood.

Deidamia.who: Deidamia, daughter of King Lycomedes of Scyros, by whom Achilles, hidden there in women's clothes, fathered Pyrrhus (Neoptolemus).

Deiotarus.who: Deiotarus (d. c. 40 BC), tetrarch and later king of Galatia, an ally of Rome whom Cicero defended in his speech Pro rege Deiotaro.

Del Zur.who: The Mar del Sur ('South Sea'), the Spanish name for the Pacific Ocean.

Delft.who: Delft, a town in the province of Holland in the Netherlands, where the physician Pieter van Foreest (Forestus) practised.

Delia.basis: It appears in a list of literary mistresses' names, e.g. Laura.
Delia.who: Delia, a conventional name for a poet's mistress, made famous by Tibullus's elegies and Samuel Daniel's sonnet sequence Delia (1592).

Delilah.who: Delilah, the Philistine woman in Judges 16 who betrayed Samson.

Deliro.who: Signior Deliro, the doting husband of Fallace in Ben Jonson's comedy Every Man out of His Humour (1599).

Delos.who: Delos, a small island in the Cyclades of the Aegean, the mythical birthplace of Apollo and Artemis and a great sanctuary of Apollo.

Delphis.who: Delphis, the beloved woman in one of the fictional Greek love letters of Aristaenetus (c. 5th century AD).

Delphos.who: Delphi, the seat of Apollo's oracle in Phocis, central Greece; 'Delphos' is the older English form of the name.

Demades.who: Demades (c. 380–319 BC), Athenian orator. After the battle of Chaeronea he famously rebuked Philip II of Macedon.

Demaeneta.who: Demaeneta, the stepmother of Cnemon in Heliodorus's Greek romance the Aethiopica.

Demaratus.who: Demaratus of Corinth (4th century BC), a guest-friend and trusted adviser of Philip II of Macedon.

Demaretus.who: Demaretus, the fictional friend to whom one of Aristaenetus's Greek love letters is addressed.

Demea.who: Demea, the strict father in Terence's comedy Adelphoe (The Brothers); his indulgent brother is Micio.

Demetrius.basis: Each passage's context points to a different bearer.
Demetrius.who: Different bearers: a pirate who rebuked Alexander; Demetrius the Cynic (1st century AD), Seneca's friend; and Demetrius Poliorcetes (d. 283 BC), king of Macedon, who died as Seleucus's captive.

Demochares.basis: The passages do not settle which Demochares is meant.

Democritus.who: Democritus of Abdera (c. 460–c. 370 BC), Greek atomist philosopher known as the 'laughing philosopher', whose name Burton takes as his pen name.

Democritus Christianus.who: Democritus Christianus (Cologne, 1616), a moral treatise on contempt of the world's vanities by the French preacher Pierre de Besse (Petrus Bessaeus).

Democritus Junior.who: Democritus Junior, the pen name under which Robert Burton (1577–1640) published The Anatomy of Melancholy.

Democritus’ Collyrium.basis: 'Collyrium' means eye-salve, and the name follows the old custom of naming remedies after authorities.
Democritus’ Collyrium.who: An eye-salve (collyrium) named after the philosopher Democritus.

Demonax.who: Demonax (c. AD 70–170), Cynic philosopher at Athens, known from Lucian's life of him.

Demoniacal.who: An adjective meaning 'caused by demons'; here a class of dreams.

Demophantus.who: Demophantus, a rich suitor mentioned by a courtesan in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans.

Demophoon.who: Demophoon, son of Theseus, who left Phyllis of Thrace. She hanged herself when he did not return, as Ovid's Heroides 2 relates.

Demosthenes.who: Demosthenes (384–322 BC), the greatest Athenian orator and an opponent of Philip II of Macedon.

Denis.who: Saint Denis (3rd century), first bishop of Paris, a martyr and patron saint of France, buried at Saint-Denis.

Derbyshire.who: Derbyshire, a county in the English Midlands.

Derision.who: A personified abstraction (mockery) in an allegorical list.

Dervishes.who: Dervishes, members of Muslim Sufi religious orders, known for their poverty and ascetic practices.

Desire.who: An ordinary word (desire), capitalised in the text.

Despair.who: A personified abstraction in an allegorical list.

Destiny.who: Fate, the necessity in which the Stoics believed; an ordinary word, capitalised in the text.

Deucalion.who: Deucalion, in Greek myth the son of Prometheus. With his wife Pyrrha he survived the flood and repeopled the earth by throwing stones.

Deverra.who: Deverra, a minor Roman goddess whose broom-sweeping rite protected women after childbirth; Augustine mentions her.

Devizes.who: Devizes, a market town in Wiltshire, England, whose castle was built by Roger, Bishop of Salisbury, in the 12th century.

Diacapers.who: An old compound medicine (electuary) made with capers.

Diacassia.who: An old laxative electuary made with cassia pulp.

Diacatholicon.who: Diacatholicon, an old 'universal' purgative electuary made with senna, cassia and similar drugs.

Diacodion.who: Diacodion, an old syrup made from poppy heads, used as a sedative.

Diacorolli.who: Diacorallion, a cooling compound medicine made with coral.

Diacosmus.who: The *Diakosmos* ("World-Order"), cosmological treatise listed among Democritus's works by Diogenes Laertius; now lost.

Diagalinga.who: Diagalanga, a warming electuary made with galingale root.

Diagoras.who: Diagoras of Melos (fl. late 5th century BC), Greek lyric poet notorious in antiquity as an atheist.

Diambra.who: Diambra, a warming aromatic confection made with ambergris.

Diamond.who: The gemstone, credited with occult virtues in Renaissance lapidaries.

Diana.who: Diana, Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon, identified with Artemis, whose great temple stood at Ephesus.

Dianthus.who: Dianthos, a warming aromatic cordial confection of the old pharmacopoeias.

Diapason.who: Musical term for the octave, used figuratively for perfect harmony.

Diapolypodium.who: A purging electuary made with polypody fern.

Diarbecha.who: Diyarbakır (Diyarbekir), region of Upper Mesopotamia on the upper Tigris, now in south-eastern Turkey.

Diarrhodon Abbatis.who: Diarrhodon Abbatis, the "Abbot's" cooling confection of roses in the old pharmacopoeias.

Diasenna.who: A purging electuary made with senna.

Diaserum Fernelii.basis: The name means 'Fernel's diaserum'. Its exact composition is not certain.
Diaserum Fernelii.who: A purging preparation named after the French physician Jean Fernel (1497–1558).

Diazinziber.who: Diazingiber, a warming confection made with ginger.

Dibrenses.who: Inhabitants of Dibra (Debar), on the modern Albania–North Macedonia border; the dead-dog story concerns the Turkish siege of Sfetigrad (1448).

Dibutades.who: Butades (Dibutades) of Sicyon, legendary potter whose daughter traced her lover's shadow; Pliny tells the story as the origin of modelling in clay.

Dicaearchus.who: Dicaearchus of Messana (fl. c. 320 BC), Peripatetic philosopher and geographer, pupil of Aristotle, who measured mountain heights and criticised Plato.

Dictis Cretensis.who: Dictys Cretensis, supposed Cretan eyewitness of the Trojan War, whose diary survives in a late-antique Latin version.

Didacus à Stunica.who: Diego de Zúñiga (1536–c. 1598), Spanish Augustinian whose commentary on Job (1584) endorsed the Copernican motion of the earth.

Dido.who: Dido, legendary founder and queen of Carthage, who killed herself when Aeneas left her (Virgil, *Aeneid* 4).

Dido Virg.who: Dido, queen of Carthage, speaking in Virgil's *Aeneid* (1.630); the form is a margin note, 'Dido, Virg.'

Diet.who: Diet, i.e. regimen; personified as 'Dr. Diet' in the Salernitan proverb.

Differences.who: Ordinary word: the kinds or species of melancholy.

Digestion.who: One of the four powers of the nutritive faculty in Galenic physiology.

Digges.who: Thomas Digges (c. 1546–1595), English mathematician and astronomer, the first to publish an English defence of the Copernican system (1576).

Diggseus.who: Thomas Digges (c. 1546–1595), English astronomer and early English defender of Copernicus.

Dinah.who: Dinah, daughter of Jacob and Leah, violated by Shechem (Genesis 34).

Dinias.basis: Burton cites Lucian's Charidemus. I cannot confirm Dinias's exact role in it.
Dinias.who: Dinias, a guest at Androcles' feast in the pseudo-Lucianic dialogue *Charidemus*, on beauty.

Dinomachus.basis: Burton cites Lucian's courtesan dialogues. I cannot place the exact dialogue.
Dinomachus.who: A fictional young lover in Lucian's *Dialogues of the Courtesans*.

Dio Nicaeus.who: Cassius Dio (c. 155–c. 235), Greek historian from Nicaea, author of a Roman History that covers Septimius Severus.

Diocles.who: Diocles of Carystus (4th century BC), Greek physician whose account of hypochondriac melancholy Galen quotes and criticises.

Dioclesiani Therma.who: The Baths of Diocletian in Rome, the largest of the imperial baths, completed c. 306.

Dioclesianus Herculeus.basis: Burton pairs 'Maximus Jovianus' with 'Dioclesianus Herculeus'. Historically Diocletian was Jovius and Maximian Herculius.
Dioclesianus Herculeus.who: The tetrarch emperors Diocletian (Jovius) and Maximian (Herculius), who styled themselves after Jupiter and Hercules; Burton seems to transpose the epithets.

Diocletian.who: Diocletian, Roman emperor 284–305, who abdicated and retired to his palace at Split to grow cabbages; builder of great baths in Rome.

Diogenes.who: Diogenes of Sinope (c. 400–c. 323 BC), the Cynic philosopher who lived in a tub.

Diogenianus.who: Diogenianus of Heraclea (2nd century AD), Greek grammarian in Hadrian's time whose collection of proverbs survives.

Diognetus.basis: Burton's 'Idem' points to Parthenius. The Polycrite story there matches.
Diognetus.who: Diognetus, the Erythraean commander besieging Naxos who loved Polycrite and betrayed his own side, in Parthenius's *Love Stories* 9.

Diomede.who: Diomedes, Greek hero of the Trojan War, who wins Cressida from Troilus in the medieval story told by Boccaccio, Chaucer and Shakespeare.

Diomedes.who: Diomedes, mythical king of the Bistones in Thrace, whose man-eating mares Hercules took; Hercules killed the king in one of his labours.

Dion.who: Cassius Dio (c. 164–after 229), Greek-writing Roman senator and historian, author of a Roman History that includes the emperors.

Dionysian.who: The Dionysia, festivals of Dionysus (Bacchus), known for licence and revelry.

Dionysius.basis: Passages 2–3; in passage 1 the name means the Dionysius to whom one of the spurious Hippocratic letters is addressed.
Dionysius.who: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite (c. 500), Christian Neoplatonist author of the Celestial Hierarchy, which ranks the angels in nine orders.

Dionysius Halicarnasseus.who: Dionysius of Halicarnassus (fl. c. 30–8 BC), Greek historian and rhetorician at Rome, author of the Roman Antiquities.

Dionysius Junior.who: Dionysius II, the Younger, tyrant of Syracuse in the 4th century BC, twice driven from power, who ended his life in exile at Corinth.

Dionysodorus.who: Dionysodorus of Melos, Greek geometer; Pliny (Natural History 2.112) tells the story of his letter from the centre of the earth.

Dioscorides.who: Pedanius Dioscorides (fl. 1st century AD), Greek physician whose De materia medica was the standard herbal; Mattioli wrote a famous commentary on it.

Dioscorides’ Rhododaphne.who: Pedanius Dioscorides (fl. 1st century AD), Greek physician and herbalist; his rhododaphne is the oleander, a handsome but poisonous shrub.

Dioscuri.who: The Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, twin sons of Zeus who protected sailors; their name was given to the lights seen on masts (St Elmo's fire).

Diphilus.who: Diphilus, the lover of the courtesan Philinna in one of Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans; a fictional character.

Disarius.who: Dysarius, a physician who speaks in Macrobius's Saturnalia (early 5th century) and answers the questions about medicine and the body.

Dithmarus Blefkenius.who: Dithmar Blefken, German traveller and pastor, whose Islandia (1607) gave a much-disputed account of Iceland and its people.

Ditmarsh.who: Dithmarschen, a low marshy district on the North Sea coast of western Holstein, in northern Germany.

Divus Augustus.who: Augustus (63 BC–AD 14), first Roman emperor, who was declared a god ('divus') after his death.

Dodona.who: Dodona, in Epirus in north-western Greece, site of the ancient oracle of Zeus.

Dodonaeus.who: Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), Flemish physician and botanist, author of a widely translated herbal.

Doll.who: Doll, pet form of Dorothy, used here as a stock girl's name in an alliterative list.

Dominicans.who: The Dominicans, the Order of Preachers, a mendicant order of friars founded by St Dominic in 1216.

Dominicus Niger.who: Domenico Mario Negri (1475–c. 1528), Venetian humanist geographer, author of the Geographiae commentarii.

Dominicus Sylvius.who: Domenico Selvo, Doge of Venice 1071–1084, who married a Byzantine princess remembered for her extreme luxury.

Domitian.who: Domitian (51–96), Roman emperor 81–96, known for his cruelty and for demanding to be addressed as 'lord and god'.

Domitian Agricola.basis: Domitian's jealousy of Agricola is told in Tacitus' Agricola
Domitian Agricola.who: Two names run together: the emperor Domitian envied Gnaeus Julius Agricola (40–93), Roman general, governor of Britain and father-in-law of Tacitus.

Domitians.who: Domitian (51–96), Roman emperor, used here in the plural to mean tyrants like him.

Domitian’s Parthenius.who: Parthenius, chamberlain and favourite freedman of the emperor Domitian, and one of the plotters in his murder in 96.

Dompius.who: François Domptius, Flemish Dominican who, with Sébastien Michaëlis, exorcised Madeleine de Demandolx at Sainte-Baume in the Gaufridy witchcraft case (1610–11).

Don Garcia de Sylva.who: García de Silva y Figueroa (1550–1624), Spanish diplomat, Philip III's ambassador to Shah Abbas of Persia, who wrote an account of his embassy.

Don Quixote.who: Don Quixote, the hero of Cervantes' novel (1605–15), driven mad by reading romances of chivalry.

Donatists.who: The Donatists, a schismatic Christian church of 4th–5th-century North Africa; its extreme wing sought martyrdom.

Donatus Altomarus.who: Donato Antonio Altomare (c. 1506–1566), Neapolitan physician and medical writer.

Donatus ab Altomari.who: Donato Antonio Altomare (c. 1506–1566), Neapolitan physician, author of an Ars medicinalis.

Doric.who: Doric, the Greek dialect, used proverbially to mean a rustic, unpolished style.

Dorinda.basis: a stock name for a girl; no particular bearer

Doris.basis: In passages 1 and 3 this is Doris the sea-nymph (Lucian, Dialogues of the Sea-Gods). In passage 2 it is Doris, the old mistress in Petronius' Satyricon.

Dorotheus.who: Dorotheus of Sidon (1st century AD), Greek astrological poet whose work survived chiefly through Arabic astrologers.

Dorothy.basis: a Christian name used generically; no particular bearer

Dort.who: Dordrecht, a town in the province of Holland in the Netherlands.

Dosicles.who: Dosicles, the hero of Theodore Prodromos' 12th-century Byzantine verse romance Rhodanthe and Dosicles.

Dotage.who: Dotage, a general term for disorder of the mind.

Dousabel.basis: the name and the pastoral context fit Drayton's ballad of Dowsabel in his eclogues
Dousabel.who: Dowsabel, the country lass of Michael Drayton's pastoral ballad of Dowsabel, coupled here with Chaucer's Sir Thopas.

Dove.who: John Dove (1561–1618), English divine, author of A Confutation of Atheism (1605).

Dover.who: Dover, the Channel port in Kent, whose harbour suffered from silting.

Drake.who: Sir Francis Drake (c. 1540–1596), English navigator who sailed round the world in 1577–80.

Drakesly.who: Drakelow, on the Trent near Burton upon Trent in Derbyshire, seat of the Gresley family.

Drayton.who: Fenny Drayton, Leicestershire, near Burton's birthplace of Lindley, seat of the Purefoy family.

Dresden.who: Dresden, capital of the Electorate of Saxony, in the region of Meissen.

Dropax.who: Dropax, a pitch plaster applied to the skin as a counter-irritant.

Druids.who: The Druids, priests of the ancient Gauls and Britons, who taught according to Caesar that the soul passes after death into another body.

Drusianus.who: Pietro Torrigiano (Turisanus or Drusianus, d. c. 1320), Florentine physician and commentator on Galen, who gave up medicine to become a Carthusian monk.

Dryades.who: Dryads, the tree and wood nymphs of Greek myth.

Du Bartas.who: Guillaume de Salluste Du Bartas (1544–1590), Gascon Huguenot poet, author of La Sepmaine, a poem on the Creation.

Du Plessis.who: Philippe Duplessis-Mornay (1549–1623), French Huguenot statesman and theological writer.

Dublin.who: Dublin, in Ireland, where Henry II kept his Christmas in 1171.

Dubliulius.basis: the cited title matches a pilgrimage narrative under this name; details about the author are uncertain
Dubliulius.who: Johannes Dubliulius, author of a Latin account (Hodoeporicon) of a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, published around 1599.

Dubravius.who: Jan Dubravius (Skála z Doubravky, c. 1486–1553), Bishop of Olomouc, author of De piscinis, a treatise on fishponds.

Dudithus.who: Andreas Dudith (1533–1589), Hungarian humanist and former Catholic bishop who turned Protestant; he corresponded with Jacob Monau.

Duff.who: Dub (Duff), 10th-century King of Scots; Boece tells how witches made him waste away by melting a wax image of him.

Duke.who: A title, here the 'Duke' in Duke Humphrey of Gloucester.

Dulcinea.who: Dulcinea del Toboso, the peasant girl Don Quixote idolises as his lady in Cervantes' novel.

Dunmow.who: Dunmow (Little Dunmow), Essex, whose priory was linked by legend to Matilda Fitzwalter, the lady pursued by King John.

Durand.who: Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), French Dominican scholastic theologian and commentator on Peter Lombard's Sentences.

Durazzo.who: Durazzo, the Adriatic port of Albania, now Durrës.

Duretus.who: Louis Duret (1527–1586), French physician at Paris, who annotated Jacques Houllier's (Hollerius) works on internal diseases.

Dutch.who: In Burton's usage 'Dutch' usually means German (High or Low), not only Netherlandish; so a 'Dutch mile' is a German mile.

Dutchman.who: A Netherlander; here a soldier from the Low Countries fighting at 's-Hertogenbosch in Brabant.

Dutchmen.who: Germans and Netherlanders; Burton's 'Dutch' covers the German peoples generally.

Dux Polonus.basis: 'The Polish duke' among travel writers fits Radziwiłł's widely read Hierosolymitana peregrinatio.
Dux Polonus.who: Mikołaj Krzysztof 'Sierotka' Radziwiłł (1549–1616), Polish-Lithuanian prince whose account of his pilgrimage to Jerusalem and Egypt was published in Latin in 1601.

E Graeco Ruf.basis: 'Ruf.' with 'e Graeco' and an amatory epigram suggests Rufinus of the Anthology.
E Graeco Ruf.who: Rufinus, Greek epigrammatist whose love epigrams are preserved in the Greek Anthology; Burton's marginal note means 'from the Greek of Rufinus'.

E Graeco Simonidis.basis: The verses on a wife loathing her husband fit Semonides' poem on women, which was usually ascribed to 'Simonides'.
E Graeco Simonidis.who: Semonides (often called Simonides) of Amorgos, 7th-century BC Greek iambic poet whose satire on the types of women is quoted here in Latin.

E Grec.who: A source note meaning 'from the Greek', not a name.

E Luciano.who: Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–after 180), Greek satirist; the note means 'from Lucian'.

E Stobaeo.who: Joannes Stobaeus (5th century), Greek compiler of an anthology of extracts from earlier poets and prose writers; the note means 'from Stobaeus'.

Easily.who: An ordinary word, not a name.

East Indies.who: The East Indies: in Burton's time, India and all of South and East Asia, including Japan.

Eastern.who: An ordinary adjective, not a name.

Eban.who: 'Ebon' (ebony) stone, a polishing stone; not a proper name.

Ecbatana.who: Ecbatana, the ancient Median capital and summer residence of the Persian kings, now Hamadan in western Iran.

Eccentricity.who: An astronomical term, not a name.

Eccentrics.who: An astronomical term (eccentric orbs), not a name.

Ecclesiast.who: Erasmus's Ecclesiastes, sive de ratione concionandi (1535), his treatise on preaching.

Echo.basis: The common noun and the nymph both appear.
Echo.who: Mostly the ordinary word 'echo', but in the Ausonius passage it is Echo, the nymph who was reduced to a voice.

Echo Satyrus.who: Echo, the nymph; in Moschus' epigram Pan loves Echo, Echo loves a Satyr, and the Satyr loves Lyde.

Echoes.who: An ordinary word, not a name.

Echoes. Blancanus.who: Giuseppe Biancani (Blancanus) (1566–1624), Italian Jesuit mathematician and astronomer, author of an Echometria on echoes.

Ecstasis.who: A medical term (ecstasy, trance), not a name.

Ecstasy.who: A medical term, not a name.

Edgar Ætheling.who: Edgar Ætheling (c. 1051–c. 1126), last male of the West Saxon royal house, proclaimed king after Hastings in 1066 but never crowned.

Edgemond.who: Mount Edgcumbe, the Edgcumbe family's seat on the Cornish shore of Plymouth Sound, praised in Richard Carew's Survey of Cornwall.

Edinus.basis: The story of a Danish king maddened by a sound, told by Krantz, matches the tale of Eric the Good; the form 'Edinus' is odd.
Edinus.who: Probably Eric I Ejegod (r. 1095–1103), king of Denmark, who according to Saxo was driven to frenzy by a harper's music and killed some of his own men.

Edmond Ironside.who: Edmund II Ironside (d. 1016), English king, said in legend to have fought Cnut in single combat at Alney on the Severn.

Edmund Gunter.who: Edmund Gunter (1581–1626), English mathematician and Gresham professor of astronomy, who published tables of logarithmic sines and tangents in 1620.

Edmundsbury.who: Bury St Edmunds in Suffolk, seat of a great and wealthy Benedictine abbey.

Education.who: A section heading, not a name.

Edulica.who: Edulica (Educa, Edusa), a minor Roman goddess who presided over children's eating, mocked by Augustine in the City of God.

Edward.basis: Each passage names a different Edward.
Edward.who: Different English kings: Edward IV (the 26 battles), Edward II (imprisoned and deposed) and Edward I (father of Edward of Caernarvon).

Edward Senior.who: Edward the Elder (r. 899–924), son of Alfred, king of the Anglo-Saxons.

Edwin Sandys.who: Sir Edwin Sandys (1561–1629), English politician, author of A Relation of the State of Religion (1605), a survey of religion in Europe.

Egnatius.who: Giovanni Battista Egnazio (Egnatius) (1478–1553), Venetian humanist, author of a De Caesaribus on the Roman emperors.

Egyptian.basis: generic adjective; different bearers in each passage
Egyptian.who: A native of ancient Egypt; Burton applies the word to different Egyptians: a man in Plutarch, Egyptian priests, and an Egyptian prince.

Egyptian Pharaohs.who: The kings of ancient Egypt, here Moeris and Sesostris, remembered for their great building works.

Egyptian Pyramids.who: The ancient royal tombs of Egypt, chiefly the pyramids at Giza near Cairo.

Egyptians.who: The ancient Egyptians, the people of Egypt.

Ela.basis: the story of Joshua ben Hananiah and the lion matches the Talmudic passage; Burton's spelling of the name is garbled
Ela.who: The forest of 'Be Ilai' in the Talmudic story of Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah and the emperor (Babylonian Talmud, Hullin 59b), home of a monstrous lion.

Eldorado.who: El Dorado, the legendary golden city or kingdom of South America (also called Manoa), sought by Ralegh and other explorers.

Elean.who: Of Elis, the city-state of the north-western Peloponnese that controlled Olympia.

Eleazar.who: Eleazar, a Jewish exorcist who, according to Josephus (Antiquities 8), drove out demons before Vespasian using charms ascribed to Solomon.

Electra.who: In the first passage, Electra the sister of Orestes in Euripides' Orestes; in the second, Electra the maid whom Stratonice gave to King Deiotarus of Galatia (Plutarch).

Elege.who: One of the Proetides, the daughters of King Proetus of Argos or Tiryns, cured of madness by the seer Melampus.

Elenora.basis: the first is certain from Drayton; for the second, Burton says 'St. Lewis', but the famously ill-matched wife is Eleanor of Aquitaine, wife of Louis VII
Elenora.who: First, Eleanor Cobham (d. 1452), Duchess of Gloucester, exiled for witchcraft, in Drayton's Englands Heroicall Epistles; second, apparently Eleanor of Aquitaine, wife of Louis VII of France.

Eleonora.basis: Philip the Good's Portuguese marriage at Bruges in winter was to Isabella; the name 'Eleonora' seems to be an error in Burton or his source
Eleonora.who: Apparently Isabella of Portugal (1397–1471), daughter of John I of Portugal, who married Philip the Good of Burgundy at Bruges in January 1430.

Eleonora Meliorina.basis: known only from Donati's case report
Eleonora Meliorina.who: A gentlewoman of Mantua whose delusion of being married to a king is recorded by the physician Marcello Donati.

Elephantine.who: Elephantis, a Greek woman writer of erotic manuals, mentioned by Martial and Suetonius (Tiberius).

Eliacis.who: Pausanias's Eliaca, the books (5–6) of his Description of Greece on Elis and Olympia.

Elias.who: In the first passage, 'Elias Artista', the Paracelsian restorer of the arts whose coming was prophesied; in the others, the prophet Elijah.

Elias Artifex.who: 'Elias Artista', the legendary adept whose coming Paracelsus and his followers foretold as the restorer of all arts and sciences.

Eliases.who: Impostors and enthusiasts who claimed to be the prophet Elijah returned.

Eliphaz.who: Eliphaz the Temanite, the first of Job's three comforters in the Book of Job.

Elis.who: Elis, the region and city in the north-western Peloponnese of Greece, which controlled Olympia.

Eliseus.who: Elisha (Latin Eliseus), Hebrew prophet and successor of Elijah.

Elisha.who: Elisha, Hebrew prophet and successor of Elijah, who cured Naaman the Syrian of leprosy (2 Kings 5).

Elixation.who: Boiling or seething, a term of the old physiology of digestion.

Elizabeth.who: First, Queen Elizabeth I of England (1533–1603); second, Elizabeth of York (1466–1503), daughter of Edward IV and queen of Henry VII.

Elkanah.who: Elkanah, husband of Hannah and father of the prophet Samuel (1 Samuel 1).

Elpenor.who: Elpenor, companion of Odysseus whom Circe turned into a swine in Homer's Odyssey.

Ely.who: Ely, cathedral city in Cambridgeshire; the bishop meant is William Longchamp (d. 1197), chancellor and justiciar under Richard I.

Elyot.who: Sir Thomas Elyot (c. 1490–1546), English humanist and diplomat, author of the popular health manual The Castel of Helth.

Elysian.who: The Elysian Fields, the classical paradise of the blessed dead.

Emanuel.who: Manuel I (1469–1521), King of Portugal, whose reign Jerónimo Osório chronicled in De rebus Emmanuelis gestis.

Emblem.who: An emblem, a symbolic picture with a motto, from the emblem books Burton cites.

Embryo.who: The unborn child in the womb.

Emerald.who: The emerald, a green precious stone.

Emilia.who: Emilia Pia (d. 1528), lady of the court of Urbino and a speaker in Castiglione's Book of the Courtier.

Emily.who: Emelye, the lady whom Palamon and Arcite both love in Chaucer's Knight's Tale.

Emma.who: Emma of Normandy (d. 1052), queen of Æthelred II and Cnut and mother of Edward the Confessor, said in legend to have passed an ordeal of red-hot ploughshares.

Emmanuel Philibert.who: Emmanuel Philibert (1528–1580), Duke of Savoy, general for Spain who won the battle of St Quentin.

Emmetris.basis: a green stone named in Cardano; which mineral is meant is uncertain

Empedocles.who: Empedocles of Acragas (c. 495–435 BC), Greek philosopher-poet; legend says he threw himself into Etna, and he was said to calm madness with music.

Emporiums. Valois.basis: The text runs 'Emporiums' into the name; the name meant is Valois.
Emporiums. Valois.who: The Valois, the royal house of France from 1328 until it died out with Henri III in 1589.

Empyrean.who: The empyrean, the highest and outermost heaven in the old cosmology.

Encelius.who: Christoph Entzelt (Encelius), 16th-century German Lutheran pastor, author of De re metallica, a treatise on metals, stones and gems and their virtues.

Encyclopaedian.who: Encyclopaedic, i.e. covering the whole circle of learning.

Endor.who: Endor, a village in ancient Israel where Saul consulted a witch who called up Samuel's ghost (1 Samuel 28).

Endymion.who: Endymion, the beautiful youth of Greek myth whom the Moon (Selene) loved and who was laid in an endless sleep.

English.who: The English, or the English language.

Enneades.who: The Enneades (Rhapsodiae historiarum), a universal history by the Venetian humanist Marcantonio Coccio Sabellico (c. 1436–1506).

Enneads.who: The Enneads, the treatises of the Neoplatonist Plotinus (c. 204–270), arranged by his pupil Porphyry in six groups of nine.

Ennia.basis: Known only as the wife named on Rubenius Celer's epitaph; I know nothing more of her.

Ennius.who: Quintus Ennius (239–169 BC), early Roman poet, author of the Annales; he praised Scipio Africanus, who was his patron.

Enthusiasms.who: Enthusiasms, i.e. states of divine inspiration or possession.

Enthusiasmus.who: Enthusiasm, i.e. divine inspiration or frenzy.

Enthusiasts.who: Enthusiasts, i.e. people who claim direct divine inspiration.

Entisberus.who: William Heytesbury (Hentisberus, d. c. 1372), Oxford logician, one of the Merton 'Calculators', known for his subtle sophismata.

Envy.who: Envy, a passion and a heading.

Eobanus Hessus.who: Helius Eobanus Hessus (1488–1540), German humanist Latin poet, author among other works of a verse regimen of health.

Epaminondas.who: Epaminondas (d. 362 BC), Theban general who won at Leuctra (371 BC) and died at Mantinea; he never married.

Ephemer.who: The Ephemerides of David Origanus (1558–1628), German astronomer and astrologer at Frankfurt an der Oder.

Ephemerides.who: Ephemerides, i.e. astronomical tables giving the daily positions of the planets.

Ephesian.basis: The two passages mean different people.
Ephesian.who: In the first passage, the Widow of Ephesus in Petronius' Satyricon, a faithful mourner seduced by a soldier; in the second, a different Ephesian, in Philostratus' Life of Apollonius.

Ephesians.who: St Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians.

Ephesus.who: Ephesus, an ancient Greek city in Ionia, near modern Selçuk in Turkey, famous for its temple of Artemis (Diana).

Epicharmus.who: Epicharmus (fl. early 5th century BC), Sicilian Greek comic poet, famous for maxims such as 'remember to distrust'.

Epichthonius Cosmopolites.who: 'Epichthonius Cosmopolites', the pseudonym of the unidentified maker of the engraved 'Fool's Cap' world map (c. 1590).

Epicure.who: An epicure, i.e. a follower of Epicurus, or a pleasure-seeker and unbeliever.

Epicurean.who: Epicurean, i.e. given to pleasure or irreligion, after Epicurus.

Epicures.who: Epicureans, followers of Epicurus; also used loosely for gluttons and unbelievers.

Epicurus.who: Epicurus (341–270 BC), Athenian philosopher who taught atomism and that pleasure is the highest good.

Epicycles.who: Epicycles, the small circles of Ptolemaic astronomy.

Epidaurus.who: Epidaurus, a city in the Argolid, Greece, home of the chief sanctuary of Asclepius (Aesculapius).

Epidicus.who: Epidicus, the scheming slave who gives his name to Plautus' comedy Epidicus.

Epiphanius.who: Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403), bishop in Cyprus, author of the Panarion, a catalogue and refutation of eighty heresies.

Epirus.who: Epirus, mountainous region of north-western Greece and southern Albania on the Ionian Sea.

Erasistratus.who: Erasistratus of Ceos (c. 304–c. 250 BC), Greek physician and anatomist at Alexandria, famed for diagnosing Antiochus's love for Stratonice.

Eratosthenes.who: Eratosthenes Batavus (1617), Willebrord Snellius's treatise on measuring the earth's size by triangulation.

Ericus.who: Erik 'Weather-hat' (Väderhatt), legendary early king of Sweden whose magic hat could turn the winds, as told by Olaus Magnus.

Erinnys.who: Erinys, one of the Furies, Greek avenging goddesses depicted as hideous hags.

Eris Armenius.who: Er, son of Armenius, the Pamphylian soldier of the myth closing Plato's Republic, who revived on his funeral pyre and described the afterlife.

Ernestus Burggravius.who: Johann Ernst Burggrav, early seventeenth-century German Paracelsian physician, author of the Biolychnium on the 'lamp of life'.

Erno.who: Lough Erne, lake in County Fermanagh, Ireland, which legend held had flooded over an earlier settlement.

Eros.who: Eros, Greek god of love, paired with Anteros, god of requited love.

Erythrae.who: Erythrae, Ionian Greek city on the Asia Minor coast opposite Chios, home of the Erythraean Sibyl and an oracle of Apollo.

Eryximachus.who: Eryximachus, Athenian physician who is one of the speakers on love in Plato's Symposium.

Eschuidus.who: John Eschenden (Ashenden), fourteenth-century English astrologer of Merton College, Oxford, author of the Summa astrologiae judicialis, which predicted events from great conjunctions.

Escorial.who: El Escorial, the monastery-palace built by Philip II in the Guadarrama hills north-west of Madrid.

Essays.who: Francis Bacon's Essays (1597, enlarged 1612 and 1625); the quoted passage comes from the essay 'Of Beauty'.

Essei.who: The Essenes, an ascetic Jewish sect of the Second Temple period, many of whom were celibate.

Estremadura.who: Extremadura, region of western Spain bordering Portugal.

Eteocles.who: Eteocles, son of Oedipus, king of Thebes, who killed his brother Polynices and was killed by him in single combat.

Eteoneus.basis: Aristides' funeral oration for Eteoneus survives; Burton's mention of Pindar here is unclear
Eteoneus.who: Eteoneus, a youth whose early death the rhetorician Aelius Aristides (2nd century AD) lamented in a funeral oration.

Ethics.who: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, his treatise on virtue, happiness and friendship.

Ethiopia.who: Ethiopia, the land south of Egypt, which Burton's age identified with Abyssinia, the realm of Prester John.

Ethiopian.who: An inhabitant of Ethiopia, which in Burton's day meant Black Africa generally, or Abyssinia in particular.

Ethiopian Gymnosophists.who: The 'naked sages', ascetic philosophers whom ancient writers, especially Philostratus in his Life of Apollonius, placed in Ethiopia as well as India.

Ethiopians.who: The people of Ethiopia; in the second passage, the Abyssinians, ruled by the legendary Christian king Prester John.

Ethocles.basis: Burton's margin cites Lucian's courtesan dialogues; I can't confirm the exact dialogue.
Ethocles.who: A suitor of a courtesan in one of Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans; a fictional character.

Etna.who: Mount Etna, the active volcano in eastern Sicily.

Eubocar.basis: Listed with Ali, Omar and Othman as Muhammad's successors.
Eubocar.who: Abu Bakr (c. 573–634), Muhammad's father-in-law and the first caliph.

Eubulides.basis: Burton's margin cites Aristaenetus, Epistle 12 of book 2.
Eubulides.who: A fictional letter-writer in the Love Letters of Aristaenetus, the Greek epistolographer (5th–6th century AD).

Euclid.basis: The third passage, from Plutarch on brotherly love, means a different man: Euclides of Megara (c. 435–c. 365 BC), Socrates' pupil.
Euclid.who: Euclid (fl. c. 300 BC), Greek mathematician of Alexandria and author of the Elements.

Euclio.who: Euclio, the miser who guards his pot of gold in Plautus's comedy Aulularia.

Eucrates.who: Two different characters of Lucian: the credulous host who tells the stories in the Philopseudes, and a rich man in The Cock (Gallus).

Eudo de Stellis.who: Éon de l'Étoile (d. c. 1148), Breton heretic and supposed wonder-worker, condemned at Reims in 1148; William of Newburgh tells his story.

Eudocia.who: Aelia Eudocia (c. 401–460), born Athenais, daughter of an Athenian sophist and wife of the Eastern emperor Theodosius II.

Eudocia. Theodosius.basis: Two names wrongly joined across a sentence break: Eudocia and Theodosius II.

Eugenia.basis: Probably a fictional figure from a Greek love-story or letter collection, but I can't confirm the source.

Eugubine.who: Gubbio (Latin Eugubium), a town in Umbria, central Italy.

Euhemerus.who: A fictional lover who writes one of the Love Letters of Aristaenetus.

Eumenes.who: Eumenes II, king of Pergamon (r. 197–159 BC), Rome's ally and enemy of Perseus of Macedon.

Eumenides.who: The Eumenides, a euphemistic name for the Furies (Erinyes), Greek goddesses of vengeance; Burton applies it to bawds.

Eumo.who: Eunus (d. c. 132 BC), Syrian slave and devotee of the Syrian goddess; he led the First Servile War in Sicily and was said to breathe fire.

Eunapius.who: Eunapius of Sardis (c. 345–after 414), Greek historian and author of the Lives of the Sophists.

Eunoe.who: Eunoe, wife of Bogud, king of Mauretania; Suetonius names her as one of Julius Caesar's mistresses.

Eunuch.who: The Ethiopian eunuch, treasurer of Queen Candace, whom Philip the Deacon baptised (Acts 8).

Euonymus.who: 'Euonymus Philiatrus', the pseudonym of Conrad Gesner (1516–1565), Swiss physician, under which he published the Thesaurus of secret remedies (1552), a book of distilled medicines.

Euphorbia.basis: Burton cites Pontano's dialogue Antonius; she seems to be a figure in it.
Euphorbia.who: A shrewish wife who appears in Giovanni Pontano's dialogue Antonius.

Euphorbus.who: Euphorbus, a Trojan son of Panthous who wounded Patroclus; Pythagoras claimed to have been him in a former life.

Euphormio.who: Euphormionis Satyricon (1603–07), John Barclay's Latin satirical romance, and its hero Euphormio.

Euphormio Satyr.who: Euphormionis Satyricon (1603–07), the Latin satirical romance by John Barclay (1582–1621).

Euphranor.who: Euphranor of Corinth (fl. c. 360 BC), Greek painter and sculptor.

Euphrates.who: The Euphrates, the great river of Mesopotamia.

Euphrosyne.who: Euphrosyne, Byzantine empress, wife of Michael II and stepmother of Theophilus, for whom she held a bride-show in 830.

Euripes.basis: A common noun for tidal channels or straits: the four in-drawing channels around the North Pole shown on Mercator's map.

Euripi.basis: A common noun: the Latin plural for straits or channels.

Euripides Menalip.who: Melanippe, a lost tragedy by Euripides that survives only in fragments.

Eurippe.basis: Burton cites Parthenius, chapter 8, which tells the story of Herippe and Xanthus.
Eurippe.who: Herippe of Miletus, wife of Xanthus, who was carried off by the Gauls; her husband searched for her, in Parthenius's Love Stories, chapter 8.

Euripus.basis: The third passage uses the strait as a figure of speech.
Euripus.who: The Euripus, the narrow strait between Euboea and mainland Greece at Chalcis, famous for its puzzling reversing currents.

Euristium.who: Eurystheus, the mythical king of Tiryns who set Hercules his labours.

Europa.who: Europa, the Phoenician princess whom Zeus, disguised as a bull, carried off to Crete.

Europae.who: Europe (Latin genitive: 'to the gods of Europe').

European.who: A native of Europe; used here as an adjective for Europeans or for things belonging to Europe.

Eurotas.who: The Eurotas (modern Evrotas), the chief river of Laconia in the Peloponnese, which flows past Sparta.

Euryalus.who: Two bearers: Euryalus, the lover of Lucretia in Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini's novella *Historia de duobus amantibus* (passages 1, 3); and Euryalus, Nisus's young friend in Virgil's *Aeneid* 9 (passage 2).

Eurydice.who: Eurydice, the wife of Orpheus in Greek myth; after her death he went down to the underworld to bring her back.

Eustathius.basis: Different bearers. Passage 2 is Eustathius of Antioch, the 4th-century opponent of Arius. Passage 3 is Eustathius (Eumathius) Macrembolites, author of the Greek romance *Hysmine and Hysminias*. Passage 1 is unclear; it may be Eustathius of Thessalonica, the Homer commentator.

Eutrapelus.who: Publius Volumnius Eutrapelus (1st century BC), Roman knight and wit, friend of Mark Antony and Cicero, mentioned in Horace's *Epistles* 1.18.

Euxine.who: The Euxine (Pontus Euxinus), the classical name for the Black Sea.

Euxitheus.who: Euxitheus, a fictional lover who writes to Pythias in the *Love Letters* of Aristaenetus, a Greek letter-writer of late antiquity.

Evangelus.basis: In Macrobius's *Saturnalia* 1.11 the defence of slaves is given by Praetextatus in reply to Evangelus, so Burton's attribution is loose. Lucian's 'piper' may be a confusion with another musician.
Evangelus.who: Two bearers: Evangelus, a Tarentine musician whom Lucian mocks (passage 1); and Evangelus, a speaker in Macrobius's *Saturnalia* (passages 2, 3).

Evax.who: Evax, legendary king of Arabia, the supposed author of a Latin lapidary (a treatise on precious stones) that is said to have been sent to Nero.

Eve.who: Eve, the first woman in Genesis and the wife of Adam.

Evenus.who: The Evenus (modern Evinos), a river in Aetolia in western Greece; in myth Nessus ferried Deianira across it.

Evesham.who: Evesham, a town in Worcestershire with a Benedictine abbey; one of its monks had a famous vision of the otherworld in 1196, recorded by Matthew Paris.

Ewelme.who: Ewelme, a village in south Oxfordshire.

Ewichius.who: Johann Ewich (1525–1588), physician of Bremen, who wrote against the trial of witches by water and against harsh witch prosecution.

Excess.who: An ordinary word: 'excess', the opposite of 'defect'.

Exeter.who: Exeter, the cathedral city of Devon; it also gives its name to a dukedom and to a bishopric.

Experience.who: An ordinary word: 'experience', named as one kind of knowledge.

Expulsion.who: A term of art: 'expulsion', the faculty in Galenic physiology by which the body casts out waste.

Fabatus.basis: An Italian quoted in Gaspar Ens's *Moros*; I cannot identify him.

Faber Stapulensis.who: Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (c. 1455–1536), French humanist, scholar of Aristotle and biblical translator.

Fabii.who: The Fabii, a Roman patrician family; traditionally 306 of its men fell in one day against Veii at the river Cremera in 477 BC.

Fabius.who: Two bearers: Quintilian (Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, c. 35–c. 100), the Roman writer on rhetoric (passages 1, 3); and Fabius, the talkative Stoic in Horace's *Satires* 1.1 (passage 2).

Fabius Pictor.who: Quintus Fabius Pictor (fl. c. 200 BC), the earliest Roman historian; spurious fragments under his name were published by Annius of Viterbo.

Fabricius.who: Two bearers: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus (3rd century BC), Roman consul famous for honest poverty (passages 1, 3); and Johannes Fabricius, Frisian astronomer who published on sunspots in 1611 (passage 2).

Fabritii.who: Men like Gaius Fabricius Luscinus (3rd century BC), the Roman consul who became a byword for frugality and incorruptibility.

Facius Cardan.who: Fazio Cardano (1444–1524), Milanese jurist and mathematician, father of Girolamo Cardano.

Faerie Queene.who: *The Faerie Queene* (1590–96), Edmund Spenser's allegorical epic poem.

Fagos.basis: The plural sits in a list with Apiciuses and Heliogabaluses, which suits Phagon; but it might simply be the Greek word phagos, 'glutton'.
Fagos.who: Phagon, a notorious glutton of the time of the emperor Aurelian, described in the *Historia Augusta*; used here as a type of the glutton.

Fairies.who: Fairies, the supernatural beings of folklore.

Fairy.who: An adjective meaning 'of Faerie land', as in the knights of Spenser's *Faerie Queene*.

Faith.who: An ordinary word: 'faith', named as one kind of knowledge.

Falaise.who: Falaise, a town in Normandy, northern France, where William the Conqueror was born.

Fallace.who: Fallace, the wife whom her husband Deliro dotes on in Ben Jonson's comedy *Every Man out of his Humour* (1599).

Falling Sickness.who: A disease: the falling sickness, an old name for epilepsy.

Fallopius.who: Gabriele Falloppio (1523–1562), Italian anatomist and physician who taught at Padua.

Falmouth.who: Falmouth, a harbour town in Cornwall.

Familists.who: The Familists, or Family of Love, a mystical sect founded by Hendrik Niclaes (16th century) with followers in England.

Farmack.who: Foremark (Formark), Derbyshire, near Repton on the Trent; seat of the Burdett baronets.

Fastidious Brisk.who: Fastidious Brisk, the foppish would-be courtier in Ben Jonson's comedy Every Man Out of His Humour (1599).

Fauld.who: Fauld, a hamlet in Hanbury parish, east Staffordshire, the Burton family estate.

Fauns.who: Fauns, Roman rustic woodland spirits, half man and half goat, akin to the Greek satyrs.

Faustina.who: Faustina the Younger (d. 175/176), Roman empress and wife of Marcus Aurelius, rumoured to have loved a gladiator.

Faustinam Marci Aurelii.who: Faustina the Younger (d. 175/176), wife of the emperor Marcus Aurelius; the gladiator story appears in the Historia Augusta.

Faustus.who: Faustus, the lovesick shepherd who tells of his love for Galla in the first eclogue of Baptista Mantuanus (Mantuan).

Faventinus.who: Benedetto Vittori of Faenza (Benedictus Victorius Faventinus, 1481–1561), Italian physician who taught at Bologna and wrote on medical practice.

Favonius.who: Favonius, the Roman name for Zephyrus, the gentle west wind.

Favorinus.who: Favorinus of Arelate (c. 80–c. 160), Gallic-born sophist and philosopher, friend of Aulus Gellius and Plutarch.

Felinus.who: Felino Sandeo (Felinus Sandeus, 1444–1503), Italian canonist of Ferrara and bishop of Lucca, who wrote commentaries on the Decretals.

Felix Kingston.who: Felix Kingston (fl. 1597–1651), London printer and stationer.

Felix Malleolus.who: Felix Hemmerlin (Malleolus, c. 1388–c. 1460), Swiss canon of Zurich and polemicist who wrote treatises on demons and exorcism.

Felix Plater.who: Felix Platter (1536–1614), Basel physician and professor, author of the Praxis medica and Observationes.

Felix Platerus.who: Felix Platter (1536–1614), Basel physician and professor, author of the Praxis medica and Observationes; he also kept a famous cabinet of curiosities.

Ferdinand.who: Ferdinand II of Aragon (1452–1516), conqueror of Granada; in the third passage, Ferdinand I (1503–1564), Holy Roman Emperor and son of Joanna.

Feribrigge.basis: Bale's catalogue names him beside Ralph Strode, a fellow Oxford logician
Feribrigge.who: Richard Ferrybridge (Feribrigge, fl. later 14th century), Oxford logician who wrote on consequences, listed by John Bale.

Feronia.who: Feronia, an ancient Italic goddess of groves and freedmen, with a famous grove and shrine near Mount Soracte.

Ferrandus.who: Jacques Ferrand (fl. 1610–1623), French physician, author of a treatise on love-melancholy (De la maladie d'amour ou mélancolie érotique).

Ferrara.who: Ferrara, city in the Po valley of northern Italy, seat of the Este dukes.

Festus.who: First passage: Porcius Festus, Roman procurator of Judaea (Acts 26); others: Sextus Pompeius Festus (late 2nd century), Latin grammarian and lexicographer.

Fez.who: Fez (Fès), city and former royal capital in northern Morocco.

Fienus.who: Thomas Fienus (Feyens, 1567–1631), Antwerp-born physician and Louvain professor, author of De viribus imaginationis (1608).

Filesacus.who: Jean Filesac (c. 1550–1638), Paris theologian of the Sorbonne, who wrote short learned treatises including De justa uxore.

Finland.who: Finland, then a province of the Swedish kingdom.

Finmark.who: Finnmark, the northernmost region of Norway.

Fischartus.who: Johann Fischart (c. 1546–1591), German Protestant satirist, translator and adapter of Rabelais.

Flaminian.who: The Via Flaminia, the Roman road from Rome north to Ariminum (Rimini), built by Gaius Flaminius in 220 BC.

Flanders.who: Flanders, the county in the southern Low Countries, now divided between Belgium, France and the Netherlands.

Flavia.basis: a stock name for a lover's mistress, not a particular woman

Flora.who: Flora, Roman goddess of flowers and springtime.

Florence.who: Florence, the city in Tuscany, Italy.

Florentine.who: A native or citizen of Florence.

Florentius.who: Florentinus (3rd century AD), Greek writer on agriculture whose Georgics survive in excerpts in the Byzantine Geoponica compiled under Constantine VII.

Floriat.basis: one of a string of stock pastoral mistress names

Florilegus.who: 'Matthew of Westminster', the supposed author of the medieval English chronicle Flores Historiarum, hence called Florilegus.

Florimel.who: Florimel, a beautiful lady pursued by many knights in Spenser's Faerie Queene, Books III–IV.

Florus.who: Lucius Annaeus Florus (2nd century AD), Roman historian, author of an Epitome of Roman history that praises Campania.

Foelicitas.who: Felicitas, Roman goddess personifying good fortune and prosperity.

Foliot.basis: Latin form Folieta fits, and Foglietta wrote a work on Naples
Foliot.who: Uberto Foglietta (1518–1581), Genoese historian and humanist, who wrote in praise of Naples.

Foliots.who: Folletti, Italian household goblins or mischievous sprites.

Fonseca.who: Cristóbal de Fonseca (c. 1550–1621), Spanish Augustinian friar whose treatise on love appeared in Latin as Amphitheatrum amoris.

Fontainbleau.who: Fontainebleau, the French royal palace southeast of Paris.

Fortune.who: Fortuna, the Roman goddess of fortune, here personified.

Fortunius Licetus.who: Fortunio Liceti (1577–1657), Italian physician and natural philosopher at Padua, who disputed Galileo's discoveries.

Fortunus Licetus.who: Fortunio Liceti (1577–1657), Italian physician and natural philosopher at Padua, writer on lamps, monsters and occult questions.

Forum Julii.who: Friuli, the region of northeast Italy named after Forum Julii (modern Cividale del Friuli), then a Venetian territory.

Fotherby.who: Martin Fotherby (c. 1560–1620), Bishop of Salisbury, author of Atheomastix (1622), a treatise against atheism.

Fotoqui.basis: apparently a native word for a temple in Purchas's travel narrative

Fox.who: Luke Foxe (1586–1635), English explorer of Hudson Bay in search of the Northwest Passage, author of North-West Fox (1635).

Foxe.who: John Foxe (1516/17–1587), English Protestant martyrologist, author of the Acts and Monuments ('Book of Martyrs').

Fracastorius Naugerio.who: Girolamo Fracastoro (1478–1553), Veronese physician and Latin poet, in a poem addressed to the Venetian humanist Andrea Navagero (Naugerius).

Frambesarius.who: Nicolas Abraham de La Framboisière (c. 1560–1636), French physician to Louis XIII, author of medical works including Consultationes.

Fran.who: Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), Italian philosopher, nephew of Giovanni Pico.

France (Dauphine.who: Dauphiné, a province of southeast France acquired by the crown in 1349, which gave its name to the heir's title of Dauphin.

Frances.who: Frances Brydges (d. 1663), Countess of Exeter, widow of Thomas Cecil, 1st Earl of Exeter, and Burton's patroness.

Francis.who: Francis I (1494–1547), King of France; met Henry VIII at the Field of the Cloth of Gold in 1520 and was captured by Charles V at Pavia in 1525.

Francis Alexander.basis: The physician's name and the title 'Apol.' in a pharmacological context fit Alessandri's work.
Francis Alexander.who: Francesco Alessandri, sixteenth-century Italian physician of Vercelli, author of the medical work *Apollo*.

Francis Bacon.who: Francis Bacon (1561–1626), English philosopher and statesman, Viscount St Albans, author of the *Essays*.

Francis Philelphus.who: Francesco Filelfo (1398–1481), Italian humanist, known for his large collection of Latin letters.

Francis Sforza.basis: The broken match with Dorotea Gonzaga of Mantua belongs to the reign of Francesco I, though it was for his son Galeazzo Maria.
Francis Sforza.who: Francesco Sforza (1401–1466), Duke of Milan; a Gonzaga marriage with his family fell through over fears that the bride was deformed.

Francis Spira.who: Francesco Spiera (1502–1548), Italian lawyer who renounced his Protestant faith and died in despair; his case became a famous Protestant warning.

Francis Willoughby.who: Sir Francis Willoughby (1546–1596), who built Wollaton Hall near Nottingham.

Francis Ximenius.who: Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros (1436–1517), cardinal, Archbishop of Toledo and regent of Castile; Álvar Gómez de Castro wrote his life.

Franciscan.who: A friar of the Franciscan order, founded by St Francis of Assisi.

Franciscans.who: Friars of the Franciscan order, founded by St Francis of Assisi.

Francisco Sansovino.who: Francesco Sansovino (1521–1586), Venetian writer, editor and compiler.

Franciscus Barbarus.who: Francesco Barbaro (1390–1454), Venetian humanist and statesman, author of *De re uxoria*, a treatise on marriage.

Franciscus Boussuetus.who: François Boussuet, sixteenth-century French physician, author of a Latin poem on aquatic animals, *De natura aquatilium carmen*.

Franciscus Collius.who: Francesco Collio (d. 1640), Milanese theologian, author of *De animabus paganorum*, on whether pagans can be saved.

Franciscus Modius.who: François Modius (1556–1597), Flemish humanist, compiler of the *Pandectae triumphales* (1586), a collection on triumphs and solemnities.

Franconia.who: Franconia, a region of central Germany centred on Würzburg, Bamberg and Nuremberg.

Frank.who: A pet form of Frances, used here as a stock girl's name in an alliterative list.

Frankfurt.who: Frankfurt am Main, in Germany, whose twice-yearly fairs were Europe's chief book market.

Fratres à Bry.who: Theodor de Bry (1528–1598) and his sons, Frankfurt engravers and publishers of the illustrated *America* series of voyages.

Fredegund.who: Fredegund (d. 597), Frankish queen and wife of Chilperic I, notorious for her murders and her feud with Brunhild.

Frederick.basis: The second passage is the Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa; the King of Naples in the first is uncertain (possibly Frederick of Aragon).

Fredericus Matenesius.who: Friedrich Matenes, Cologne theologian, author of *De luxu et abusu vestium* (1612), a treatise against luxury in dress.

Fregosi.who: The Fregoso (Campofregoso) family of Genoa, whose feud with the Adorno family divided the city in the 14th and 15th centuries.

Freiburg.basis: The passages name Fribourg in Switzerland, apparently Freiberg in Saxony (silver mines) and a German Freiburg (perhaps im Breisgau).

Frescobald.who: Francesco Frescobaldi, Florentine merchant who helped the young Thomas Cromwell, who later repaid him; the story is told in Foxe's *Acts and Monuments*.

Friesland.who: Friesland, the coastal region of the northern Netherlands and north-west Germany.

Frigemelica.who: Francesco Frigimelica (1491–1558), Paduan physician who took part in consultations recorded in Giambattista da Monte's *Consilia*.

Frisian.who: Frisian, of Frisia; the prince meant is Radbod (d. 719), the pagan Frisian king who refused baptism.

Fromundus.who: Libert Froidmont (1587–1653), Louvain philosopher and theologian, author of *Meteorologicorum libri*.

Frontinus.who: Sextus Julius Frontinus (c. 40–103), Roman administrator, author of *De aquaeductu* and the *Strategemata*.

Fuchsius). Jejunum.basis: The form is a fragment; the name meant is Fuchsius.
Fuchsius). Jejunum.who: Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), German physician and botanist, author of anatomical and medical works.

Fucinus Lacus.who: Lake Fucino in the Abruzzo, Italy, which Claudius tried to drain through a great tunnel; it was finally drained in the 19th century.

Fuggeri.who: The Fuggers, the great banking family of Augsburg, several of whom were noted patrons and collectors of books.

Fulbertus.who: Fulbert, canon of Notre-Dame in Paris, uncle of Heloise, who had Abelard castrated.

Fulco Argelanus.basis: A servant known only from the author Burton cites.

Fulda.who: Fulda in Hesse, Germany, seat of the rich Benedictine abbey founded in 744.

Fulgentius.basis: Different bearers: the mythographer Fabius Planciades Fulgentius (on Apuleius), Fulgentius of Ruspe (on God's mercy), and a medical writer cited via Gordonius.

Fulgosus.who: Battista Fregoso (Baptista Fulgosus), Doge of Genoa (1478–83), compiler of a Latin collection of memorable deeds and sayings.

Fulke’s Metromachia.who: *Metromachia*, a geometrical board game devised by William Fulke (1538–1589), English Puritan divine, who also wrote the astronomical game *Ouranomachia*.

Fulvius.basis: The list of bestial unions matches the pseudo-Plutarchan story of Fulvius Stellus.
Fulvius.who: Fulvius Stellus, figure in a tale in pseudo-Plutarch's *Parallela minora*, who lay with a mare and fathered the goddess Epona.

Fulvius Flaccus.who: Young son of Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, the Gracchan partisan; imprisoned and put to death by the consul Opimius in 121 BC.

Fumitoria.who: Pills of fumitory (*pilulae de fumoterrae*), a purging compound named after the herb.

Furies.who: The Furies (Erinyes), Greek goddesses of vengeance who pursued Orestes; in the first passage 'Poetical Furies' means poetic frenzies.

Furius.who: Lucius Furius Philus, consul 136 BC, member of the Scipionic circle and patron of Terence.

Fury.who: Frenzy or madness; in the last passage 'fourth Fury' alludes to the three mythical Furies.

Fuscinum.who: Fushimi, near Kyoto in Japan, struck by a great earthquake in 1596.

Gab. Prateolus.who: Gabriel du Préau (Prateolus) (1511–1588), French Catholic theologian, author of the *Elenchus haereticorum*, a catalogue of heresies.

Gabba.who: Galba (Gabba), a Roman wit of Augustus's time, who pretended to sleep at dinner while Maecenas courted his wife (Plutarch, *Amatorius*).

Gabinius.who: Aulus Gabinius, Roman politician and consul in 58 BC, whose wife Lollia was said to be Caesar's mistress.

Gabriel.who: The archangel Gabriel, who Muslims believe revealed the Qur'an to Muhammad.

Gaia.who: Stock feminine name in the Roman wedding formula 'Where you are Gaius, I am Gaia', which the bride spoke to the groom.

Gaius.who: Stock name for the husband in the Roman wedding formula 'Where you are Gaius, I am Gaia'.

Galatea.who: Galatea, sea-nymph (Nereid) of Greek myth; the first passage names Sannazaro's piscatory eclogue about her.

Galateus.who: *Galateo* (1558), the treatise on manners and conversation by Giovanni della Casa (1503–1556).

Galba.who: Servius Sulpicius Galba, Roman emperor (68–69), bald and crook-backed, killed in the year of the four emperors.

Galbots.who: The Cagots, an outcast group in Gascony and the Pyrenees, popularly believed to be hereditary lepers.

Galeacius Sforza.who: Galeazzo Maria Sforza (1444–1476), tyrannical Duke of Milan, assassinated by conspirators in 1476.

Galeatius.who: Galeazzo II Visconti (c.1320–1378), lord of Milan, who married his children into the French and English royal houses at great cost.

Galen Temperament.who: Galen (129–c.216), Greek physician, who described the ideal balanced temperament in his *De temperamentis*.

Galenist.who: A follower of Galen's medicine and natural philosophy.

Galenists.who: Followers of Galenic humoral medicine, opposed by the Paracelsians.

Galens.who: Galen (129–c.216), the Greek physician, pluralised to stand for learned physicians.

Galeottus.who: Galeotto Marzio (c.1424–c.1497), Italian humanist and physician, author of *De doctrina promiscua*.

Galeottus Martius.who: Galeotto Marzio (c.1424–c.1497), Italian humanist, prosecuted for teaching that virtuous pagans could be saved.

Galileo.who: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), Italian astronomer, who used the telescope to resolve the Milky Way into countless stars.

Galileo’s Nuncius Sidereus.who: *Sidereus Nuncius* (1610), Galileo's report of his telescopic discoveries, to which Kepler replied in his *Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo*.

Galileus.who: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), who argued in the fourth day of his *Dialogue* (1632) that the tides come from the earth's motion.

Galileus à Galileo.who: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), Italian astronomer, author of the *Sidereus Nuncius* (1610).

Gallieni Epithal.who: Epithalamium (wedding poem) by the Roman emperor Gallienus (r. 253–268), preserved in the *Historia Augusta*.

Gallucius.basis: An Italian cosmographer who mapped the regions of the universe, including the underworld; this fits the context of mapping limbo.
Gallucius.who: Giovanni Paolo Gallucci of Salò, late-16th-century Italian astronomer and cosmographer, author of *Theatrum mundi et temporis*.

Gallus.basis: Different bearers: Lucian's dialogue *Gallus* (The Cock), Pliny the Younger's correspondent Gallus, and the elegiac poet Cornelius Gallus.

Ganges.who: The Ganges, the great sacred river of northern India.

Ganymede.who: Ganymede, Trojan youth carried off by Zeus to be cupbearer of the gods.

Garcaeus.who: Johannes Garcaeus (Gartze) (1530–1574), German Lutheran theologian and astrologer, author of a method of judging nativities (*Astrologiae methodus*).

Garcia ab Horto.who: Garcia de Orta (c. 1501–1568), Portuguese physician at Goa, author of the *Colóquios dos simples e drogas da India* (1563) on Indian drugs and plants.

Gargarus.who: Gargarus (Gargara), a peak of Mount Ida in the Troad, northwest Asia Minor, proverbial for its rich cornfields.

Gariopontus.who: Gariopontus (fl. 11th century), physician of the Salerno school, compiler of the medical handbook *Passionarius*.

Garisenda.who: The Garisenda, a 12th-century leaning tower in Bologna, standing beside the Asinelli tower.

Garter.who: The Order of the Garter, the English order of chivalry founded by Edward III in the 1340s.

Gascony.who: Gascony, a region of southwestern France.

Gaspar Schlick.who: Kaspar Schlick (c. 1396–1449), imperial chancellor under Sigismund, Albert II and Frederick III; patron and friend of Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini.

Gasper Varrerius.who: Gaspar Barreiros (d. 1574), Portuguese scholar whose *Censura* (1565) exposed the 'Berosus' published by Annius of Viterbo as a forgery.

Gataker.who: Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), English Puritan divine, author of *Of the Nature and Use of Lots* (1619), which defends games of chance as lawful.

Gauls.who: The Gauls, the Celtic peoples of ancient Gaul, described in Caesar's *Gallic War*.

Gaunt.who: Ghent, the cloth-making city of Flanders, now in Belgium.

Gazaeus.basis: Lipsius usually cites Aeneas of Gaza as 'Gazaeus', and the topic of spirits fits.
Gazaeus.who: Aeneas of Gaza (fl. late 5th century), Christian Neoplatonist, author of the dialogue *Theophrastus* on the soul and immortality.

Geber.basis: The alchemical context is clear in the second passage. Burton's 'inventor of Algebra' is a confusion, so it is uncertain whether Cardan meant the same Geber.
Geber.who: Geber, the Latin name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (8th century?), Arab alchemist; many medieval Latin alchemical works went under his name.

Gellia.who: Gellia, a woman addressed in Martial's *Epigrams* (5.29), who sent him a hare with the jest that eating it made one handsome.

Genoa.who: Genoa, the port city and republic in northwestern Italy.

Gentiles.who: The Gentiles, non-Jewish peoples; in Burton, heathens as opposed to Jews and Christians.

Gentilis.basis: several Gentili/Gentilis writers; satirist not settled

Gentilletus.who: Innocent Gentillet (c. 1535–1588), French Huguenot jurist, author of the *Anti-Machiavel* (1576).

Geoffrey Chaucer.who: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400), English poet of the *Canterbury Tales*; the first tale is the Knight's Tale.

Geog.who: The *Geographia* of Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617), Italian mathematician and geographer.

Geogr.who: The *Geography* of Strabo (c. 64 BC – c. AD 24), Greek geographer.

Geoponics.who: The *Geoponica*, a 10th-century Byzantine compilation on agriculture made under Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus.

Geor.who: Virgil's *Georgics*; the lines quoted are from Book 1.

George.who: Saint George, the warrior martyr and patron saint of England.

George Burton.who: George Burton, a brother of Robert Burton.

George Handschius.who: Georg Handsch (1529–1578), Bohemian physician of Prague, pupil and correspondent of Pietro Andrea Mattioli.

George Purefoy.who: George Purefoy, Leicestershire gentleman of the Purefoy family, owner of Drayton (Fenny Drayton) in Burton's home county.

Georgians.who: The Georgians, the Orthodox Christians of Georgia in the Caucasus.

Georgius Agricola.who: Georgius Agricola (Georg Bauer, 1494–1555), German physician and mineralogist, author of *De re metallica* and *De animantibus subterraneis*.

Georgius Braunus.who: Georg Braun (1541–1622), Cologne cleric and topographer, editor of the city atlas *Civitates orbis terrarum*.

Georgius Wicelius.who: Georg Witzel (1501–1573), German theologian who went back from Lutheranism to Catholicism and argued for reform within the Church.

Gerar.who: Gerar, a biblical town in the Philistine country of southwest Canaan, where Abraham stayed (Genesis 20).

Gerard.who: John Gerard (c. 1545–1612), English herbalist and barber-surgeon, author of *The Herball* (1597).

Gerardus de Solo.who: Gérard de Solo (fl. 14th century), physician of Montpellier, author of a commentary on the ninth book of Rhazes' *Almansor*.

Gerhardus.who: Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), Lutheran theologian of Jena, author of the devotional *Meditationes sacrae*.

German.who: German, of Germany or the Germans.

Gerson.who: Jean Gerson (1363–1429), French theologian, chancellor of the University of Paris, and a devotional writer.

Geryon.who: Geryon, the three-bodied giant of Greek myth killed by Heracles; a symbol of several bodies joined as one.

Geryons.who: Geryon, the three-bodied giant of Greek myth killed by Heracles; used as a figure for friends united as one body.

Gesner Bibliotheca.who: Conrad Gesner's *Bibliotheca universalis* (1545), a great bibliography of writers in Latin, Greek and Hebrew.

Geta.who: Publius Septimius Geta (189–211), Roman co-emperor murdered by his brother Caracalla (Antoninus).

Getuli.who: Getuli, a kind of goblin or mine spirit named in Georgius Agricola's *De animantibus subterraneis*.

Getulos.who: Getuli, a kind of goblin or household spirit named by Agricola and, after him, by Tholosanus.

Ghent.who: Ghent, city in Flanders, now in Belgium.

Ghibelline.who: The Ghibellines, the imperial party in medieval Italy, enemies of the papal Guelphs.

Ghibellines.who: The Ghibellines, the imperial party in medieval Italy, enemies of the papal Guelphs.

Giants.who: The Giants (Gigantes) of Greek myth, who made war on the Olympian gods.

Giaours.who: Giaour, a Turkish term of contempt for non-Muslims, especially Christians.

Gibraltar.who: The Strait of Gibraltar, between Spain and Morocco.

Gilbert.who: William Gilbert (1544–1603), English physician and natural philosopher, author of *De magnete* (1600).

Gilbertines.who: The Gilbertines, the English order founded by Gilbert of Sempringham, whose double houses held nuns and canons side by side.

Gilbertus.basis: He is cited with Origanus on the heavens, as Gilbert is elsewhere with Origanus on Copernicanism.
Gilbertus.who: William Gilbert (1544–1603), English natural philosopher, whose writings also took up cosmological questions.

Gilbertus Cognatus.who: Gilbert Cousin (Gilbertus Cognatus, 1506–1572), French humanist and secretary to Erasmus, who edited and defended Lucian.

Giles Goosecap.who: Sir Giles Goosecap, the foolish knight who is the title character of an anonymous comedy printed in 1606.

Gillius.who: Pierre Gilles (Petrus Gyllius, 1490–1555), French naturalist and topographer, author of *De topographia Constantinopoleos*.

Giovanni de la Casa.who: Giovanni della Casa (1503–1556), Italian poet and archbishop of Benevento, author of the *Galateo*, also known for his sonnets.

Giraldus Cambrensis Itinerar.who: Gerald of Wales (Giraldus Cambrensis, c. 1146–c. 1223), Welsh churchman and chronicler, author of the *Itinerarium Cambriae*.

Girava.who: Jerónimo Girava, 16th-century Spanish cosmographer, author of *Dos libros de cosmographía* (1556).

Gismunda.who: Ghismonda, daughter of Tancredi, Prince of Salerno, heroine of Boccaccio's *Decameron* IV.1, whose lover Guiscardo is killed by her father.

Glastonbury.who: Glastonbury in Somerset, whose tower stands on Glastonbury Tor.

Glauco.who: Glaucon, the physician to whom Galen addressed his *Therapeutics to Glaucon* (*Ad Glauconem de methodo medendi*).

Glaucus.who: Glaucus, Lycian hero of the *Iliad*, companion and cousin of Sarpedon.

Gloucester.who: Gloucester, the English city (with its cathedral's whispering gallery), and also the dukedom held by Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester.

Gloucestershire.who: Gloucestershire, English county on the Severn.

Gluten.who: Gluten, in old physiology a glue-like secondary humour that nourishes the body's parts.

Glycere.basis: Glycera is a conventional mistress's name, but I have not traced the epigram's source.
Glycere.who: Glycera, a stock name for a courtesan in Latin love poetry, addressed here in an epigram.

Glycerium.who: Glycerium, the girl loved by Pamphilus in Terence's comedy *Andria*.

Gnaeus Manlius.who: Gnaeus Manlius Vulso, Roman consul of 189 BC, whose army returning from Asia brought eastern luxury to Rome, according to Livy (book 39).

Gnaeus Maximus.who: Claudius Maximus, proconsul of Africa, before whom Apuleius was tried for magic (c. 158–159 AD), as described in his *Apologia*.

Gnaeus Papirius.basis: He is paired with Quintus Fabius in a famous feud; Burton seems to have the first name wrong.
Gnaeus Papirius.who: Lucius Papirius Cursor, Roman dictator, whose quarrel with his master of horse Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus (325 BC) became famous.

Gnatho.who: Gnatho, the flattering parasite in Terence's comedy *Eunuchus*.

Gnathos.who: Gnatho, the parasite of Terence's *Eunuchus*, used here as a type name for flatterers and hangers-on.

Gniphon.who: Gniphon, the usurer in Lucian's dialogue *The Dream, or the Cock*.

Goa.who: Goa, the Portuguese colonial city on the west coast of India.

Gobryas.who: Gobryas, a captain in Theodore Prodromus' twelfth-century Byzantine verse romance *Rhodanthe and Dosicles*.

Goclenius.basis: The weapon-salve defence is his; the astrology and meteor references fit his writings, though his father, the philosopher of the same name, cannot be ruled out.
Goclenius.who: Rudolph Goclenius the Younger (1572–1621), Marburg professor of physic and mathematics; he wrote on astrology and defended the magnetic cure of wounds by the weapon-salve.

God.who: God in the Christian sense; in the Plotinus passage it means 'a god' in general.

Godefridus.basis: I recall a Latin treatise on love in three books under this name; I am unsure of the details.
Godefridus.who: Pierre Godefroy (Petrus Godefridus), sixteenth-century French jurist, author of *De amoribus libri tres*, a treatise on love.

Godelman.who: Johann Georg Godelmann (1559–1611), German jurist, author of *Tractatus de magis, veneficis et lamiis* (1591), on witchcraft.

God’s Epistle.who: Gregory the Great's name for Holy Scripture, seen as God's letter to his creatures.

Goebelius.basis: An author on German baths; I cannot tell which Göbel is meant.

Golden Fleece.who: The Order of the Golden Fleece, an order of chivalry founded in 1430 by Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.

Golden Legend.who: The *Golden Legend* (*Legenda aurea*), Jacobus de Voragine's popular thirteenth-century collection of saints' lives.

Goltzius.who: Hendrick Goltzius (1558–1617), Dutch engraver and painter of Haarlem.

Gomorrah.who: Gomorrah, the biblical city destroyed with Sodom (Genesis 19).
