Gonsalva.who: Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba (1453–1515), 'the Great Captain', Spanish general who fell out of favour with Ferdinand of Aragon; Paolo Giovio wrote his life.

Gonzaga.who: The Gonzaga family, who ruled Mantua as marquises and later dukes; Burton does not say which duke used this emblem.

Gordian.who: The Gordian knot: proverbially a knot that cannot be untied.

Gorgias.who: Gorgias of Leontini (c. 483–c. 376 BC), Greek sophist and teacher of rhetoric.

Gorgo.who: Gorgo, one of the two Syracusan housewives at the Adonis festival in Alexandria in Theocritus' Idyll 15.

Gorgons.who: The Gorgons, the snake-haired monsters of Greek myth, Medusa among them.

Goropius.who: Johannes Goropius Becanus (1519–1572), Antwerp physician and antiquary known for eccentric etymological and geographical theories.

Goth.basis: This is the well-known anecdote, told by Zonaras.
Goth.who: A Goth at the Gothic sack of Athens (AD 267), who supposedly argued that the Greeks' books be spared because study made them unwarlike.

Gotham.who: Gotham, a village in Nottinghamshire whose 'wise men' were proverbial fools.

Gothardus Arthus.who: Gotthard Arthus (1570–c. 1630), writer from Danzig working at Frankfurt; he compiled the Latin texts of the de Bry *India Orientalis* travel collection.

Gotherinus.basis: A Portuguese nobleman known only from Osorius's narrative.

Goths.who: The Goths, the Germanic peoples who invaded the Roman Empire.

Goulart.who: Simon Goulart (1543–1628), Genevan Protestant pastor, compiler of the *Histoires admirables et mémorables*, a collection of strange cases.

Gracchi.who: Tiberius and Gaius Sempronius Gracchus, Roman tribunes and reformers of the second century BC, sons of Cornelia.

Graces.who: The three Graces (Charites), goddesses of charm and beauty who attended Venus.

Grafton.who: Richard Grafton (c. 1511–1573), London printer and English chronicler, who continued and printed Edward Hall's chronicle.

Granada.who: Granada, the city and former Moorish kingdom in Andalusia, southern Spain.

Grand Signior.who: The 'Grand Signior' was the usual European title for the Ottoman sultan of Constantinople.

Grecian Calis.basis: The match with the Doge of Venice and the story of an over-fastidious Greek princess fits Selvo's wife; Burton's name 'Calis' and his naming of her brother are not standard.
Grecian Calis.who: Probably Theodora Doukaina, Byzantine princess and wife of Doge Domenico Selvo (r. 1071–84), whom the chroniclers condemned for her luxury.

Greece.who: Greece; 'Emperor of Greece' means the Byzantine emperor.

Greece. Apollo.basis: A mis-split form that runs together 'Greece' and 'Apollo' across a sentence break.

Greece. Nuremberg.basis: A mis-split form that runs together 'Greece' and 'Nuremberg' across a sentence break.

Greenham.who: Richard Greenham (c. 1535–c. 1594), Puritan divine and rector of Dry Drayton, known for his counsel to afflicted consciences.

Greenland.who: Greenland, the Arctic land north-east of North America.

Greenwich.who: Greenwich, on the Thames east of London, site of a royal palace and of the tower in its park.

Greg.basis: In Burton a bare 'Greg.' in a marginal citation on moral or spiritual topics usually means Gregory the Great.
Greg.who: Pope Gregory I, 'the Great' (c. 540–604), Church Father and moral writer.

Gregorian.who: The Gregorian calendar, the reformed calendar issued by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582.

Gregorius Magnus.who: Pope Gregory I, 'the Great' (c. 540–604), whose answers to Augustine of Canterbury's questions Bede preserves.

Gregorius Tholosanus.who: Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse (c. 1540–1597), French jurist, author of the encyclopaedic Syntaxes artis mirabilis.

Gregory.basis: In the first passage 'Gregory Tholosanus' means Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, the jurist.
Gregory.who: In the visions passages, Pope Gregory I, 'the Great' (c. 540–604), whose Dialogues tell of visions and apparitions.

Gregory Nazianzen.who: Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), Cappadocian Church Father, orator and poet.

Gregory Tholosanus.who: Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse (c. 1540–1597), French jurist, author of the Syntaxes artis mirabilis.

Gregory de Valentia.who: Gregory of Valencia (1549–1603), Spanish Jesuit theologian who taught at Ingolstadt and was a leading Counter-Reformation controversialist.

Greichgea.who: The Kraichgau, a hilly district of south-west Germany between the Neckar and the Rhine, now in Baden-Württemberg.

Gresham.who: Gresham College, London, founded under the will of Sir Thomas Gresham and opened in 1597, with professorships including astronomy.

Grevinus.who: Jacques Grévin (1538–1570), French physician and poet, author of a treatise on poisons (1568).

Grisons.who: The Grisons, the Grey Leagues of the Rhaetian Alps, now the Swiss canton of Graubünden.

Grizels.who: Griselda, the patient wife of Boccaccio's last Decameron tale, retold by Petrarch and in Chaucer's Clerk's Tale.

Grobians.who: Boors and slovens, after Grobianus, the mock patron of bad manners in Friedrich Dedekind's Latin satire Grobianus (1549).

Groningen.who: Groningen, a city in the north-east of the Netherlands.

Grotta de Sibylla.who: The Grotto of the Sibyl, the cave associated with the Cumaean Sibyl near Cumae and Lake Avernus, west of Naples.

Grunnius Corocotta Porcellus.who: The pig who is the testator of the Testamentum Porcelli, a late Latin burlesque will that Jerome says schoolboys recited.

Gryllus.who: Gryllus, the companion of Odysseus turned into a pig by Circe who, in Plutarch's dialogue named after him, refuses to become a man again.

Guagninus.who: Alessandro Guagnini (1534–1614), Italian soldier in Polish service, author of Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio (1578), which includes Muscovy.

Gualter.who: Rudolf Gwalther (1519–1586), Zurich Reformed theologian, Bullinger's successor, author of homilies on many books of the Bible.

Gualter Bruele.who: Gualtherus Bruele (Walter Bruel), Flemish physician, author of Praxis medicinae, a practical handbook of diseases and cures.

Gualter Mapes.who: Walter Map (c.1140–c.1210), Welsh-born cleric and courtier of Henry II, author of the anecdotal miscellany *De nugis curialium*.

Gualterus Mapes.who: Walter Map (c.1140–c.1210), Welsh-born cleric and courtier of Henry II, author of the anecdotal miscellany *De nugis curialium*.

Guarinonius.basis: The cited 'cons. med.' matches Guarinoni's published Consilia; there are other physicians of the same family name.
Guarinonius.who: Cristoforo Guarinoni, Italian physician of Verona, physician to the Emperor Rudolf II, author of *Consilia medicinalia* (1610).

Guastavinius.who: Giulio Guastavini, Genoese physician who wrote a Latin commentary on the pseudo-Aristotelian *Problems* (1608).

Guazzo.who: Stefano Guazzo (1530–1593), Italian writer whose dialogue *La civil conversazione* (1574) was translated into English as *Civil Conversation*.

Guelph.who: The Guelphs, the medieval Italian faction that supported the papacy against the imperial Ghibellines.

Guelphs.who: The Guelphs, the medieval Italian faction that supported the papacy against the imperial Ghibellines.

Guevara.basis: Burton often cites Guevara, and moral advice about wives fits his works.
Guevara.who: Antonio de Guevara (c.1481–1545), Spanish Franciscan bishop and court preacher, author of the much-translated moral works *Dial of Princes* and *Familiar Epistles*.

Guiana.who: Guiana, the region of north-eastern South America where Ralegh sought El Dorado on his failed voyages (1595, 1617).

Guicciardine.basis: The Francis I passage and 'Hiponest' (Hypomneses) fit Francesco; the Mully-Hamet anecdote might come from his nephew Lodovico Guicciardini.
Guicciardine.who: Francesco Guicciardini (1483–1540), Florentine statesman and historian, author of the *Storia d'Italia* and the maxims called *Ricordi* (Latin *Hypomneses*).

Guido Bonat.who: Guido Bonatti (d. c.1300), Italian astrologer of Forlì, author of the *Liber astronomicus*.

Guidus Ubaldus.who: Guidobaldo del Monte (1545–1607), Italian mathematician and patron of Galileo, author of *Perspectivae libri sex* (1600).

Guil. Postellus.who: Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), French orientalist and visionary, author of *De orbis terrae concordia*.

Guinea.who: New Guinea, the large island north of Australia; Burton is unsure whether it is an island or part of the southern continent.

Guines.who: Guînes, a town near Calais, where Henry VIII met Francis I at the Field of the Cloth of Gold (1520).

Guipuzcoa.who: Guipúzcoa (Gipuzkoa), a Basque province of northern Spain known for its cider.

Guiscardus.who: Guiscardo, the low-born lover of Ghismonda in Boccaccio's *Decameron* (IV.1); her father Tancredi has him killed and sends her his heart.

Guise.who: Henri I de Lorraine, Duke of Guise (1550–1588), leader of the Catholic League, murdered at Blois on the orders of Henry III.

Guithera.who: Guinevere, King Arthur's queen in legend, discussed by John Leland in his defence of Arthur.

Gujarat.who: Gujarat, the region of western India; its Banian (Hindu and Jain merchant) communities were known to travellers for refusing to kill living creatures.

Gulielmus Parisiensis.who: William of Auvergne (d. 1249), Bishop of Paris and scholastic theologian, author of *De universo*, which treats demons and marvels.

Gurmunde.who: Gorm the Old (d. c.958), King of Denmark, whose wife Thyra was remembered as a wise and virtuous queen.

Guthlac.who: St Guthlac (c.674–714), Mercian hermit of Crowland in the Fens, famed for his struggles with demons.

Guyenne.who: Guyenne (Guienne), the historic province of south-western France around Bordeaux, part of old Aquitaine.

Gwinne.who: Matthew Gwinne (c.1558–1627), English physician and Gresham professor, who attacked Francis Anthony's *aurum potabile* in print (1611).

Gyges.who: Gyges, king of Lydia (7th century BC), who in Herodotus is made to see Candaules' wife naked and then kills Candaules and takes his throne.

Gymnosophist.who: One of the Gymnosophists, the naked Indian ascetic philosophers whom Alexander questioned (Plutarch, *Life of Alexander*).

Gymnosophists.who: The Gymnosophists, the 'naked philosophers' (ascetic sages of India, also placed by ancient writers in Ethiopia) described by Greek writers.

Habakkuk.who: Habakkuk, Hebrew prophet; in the apocryphal *Bel and the Dragon* an angel carries him by the hair to feed Daniel in the lions' den.

Habbakuk.who: Habakkuk, Hebrew prophet; his book opens by complaining that the wicked prosper.

Habundia.who: Dame Habundia (Abundia), a fairy queen of medieval European folklore, said to lead night-roaming spirits.

Hacket.who: William Hacket (d. 1591), English fanatic who claimed to be Christ and was executed in London; Coppinger and Arthington were his followers.

Hadrian Antinous.who: Two names: the Roman emperor Hadrian (76–138) and his beloved favourite Antinous (d. 130), deified after drowning in the Nile.

Haed.who: Pietro Edo (Petrus Haedus, Capretto) (1427–1504), priest of Pordenone, author of *De contemnendis amoribus* (*Anterotica*, 1492).

Haedus.who: Pietro Edo (Petrus Haedus, Capretto) (1427–1504), priest of Pordenone, author of *De contemnendis amoribus* (*Anterotica*, 1492).

Hagar.who: Hagar, Sarah's Egyptian handmaid and mother of Ishmael, comforted by an angel in the wilderness (Genesis 16 and 21).

Hagthorpe.who: John Hagthorpe (fl. 1620s), English writer whose *England's Exchequer* (1625) urged sea power, trade and colonies.

Hakluyt.who: Richard Hakluyt (c. 1552–1616), English clergyman who collected voyage narratives in *The Principal Navigations of the English Nation*.

Halcyonian.who: An adjective from 'halcyon days': calm and peaceful times, named from the kingfisher (Alcyone in myth), said to calm the seas while it nests.

Hall.basis: The second passage is the chronicler Edward Hall (d. 1547). The first, a side-note on a definition of ambition, may be Joseph Hall, but this is not certain.

Halyabbas.who: Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi (d. c. 990), Persian physician known in Latin as Haly Abbas, author of the medical encyclopedia *Kitab al-Maliki* (*Liber regius*).

Hamadryades.who: The Hamadryads, nymphs in Greek myth whose lives were bound up with particular trees.

Haman.who: Haman, chief minister of King Ahasuerus in the Book of Esther, hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai.

Hamathites.who: The people of Hamath (modern Hama, Syria), resettled in Samaria, who made the god Ashima (2 Kings 17:30).

Hamburg.who: Hamburg, the Hanseatic port on the Elbe in northern Germany.

Hamech.basis: Burton's own wording and the well-known compound 'confectio Hamech'. No historical author can be securely identified.
Hamech.who: Hamech, a supposed Arab physician who gave his name to the 'confection of Hamech', a strong purgative electuary in the Arabic–Latin pharmacopoeia.

Hammel.who: Hameln (Hamelin), a town on the Weser in Lower Saxony, Germany, home of the Pied Piper legend of 1284.

Hanbury.who: Hanbury, a village in east Staffordshire near Tutbury, next to Fauld, where the Burton family lived.

Hanea.basis: 'Hanea' looks like a corrupt form of Greek hagnos. Ancient sources tie this plant to the Thesmophoria and to chastity.
Hanea.who: The Greek *agnos*, the chaste-tree (*Vitex agnus-castus*), which Athenian women strewed on their beds at the Thesmophoria.

Hannah.who: Hannah, wife of Elkanah and mother of the prophet Samuel, who prayed in distress for a child (1 Samuel 1).

Hannibal.who: Hannibal (247–c. 183 BC), Carthaginian general, defeated at Zama, who later poisoned himself to avoid being handed over to Rome.

Harpax.who: Harpax, the Macedonian soldier's servant in Plautus's comedy *Pseudolus*.

Harpedone.who: Harpedone, the fictional addressee of a love letter in the *Epistles* of Aristaenetus (late antique Greek letter-writer).

Harpies.who: The Harpies, rapacious winged monsters of Greek myth, half woman and half bird, described by Virgil in *Aeneid* 3.

Harpy.who: Used figuratively of a grasping person, after the Harpies, the rapacious winged monsters of Greek myth.

Hassia.who: Hesse, a landgraviate in central Germany.

Haterius.basis: Several Roman bearers named Haterius are possible, and the cited passages are not certain.

Hatred.basis: A word in a section heading.

Hatto.who: Hatto II (d. 970), Archbishop of Mainz, who in legend was eaten by mice in the Mouse Tower at Bingen.

Hayward.basis: The context is a list of consolatory writers for troubled consciences, and Hayward's *Sanctuarie* fits.
Hayward.who: Sir John Hayward (c. 1564–1627), English historian, who also wrote the devotional work *The Sanctuarie of a Troubled Soule* (1601).

Heautontimorumenos.who: *Heauton Timorumenos* ('The Self-Tormentor'), comedy by Terence (163 BC).

Hebe.who: Hebe, Greek goddess of youth, daughter of Zeus and Hera and cupbearer to the gods.

Hebrew.who: A Hebrew, i.e. a Jewish writer; used alongside Greek and Latin for the writers of antiquity.

Hebrides.who: The Hebrides, the island groups off the west coast of Scotland.

Hebrus.who: The Hebrus, the river of ancient Thrace, now the Maritsa/Evros, flowing from Bulgaria to the Aegean.

Hecate.who: Hecate, Greek goddess of witchcraft and crossroads, often shown in triple form.

Hecklebirg.basis: Hekla was famous in the period for cries of the damned, and 'Hecklebirg' = Hekla-berg. 'Norway' reflects Iceland's political tie.
Hecklebirg.who: Hekla, the volcano in southern Iceland (then under the Danish–Norwegian crown), believed to be a mouth of hell.

Hecla.who: Hekla, an active volcano in southern Iceland, popularly held to be a mouth of hell.

Hector.who: Hector, the Trojan champion of Homer's *Iliad*, son of Priam, killed by Achilles.

Hectors.who: Hector, the Trojan champion of the *Iliad*; used in the plural for great warriors.

Hecuba.who: Hecuba, legendary queen of Troy, wife of Priam, said in myth to have been turned into a dog after her griefs.

Hedieia.who: Hedeia, Athenian courtesan named by Plutarch among the women who kept company with Epicurus and his followers in the Garden.

Hedinga.who: Jadwiga (Hedwig) of Anjou (c. 1374–1399), queen of Poland, whose 1386 marriage to Jogaila of Lithuania brought his baptism as Władysław II.

Hegesippus.who: 'Hegesippus' (Pseudo-Hegesippus), name attached to a fourth-century Latin adaptation of Josephus's Jewish War, De excidio Hierosolymitano.

Heider.who: Wolfgang Heider (1558–1626), professor of ethics at Jena, author of a Systema philosophiae moralis.

Heins.who: Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), Dutch classical scholar, Latin poet and dramatist of Leiden.

Heinsius Austriac.basis: Heinsius is certain; the cited title 'Austriaco' seems a corruption of his tragedy Auriacus.
Heinsius Austriac.who: Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), Dutch scholar and poet, quoted from his Latin tragedy Auriacus (1602) on the murder of William of Orange.

Heinsius Austriaco.basis: Heinsius is certain; the cited title 'Austriaco' seems a corruption of his tragedy Auriacus.
Heinsius Austriaco.who: Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), Dutch scholar and poet, quoted from his Latin tragedy Auriacus (1602) on the murder of William of Orange.

Heinsius Primerio.basis: Burton's usual Heinsius; the work cited as 'Primerio' is not settled.
Heinsius Primerio.who: Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), Dutch classical scholar and Latin poet of Leiden.

Helen.who: In the first passage, the baths of St Helena (Sant'Elena) in northern Italy; in the others, Helen of Troy, the legendary beauty whose abduction caused the Trojan War.

Helena.who: Helen of Troy, legendary wife of Menelaus, carried off by Paris; in the Odyssey she receives the drug nepenthe in Egypt.

Helena Alba.who: Guinevere, legendary queen of King Arthur, whose name John Leland rendered as 'Helena Alba' (white Helen).

Helenae.who: Helen of Troy, legendary beauty; Pliny mentions paintings of Atalanta and Helen at Lanuvium.

Helicon.who: Mount Helicon in Boeotia, Greece, sacred to the Muses; here standing for the Muses themselves.

Heliodorus’ Chariclea.who: The Aethiopica of Heliodorus of Emesa (3rd or 4th century AD), Greek romance whose heroine is Chariclea.

Heliogabali.who: Elagabalus (Heliogabalus), Roman emperor 218–222, notorious for debauchery and extravagance.

Heliogabalus.who: Elagabalus (Heliogabalus), Roman emperor 218–222, notorious for debauchery and extravagance; murdered by his guards.

Heliogabaluses.who: Elagabalus (Heliogabalus), Roman emperor 218–222, a byword for gluttony and debauchery; used here as a type.

Helisaeus Roeslin.who: Helisaeus Röslin (1545–1616), Alsatian physician and astrologer, author of Theoria nova coelestium meteoron (1578) on the comet of 1577.

Hellebore.who: Hellebore, a plant used since antiquity as a purge for madness and melancholy.

Hellebores.who: White and black hellebore, purgative plants used against melancholy.

Helleborism.who: A course of purging with hellebore.

Hellespont.who: The Hellespont, the strait between Europe and Asia Minor, now the Dardanelles.

Helmstad.who: Helmstedt in Lower Saxony, Germany, seat of a Lutheran university founded in 1576.

Heloissa.who: Héloïse (c. 1100–1164), niece of Canon Fulbert, lover and later wife of Peter Abelard, afterwards abbess of the Paraclete.

Helvetia.who: Helvetia, the Latin name for Switzerland.

Hemmingius.who: Niels Hemmingsen (1513–1600), Danish Lutheran theologian at Copenhagen, who wrote on witchcraft and pastoral consolation.

Hen.basis: 'Hen.' is the abbreviated first name of Neuhusius, who wrote on the Rosicrucians.
Hen.who: Henricus Neuhusius (Heinrich Neuhaus), German writer of a 1618 pamphlet questioning whether the Rosicrucian brethren existed.

Hen. Nicholas.who: Hendrik Niclaes (c. 1502–c. 1580), Dutch mystic who founded the Family of Love and claimed divine inspiration.

Hengist.who: Hengist, legendary fifth-century Saxon leader who settled in Kent; in legend, father of Rowena, Vortigern's wife.

Henricus Abrincensis.who: Henry of Avranches (d. c. 1260), Anglo-Norman Latin poet at the court of Henry III, who wrote verses mocking English beer.

Henricus Ayrerus.basis: The Hildesheim citations fit; I have no further details of his life.
Henricus Ayrerus.who: Heinrich Ayrer, German physician whose consultations on melancholy were printed in Hildesheim's Spicilegia.

Henricus Bavarus.who: Emperor Henry II (973–1024), formerly Duke of Bavaria, husband of St Cunigunde, who was said to have walked unharmed over red-hot ploughshares.

Henry.who: Different English kings: Henry VI (Wars of the Roses), Henry VIII (Field of the Cloth of Gold, 1520) and Henry I (who imprisoned his brother Robert).

Henry Landgrave.who: Henry II 'the Iron', Landgrave of Hesse, father of Adelaide, wife of King Casimir III of Poland.

Henry Spelman.who: Sir Henry Spelman (c. 1562–1641), English antiquary, author of De non temerandis ecclesiis (1613) against the lay seizure of church property.

Henry Stephan.who: Henri Estienne (1531–1598), French printer and scholar, author of the satirical Apologie pour Hérodote (1566).

Hepatic.who: Relating to the liver; here a kind of hypochondriacal melancholy.

Hephaestion.who: Hephaestion (d. 324 BC), Macedonian general and Alexander the Great's closest friend.

Heraclea.who: Heraclea in Thrace (ancient Perinthus), on the Sea of Marmara; now Marmara Ereğlisi, Turkey.

Heraclitus.who: Heraclitus of Ephesus (fl. c. 500 BC), Greek philosopher, traditionally the 'weeping philosopher' set against the laughing Democritus.

Herberstein.basis: Fits the Muscovy passages; the husbandry passage (with Porta, Camerarius) probably means Conrad Heresbach, the writer on husbandry.
Herberstein.who: Sigismund von Herberstein (1486–1566), Austrian diplomat whose Rerum Moscoviticarum commentarii described Muscovy.

Herc. de Saxonia.who: Ercole Sassonia (Hercules Saxonia, 1551–1607), Paduan professor of medicine whose treatise on melancholy appeared posthumously in 1620.

Herculean.basis: adjective: a task fit for Hercules

Hercules.who: Hercules (Heracles), the Greek hero of the twelve labours, deified after death.

Hercules Furens.who: Hercules in his madness, when he killed his own children, as shown in Seneca's tragedy Hercules Furens.

Hercules Gallus.who: The Gallic Hercules (Ogmios), whom Lucian describes leading men by chains from his tongue, an emblem of eloquence.

Hercules Hylam.who: Hercules, the Greek hero, here with his favourite Hylas (Latin accusative 'Hylam').

Hercyne.who: The Hercyna, a spring and stream at Lebadea (modern Livadeia) in Boeotia, beside the oracle of Trophonius.

Hercynian.who: The Hercynian Forest, the ancient name for the vast wooded uplands of central Germany.

Herebertus.who: St Heribert (c. 970–1021), Archbishop of Cologne, who in the legend of the dancers of Kölbigk absolves them.

Heresbachius.who: Conrad Heresbach (1496–1576), German humanist and councillor of Cleves, author of De educandis principum liberis and a treatise on husbandry.

Hermaphroditus.who: Hermaphroditus, son of Hermes and Aphrodite, loved by the nymph Salmacis, with whom he was fused into one body (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4).

Hermes.basis: Fits the astrological and magical passages; the third ('Hermes Polit.', on birds in Poland) is a different, unidentified author.
Hermes.who: Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage to whom astrological, magical and philosophical writings were ascribed.

Hermione.basis: Two bearers: the town of Hermione (Ermioni) in the Argolid, and Hermione, daughter of Menelaus, in Euripides.

Hermolaus.who: Hermolaus, a Macedonian royal page who led the conspiracy of the pages against Alexander the Great in 327 BC (Curtius, book 8).

Hermon.who: Mount Hermon, the high mountain on the border of modern Lebanon and Syria, north of Palestine.

Hermotimus.basis: 'the said Author', Epist. lib. 2, points to Aristaenetus' letters, cited nearby.
Hermotimus.who: Hermotimus, a young lover in one of the fictional love letters of Aristaenetus (fl. c. AD 500).

Hero.who: Hero, priestess of Sestos and beloved of Leander, as in Musaeus and Marlowe's Hero and Leander.

Herod.basis: Different Herods: Herod Antipas (John the Baptist), Herod the Great (Hegesippus), Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12).

Herodes Atticus.who: Herodes Atticus (c. 101–177), wealthy Athenian sophist and benefactor who planned to cut a canal through the Isthmus of Corinth.

Herodians.who: The Herodians, a Jewish party in the Gospels that supported the Herodian dynasty and opposed Jesus.

Herodias.who: Herodias, wife of Herod Antipas, who obtained John the Baptist's head; in the Gospels, her daughter (Salome) danced.

Herod’s Mariamne.who: Mariamne (d. 29 BC), Hasmonean princess famed for her beauty, wife of Herod the Great, who had her executed.

Herophilus.who: Herophilus of Chalcedon (c. 335–c. 280 BC), Alexandrian physician and anatomist, who called medicines the 'hands of the gods'.

Herrera.who: Antonio de Herrera y Tordesillas (1549–1626), Spanish royal chronicler and historian of the Spanish Indies.

Hesione.who: Hesione, daughter of King Laomedon of Troy, rescued by Hercules from a sea monster.

Hesperius.who: Hesperius, a former tribune in Augustine's North Africa whose farm near Hippo is mentioned in City of God 22.8.

Hesperus.who: Hesperus, the evening star (the planet Venus), personified in Greek myth.

Hessen.who: Hesse, a landgraviate in central Germany.

Hetoemocles.who: Hetoemocles, a fictional Stoic philosopher in Lucian's Symposium (The Carousal, or Lapiths), who writes a letter complaining that he was not invited.

Heurnius. Scherertzius.basis: The form runs two names together; Heurnius, the Leiden physician Burton often cites, is meant; Scherertzius is a separate, unidentified author.
Heurnius. Scherertzius.who: Johannes Heurnius (1543–1601), Dutch professor of medicine at Leiden.

Heuter.who: Pontus Heuterus (Pontus de Huyter, 1535–1602), Dutch priest and historian, author of the Rerum Burgundicarum libri, a history of the Burgundian dukes.

Hevaei.basis: Burton's list follows 2 Kings 17, and the Vulgate gives the Avvites as Hevaei/Evaei.
Hevaei.who: The Avvites (Vulgate 'Hevaei'), people settled in Samaria who worshipped Tartak, according to 2 Kings 17:31.

Hexamilium.who: The Hexamilion, the six-mile Byzantine defensive wall across the Isthmus of Corinth, rebuilt in the fifteenth century and repeatedly destroyed by the Ottomans.

Hezekiah.who: Hezekiah, King of Judah (late 8th–early 7th century BC); Isaiah's poultice of figs cured him after he prayed (2 Kings 20).

Hier.who: St Jerome (c. 347–420), Latin Church Father and translator of the Vulgate; his letter to Laeta deals with bringing up a daughter.

Hier. Capivaccius.who: Girolamo Capivaccio (d. 1589), physician and professor of medicine at Padua.

Hier. Wolfius.who: Hieronymus Wolf (1516–1580), German humanist and Greek scholar of Augsburg, who wrote a preface to Cyprianus Leovitius's astrological work on nativities.

Hiera.who: First passage: Hiera, the ancient name of Vulcano in the Aeolian Islands. Second passage: hiera, a classic purgative electuary of ancient pharmacy (e.g. hiera picra).

Hieralogodion.basis: Standard name in the old pharmacopoeias; the attribution to Logadius is traditional.
Hieralogodion.who: Hiera Logadii, a compound purgative electuary named after its supposed inventor Logadius, prescribed against melancholy.

Hieram Rufi.who: Hiera Rufi, a purgative electuary attributed to the physician Rufus of Ephesus and recorded by Aetius.

Hierocles.who: Sossianus Hierocles (fl. c. 300), Roman governor under Diocletian whose Philalethes compared Apollonius of Tyana to Christ; Eusebius wrote a rebuttal.

Hieroglyph.who: The Hieroglyphica (1556) of Pierio Valeriano, a large Renaissance encyclopedia of Egyptian and other symbolic meanings.

Hieroglyphics.who: Pierio Valeriano's Hieroglyphica (1556), an encyclopedia of symbols; in the first and third passages the word also means the Egyptians' own hieroglyphic signs.

Hierom Wolfius.who: Hieronymus Wolf (1516–1580), German humanist, Greek scholar and librarian of Augsburg.

Hieronym.who: St Jerome (c. 347–420), Latin Church Father and translator of the Vulgate.

Hieronym. Paulus.who: Jeroni Pau (Hieronymus Paulus, d. 1497), Catalan humanist of Barcelona, author of a treatise on the rivers and mountains of Spain.

Hieronymus Henninges.who: Hieronymus Henninges (d. 1597), German Lutheran pastor and genealogist, author of the Theatrum genealogicum.

Hieronymus Massainus.basis: Known only as the questioner in Alexander ab Alexandro's Genialium dierum.

Hieronymus Mengus.who: Girolamo Menghi (1529–1609), Italian Franciscan exorcist, author of the Flagellum daemonum and other exorcism manuals.

Hieronymus Wolfius.who: Hieronymus Wolf (1516–1580), German humanist and Greek scholar of Augsburg, who was interested in astrology.

Hieronymus. Aristotle.basis: 'Hieronymus' is Burton's usual citation form for Jerome, and the form joins a marginal note to the following sentence.
Hieronymus. Aristotle.who: St Jerome (c. 347–420), Latin Church Father, cited in a margin as the source of the Latin tag; Aristotle begins the next sentence.

Hilarion.who: St Hilarion (c. 291–371), hermit of Gaza and Palestine, whose life Jerome wrote.

Hilary.who: Hilary term, the law and university term beginning in January, named after the feast of St Hilary; used here figuratively for a short spell.

Hilarys.basis: Named alongside Paul and Antony as an anchorite, and the next sentence names Hilarion.
Hilarys.who: St Hilarion (c. 291–371), Palestinian hermit, named here with Paul the Hermit and Antony as a model desert ascetic.

Hildebertus Cenomanensis Episc.who: Hildebert of Lavardin (c. 1055–1133), Bishop of Le Mans and later Archbishop of Tours, Latin poet who wrote verses on Berengar of Tours.

Hildebrand.who: Hildebrand, Pope Gregory VII (c. 1015–1085), whom his imperialist and Protestant enemies accused of sorcery.

Hipparchus.who: Hipparchus of Nicaea (2nd century BC), Greek astronomer who discovered precession and compiled a star catalogue.

Hippo.who: Hippo Regius, Augustine's episcopal city in North Africa, modern Annaba in Algeria.

Hippocrates Cous.who: Hippocrates of Cos (c. 460–c. 370 BC), Greek physician and father of medicine.

Hippocrates’ Aphorisms.who: The Aphorisms, a collection of short medical maxims in the Hippocratic Corpus.

Hippodamus.who: Hippodamus of Miletus (5th century BC), Greek town planner associated with the grid layout of streets.

Hippolytus.who: First passage: Hippolytus à Collibus (Hippolyt von Colli, 1561–1612), jurist and author of Incrementa urbium. Other passages: mythical Hippolytus, son of Theseus, loved by Phaedra.

Hippolytus Salvianus.who: Ippolito Salviani (1514–1572), Roman physician and naturalist, author of an illustrated history of fishes (Aquatilium animalium historiae).

Hippolytus à Collibus.who: Hippolyt von Colli (Hippolytus à Collibus, 1561–1612), Swiss-born jurist and Palatine counsellor, author of the political treatise Incrementa urbium.

Hippolytus. Joessa.who: Hippolytus is the son of Theseus, loved by Phaedra in Seneca's tragedy; Joessa is a courtesan in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans who pleads with Lysias.

Hippomanes.who: Hippomanes, a substance from a mare or newborn foal that the ancients believed to be a potent love-charm.

Hippomenes.who: Hippomenes (or Melanion), the mythical suitor who beat Atalanta in a footrace by dropping golden apples and so won her as his wife.

Hipponax.who: Hipponax of Ephesus (6th century BC), Greek iambic satirist whose lampoons were said to have driven the sculptors Bupalus and Athenis to hang themselves.

Hiscere.who: A Latin verb meaning 'to open the mouth' or 'to mutter', from Juvenal's Satire 5.

Hispaniola.who: Hispaniola, the Caribbean island now divided between Haiti and the Dominican Republic.

Hispulla.who: Hispulla, wife of the Roman senator Corellius Rufus, whose suicide by starvation Pliny the Younger describes in Letters 1.12.

Histria.who: Istria, the peninsula at the head of the Adriatic, now divided between Croatia and Slovenia; the 'Mons maior' here is Monte Maggiore (Učka).

Hobgoblins.who: Hobgoblins: in English folklore, mischievous household sprites of the Robin Goodfellow kind.

Hodaeporicons.who: Hodoeporicons: travel narratives or itineraries, from the Greek word for a journey.

Hofmannus.who: Daniel Hoffmann (c.1538–1611), Lutheran theologian and professor at Helmstedt, known for his controversy over the claims of philosophy against theology.

Hogenbergius.who: Frans Hogenberg (c.1535–c.1590), Flemish engraver who produced the city atlas Civitates orbis terrarum with Georg Braun.

Holland.who: Holland, the leading province of the United Provinces of the Netherlands.

Hollander.who: A native of Holland; a Dutchman.

Hollanders.who: The Dutch, people of Holland and the United Provinces.

Hollerius.who: Jacques Houllier (c.1498–1562), Paris physician whose De morbis internis was annotated by Louis Duret.

Holofernes.who: Holofernes, the Assyrian general in the apocryphal Book of Judith, whom Judith seduced and then beheaded.

Homer. Jacob.basis: A parsing artefact that runs together 'Homer' (end of one sentence) and 'Jacob' (start of the next).

Homer’s Iliads.who: Homer's Iliad, the Greek epic of the Trojan War.

Homer’s Mars.who: Ares (Mars), who roars like nine or ten thousand men when Diomedes wounds him in Iliad 5.

Homer’s Nireus.who: Nireus of Syme, called by Homer (Iliad 2) the handsomest Greek at Troy after Achilles.

Homogeneal.who: Homogeneal: an anatomical term for parts of uniform substance.

Hondius.who: Jodocus Hondius (1563–1612), Flemish engraver and cartographer of Amsterdam who published enlarged editions of Mercator's Atlas.

Honorius.basis: Two different bearers; the patient is not otherwise identifiable.
Honorius.who: In the second passage, Western Roman emperor Honorius (384–423), who reigned alongside his brother Arcadius; in the first, a deluded patient known only from Victorius Faventinus.

Honour.who: Honos, the Roman personification of honour, who had temples at Rome.

Hor.who: Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus, 65–8 BC), Roman lyric and satiric poet, quoted here.

Horatii.who: The Horatii, three Roman brothers of legend who fought the three Alban Curiatii for Rome under Tullus Hostilius.

Horatius Augenius.who: Orazio Augenio (1527–1603), Italian physician and professor at Padua, author of a large treatise on bloodletting.

Horta.who: Horta, a minor Roman goddess who urged people to action, mentioned by Augustine in City of God 4.16.

Hortensius.who: Quintus Hortensius Hortalus (114–50 BC), Roman orator and Cicero's rival, who married Marcia after Cato divorced her.

Hostius.who: Hostius Quadra, a Roman debauchee whose use of magnifying mirrors Seneca condemns in Natural Questions 1.16.

Hostratus.who: Jacob van Hoogstraten (c.1460–1527), Dominican inquisitor at Cologne, Reuchlin's chief opponent and a target of the Epistolae obscurorum virorum.

Hotherus.who: Hotherus (Höðr), legendary Scandinavian king in Saxo Grammaticus, who met wood-maidens while lost hunting; Olaus Magnus retells the story.

Hovatus.basis: Camden records Hamont's burning at Norwich, and the Latinised form looks like his name, but this is not certain.
Hovatus.who: Probably Matthew Hamont, a ploughwright burned at Norwich in 1579 for heretical opinions, as recorded in Camden's Annals.

Huena.who: Hven (now Ven), an island in the Øresund, now Swedish, where Tycho Brahe built his observatory Uraniborg.

Hugh Broughton.who: Hugh Broughton (1549–1612), English Puritan Hebraist and biblical chronologer, author of A Concent of Scripture.

Hugh Middleton Baronet.who: Sir Hugh Myddelton (1560–1631), goldsmith and entrepreneur who built the New River to bring water to London; made a baronet in 1622.

Hugo.basis: Several medieval Hugos (of St Victor, of St Cher, etc.) are possible; the passage does not settle which.

Hugo de Prato Florido.basis: The name and the sermon reference fit this preacher; I am not sure of his dates.
Hugo de Prato Florido.who: Hugh of Prato (Hugo de Prato Florido), 14th-century Italian Dominican preacher whose Latin sermon collections for Sundays and feasts were widely printed.

Huguenots.who: The Huguenots, French Calvinist Protestants, one side in the French Wars of Religion.

Hull.who: Kingston upon Hull, port town on the Humber estuary in Yorkshire.

Humfrey Llwyd.who: Humphrey Llwyd (1527–1568), Welsh antiquary and map-maker, friend of Ortelius, to whom he addressed his description of Britain.

Humphrey.who: Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester (1390–1447), youngest son of Henry IV, whose wife Eleanor Cobham was exiled for witchcraft.

Hungary.who: The kingdom of Hungary in central Europe.

Huniades.basis: Being freed from prison to be crowned king fits Matthias Hunyadi rather than his father John.
Huniades.who: Matthias Corvinus (1443–1490), son of John Hunyadi, held prisoner in Prague and then released to be elected King of Hungary in 1458.

Huns.who: The Huns, nomadic people who invaded the Roman Empire in the 4th–5th centuries.

Hydamardia.who: Hydamargia, a made-up city on the island of Cabbalusa in Lucian's True History, where women with asses' legs prey on strangers.

Hylas.who: Hylas, the young companion of Hercules on the Argonauts' voyage, carried off by water-nymphs, whom Hercules searched for frantically.

Hymen.who: Hymen, the Greek god of marriage; in the third passage the word means the anatomical membrane.

Hymenaeus.who: Hymenaeus, the god of weddings and the wedding song; in the third passage, the heretic whom Paul delivered to Satan (1 Timothy 1:20).

Hyperborean.who: The unnamed Hyperborean magician in Lucian's Philopseudes, who uses love-magic to draw a woman to a young man.

Hyperchen.basis: Burton names it as Cardan's work, and the title fits one of Cardano's dialogues.
Hyperchen.who: Hyperchen, a dialogue by Girolamo Cardano that discusses spirits and daemons.

Hyperides.who: Hyperides (c.390–322 BC), Athenian orator, famous for his defence of the courtesan Phryne.

Hyperius.who: Andreas Hyperius (1511–1564), Flemish Protestant theologian at Marburg, author of a treatise on daily reading of Scripture.

Hypocrit.basis: The marginal 'Hypocrit.' comes before Scaliger's verdict on Homer, which fits the Hypercriticus.
Hypocrit.who: Hypercriticus, the sixth book of Julius Caesar Scaliger's Poetices libri septem, which judges the poets critically.

Iago.who: St James the Greater (Santiago), apostle and patron saint of Spain, whose shrine at Santiago de Compostela drew pilgrims.

Iamblichus.who: Iamblichus (c.245–c.325), Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher, who wrote on daemons and theurgy and was later reputed a magician.

Iarthae Indorum.who: Iarchas, the chief of the Indian sages (Brahmans) whom Apollonius visits in Philostratus' Life of Apollonius.

Iberina.who: Hiberina, a woman in Juvenal's sixth satire who cannot be content with a single man.

Icaromenippus.who: Icaromenippus, Lucian's satirical dialogue in which Menippus flies to heaven and overhears men's prayers to Zeus.

Iceland.who: Iceland, the island in the North Atlantic.

Idalian Ganymede.who: Ganymede, the beautiful Trojan youth whom Jupiter carried up to heaven to be his cupbearer.

Ignatius.basis: Cited as an author on St Mark's in Venice; Burton elsewhere cites Egnatius, and the Latin form fits.
Ignatius.who: Giovanni Battista Egnazio (Egnatius, c. 1478–1553), Venetian humanist and historian who wrote on Venice and its notable men.

Ignatius Loyola.who: Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556), Basque soldier turned priest, founder of the Society of Jesus.

Ilissus.who: The Ilissos, a small river flowing past ancient Athens, setting of Plato's Phaedrus.

Illyricum.who: Illyricum, the Roman name for the region along the eastern Adriatic coast (roughly modern Croatia, Bosnia, Montenegro and Albania).

Illyricus.basis: The best-known Latin writer called simply Illyricus, listed among Protestant theological authors.
Illyricus.who: Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), Croatian-born Lutheran theologian and polemicist.

Imagin.who: Lucian's Imagines (Eikones), a dialogue describing an ideal beauty assembled from famous statues and paintings.

Imagines.who: Lucian's Imagines (Eikones), a dialogue describing an ideal beauty, Panthea, assembled from famous statues and paintings.

Imbram Bassa.basis: Radziwiłł visited Cairo in the early 1580s, when Ibrahim Pasha governed Egypt.
Imbram Bassa.who: Ibrahim Pasha, Ottoman governor of Egypt in the 1580s, later grand vizier.

Impudency.who: Shamelessness (Greek Anaideia) personified as a deity, said to have had a shrine at Athens.

In Charidemo.who: Charidemus, a dialogue on beauty transmitted among Lucian's works.

In Clio.who: Clio, the first book of Herodotus' Histories.

In Cosmogr.who: Sebastian Münster's Cosmographia (1544), a German description of the world.

In Gallo.who: Lucian's Gallus (The Dream, or the Cock), in which a cock claims to be the reincarnated Pythagoras.

In Hygiasticon.who: Leonard Lessius' Hygiasticon (1613), a Jesuit treatise on temperate diet and health.

In Hyperchen.basis: Attributed to Cardan in the passage; the title matches a little-known dialogue of his.
In Hyperchen.who: Hyperchen, a dialogue by the Italian physician and philosopher Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576).

In Jovinianum.who: Jerome's Adversus Jovinianum (c. 393), a polemic against the monk Jovinian.

In Lysandro.who: Plutarch's Life of Lysander, the Spartan commander.

In Micro.basis: 'Micro' abbreviates the Microtechne, i.e. Galen's Ars parva, on which Crato wrote.
In Micro.who: Johann Crato von Krafftheim's Microtechne, a commentary on Galen's Ars parva.

In Muscovia.who: Paolo Giovio's Moscovia (1525), an account of Muscovy based on the Russian embassy to Rome.

In Phaedon.who: Plato's Phaedo, the dialogue on Socrates' last day and the immortality of the soul.

In Philebo.who: Plato's Philebus, a dialogue on pleasure and the good.

In Phoeniss.who: Euripides' Phoenissae (The Phoenician Women), a tragedy on the war of Polynices and Eteocles.

In Satyr.who: Petronius' Satyricon, the first-century Latin comic novel.

In Satyricon.who: Petronius' Satyricon, the first-century Latin comic novel.

In Syntax.who: Johann Jacob Wecker's Medicinae syntaxes (1576), a systematic compendium of medicine.

In Syntaxi.who: Johann Jacob Wecker's Medicinae syntaxes (1576), a systematic compendium of medicine.

In Syria.who: Syria, the region of the eastern Mediterranean around Damascus.

In Theaetet.who: Plato's Theaetetus, a dialogue on the nature of knowledge.

In Theoricis Planetarum.who: Giovanni Antonio Magini's Theoricae orbium coelestium et planetarum (1589), a treatise on planetary theory.

In Toxari.who: Lucian's Toxaris, a dialogue on friendship told through Greek and Scythian tales.

In Tusc.who: Cicero's Tusculan Disputations, philosophical dialogues on death, pain, grief and happiness.

Inachus.who: Inachus, river and river-god of Argos in Greek myth, father of Io.

Incubi.basis: class of demons, not a proper name

India.who: India, the South Asian subcontinent, loosely the East Indies in Burton's usage.

Indian.who: Of India or the Indies, used adjectivally of their peoples, priests and creatures.

Indian Brachmanni.who: The Brahmins, the priestly and philosophic caste of ancient India, admired by Greek writers for their austerity and wisdom.

Indian Capes.basis: generic phrase paired with Africa and the islands on the sea route
Indian Capes.who: The headlands and coasts of the East Indies, reached by Dutch and English voyages round Africa.

Indian Havana.who: Havana, the great Spanish harbour of Cuba in the West Indies.

Indians.who: The native peoples of the Indies, East and especially West (the Americas).

Indies.who: The West Indies (Spanish America) in the first two passages; the East Indies (South and Southeast Asia) in the third.

Indigetes.who: The Di Indigetes, Roman native gods or deified heroes of the homeland, distinguished from gods imported from abroad.

Innocentius Gentilletus.who: Innocent Gentillet (c.1535–1588), French Huguenot jurist, author of the Discours contre Machiavel (1576), the so-called Anti-Machiavel.

Invading. Aristotle.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher (the form wrongly includes the preceding word "Invading").

Ionia.who: Ionia, the Greek-settled central west coast of Asia Minor (modern Aegean Turkey).

Ionian.who: The Ionian Sea, between western Greece and southern Italy.

Iphicrates.who: Iphicrates (c.415–c.353 BC), Athenian general and military reformer, said to be a shoemaker's son.

Iphigenia.who: First, Efigenia, heroine of Boccaccio's tale of Cimone (Decameron V.1); second, Iphigenia, Agamemnon's daughter sacrificed at Aulis, painted by Timanthes.

Irenaeus.who: Irenaeus (c.130–c.202), bishop of Lyons, whose Against Heresies attacks the Gnostics, including Marcus and Valentinus.

Irene.who: First, the Greek captive loved by Mehmed II after 1453; second, Empress Irene of Byzantium (c.752–803); third, Irene, daughter of Ptolemy I and Thais.

Iris.who: Iris, Greek goddess of the rainbow and messenger of the gods.

Irish.who: The Irish (the "Irish Sea" between Britain and Ireland in one passage).

Irus.who: Irus, the beggar of Ithaca in Homer's Odyssey (book 18), proverbial for poverty.

Isaac.who: Isaac Israeli (c. 855–c. 955), Jewish physician and philosopher at Kairouan, whose book on diets was widely used in Latin translation.

Isabella.who: Different bearers: a stock name for a mistress; Isabella of France (1295–1358), queen of Edward II; Isabella of Valois, French princess married to Gian Galeazzo Visconti.

Isacius.basis: Nicetas is cited, but which Isaac he means is not certain.
Isacius.who: Probably a Byzantine prince or emperor of the Comnenian age, given to learning, named in Nicetas Choniates' history.

Isaeus.who: Isaeus (fl. late 1st century AD), Assyrian sophist and rhetorician praised by Pliny the Younger, whose life Philostratus wrote.

Isaurus.basis: Pliny's account of this battle places it at the Isara; Burton's form is garbled.
Isaurus.who: The river Isère in south-eastern France, where Q. Fabius Maximus defeated the Allobroges in 121 BC.

Isidore.basis: Could be Isidore of Pelusium (letters) or Isidore of Seville.

Isis.who: Egyptian goddess, sister and wife of Osiris; in the Leland passage, the Isis, the name of the Thames at Oxford.

Ismene.who: Hysmine, heroine of the 12th-century Byzantine romance Hysmine and Hysminias by Eustathius (Eumathios) Makrembolites.

Ismenias.who: Different bearers: Ismenias, Theban aulos-player said to cure ailments by music; and Hysminias, hero of Eustathius Makrembolites' romance Hysmine and Hysminias.

Ismenodora.who: Ismenodora, rich widow of Thespiae who carried off the youth Bacchon to marry him, as told in Plutarch's Amatorius.

Isocrates.who: Isocrates (436–338 BC), Athenian orator and teacher of rhetoric.

Israel.who: The people of Israel, the Hebrews of the Old Testament.

Israelites.who: The Hebrew people of the Old Testament.

Issus.who: Issus, town in Cilicia near modern Iskenderun, Turkey, where Alexander defeated Darius III in 333 BC.

Ister.who: Ister, the ancient name of the lower Danube.

Isthmian.who: The Isthmian Games, held at the Isthmus of Corinth in honour of Poseidon.

Isthmus.who: The Isthmus of Corinth, joining the Peloponnese to mainland Greece.

Italian (Crusianus.basis: Drusianus/Trusianus is the Latin name of Torrigiano, who left medicine for the cloister.
Italian (Crusianus.who: Pietro Torrigiano (Drusianus/Trusianus, d. c. 1320), Florentine physician and commentator on Galen who became a Carthusian monk.

Ithaca.who: Ithaca, Ionian island off western Greece, home of Odysseus.

Itinerary.who: Abraham Ortelius's Itinerarium per nonnullas Galliae Belgicae partes (1584), an account of a journey through the Low Countries and the Ardennes.

J. Aubanus Bohemus.who: Johann Boemus (Aubanus) (c. 1485–1535), German Hebraist and author of Omnium gentium mores, an early ethnographic compendium.

J. Bayerus.who: Johann Bayer (1572–1625), German astronomer, author of the star atlas Uranometria (1603).

J. Caesar Claudinus.who: Giulio Cesare Claudini, Bolognese physician and professor, author of a collection of medical consultations and responses.

J. Kevenheder.basis: Kevenheder is a form of Khevenhüller; which family member is uncertain.
J. Kevenheder.who: A Khevenhüller, Carinthian baron whose device appears among the emblems of Johannes Sambucus.

Jac. Boissardus.who: Jean-Jacques Boissard (1528–1602), French antiquary and Latin poet, author of De divinatione et magicis praestigiis.

Jacchinus.who: Leonardo Giacchini (Jacchinus) (d. 1557), Italian physician and professor at Pisa, author of a commentary on the ninth book of Rhazes ad Almansorem.

Jack Cade.who: Jack Cade (d. 1450), leader of the Kentish rebellion of 1450 against Henry VI's government.

Jackson.basis: An English 'Doctor' of Burton's day who wrote on unbelief; Jackson is the obvious candidate.
Jackson.who: Thomas Jackson (1579–1640), Oxford divine, later President of Corpus Christi College, who wrote at length against atheism and unbelief.

Jacobins.who: The Jacobites: Syrian Monophysite Christians, named after Jacob Baradaeus (6th century).

Jacobus Boissardus.who: Jean-Jacques Boissard (1528–1602), French antiquary and Latin poet of Besançon, who wrote on divination, magic and spirits.

Jacobus Ferrandus.who: Jacques Ferrand (c.1575–after 1623), French physician of Agen, author of a treatise on love-melancholy (1610; enlarged 1623).

Jacobus Grevinus.who: Jacques Grévin (1538–1570), French physician and poet, author of a treatise on poisons that attacked the medical use of antimony.

Jacobus Micyllus.who: Jacob Micyllus (1503–1558), German humanist and Latin poet, who translated Lucian.

Jacobus Sprenger.who: Jacob Sprenger (c.1436–1495), German Dominican inquisitor, named as co-author of the witch-hunters' manual *Malleus Maleficarum* (1487).

Jacobus de Dondis.who: Jacopo de' Dondi (1298–1359), physician of Padua, known as 'the Aggregator' from his compilation of remedies.

Jacobus de Voragine.who: Jacobus de Voragine (c.1230–1298), Dominican archbishop of Genoa, compiler of the *Golden Legend* of saints' lives.

Jagello.who: Jogaila (d. 1434), Grand Duke of Lithuania, who was baptised as Władysław and married Queen Jadwiga of Poland in 1386, becoming King of Poland.

Jakarta.who: Jakarta (Burton's 'Jacatra'), a port on Java, later the Dutch Batavia and now the capital of Indonesia.

Jakeh.who: Jakeh, father of Agur, to whom Proverbs 30 is attributed.

Jambres.who: Jambres, one of the two Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses, named in 2 Timothy 3:8 and in Jewish tradition.

James Dubravius.who: Jan Dubravius (Jan Skála z Doubravky, c.1486–1553), bishop of Olomouc in Moravia, author of a Latin treatise on fishponds, *De piscinis*.

James Lernutius.who: Janus Lernutius (Jan Lernout, 1545–1619), Flemish neo-Latin poet of Bruges, author of the *Ocelli* ('Little eyes') poems.

James Rossa.basis: The office, the royal kinship, the death at Florence and the story of chastity match; the form 'Rossa' and the date are garbled.
James Rossa.who: Jaime of Portugal (1433–1459), the 'Cardinal of Portugal', archbishop of Lisbon, nephew of King Duarte, who died at Florence and was famed for his chastity.

James Sempill.who: Sir James Sempill (1566–1625), Scottish courtier and writer, author of *Sacrilege Sacredly Handled* (1619), a defence of tithes.

James Whitehall.who: James Whitehall, Burton's friend from Christ Church, Oxford, and rector of Checkley in Staffordshire.

Janissaries.who: The Janissaries, the Ottoman sultan's standing infantry, here meaning armed guards hired to escort caravans.

Jannes.who: Jannes, one of the two Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses, named in 2 Timothy 3:8 and in Jewish tradition.

Jansenius.who: Cornelius Jansen the elder (1510–1576), first bishop of Ghent, biblical commentator who wrote on Ecclesiasticus. He is not the Jansen of Jansenism.

Jansonius Caesius.who: Willem Janszoon Blaeu (1571–1638), Dutch cartographer and maker of globes, who signed in Latin as Guilielmus Janssonius Caesius and wrote on the use of globes.

January.who: January, the old knight married to young May in Chaucer's Merchant's Tale. In the third passage 'January' is simply the month.

Janus Cornarius.who: Janus Cornarius (Johann Haynpol, c.1500–1558), German physician and humanist, translator of Hippocrates and Galen.

Jason.who: Jason, leader of the Argonauts and lover of Medea. In the third passage the name is the physician Jason Pratensis.

Jasonem Pratensem.who: Jason Pratensis (Jason van de Velde, 1486–1558), physician of Zeeland, author of *De cerebri morbis* (1549), on diseases of the brain.

Jasper Belga.basis: 'Belga' marks a Low Countries Jesuit named Gaspar in the Jesuit mission letters; Barzaeus is the best-known one.
Jasper Belga.who: Gaspar Barzaeus (Gaspard Berse, 1515–1553), Jesuit missionary from Zeeland who worked at Ormuz and Goa.

Jaucis.basis: A mythical mother of Branchus by Apollo; I cannot confirm the source or the correct form of her name.

Java.who: Java, island of present-day Indonesia, where the English had a trading factory at Bantam.

Jaxares.who: The Jaxartes, now the Syr Darya, a Central Asian river that flows into the Aral Sea, though ancient writers thought it fed the Caspian.

Jealousies.who: Not a name: the passion of jealousy.

Jealousy.who: Not a name: the passion of jealousy, and a section heading.

Jeremy.who: The prophet Jeremiah and the biblical book named after him.

Jerome Osorius.who: Jerónimo Osório (1506–1580), Portuguese humanist and bishop of Silves, author of a Latin history of King Manuel I's reign.

Jesuit.who: A member of the Society of Jesus. 'T. W. Jesuit' is Thomas Wright, author of *The Passions of the Mind*.

Jesuits.who: The Jesuits, members of the Society of Jesus founded by Ignatius Loyola in 1540.

Jew.who: A Jew. In the third passage it is the legendary Wandering Jew, condemned to roam until the Second Coming.

Jewish.who: The Jews, here their religious traditions and legends.

Jewry.who: Judaea, the land of the Jews in Palestine.

Jews’ Talmud.who: The Talmud, the body of rabbinic law and commentary of Judaism.

Jezebels.who: Jezebel, wife of King Ahab of Israel, who painted her face (2 Kings 9); used here for painted, shameless women.

Jo. Aubanus.who: Johann Boemus Aubanus (c.1485–1535), German Hebraist and author of *Omnium gentium mores* (1520), an early survey of the customs of the world's peoples.

Jo. Dubliulius.basis: He is listed with other authors of pilgrimage accounts; I recall such a printed account under this name, but I am not sure of the details.
Jo. Dubliulius.who: Johannes Dubliulius, sixteenth-century German pilgrim who wrote an account of a journey to Jerusalem.

Jo. Gorraeus.who: Jean de Gorris (Gorraeus) (1505–1577), Paris physician and author of the *Definitionum medicarum libri XXIV* (1564).

Jo. Voschius.basis: The citation is to a work on plague, and I recall a physician of this name, but I am not sure of his details.
Jo. Voschius.who: Johannes Voschius, late sixteenth-century Low Countries physician and author of a treatise on the plague (*De peste*).

Joachimus Camerarius.who: Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), Nuremberg physician and botanist, author of the *Symbolorum et emblematum centuriae*.

Joan.who: Joanna I, Queen of Naples (1326–1382), notorious for her marriages and suspected of complicity in the murder of her first husband, Andrew of Hungary.

Joanna.who: Joanna ('the Mad') of Castile (1479–1555), wife of Philip the Handsome and mother of the Emperors Charles V and Ferdinand I; known for her jealousy.

Jocasta.who: Jocasta, mother and wife of Oedipus and mother of Polynices, in Euripides' *Phoenician Women*.

Jocundo.who: Giocondo, a character in a tale in canto 28 of Ariosto's *Orlando Furioso* who discovers his wife's unfaithfulness.

Jod. à Meggen.who: Jost von Meggen (Jodocus a Meggen) (1509–1559), Swiss of Lucerne who wrote an account of his 1542 pilgrimage to Jerusalem (*Peregrinatio Hierosolymitana*).

Jodocus Damhoderius.who: Joos de Damhouder (1507–1581), Flemish jurist of Bruges, author of the *Praxis rerum criminalium*.

Jodocus Lorichius.who: Jodocus Lorichius (1540–1612), Catholic theologian at Freiburg, author of a *Thesaurus* of theology.

Jodocus Sincerus.who: 'Jodocus Sincerus', pen name of Justus Zinzerling, German author of the travel guide *Itinerarium Galliae* (1616).

Jodocus Sincerus Itinerario Galliae.who: 'Jodocus Sincerus', pen name of Justus Zinzerling, whose *Itinerarium Galliae* (1616) is a travel guide to France.

Jodocus à Meggen.who: Jost von Meggen (1509–1559), Swiss of Lucerne, author of an account of his pilgrimage to Jerusalem by way of Cyprus.

Joh. Major.who: John Major or Mair (1467–1550), Scottish scholastic who taught at Paris, author of a *History of Greater Britain* (1521).

Joh. Valent. Andreas.who: Johann Valentin Andreae (1586–1654), Lutheran theologian of Württemberg, author of the utopia *Christianopolis* (1619).

Joh. de Indagine.who: Johannes ab Indagine (Johann Rosenbach, d. 1537), German priest and author of a popular work on palmistry and astrology.

Johannes Hasfurtus.basis: 'Hasfurtus' fits Virdung's toponym, and the passage is about astrology in medicine.
Johannes Hasfurtus.who: Johannes Virdung of Hassfurt (1463–c.1538), German astrologer and physician.

Johannes Lansbergius.basis: In 1633 the son published a defence of his father against Fromondus; Burton's 'Johannes' may be a mistake.
Johannes Lansbergius.who: Probably Jacob van Lansberge, son of the Copernican astronomer Philips van Lansberge, who defended his father against Fromondus in 1633.

Johannes Montanus Strigoniensis.basis: The name and the Paracelsian context fit; I am not sure of the details.
Johannes Montanus Strigoniensis.who: Johannes Montanus of Esztergom (Strigonium), late sixteenth-century Hungarian Paracelsian physician who promoted the writings of Paracelsus.

Johannes Stuckius.who: Johann Wilhelm Stucki (1542–1607), Zurich theologian, author of *Antiquitatum convivialium libri III* (1582), on ancient feasting.

Johannes de Monteforti.who: John of Montfort (d. 1345), claimant to the duchy of Brittany in the War of the Breton Succession.

Johannes de la Casa.who: Giovanni della Casa (1503–1556), Archbishop of Benevento and author of the *Galateo*; he was accused of praising sodomy in an early comic poem.

John Bancroft.who: John Bancroft (1574–1641), Burton's tutor at Christ Church and Bishop of Oxford from 1632; he built the bishop's palace at Cuddesdon.

John Baptist.basis: The second passage names a different man, a Neapolitan patient in Valleriola's observations.
John Baptist.who: John the Baptist, the prophet beheaded by Herod Antipas (first and third passages).

John Baptista Alfaqui.basis: He was a converted alfaquí who wrote a confutation of the Qur'an; Burton's 'Mauretanian' and 'Baptista' do not fit exactly.
John Baptista Alfaqui.who: Juan Andrés, a former Muslim alfaquí of Xàtiva who converted to Christianity and wrote *Confusión de la secta mahomática* (1515) against the Qur'an.

John Beheim.who: Hans Böhm, the 'Drummer of Niklashausen' (d. 1476), a herdsman and popular preacher in Franconia, burned as a heretic.

John Foxe.who: John Foxe (1516/17–1587), English martyrologist, author of the *Acts and Monuments* ('Book of Martyrs').

John Galeatius.who: Gian Galeazzo Visconti (1351–1402), later Duke of Milan, who married Isabella of Valois, daughter of King John II of France.

John Huniades.who: John Hunyadi (c.1406–1456), Hungarian general and regent, of modest birth, famous for his wars against the Turks.

John Lerius.who: Jean de Léry (1536–1613), Burgundian Huguenot minister, author of *Histoire d'un voyage fait en la terre du Brésil* (1578).

John Major.basis: The cited 'life of John the Monk' (John of Lycopolis) fits that collection of exempla, not the Scottish historian.
John Major.who: Johannes Major (1564–1608), Jesuit compiler of the *Magnum speculum exemplorum*, a collection of edifying stories including lives of the desert fathers.

John Medices.who: Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici (1360–1429), Florentine banker, father of Cosimo and Lorenzo de' Medici.

John Pena.who: Jean Pena (1528–1558), French mathematician whose preface to his edition of Euclid's *Optics* and *Catoptrics* (1557) denied the sphere of fire.

John Reppington.basis: The Repington family of Amington fits Burton's list of Warwickshire neighbours; the details of this John are not certain.
John Reppington.who: Sir John Repington (Rippington), knight of a Warwickshire gentry family associated with Amington near Tamworth.

John Secundus.who: Janus Secundus (Jan Nicolaes Everaerts, 1511–1536), Dutch neo-Latin poet, best known for his Basia (Kisses).

John White.who: John White, London bookseller for whom William Burton's Description of Leicestershire was printed in 1622.

John Williams.who: John Williams (1582–1650), bishop of Lincoln and Lord Keeper, later archbishop of York; he paid for the library of St John's College, Cambridge.

John de Indagine.who: Johannes ab Indagine (Johann von Hagen, c. 1467–1537), German priest, author of the Introductiones apotelesmaticae on chiromancy, physiognomy and astrology.

Johnson.basis: Listed among medical authorities for remedies; Jonstonus is the likeliest physician behind the anglicised 'Johnson'.
Johnson.who: Jan Jonston (Joannes Jonstonus, 1603–1675), Polish-Scottish physician and naturalist, author of a compendium of practical medicine.

Jonathan.who: Jonathan, son of King Saul and devoted friend of David (1 Samuel).

Jones.who: John Jones (fl. 1562–1579), English physician who wrote on the baths of Bath and of Buxton.

Jonuses Bassa.basis: Burton's marginal note cites Knolles, and 'Ionuses Bassa' is Knolles's form of the name.
Jonuses Bassa.who: Yunus Pasha, Ottoman pasha whose jealous killing of his wife Manto is told in Richard Knolles's Generall Historie of the Turkes (1603).

Joppa.who: Joppa, the ancient port on the coast of Palestine, now Jaffa (part of Tel Aviv), where pilgrims landed for Jerusalem.

Jordan.who: The River Jordan, flowing from the Lebanon region south through the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea.

Jordanus Brunus.who: Giordano Bruno (1548–1600), Italian philosopher and cosmologist, burned in Rome for heresy.

Jos. Scaliger.who: Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), French classical scholar, author of the Ausonianae lectiones on the poet Ausonius.

Joseph.who: Joseph, son of Jacob, sold into Egypt, imprisoned, and later made ruler over Pharaoh's house (Genesis 37–50).

Josephus Blancanus.who: Giuseppe Biancani (Josephus Blancanus, 1566–1624), Italian Jesuit mathematician, author of Aristotelis loca mathematica (1615).

Josephus Struthius.who: Józef Struś (Josephus Struthius, 1510–1568), Polish physician, author of Sphygmicae artis libri V on the pulse.

Josiah.who: Josiah, king of Judah (r. c. 640–609 BC), famed for restoring the true worship and reforming religion (2 Kings 22–23).

Joubertus.who: Laurent Joubert (1529–1583), French physician of Montpellier, author of the Paradoxa and a treatise on quartan fever.

Jove.who: Jove, that is Jupiter, king of the Roman gods.

Jovial.who: Adjective meaning 'of the planet Jupiter', here a class of spirits.

Jovianus Pont.who: Giovanni Pontano (Jovianus Pontanus, 1426–1503), Neapolitan humanist, statesman and Latin poet.

Jovianus Pontanus.who: Giovanni Pontano (1426–1503), Neapolitan humanist and statesman, author of the dialogue Antonius, De bello Neapolitano and De rebus coelestibus.

Jovinianus.who: Jovian (Flavius Jovianus), Roman emperor 363–364, a Christian who succeeded Julian the Apostate.

Jovius Musc.who: Paolo Giovio (Paulus Jovius, 1483–1552), Italian historian and bishop of Nocera; the reference is to the Elogia of learned men displayed in his Museum.

Joyeux.who: Henri de Joyeuse (1563–1608), Duke of Joyeuse, French courtier and soldier who became a Capuchin friar as Father Ange.

Judah.who: In the first passage, the southern Hebrew kingdom of Judah; in the second, Judah, son of Jacob, who lay with Tamar (Genesis 38).

Judas.who: Judas Iscariot, the apostle who betrayed Christ and then hanged himself.

Judas Maccabeus.who: Judas Maccabeus (d. c. 160 BC), Jewish leader of the revolt against the Seleucid kings (1 Maccabees).

Judgement.who: A faculty of the understanding, not a name.

Judith’s Pantofles.who: Judith, heroine of the apocryphal Book of Judith, whose sandals ravished Holofernes' eyes before she beheaded him (Judith 16:9).

Jugurtha.who: Jugurtha (c. 160–104 BC), king of Numidia who fought Rome; Sallust wrote his war; he died in prison after Marius's triumph.

Jul. Caesar la Galla.who: Giulio Cesare Lagalla (1571–1624), Italian philosopher at Rome, author of De phaenomenis in orbe lunae (1612), answering Galileo.

Julia.who: Julia, the beloved addressed in a short Latin poem attributed to Petronius.

Julia Augusta.who: Julia Domna (d. 217), wife of Emperor Septimius Severus; Cassius Dio records her exchange with the Caledonian woman.

Julian.who: Julian the Apostate (331/2–363), Roman emperor 361–363, who renounced Christianity for paganism.

Julianus.who: Julian the Apostate (331/2–363), Roman emperor 361–363, pagan restorer and friend of the philosopher Maximus of Ephesus.

Julianus Apostata.who: Julian the Apostate (331/2–363), Roman emperor 361–363, who renounced Christianity and was devoted to pagan rites and divination.

Juliet.who: Juliet, the tragic heroine of the story of Romeo and Juliet, best known from Shakespeare's play.

Julius Alexandrinus.who: Giulio Alessandrini (1506–1590), physician of Trent, physician to the Habsburg emperors and author of medical consilia.

Julius Caesar.who: Gaius Julius Caesar (100–44 BC), Roman general and dictator, reformer of the calendar and author of the Commentaries.

Julius Caesar Claudinus.who: Giulio Cesare Claudini (d. 1618), physician and professor at Bologna, author of medical Responsiones et consultationes.

Julius Caesar La Galla.who: Giulio Cesare Lagalla (d. 1624), professor of philosophy at Rome, author of a treatise on the immortality of the soul.

Julius Caesar Scaliger.who: Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), Italian-born humanist and physician in France, who attacked Cardano's De subtilitate in his Exotericae exercitationes.

Julius Pollux.who: Julius Pollux (2nd century AD), Greek grammarian and rhetorician of Naucratis, compiler of the Onomasticon, a thesaurus of Attic words.

Julius Proculus.who: Julius Proculus, legendary Roman who claimed that the dead Romulus appeared to him as a god, as told by Livy.

Julius Scaliger.who: Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), Italian-born humanist, physician and critic in France, author of the Poetices libri septem; married a very young wife late in life.

Junctine.who: Francesco Giuntini (Junctinus) (1523–1590), Florentine astrologer, author of the Speculum astrologiae.

Juniors.who: Ordinary word: the moderns, recent writers.

Junius.basis: political, academic and biblical contexts point to different Junii (e.g. Franciscus Junius in the biblical one)

Junius Brutus.basis: suicide context fits Marcus, not Lucius Junius Brutus
Junius Brutus.who: Marcus Junius Brutus (85–42 BC), Caesar's assassin, who killed himself after defeat at Philippi.

Juno.who: Juno, Roman queen of the gods and wife of Jupiter (Greek Hera), hostile to Troy.

Jupiter.who: Jupiter, chief Roman god (Greek Zeus); in the first passage the planet Jupiter in Burton's horoscope.

Jupiter Ammon.who: Zeus Ammon, the ram-horned Egyptian god Amun identified with Jupiter, whose famous oracle stood at the Siwa oasis in the Libyan desert.

Jupiter Belus.who: Bel (Marduk), chief god of Babylon, identified by Herodotus with Zeus; his great temple stood in Babylon.

Jupiter Menecrates.who: Menecrates of Syracuse (4th century BC), physician who called himself Zeus and claimed divine cures.

Jupiter Tragoedus.who: Zeus Tragoedus ('Zeus the Tragedian'), satirical dialogue by Lucian in which Zeus is at a loss for words before the assembled gods.

Jupiters.who: Jupiter, chief Roman god, of whom Varro reckoned many local forms.

Justa.basis: Galen's anecdote; Burton has garbled the names of husband and wife
Justa.who: The Roman lady in Galen's On Prognosis, wife of one Justus, whom Galen found lovesick for the dancer Pylades by her pulse.

Justin.who: Marcus Junianus Justinus (fl. 2nd–3rd century AD?), Roman historian who epitomised the Philippic Histories of Pompeius Trogus.

Justin Martyr.who: Justin Martyr (c. 100–c. 165), Christian apologist, who reported a Roman statue he took to be dedicated to Simon Magus.

Justinians.who: Justinian I (r. 527–565), Byzantine emperor under whom Roman law was codified; used here for lawyers generally.

Justus Baronius.basis: the name form matches; the quoted work is not certain
Justus Baronius.who: Justus Baronius (Justus Calvinus), German convert from Calvinism to Catholicism and controversial writer of the early seventeenth century.

Juv.who: Juvenal (Decimus Junius Juvenalis, fl. early 2nd century AD), Roman satirist.

Juvenalis Sat.who: The Satires of Juvenal (early 2nd century AD); the line on Thessalian love potions is from Satire 6.

Juvenal’s Iberina.who: Hiberina, the lustful wife in Juvenal's Satire 6, who would sooner be content with one eye than with one man.

Kate.who: A generic woman's name in Burton's alliterative list, not any particular person.

Katharine Cobham.who: Eleanor Cobham (c. 1400–1452), wife of Humphrey Duke of Gloucester, convicted of witchcraft in 1441; Burton calls her Katharine.

Kemnisius.who: Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), Lutheran theologian, author of the anti-Catholic Examen Concilii Tridentini.

Kemnitius.who: Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), Lutheran theologian, author of the Examen Concilii Tridentini, which attacks clerical celibacy.

Kennethus.who: Kenneth II (d. 995), King of Scots, said by Buchanan to have had Malcolm son of King Duff murdered so that his own son could succeed.

Ketellus.basis: the book and chapter reference matches William of Newburgh's story of Ketell
Ketellus.who: Ketell, a pious Englishman who could see demons, according to William of Newburgh's Historia rerum Anglicarum.

Kett.who: Robert Kett (d. 1549), leader of the Norfolk rebellion of 1549, hanged at Norwich.

Knipperdoling.who: Bernhard Knipperdolling (c.1495–1536), Anabaptist leader at Münster, executed with Jan of Leiden after the city fell.

Korah.who: Korah, the Levite who led a revolt against Moses and Aaron and was swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16).

Kornmannus.who: Heinrich Kornmann, German jurist of the early seventeenth century, author of De miraculis mortuorum, De linea amoris and De virginum statu.

Krechting.who: Bernhard Krechting (d. 1536), Anabaptist leader at Münster, executed with Jan of Leiden and Knipperdolling.

Krems.who: Krems, a town on the Danube in Lower Austria.

Kurds.who: The Kurds, a mountain people of the Middle East; Burton's 'devil-worshippers' are probably the Yazidis, who are Kurdish-speaking.

Labden.basis: a district in Aquitaine cited from Bodin; perhaps Labourd, but not certain

Labedum.who: Lebedus, a Greek city on the Ionian coast of Asia Minor, seat of the guild of Dionysiac performers in Hellenistic times.

Labeo.who: Marcus Antistius Labeo (d. c. AD 10), Augustan Roman jurist; Gellius (4.2) quotes his definition of disease.

Lacedaemon.who: Lacedaemon, that is, Sparta, the chief city of Laconia in the Peloponnese.

Lacedaemonians.who: The Lacedaemonians, that is, the Spartans.

Lacinius.who: Lacinius, a mythical brigand near Croton whom Hercules killed; the Lacinian promontory was named after him.

Laconia.who: Laconia, the region of the south-eastern Peloponnese ruled from Sparta.

Laconian.who: Laconian means Spartan; the boy who chose death over slavery is told by Seneca (Epistles 77).

Laconic.who: Laconic means Spartan in style: terse and brief.

Ladislaus.who: Three kings: Władysław III of Hungary and Poland (killed at Varna, 1444); Ladislaus Posthumus of Bohemia and Hungary (1440–1457); Ladislaus of Naples (1377–1414).

Lady.who: An ordinary word here: a woman of rank.

Laelii.who: Men like Gaius Laelius 'Sapiens', friend of Scipio Aemilianus, used by Cicero as a type of the wise and noble Roman.

Laelius.who: Gaius Laelius 'Sapiens' (consul 140 BC), friend of Scipio Aemilianus and patron of Terence, a speaker in Cicero's De amicitia.

Laelius Eugubinus.who: Lelio della Fonte (Laelius a Fonte Eugubinus), Italian physician of Gubbio, fl. late sixteenth century, whose medical Consultationes were published.

Laelius à Fonte Eugubinus.who: Lelio della Fonte (Laelius a Fonte Eugubinus), Italian physician of Gubbio, fl. late sixteenth century, whose medical Consultationes were published.

Lagus.who: Lagus, a son of Ptolemy I Soter of Egypt by the Athenian courtesan Thais.

Lais.who: Lais of Corinth, the celebrated Greek courtesan of the late fifth and fourth centuries BC.

Lalage.who: Lalage, the girl Horace's speaker loves in Odes 1.22 ('Integer vitae').

Lampido.who: Lampido of Sparta, daughter of King Leotychidas, wife of Archidamus II and mother of Agis II.

Lamprias.who: Lamprias, a character in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans (no. 3), Diphilus's rival in the courtesans' quarrel.

Lamprid.who: Aelius Lampridius, one of the supposed authors of the Historia Augusta, credited with its Life of Elagabalus.

Lampsacus.who: Lampsacus, a Greek city on the Hellespont famous for Priapus-worship and wine; it is modern Lapseki in Turkey.

Lancaster.who: The House of Lancaster, the royal line that fought the House of York in the Wars of the Roses.

Lancelot.who: Sir Lancelot, knight of the Round Table in Arthurian romance.

Lancelots.who: Men like Sir Lancelot, the Arthurian knight; a type of the chivalrous lover.

Landgrave.who: Landgrave is a German princely title; in the first passage it means William IV of Hesse-Kassel (1532–1592), who employed the astronomer Christoph Rothmann.

Lanes.basis: Spanish 'llanos' (plains) is named alongside the sierras and Andes in Acosta and Herrera
Lanes.who: The llanos, the great tropical grassland plains of northern South America.

Langium.who: Johann Lange (1485–1565), German physician, author of the Medicinalium epistolarum miscellanea.

Langius.who: Johann Lange (1485–1565), German physician, author of the Medicinalium epistolarum miscellanea.

Languedoc.who: Languedoc, a province of southern France with Montpellier and Toulouse among its cities.

Lanhadron.basis: Carew's Survey of Cornwall is cited, and I recall the estate's location but am not fully certain
Lanhadron.who: Lanhadron, an estate in the parish of St Ewe, near Mevagissey in south Cornwall.

Lansbergius.who: Philips van Lansberge (1561–1632), Flemish-Dutch astronomer who defended Copernicus in Commentationes in motum terrae (Middelburg, 1630).

Lansius.who: Thomas Lansius (1577–1657), German jurist at Tübingen, author of the Consultatio de principatu inter provincias Europae and published orations.

Laodamia.who: Laodamia, in Greek legend the wife of Protesilaus, the first Greek killed at Troy; she so mourned him that she kept his image and died with him.

Laodice.basis: She is the best-known Laodice called Mithridates' sister who was accused of poisoning; Burton's reference is confused.
Laodice.who: Laodice, sister and wife of Mithridates VI Eupator of Pontus, who took lovers while he was away and tried to poison him.

Laodiceans.who: The Christians of Laodicea in Asia Minor, rebuked in Revelation 3:14–16 for being 'lukewarm, neither cold nor hot'.

Lapis Armenus.basis: 'Armenian stone', a mineral remedy (an index entry)

Lapithae.who: The Lapiths, a legendary Thessalian people whose wedding feast for Pirithous ended in a drunken brawl with the Centaurs.

Lapland.who: Lapland, the far north of Scandinavia and Finland, home of the Sami.

Larissean Coronis.who: Coronis of Larissa in Thessaly, a mythical beauty loved by Apollo and mother of Asclepius.

Lateran.who: The Lateran in Rome, site of the basilica of St John Lateran, the pope's cathedral, and of the Lateran councils; canon 22 of the Fourth Council (1215) concerns physicians.

Latin.basis: The Latin language or Latin writers in general

Latin Epigrammatists.basis: A general term for Latin writers of epigrams

Latins.who: The Latin (Western) writers, especially physicians, as distinct from the Greeks and Arabs.

Latmos.who: Mount Latmus in Caria, near Miletus in western Turkey (modern Beşparmak Dağları), where the Moon was said to visit the sleeping Endymion.

Latona.who: Latona (Greek Leto), mother of Apollo and Diana by Jupiter; the giant Tityus was punished in Hades for trying to rape her.

Laudanum Paracelsi.basis: A preparation of opium named after Paracelsus

Laufenberg.who: Laufenburg, a town on the Upper Rhine on the Swiss–German border, once known for its dangerous rapids.

Laura.who: Laura, the woman Petrarch celebrated in his poems, traditionally identified with Laura de Noves (d. 1348).

Laurel.basis: The plant, used as a purge

Laurence.basis: The first is the son of Giovanni de' Medici, brother of Cosimo; the second is a proverbial English figure, not a historical person.
Laurence.who: In the first passage, Lorenzo de' Medici the elder (1395–1440), son of Giovanni di Bicci; in the second, 'lusty Laurence', a proverbial lecher.

Laurence Medices.who: Lorenzo de' Medici, 'the Magnificent' (1449–1492), ruler of Florence and patron of the arts.

Laurentium.basis: He appears in a list of medical writers on cures for love, and he wrote on love-melancholy.
Laurentium.who: André du Laurens (Laurentius, 1558–1609), French royal physician whose treatise on melancholy includes a section on love-melancholy.

Laurentius Pignorius.who: Lorenzo Pignoria (1571–1631), Paduan antiquary who wrote a commentary on the Egyptian Mensa Isiaca (Bembine Table).

Lauretan.who: The Laurentine villa of Pliny the Younger, near ancient Laurentum on the Latin coast south of Ostia.

Lauretta.who: Loreto, in the Marche in Italy, a pilgrimage shrine of the Virgin built around the Holy House of Nazareth.

Lauretum.who: Loreto, in the Marche in Italy, a rich pilgrimage shrine around the Holy House of the Virgin.

Lavinia.who: Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus in Virgil's Aeneid, who became Aeneas' wife in Italy.

Lazarus.who: Lazarus, the beggar at the rich man's gate in Christ's parable (Luke 16:19–31).

Lazius.who: Wolfgang Lazius (1514–1565), Viennese physician, historian and mapmaker to Ferdinand I.

Le Maire.who: Jacob Le Maire (c. 1585–1616), Dutch navigator who sailed with Willem Schouten (1615–16) and found the Le Maire Strait and the route round Cape Horn.

Lea.who: The River Lea, flowing from Hertfordshire past Ware into the Thames east of London; it was made navigable for barges.

Leah.who: Leah, Jacob's first wife and the mother of Dinah (Genesis 29–30, 34).

Leander.who: Leander of Abydos, the legendary lover of Hero who swam the Hellespont to her nightly and drowned; told by Musaeus.

Leander Albertus.who: Leandro Alberti (1479–1552), Bolognese Dominican, author of the *Descrittione di tutta Italia* (1550).

Lebadea.who: Lebadea in Boeotia (modern Livadeia, Greece), site of the oracle of Trophonius and the spring Hercyna.

Lechaeum.who: Lechaeum, the ancient western harbour of Corinth on the Gulf of Corinth; Cenchreae was its eastern port.

Leda.who: Leda, the Spartan queen whom Jupiter seduced in the form of a swan; mother of Helen and the Dioscuri.

Leicestershire.who: Leicestershire, the English Midland county where Burton was born at Lindley and held the living of Seagrave.
