Leiden.who: Leiden, university city in the province of Holland, in the Netherlands.

Leipzig.who: Leipzig, trading and university city in Saxony, eastern Germany.

Leland.who: John Leland (c. 1503–1552), English antiquary and topographer, and author of the Latin poem *Cygnea cantio* about the Thames.

Lemmer.who: Lemmings, the small Scandinavian rodents believed to fall from the sky with the rain.

Lemnian.who: Lake Geneva (Latin Lacus Lemannus), which St Bernard is said to have ridden beside all day without noticing it.

Lemnos.who: Lemnos, an island in the northern Aegean where, in myth, Vulcan (Hephaestus) landed when he was thrown from heaven.

Lemures.who: The Lemures, restless and malevolent spirits of the dead in Roman religion, appeased at the festival of the Lemuria.

Leo.basis: the two passages clearly mean different things
Leo.who: In the first passage, Leo Africanus (c. 1494–c. 1554), author of a *Description of Africa*; in the second, the zodiac sign Leo.

Leo Decimus.who: Pope Leo X (Giovanni de' Medici, 1475–1521), the worldly Renaissance pope whose life Paolo Giovio wrote.

Leo Suavius.who: Leo Suavius, pseudonym of Jacques Gohory (1520–1576), French humanist and Paracelsian who wrote commentaries on Paracelsus.

Leochaeus Anacreon.basis: Leochaeus is the Latin name John Leech used, and he wrote Latin erotic verse; the poem title is assumed
Leochaeus Anacreon.who: John Leech (Joannes Leochaeus), early 17th-century Scottish Neo-Latin poet, quoted from a set of Anacreontic love poems.

Leochaeus Panthea.basis: Leochaeus is the Latin name John Leech used, and he wrote Latin erotic verse
Leochaeus Panthea.who: John Leech (Joannes Leochaeus), early 17th-century Scottish Neo-Latin poet, quoted from a love poem titled 'Panthea'.

Leolin.basis: a Welsh prince in Walter Map's legendary anecdote; which historical Llywelyn is meant is uncertain

Leon.who: Leone Ebreo (Judah Abravanel, c. 1465–c. 1523), Jewish Neoplatonist philosopher and author of the *Dialoghi d'amore*.

Leonardus Fuchsius.who: Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), German Protestant physician and botanist, professor at Tübingen.

Leonartus Jacchinus.who: Leonardo Giachini (d. 1584), Italian physician who taught at Pisa and wrote a commentary on the ninth book of Rhazes' *Ad Almansorem*.

Leonicus.who: Niccolò Leonico Tomeo (1456–1531), Venetian humanist of Padua and author of the miscellany *De varia historia*.

Leonides.basis: the couplet is a Greek Anthology epigram; which Leonidas is meant is unclear
Leonides.who: Leonidas, a Greek epigrammatist whose poems are in the Greek Anthology (either Leonidas of Tarentum or Leonidas of Alexandria).

Leontia.who: Leontion, a hetaira and Epicurean philosopher who was a companion of Epicurus in his Garden at Athens.

Leontiscus.who: Leontiscus, son of Ptolemy I Soter of Egypt by the Athenian courtesan Thais.

Leontius.who: Leontius, 5th-century Athenian sophist and father of Athenais, who became the Empress Eudocia when she married Theodosius II.

Leotichides.who: Leotychides, son of Timaea, wife of the Spartan king Agis II; rumoured to be Alcibiades' son, he was passed over for the throne in favour of Agesilaus.

Lepanto.who: Lepanto, the Italian name of ancient Naupactus, modern Nafpaktos, on the Gulf of Corinth in Greece.

Lepidus.basis: Pliny, *Natural History* book 7, speaks of the Lepidus family rather than of a single person
Lepidus.who: A member of the Roman family of the Aemilii Lepidi, in which Pliny records an eye defect passed down through the generations.

Lerius.who: Jean de Léry (1536–1613), French Protestant pastor who wrote an account of his voyage to Brazil (1578).

Lesbia.who: Lesbia, the mistress Catullus addresses in his poems, usually identified with Clodia.

Lesbian Sappho.who: Sappho of Lesbos (fl. c. 600 BC), Greek lyric poet who, by legend, leapt from the Leucadian rock for love of Phaon.

Lesbos.who: Lesbos, a large Greek island in the eastern Aegean whose chief city is Mytilene.

Lessius.who: Leonardus Lessius (1554–1623), Flemish Jesuit theologian and author of the dietary treatise *Hygiasticon* (1613).

Lethargy.who: Lethargy, the disease of morbid drowsiness.

Lethe.who: Lethe, the river of forgetfulness in the classical underworld.

Leucadia.who: Leucas (Leucadia), the Ionian island now called Lefkada, off western Greece.

Leucadians.who: The inhabitants of Leucas (modern Lefkada), an Ionian island off western Greece.

Leucata Petra.who: Cape Leucatas, the white cliff at the southern tip of Lefkada (Santa Maura) from which lovers leapt, Sappho among them by legend.

Leucippe.who: Leucippe, the heroine of Achilles Tatius' Greek romance *Leucippe and Clitophon*.

Leucippus.who: Leucippus (5th c. BC), Greek philosopher, founder of atomism and teacher of Democritus.

Leucophrye.who: Leucophrye, legendary daughter of Mandrolytus who, in Parthenius's Erotica, betrayed her city of Magnesia to her lover Leucippus.

Leucothoe.who: First passage: Leucothoe, daughter of Orchamus, loved by Apollo in Ovid's Metamorphoses 4; second: Leucothoe, the sea-goddess (Ino deified), loved by Triton in Calcagnini's dialogue.

Leuctrian.who: Leuctra in Boeotia, where Epaminondas and the Thebans defeated the Spartans in 371 BC.

Levant.who: The Levant, the eastern Mediterranean and its coasts.

Levi.who: Levi, third son of Jacob, who with Simeon massacred the Shechemites (Genesis 34).

Leviathan.who: Leviathan, the biblical sea monster (Job 41), which Jewish legend says will be served at the messianic banquet.

Levinus Lemnius.who: Levinus Lemnius (1505–1568), Dutch physician of Zierikzee, author of De occultis naturae miraculis and De habitu et constitutione corporis.

Levinus Torrentius.who: Laevinus Torrentius (1525–1595), Flemish humanist and bishop of Antwerp, author of a commentary on Suetonius.

Lewis.who: Three kings of France: Louis IX (St Louis), who dined with Aquinas; Louis XII (d. 1515); and Louis XI (d. 1483), who imagined everything stank.

Lewis Sforza.who: Ludovico Sforza, 'il Moro' (1452–1508), Duke of Milan, whose ambitions helped bring the French invasions of Italy.

Lex Valeria.basis: Burton cites Livy on the Oppian law and Cato; Valerius proposed its repeal
Lex Valeria.who: The tribune Lucius Valerius's proposal (195 BC) to repeal the Oppian sumptuary law on women's finery, which Cato opposed (Livy 34).

Libanius.who: Libanius (314–c. 393), Greek sophist and rhetorician of Antioch, friend of Julian the Apostate, author of orations and declamations.

Libanius Sophista.who: Libanius (314–c. 393), Greek sophist and rhetorician of Antioch, who refused offices offered by the emperor.

Libanus.who: Mount Lebanon, the range in modern Lebanon where the Jordan's sources lie.

Libavius.who: Andreas Libavius (c. 1555–1616), German physician and chemist, critic of the Paracelsians, the Rosicrucians and the weapon-salve.

Liber Ariadne.who: Liber (Bacchus), who won Ariadne with a crown that was later set among the stars as the Corona Borealis.

Libertines.basis: listed among Epicures and Atheists; general sense of the term
Libertines.who: Libertines: freethinkers and loose livers, a name first given to the antinomian sect that Calvin attacked in the 16th century.

Liberty.who: Libertas, the personified Roman goddess of Liberty, who had temples in Rome.

Libra.who: Libra, the zodiac sign of the Balance.

Libya.who: Libya, the ancient name for North Africa west of Egypt, including its deserts.

Libyae.who: Libya (Latin genitive), here meaning Africa as one of the three continents, beside Asia and Europe.

Libyc.who: The Libyan Sea, the Mediterranean off the North African coast.

Licinius.who: Licinius (d. 325), Roman emperor (r. 308–324), Constantine's colleague and later rival, defeated by him in 324.

Liechtenbergius.who: Johannes Lichtenberger (d. 1503), German astrologer, author of the widely read prophetic Prognosticatio (1488).

Liege.who: Liège, a city on the Meuse in modern Belgium.

Ligorius.who: Pirro Ligorio (c. 1513–1583), Neapolitan architect, painter and antiquary, who wrote on the antiquities of Rome.

Lil. Giraldus.who: Lilio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552), Ferrarese humanist, author of De deis gentium historia, a handbook of pagan gods in syntagmata.

Lilis.who: Lilith, in Jewish legend Adam's first wife before Eve and mother of demons.

Lilius Giraldus.who: Lilio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552), Ferrarese humanist and mythographer, author of De deis gentium historia and a life of Hercules.

Limousin.who: The Limousin, a province of west-central France around Limoges.

Lincoln.who: Lincoln, the English cathedral city and seat of a bishopric.

Lincolnshire.who: Lincolnshire, the eastern English county with its Fens and Wolds.

Lindhout.basis: listed with other astrologers; name fits, details uncertain
Lindhout.who: Henricus van Lindhout, Flemish physician and astrologer of the late 16th century, author of a Speculum astrologiae.

Lindley.who: Lindley, near Higham on the Hill in Leicestershire, the Burton family seat where Robert Burton was born.

Linschoten’s Datura.who: Jan Huygen van Linschoten (1563–1611), Dutch traveller to the East Indies whose Itinerario describes datura (thorn-apple) and its stupefying effects.

Linz.who: Linz, a city on the Danube in Upper Austria.

Lionel.who: Lionel of Antwerp (1338–1368), Duke of Clarence, son of Edward III, who married Violante Visconti at Milan in 1368.

Lipari.who: Lipari, the chief of the volcanic Aeolian Islands off northern Sicily.

Lippomanus.who: Luigi Lippomano (1500–1559), Venetian-born Bishop of Verona, who compiled a large collection of saints' lives.

Lipsius’ Satire.who: Justus Lipsius's *Satyra Menippaea: Somnium* (1581), a Menippean satire set in a dream, by the Flemish humanist Justus Lipsius (1547–1606).

Literati.who: The Chinese scholar-officials, chosen for office by competitive examination.

Liternum.who: Liternum, ancient coastal town in Campania north of Cumae, where Scipio Africanus spent his retirement and died.

Lithuania.who: Lithuania, then a grand duchy joined with Poland, on the Baltic.

Little John.who: Little John, legendary companion of Robin Hood in the English outlaw ballads.

Liver.who: The liver, as an organ of the body.

Livia.who: Livia Drusilla (58 BC–AD 29), wife of the emperor Augustus.

Livonia.who: Livonia, historical Baltic region covering much of modern Latvia and Estonia.

Livy’s Horatii.who: The Horatii, three Roman brothers who fought the three Alban Curiatii in single combat for their city, as told in Livy, book 1.

Llan Avan.basis: Gerald of Wales's story of the church of St Afan in the Builth district fits Llanafan Fawr
Llan Avan.who: Llanafan Fawr, near Builth in Breconshire (now Powys), Wales, with its church of St Afan.

Lobel.who: Matthias de L'Obel (1538–1616), Flemish botanist and physician, author of herbals, later botanist to James I.

Lobelius.who: Matthias de L'Obel (1538–1616), Flemish botanist and physician, author of illustrated herbals, later botanist to James I.

Locrenses.who: The Locrians of Locri Epizephyrii in southern Italy, who defeated the much larger army of Croton at the river Sagra (6th century BC).

Lod. Guicciardine.who: Lodovico Guicciardini (1521–1589), Florentine merchant and writer in Antwerp, author of a description of the Low Countries (1567).

Lod. Mercatus.who: Luis Mercado (c.1525–1611), Spanish physician, professor at Valladolid and physician to Philip II and Philip III, writer on internal and hereditary diseases.

Lod. Vertomannus.who: Ludovico di Varthema (c.1470–1517), Italian traveller in Arabia, Persia and India, whose *Itinerario* appeared in 1510.

Lod. Vives.who: Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), Spanish humanist, author of *De causis corruptarum artium* and a commentary on Augustine's *City of God*.

Lodovicus.who: Luis Mercado (c.1525–1611), Spanish physician to Philip II and Philip III, author of *De internorum morborum curatione*.

Lodovicus Cornarus.who: Alvise (Luigi) Cornaro (c.1467–1566), Venetian nobleman whose treatise on the sober life was translated into Latin by Lessius.

Lodovicus Mercatus.who: Luis Mercado (c.1525–1611), Spanish physician to Philip II and Philip III, author of treatises on hereditary diseases and women's diseases.

Lodovicus Molina.who: Luis de Molina (1535–1600), Spanish Jesuit theologian, who wrote on the six days of creation in his commentary on Aquinas.

Lodovicus Pius.who: Louis the Pious (778–840), son of Charlemagne, Frankish king and emperor.

Lodovicus Vertomannus.who: Ludovico di Varthema (c.1470–1517), Italian traveller in Arabia, Persia and India, whose *Itinerario* appeared in 1510.

Lodovicus Vives.who: Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), Spanish humanist, author of the *Fabula de homine* and *De anima et vita*.

Lodovicus de La Cerda.basis: Spanish Jesuit of this name; the angel treatise is attributed to him
Lodovicus de La Cerda.who: Juan Luis de la Cerda (d. 1643), Spanish Jesuit, best known for his commentary on Virgil, who also wrote on guardian angels.

Lollia.who: First passage: Lollia, wife of Aulus Gabinius and one of Caesar's mistresses; second: Lollia Paulina, Claudius's prospective bride, ruined by Agrippina in AD 49.

Lomatius.who: Gian Paolo Lomazzo (1538–1592), Milanese painter and art theorist, author of the *Trattato dell'arte della pittura* (1584).

Lombards.who: First passage: Lombard moneylenders and pawnbrokers; second: the Germanic Lombards, who invaded Italy in 568, supposedly at Narses' invitation.

Lombardy.who: Lombardy, region of northern Italy around Milan.

London. Helena.basis: form wrongly joins 'London' with Helena; the name meant is Helena
London. Helena.who: St Helena (c.250–c.330), mother of Constantine the Great, who built churches in the Holy Land.

Longinus.who: Cassius Longinus (c.213–273), Greek Platonist philosopher and rhetorician, called a 'living library' by Eunapius.

Longus Sophista.who: Longus (probably 2nd–3rd century AD), Greek sophist and author of the pastoral romance *Daphnis and Chloe*.

Longus Sophista’s Daphnis.who: *Daphnis and Chloe*, the Greek pastoral romance by Longus (probably 2nd–3rd century AD).

Lonicerus.basis: several Lonicers wrote on medicine; it is unclear which one wrote on apoplexy

Lop.who: The desert of Lop, around Lop Nur in the Tarim Basin (Xinjiang, China), described by Marco Polo as haunted by spirits.

Lorarios.who: Latin *lorarii*: Roman officers or slaves who bound and flogged offenders with thongs.

Lorchan.basis: Cited with the Mercurius Gallobelgicus, but I cannot securely identify the author meant by 'Lorchan'.

Lord.who: God, as addressed in the Psalms.

Lord Verulam.who: Francis Bacon, Lord Verulam (1561–1626), English statesman and philosopher, author of the utopian fiction *New Atlantis*.

Lorraine.who: Lorraine, a duchy in north-eastern France with its capital at Nancy, ruled by its own dukes in Burton's time.

Lot.who: Lot, Abraham's nephew in Genesis, who escaped Sodom and was made drunk and lay with his daughters.

Lotichius.who: Petrus Lotichius Secundus (1528–1560), German Neo-Latin poet known for his elegies.

Louvain.who: Louvain (Leuven), university town in Brabant, now in Belgium.

Love.who: The passion of love, the subject of Burton's Third Partition; in one passage it is personified as a god.

Love-Melancholy.who: Burton's term for melancholy caused by love, the subject of his Third Partition.

Love’s Beginning.who: A subsection heading in the Third Partition.

Loxa.who: Loja, a town in the province of Granada, Andalusia, where Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba spent his last years out of royal favour.

Loyola.who: St Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556), Spanish founder of the Society of Jesus.

Loysii.basis: It is set beside 'Manderini' in a description of China drawn from Ricci and Trigault; it probably renders the Chinese honorific laoye.
Loysii.who: A title of Chinese officials and scholar-gentry, taken from the Jesuit reports on China.

Luc.who: Lucan (39–65), Roman poet; the line 'caelo tegitur qui non habet urnam' is from his *Pharsalia*, book 7.

Lucca.who: Lucca, a city and former republic in Tuscany, known for its nearby baths (Bagni di Lucca).

Lucerne.who: Lucerne, a Swiss city and canton; in the second passage it means the Luserna valley in Piedmont, a Waldensian district.

Lucia.who: An Italian girl's name, given as an example of a pretty name.

Lucian Charidemo.who: *Charidemus*, a dialogue on beauty transmitted among Lucian's works and generally thought spurious.

Lucian Imag.who: Lucian's *Imagines* (*Essays in Portraiture*), which praises the beauty of Panthea, mistress of the emperor Lucius Verus.

Lucians.who: Satirists in the manner of Lucian of Samosata (c. 120–after 180), the Greek satirist.

Lucianum.who: Lucian of Samosata (c. 120–after 180), Greek satirist; the reference is to the dialogue *Charidemus* among his works.

Lucianus Charidemo.who: *Charidemus*, a dialogue on beauty transmitted among Lucian's works.

Lucianus Timon.who: Lucian's dialogue *Timon, or the Misanthrope*, about a rich Athenian deserted by his flatterers once he became poor.

Lucianus Toxari.who: Lucian's *Toxaris, or Friendship*, a dialogue of Greek and Scythian stories about loyal friends.

Lucian’s Alexander.who: Alexander of Abonoteichus (2nd century), oracle-monger and impostor attacked in Lucian's *Alexander, or the False Prophet*.

Lucian’s Gallus.who: The talking cock in Lucian's dialogue *The Dream, or the Cock* (Gallus), who opens locked doors with a feather from his tail.

Lucian’s Icaromenippus.who: Lucian's dialogue *Icaromenippus*, in which the Cynic Menippus flies to the moon and to heaven on wings.

Lucian’s Imagines.who: Lucian's *Imagines* (*Essays in Portraiture*), a description of a beautiful woman's features.

Lucian’s Juno.who: Juno (Hera) as she appears in Lucian's *Dialogues of the Gods*.

Lucian’s Jupiter.who: Jupiter (Zeus) as Lucian portrays him, chiefly in *Icaromenippus*.

Lucian’s Leontichus.who: Leontichus, a boastful soldier in Lucian's *Dialogues of the Courtesans*.

Lucian’s Lycia.basis: Burton's marginal note points to that work, but I cannot confirm this character there.
Lucian’s Lycia.who: A courtesan Burton cites from Lucian's *Dialogues of the Courtesans*.

Lucian’s Menippus.who: Menippus of Gadara (3rd century BC), Cynic satirist, who goes down to the underworld in Lucian's *Necyomantia* (*Menippus*).

Lucian’s Mercury.who: Mercury (Hermes) in Lucian's *Dialogues of the Gods*, who would gladly be caught with Venus as Mars was.

Lucian’s Piscator.who: Lucian's dialogue *Piscator* (*The Fisherman*), a satire on the philosophers of his day.

Lucian’s Timon.who: Timon of Athens, the legendary misanthrope, as Lucian portrays him in his dialogue *Timon*.

Lucifer.who: Lucifer, Satan, chief of the fallen angels.

Lucilius.who: First passage: Gaius Lucilius (c. 180–103 BC), founder of Roman satire; the others: Lucilius Junior, Seneca's friend, addressed in his *Moral Epistles*.

Lucilla.who: Annia Lucilla (c. 150–182), daughter of Marcus Aurelius and wife of the co-emperor Lucius Verus, whom she was rumoured to have poisoned.

Lucinia.basis: An imaginary land listed beside Hall's Mundus alter et idem and More's Utopia; I cannot identify which fiction is meant.

Lucius Martius.basis: Known only as a patient in Galen's case report; nothing more is known about him.

Lucretia.who: Lucretia, legendary Roman matron who stabbed herself after being raped by Sextus Tarquinius; the archetype of a chaste wife, as in Martial's epigram.

Lucullus.who: Lucius Licinius Lucullus (c. 118–56 BC), Roman general famed for his wealth, villas and luxurious living; Plutarch wrote his Life.

Ludovicus Suessanus.basis: The Pasquino anecdote belongs to Adrian VI's reign; I know nothing more about the man.
Ludovicus Suessanus.who: Ludovico of Sessa (Suessanus), a witty courtier at Rome who talked Pope Adrian VI (1522–23) out of having the Pasquino statue thrown into the Tiber.

Lullius.who: Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), Majorcan philosopher and mystic; many alchemical works were later attributed to him.

Lumen Greciae.who: 'Light of Greece', Cicero's epithet for Corinth (Pro lege Manilia).

Luneburg.who: Lüneburg, a Hanseatic town in Lower Saxony, northern Germany.

Lupercals.who: The Lupercalia, an ancient Roman fertility festival held on 15 February and linked with Pan (Faunus).

Lupsetus.who: Thomas Lupset (c. 1495–1530), English humanist; Guillaume Budé addressed a letter to him that was printed with More's Utopia (1517).

Lupulus.basis: Latin name of the hop plant

Luscinius Grunnio.who: Ottmar Nachtgall (Othmar Luscinius, c. 1478–1537), Alsatian humanist; the citation refers to his satirical dialogue Grunnius Sophista (1522).

Lutherus.who: Martin Luther (1483–1546), German reformer, quoted from his Commentary on Galatians.

Lycaon.who: Lycaon, mythical king of Arcadia whom Jupiter turned into a wolf for serving him human flesh (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1).

Lyceus.who: The Lyceum, the gymnasium outside Athens where Aristotle later taught.

Lycia.who: Lycia, an ancient region on the south-west coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey).

Lycian Pandarus.who: Pandarus, Lycian archer and Trojan ally in Homer's Iliad; Athena turned aside his arrow so that it only grazed Menelaus.

Lycinus.who: Lycinus, Lucian's spokesman in his dialogues; here in 'The Ship, or The Wishes' (Navigium), where Timolaus also speaks.

Lycomedes.who: Lycomedes, mythical king of Scyros, at whose court Achilles was hidden in girl's clothes.

Lycoris.basis: A conventional poetic name used for different women: by Martial, by Sannazaro, and for the mistress in the elegies attributed to Gallus.

Lycurgus.basis: The first and third passages mean the Spartan lawgiver; the second means Lycurgus, the Thracian king whom Bacchus drove mad.

Lydgate.who: John Lydgate (c. 1370–c. 1451), English poet; his 'Flower of Courtesy' was printed in early editions of Chaucer's works.

Lydia.basis: The first and third passages mean the kingdom in western Asia Minor; the second is the girl addressed in a poem attributed to Petronius.

Lydians.who: The inhabitants of ancient Lydia in western Asia Minor.

Lynn.who: King's Lynn, a port town in Norfolk, England.

Lyons.who: Lyon, a city in east-central France.

Lyranus.who: Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), Franciscan biblical commentator whose Postillae were the standard medieval commentary on the Bible.

Lysander.who: Lysander (d. 395 BC), Spartan admiral; Xenophon's Oeconomicus tells the related story of Cyrus showing him his garden.

Lysander Calista.who: Lysander and Caliste, the lovers in Vital d'Audiguier's French romance Histoire tragi-comique de nostre temps (1615), translated into English in 1621.

Lysias.basis: Ficino's commentary on Plato pairs Phaedrus with Lysias; calling him 'Theban' follows Ficino, not history.
Lysias.who: Lysias (c. 445–c. 380 BC), Athenian orator whose speech on love Phaedrus admires in Plato's Phaedrus.

Lysimachus.basis: He is listed among royal physicians next to Mithridates, and Pliny's herb lore fits.
Lysimachus.who: Lysimachus (c. 360–281 BC), Alexander's general and later king of Thrace; Pliny credits him with discovering the herb lysimachia.

Lysis.who: Lysis, the Athenian youth after whom Plato's dialogue on friendship is named.

Lysistrata.who: Lysistrata, heroine of Aristophanes' comedy of that name (411 BC).

M. Aurelius.who: Marcus Aurelius (121–180), Roman emperor, here as presented in Antonio de Guevara's fictionalised Horologium principum (The Dial of Princes).

M. D.basis: The initials and the sonnet citation fit Drayton, but I cannot confirm that this sonnet is his.
M. D.who: Michael Drayton (1563–1631), English poet, author of the sonnet sequence Idea.

M. Polus.who: Marco Polo (1254–1324), Venetian merchant and traveller whose account of his travels in Asia describes the desert of Lop.

M. Polus Venetus.who: Marco Polo (1254–1324), Venetian traveller in Asia, whose book places Prester John in Asia.

M. Sergius.who: Marcus Sergius Silus, Roman soldier of the Second Punic War, famed for his many wounds; great-grandfather of Catiline.

Macbeth.who: Macbeth (d. 1057), King of Scots, whose meeting with the three weird sisters Hector Boece tells.

Maccabees.who: The Books of the Maccabees, in the Apocrypha; 2 Maccabees 14 tells of Razis's suicide.

Macedon.who: Macedon, the ancient kingdom of northern Greece ruled by Philip II and Alexander.

Macedonia.who: Macedonia, the region of northern Greece and the southern Balkans, the ancient kingdom of Macedon.

Macedonian.who: Of Macedon; here Archelaus I (r. c. 413–399 BC), King of Macedon, patron of Euripides.

Macedonian Philip.who: Philip II of Macedon (382–336 BC), father of Alexander the Great, husband of Olympias.

Maceronicon.who: Burton's coinage for a macaronic medley, a hotchpotch put together from many authors.

Machates.who: Machates, the young guest at Amphipolis visited by the revenant girl Philinnion in Phlegon of Tralles' Book of Marvels.

Machiavellian.who: Machiavellian: scheming and unscrupulous in politics, after Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527).

Machiavellians.who: Followers of Niccolò Machiavelli's (1469–1527) political maxims: men who use religion and morals only for political ends.

Madagascar.who: Madagascar, the large island off south-east Africa.

Madrid.who: Madrid, the Spanish royal seat from 1561.

Maecenas.who: Gaius Maecenas (c. 70–8 BC), friend of Augustus and patron of Horace and Virgil; hence any generous patron.

Maecenates.who: Plural of Maecenas (c. 70–8 BC), patron of Horace and Virgil: generous patrons of learning.

Maenades.who: The Maenads, frenzied female followers of Dionysus (Bacchus).

Maeotian.who: Of the Palus Maeotis, the ancient name of the Sea of Azov and its marshes, north of the Black Sea.

Maevius.basis: paired with Seius and Irus as types of mean birth
Maevius.who: Maevius, a stock Roman name, like Seius, for an obscure, ordinary man.

Magalianus.basis: Latin form and the commentary on 1 Timothy fit him
Magalianus.who: Cosme de Magalhães (Cosmas Magalianus), Portuguese Jesuit, author of commentaries on the Pastoral Epistles.

Magdalen.basis: the second passage miscalls Margaret 'Magdalen'; it tells her story of Alain Chartier
Magdalen.who: Two bearers: Madeleine of France (1443–1495), daughter of Charles VII, betrothed to Ladislaus Posthumus; and Margaret of Scotland (1424–1445), wife of the future Louis XI.

Magdeburg.who: Magdeburg, archiepiscopal city on the Elbe in Saxony, Germany.

Magdeburgenses.who: The Magdeburg Centuriators, Lutheran historians led by Matthias Flacius Illyricus, who wrote the Protestant church history 'Magdeburg Centuries' (1559–74).

Magellan.who: The Strait of Magellan, at the southern tip of South America, named after Ferdinand Magellan (c. 1480–1521).

Magellanica.who: Magellanica, an early-modern name for Terra Australis, the great southern continent then supposed to lie south of the Strait of Magellan.

Maginus Geog.who: Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617), Bolognese astronomer and geographer, editor of Ptolemy's Geography with modern regional descriptions.

Maginus Geogr.who: Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617), Bolognese astronomer and geographer, editor of Ptolemy's Geography with modern regional descriptions.

Maginus Pers.who: Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617), Bolognese geographer; cited here for his description of Persia in his geography.

Magirus.basis: his Physiologia was a standard source on the parts and faculties
Magirus.who: Johannes Magirus (d. 1596), German physician and philosopher, author of the textbook 'Physiologia peripatetica'.

Magnesia.who: Magnesia on the Maeander, a city in Ionia (western Turkey) that Xerxes gave Themistocles.

Magnus Gonsalva.who: Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba (1453–1515), 'the Great Captain', Spanish general who conquered Naples and later fell from royal favour; Paolo Giovio wrote his life.

Mahomet.who: Two bearers: Mehmed II (1432–1481), Ottoman sultan who took Constantinople (first and third passages); and the Prophet Muhammad (c. 570–632) (second passage).

Mahometan.who: Muslim: of the religion of Muhammad (c. 570–632).

Mahometan Mesquitas.who: Muslim mosques ('mesquita', the Spanish and Portuguese word for mosque).

Mainz.who: Mainz, an archiepiscopal and electoral city on the Rhine in Germany.

Majorca.who: Majorca (Mallorca), the largest of the Balearic Islands, Spain.

Malabar.who: The Malabar Coast, the south-western coast of India (modern Kerala and neighbouring areas).

Malacca.who: Malacca (Melaka), a port on the Malay Peninsula in modern Malaysia, held by the Portuguese from 1511.

Malaga.who: Málaga, a Mediterranean port in Andalusia, southern Spain.

Malatesta.basis: Known only as Brasavola's patient at the Ferrara court

Malcolm.basis: Buchanan's account of Kenneth III fits; the historical details are uncertain
Malcolm.who: Malcolm, son of King Dub (Duff) of Scotland and Prince of Cumbria, whose murder Buchanan blames on Kenneth III (late 10th century).

Maldives.who: The Maldives, an archipelago of small coral islands in the Indian Ocean, south-west of India.

Malines.who: Gerard Malynes (fl. 1586–1641), English merchant and economic writer, author of *Consuetudo, vel Lex Mercatoria* (1622).

Malmesbury.who: Malmesbury, a town in Wiltshire, England, with a Benedictine abbey whose abbot was St Aldhelm (d. 709).

Malta.who: Malta, the Mediterranean island south of Sicily.

Mamaea.who: Julia Mamaea (d. 235), mother of the emperor Severus Alexander; Heliogabalus's mother was actually her sister Julia Soaemias.

Mambrinum.basis: A place in the Val Luserna, Piedmont; I cannot match it to a modern name

Mamelukes.who: The Mamluks, a slave-soldier caste who ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250 until the Ottoman conquest of 1517.

Mammon. Psellus.basis: form joins two names by mistake
Mammon. Psellus.who: Mammon, the biblical personification of riches, treated by demonologists as prince of the tempting devils; the form also takes in the next word, 'Psellus' (Michael Psellus).

Manamotapa.who: Monomotapa, the Mutapa kingdom of south-eastern Africa, in modern Zimbabwe and Mozambique.

Manardus.who: Giovanni Manardi (1462–1536), physician of Ferrara, author of the *Epistolae medicinales*.

Manasseh.who: Manasseh, the idolatrous king of Judah who repented and was forgiven (2 Chronicles 33).

Manderini.who: Mandarins, the scholar-officials of imperial China.

Manichees.who: Manichaeans, followers of the dualist religion of Mani (3rd century), condemned as heretics by the Church.

Manna.basis: the food of the Israelites in the wilderness

Manoa.who: Manoa, the legendary golden city of El Dorado, thought to lie on a lake in Guiana, as described by Ralegh.

Mansfield.who: Mansfeld, a mining town in modern Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, known for its copper-shale fossils.

Mantinea.who: Mantinea, a city in Arcadia, Greece, site of the battle of 362 BC in which Epaminondas fell.

Manto.basis: the first is clearly the mythical seeress; the second rests only on Burton's citation of Knolles
Manto.who: First passage: Manto, the prophetess and daughter of Tiresias; second: the wife of Yunus Pasha in Knolles's *Generall Historie of the Turkes*.

Mantua.who: Mantua, a city in Lombardy, northern Italy.

Maph.basis: the quoted verses on the Rutulians' collapse seem to come from Vegio's Aeneid supplement
Maph.who: Maffeo Vegio (1407–1458), Italian humanist, author of a thirteenth book added to Virgil's *Aeneid*.

Maragnan.basis: the second passage lists it among great rivers
Maragnan.who: Maranhão in northern Brazil, including the island of São Luís; in the second passage, the river Maranhão (Marañón, the Amazon).

Marathon.who: Marathon in Attica, where the Athenians defeated the Persians in 490 BC.

Marbodeus.who: Marbod of Rennes (c. 1035–1123), bishop and poet, author of the *Liber lapidum*, a Latin verse treatise on the virtues of gems.

Marcella.who: Marcella (d. 410), a Roman noblewoman and ascetic widow, friend and correspondent of St Jerome.

Marcellus Donatus.who: Marcello Donati (1538–1602), physician of Mantua, author of *De medica historia mirabili*.

Marcolphus.who: Marcolf, the coarse, ugly peasant who trades wits with King Solomon in the medieval *Dialogue of Solomon and Marcolf*.

Marcus.who: Three bearers: the Mesopotamian monk Marcus, Psellus's informant on demons; Marcus, the 2nd-century Gnostic denounced by Irenaeus; and Marco Polo (as 'Marcus Polus').

Marcus Aurelius.who: Marcus Aurelius (121–180), Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher.

Marcus Cicero.who: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Roman orator and statesman.

Marcus de Oddis.basis: the Latin form and the medical context fit the Paduan physician
Marcus de Oddis.who: Marco degli Oddi, 16th-century physician of Padua, son of the physician Oddo degli Oddi.

Margaret.who: Second passage: Margaret Stewart (1424–1445), daughter of James I of Scotland and first wife of the future Louis XI; the first is the Margaret addressed in Barthius's love verse.

Mariamne.who: Mariamne (d. 29 BC), Hasmonean princess and wife of Herod the Great, who had her executed.

Marian.basis: The passages mean different things: the oak linked to Gaius Marius in Cicero's De legibus; a mistress named Mariana in Pontanus; and the reign of Mary I of England.

Mariana.who: Juan de Mariana (1536–1624), Spanish Jesuit historian, author of the Historiae de rebus Hispaniae (a history of Spain).

Marinus Mersennus.who: Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), French Minim friar and natural philosopher, author of the Quaestiones celeberrimae in Genesim (1623).

Mariola.who: The Sierra de Mariola, a mountain range in the Valencia region of eastern Spain, long known for its medicinal herbs.

Marius.who: Gaius Marius (157–86 BC), Roman general and seven times consul, a 'new man' of humble birth from Arpinum.

Mark Ridley.who: Mark Ridley (1560–1624), English physician, author of A Short Treatise of Magneticall Bodies and Motions (1613).

Marlianus.who: Bartolomeo Marliani (d. c.1560), Italian antiquary, author of a topography of ancient Rome.

Marrhusian Phaedrus.who: Phaedrus of Myrrhinus (late 5th century BC), Athenian friend of Socrates and a speaker in Plato's Phaedrus and Symposium; Ficino paired him with Lysias.

Mars.basis: The second passage means the god; the first and third mean the astrological planet.
Mars.who: Mars, Roman god of war, and the planet named after him, which astrologers counted a malign influence.

Marsilius Cagnatus.who: Marsilio Cagnati (1543–1612), physician of Verona, author of De sanitate tuenda (on preserving health).

Marstallerus.basis: He is named in a list of defenders of astrology, and the Latin form fits Marstaller's anthology.
Marstallerus.who: Gervasius Marstaller, 16th-century German physician who compiled a collection of writings in defence of judicial astrology (1549).

Marsyas.who: Marsyas, the satyr who challenged Apollo to a music contest and was flayed alive when he lost.

Mart.who: Martial (Marcus Valerius Martialis, c.40–c.104), Latin poet of epigrams; 'Mart.' is Burton's abbreviation.

Martha.who: Martha of Bethany, sister of Mary and Lazarus, who in Luke 10 was 'cumbered about much serving'.

Martia.who: Marcia, wife of Cato the Younger, whom Cato gave in marriage to the orator Quintus Hortensius.

Martial.who: Martial (Marcus Valerius Martialis, c.40–c.104), Latin poet of epigrams.

Martial’s Mamurra.who: Mamurra, a character in Martial's Epigrams (9.59) who looks over costly goods and slaves in the Roman market but buys almost nothing.

Martial’s Sota.who: Sotas, a physician in Martial's Epigrams (4.9); there it is his daughter Labulla who leaves her husband for Clitus.

Martian.basis: I cannot identify a physician of this name serving Philip I of Castile.

Martianus.who: Martianus Capella (fl. 5th century), Latin writer of Carthage, author of the allegory De nuptiis Philologiae et Mercurii.

Martianus Capella’s Jupiter.who: Jupiter as shown in Book 1 of Martianus Capella's De nuptiis Philologiae et Mercurii, holding a sphere that reflected all the world.

Martin.who: St Martin of Tours (d. 397), bishop, whose feast on 11 November was Martinmas.

Martin Bellius.who: 'Martinus Bellius', the pen-name under which Sebastian Castellio published De haereticis an sint persequendi (1554), arguing against executing heretics.

Martin Cromerus.who: Marcin Kromer (1512–1589), Polish historian and Prince-Bishop of Warmia, author of De origine et rebus gestis Polonorum (a history of Poland).

Martin Guerre.who: Martin Guerre, French peasant of Artigat whose identity was taken by the impostor Arnaud du Tilh; the impostor was tried at Toulouse in 1560.

Martin Rulandus.basis: His son Martin Ruland the Younger was also a physician; the reference to simple domestic remedies fits the elder better.
Martin Rulandus.who: Martin Ruland the Elder (1532–1602), German physician known for popular empirical remedies.

Mary.who: The Virgin Mary, mother of Jesus.

Mary Magdalen.who: Mary Magdalene, follower of Jesus, traditionally held to be a repentant sinner.

Mary. Antony.basis: An extraction error that joins 'Mary.' (the Virgin Mary) to 'Antony' (Mark Antony) across a sentence break.

Mary’s Oxon.who: The University Church of St Mary the Virgin, Oxford, where university sermons were preached.

Masinissa.who: Masinissa (c.238–148 BC), king of Numidia and ally of Rome, who married Sophonisba.

Masistes.who: Masistes, brother of the Persian king Xerxes; Herodotus (Book 9) tells how Queen Amestris mutilated his wife.

Massagetae.who: The Massagetae, an ancient nomadic people of Central Asia east of the Caspian Sea, described by Herodotus.

Massaria.who: Alessandro Massaria (1510–1598), physician of Vicenza and professor of medicine at Padua, author of a Practica medica.

Massilians.who: The people of Massilia, the ancient Greek colony that is modern Marseille.

Mat. Riccius.who: Matteo Ricci (1552–1610), Italian Jesuit missionary in China; his account was published by Nicolas Trigault as De Christiana expeditione apud Sinas.

Matenesius.who: Johann Friedrich Matenesius, German Catholic writer of Cologne, author of a treatise on luxury and abuse of dress (De luxu et abusu vestium).

Matholdus.basis: a physician named only in Solenander's consilia; not otherwise known to me

Matilda.basis: each passage's context settles its bearer; the third is a generic name
Matilda.who: Different bearers: the Empress Matilda (1102–1167), daughter of Henry I; Matilda Fitzwalter, the Dunmow maid said to have been pursued by King John; and a stock girl's name.

Matt. Riccius.who: Matteo Ricci (1552–1610), Italian Jesuit missionary in China, whose journals were published by Trigault as De Christiana expeditione apud Sinas (1615).

Matthew Paris.who: Matthew Paris (c. 1200–1259), Benedictine monk and chronicler of St Albans, author of the Chronica majora.

Matthew Riccius.who: Matteo Ricci (1552–1610), Italian Jesuit missionary in China, whose account of the mission appeared as De Christiana expeditione apud Sinas (1615).

Matthias Ditmarsh.basis: political writer not identifiable with confidence

Matthias à Michou.who: Maciej Miechowita (Matthias de Miechow, 1457–1523), Polish physician and historian, author of the Tractatus de duabus Sarmatiis describing Tartary and Muscovy.

Matthiolum.who: Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), Sienese physician and botanist, famous for his illustrated commentary on Dioscorides.

Matthiolus.who: Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), Sienese physician and botanist, famous for his illustrated commentary on Dioscorides.

Mauretania.who: Mauretania, ancient kingdom of north-west Africa, roughly modern northern Morocco and western Algeria.

Mauretanian.who: Mauretanian: Moorish, of the Moors of north-west Africa (Barbary).

Mauritius.who: Maurice (Mauricius), Byzantine emperor 582–602, noted for piety and frugality.

Maurolicus.who: Francesco Maurolico (1494–1575), Sicilian mathematician and astronomer of Messina.

Mausolean.who: Mausolean: grand and monumental, after the Mausoleum, the tomb of Mausolus at Halicarnassus.

Mausolus.who: Mausolus (d. 353 BC), ruler of Caria, husband of Artemisia, who built his famous tomb, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus.

Max.who: Maximus of Tyre (2nd century AD), Greek Platonist rhetorician, author of the Dissertations.

Maxentius.who: Maxentius, Roman emperor 306–312, persecutor of Christians, defeated by Constantine at the Milvian Bridge.

Maximilian.who: Maximilian I (1459–1519), Holy Roman Emperor; Trithemius supposedly raised for him the ghost of his dead wife, Mary of Burgundy.

Maximilianus Vrientius.who: Maximilian de Vriendt (Vrientius), Flemish Latin poet of Ghent, writer of epigrams.

Maximinus.basis: physical size and low birth fit Thrax; Eusebius book 9 concerns Daia
Maximinus.who: Maximinus Thrax (r. 235–238), gigantic peasant-soldier made emperor (first two passages); Maximinus Daia (r. 310–313), whose toleration edict Eusebius records (third).

Maximus Jovianus.basis: Burton appears to have transposed the titles of the two co-emperors
Maximus Jovianus.who: Maximian (r. 286–305), Diocletian's co-emperor; the two took the divine titles Jovius (Diocletian) and Herculius (Maximian).

Maximus Tyrius.who: Maximus of Tyre (2nd century AD), Greek Platonist rhetorician whose Dissertations include whether diseases of body or mind are worse.

Mecca.who: Mecca, holy city of Islam in western Arabia.

Medea.who: Medea, sorceress of Colchis in Greek myth, who loved Jason and helped him win the Golden Fleece.

Medicean.who: Medicean stars: Jupiter's four largest moons, discovered by Galileo in 1610 and named by him after the Medici.

Megaera.who: Megaera, one of the three Furies (Erinyes) of Greek myth, with Alecto and Tisiphone.

Megalopolis.who: Megalopolis, city of Arcadia in the central Peloponnese, Greece.

Megapenthus.who: Megapenthes, the tyrant in Lucian's dialogue Cataplus (The Downward Journey) who begs Clotho for more life.

Megara.who: Megara, ancient Greek city by the Isthmus of Corinth, between Athens and Corinth.

Megaris.who: Megaris, the territory of Megara in ancient Greece, by the Isthmus of Corinth.

Mela.who: Pomponius Mela (fl. c. AD 43), Roman geographer, author of De chorographia.

Melaena.who: Melaene ('the dark one'), a sea-nymph loved by Triton in Celio Calcagnini's Latin dialogue Galatea.

Melaene.who: Melaene ('the dark one'), a sea-nymph loved by Triton in Celio Calcagnini's Latin dialogue Galatea.

Melampus.who: Melampus, legendary Greek seer and healer who cured the mad daughters of King Proetus of Argos, traditionally with hellebore.

Melanagoga.who: Melanagoga, the technical term for medicines that purge black bile (melancholy).

Melancholy.who: Melancholy, the disease that is Burton's subject.

Melanelius.basis: Burton cites him as author of a book on melancholy drawn from Galen; I cannot securely identify him.

Melanippe.who: Melanippa, a lost tragedy by Quintus Ennius (239–169 BC), based on Euripides' Melanippe plays.

Melanthius.who: Melanthius, the disloyal goatherd in Homer's Odyssey who insults and kicks the disguised Odysseus.

Melchonis.basis: The Ammonite context and the name form point to Milcom.
Melchonis.who: Milcom (Malcam), the national god of the Ammonites in the Old Testament, often identified with Moloch.

Meleager.who: Meleager, Greek hero and hunter who killed the Calydonian boar sent by Artemis; Philostratus describes him in his Imagines.

Meletus.who: Meletus, Athenian who joined Anytus and Lycon in prosecuting Socrates in 399 BC.

Melibea.who: The Tragicomedia de Calisto y Melibea (Celestina, 1499), attributed to Fernando de Rojas; Melibea is its heroine, loved by Calisto.

Melichius.basis: Named among pharmacopoeia and dispensatory writers; the name form fits Melichio.
Melichius.who: Giorgio Melichio (Georg Melich), German-born apothecary in Venice, author of a guide to compounding medicines, the Avvertimenti nelle composizioni de' medicamenti.

Melinda.who: Malindi, a port on the coast of Kenya and a Portuguese trading station in the sixteenth century.

Melissa.who: In the first passage, melissa is the herb balm; in the second, Melissa is a courtesan in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans who uses a love charm.

Melissus.who: In the first passage, Melissus of Samos (fl. 5th c. BC), Eleatic philosopher; in the second, a merchant suitor in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans.

Mellona.who: Mellona, minor Roman goddess of bees and honey.

Memmius.basis: Cicero's De oratore anecdote is usually taken to refer to this Gaius Memmius.
Memmius.who: Gaius Memmius (d. 100 BC), Roman politician and tribune, mocked by the orator Crassus in an anecdote preserved in Cicero's De oratore.

Memory.who: Memory, one of the inward senses in Renaissance faculty psychology.

Memphis.who: Memphis, ancient capital of Egypt on the Nile, south of modern Cairo.

Men.who: An ordinary word meaning human beings.

Menalcas.who: Menalcas, a shepherd in Virgil's Eclogues (and Theocritus), here standing for any rustic.

Menecrates.who: Menecrates of Syracuse (4th c. BC), physician who called himself Zeus and wrote an arrogant letter to Philip II of Macedon.

Menedemus.who: Menedemus, the self-punishing old father in Terence's comedy Heauton Timorumenos, whom his neighbour Chremes questions.

Menedemus Lampsacus.who: Menedemus (3rd c. BC), Cynic philosopher and pupil of Colotes of Lampsacus, who went about dressed as a Fury claiming to be a spy from Hades (Diogenes Laertius 6.102).

Menelaus.who: Menelaus, legendary king of Sparta and husband of Helen in Homer.

Menenius Agrippa.who: Agrippa Menenius Lanatus (d. 493 BC), Roman consul who ended the plebeian secession of 494 BC with his fable of the belly and the members.

Menippus.who: Menippus of Gadara (3rd c. BC), Cynic satirist, who appears as a character in Lucian's dialogues, including the journey to Hades in the Necyomantia.

Menippus Lycius.who: Menippus of Lycia, the young man in Philostratus' Life of Apollonius (4.25) whom a lamia seduced until Apollonius exposed her.

Mentz.who: Mainz, the German city on the Rhine; St Boniface was its archbishop.

Mercator.who: Latin for 'the merchant', the subject of the quoted verse.

Mercatus.who: Luis Mercado (Ludovicus Mercatus, c. 1525–1611), Spanish physician to Philip II, author of works on women's diseases and hereditary diseases.

Mercerus.who: Josias Mercier (Mercerus, d. 1626), French classical scholar who edited the letters of Aristaenetus.

Mercurialists.who: An astrological term for people born under the planet Mercury.

Mercurius Britannicus.who: Mercurius Britannicus, the pseudonym used by Joseph Hall (1574–1656) for his satire Mundus alter et idem (c. 1605), which describes an imaginary Terra Australis.

Mercurius Gallobelgicus.who: Mercurius Gallobelgicus, a Latin news digest published at Cologne from 1594.

Mercury.who: Mercury, the Roman messenger god (father of Autolycus); in the second passage, the planet of that name in astrology.

Meresin.basis: Burton's ranking of the orders of devils follows Agrippa's list, which names Meresin.
Meresin.who: Meresin, a demon named as prince of the aerial powers in Renaissance demonology, as in Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy.

Merindol.who: Mérindol, a village in Provence where Waldensians were massacred in 1545.

Merlin.who: Merlin, the legendary Welsh prophet and enchanter, who interpreted the fight of the red and white dragons for Vortigern.

Merryman.who: Dr Merryman, a personification of cheerfulness, one of the three 'doctors' of the Salernitan health rules.

Mersennus.who: Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), French Minim friar and scholar, whose Quaestiones in Genesim (1623) attacked atheists and astrologers.

Merula.who: Paulus Merula (1558–1607), Dutch scholar and geographer, author of a Cosmographia generalis.

Mesopotamia.who: Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, mostly modern Iraq; its upper part is the Diyarbakır region of Turkey.

Messalina.who: Valeria Messalina (d. AD 48), third wife of the Emperor Claudius, notorious for her lewdness; executed after a mock marriage to Silius.

Messenian.who: The Messenians, people of Messenia in the south-western Peloponnese, Greece.

Messiah.who: The Messiah, the anointed deliverer the Jews expect, whom Christians identify with Christ.

Messina.who: Messina, port city in north-eastern Sicily.

Mesue.basis: Burton cites the standard authority of Renaissance pharmacy; which Mesue is meant isn't settled
Mesue.who: Mesue, name under which medieval Latin medical and pharmacological works circulated, linked to Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (d. 857), Christian physician of Baghdad, and a later 'Mesue the Younger'.

Meswinde.who: Merswind, a girl in the legend of the dancers of Kölbigk in Saxony, who were cursed to dance for a year (c. 1021) for dancing in a churchyard.

Metaphysics.basis: name of a subject of study

Metellus.who: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus (d. 115 BC), Roman general who defeated the Achaeans in 146 BC and was proverbial for his good fortune.

Metellus Numidicus.who: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus (censor 102 BC), Roman statesman; Gellius ascribes to him a censor's speech urging marriage, though it is probably Macedonicus's.

Methymna.who: Methymna, ancient city on the north coast of Lesbos, modern Mithymna (Molyvos).

Mevius.who: Maevius, poetaster of the 1st century BC, mocked with Bavius by Virgil (Eclogue 3) and by Horace.

Mexican.who: The lake of Mexico, i.e. Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico, round the Aztec capital, which had no outlet.

Mexico.who: Mexico, the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan and the region of New Spain around it.

Mezentius.who: Mezentius, Etruscan king in Virgil's Aeneid, father of Lausus, who chose to die after his son was killed.

Michael.basis: a Byzantine emperor, a musician patient, and a despot's son in different passages

Michael Paleologus.basis: Burton names him, but Manuel Philes worked mainly under Andronikos II, so Michael IX may be meant
Michael Paleologus.who: Michael VIII Palaiologos (r. 1259–1282), Byzantine emperor who founded the Palaiologan dynasty.

Michael Parapinatius.who: Michael VII Doukas, called Parapinakes (r. 1071–1078), Byzantine emperor and pupil of Michael Psellus.

Michaelis.who: Sébastien Michaëlis (c. 1543–1618), French Dominican inquisitor who exorcised Madeleine Demandolx at Sainte-Baume in 1610; his account was translated into English in 1613.

Micio.who: Micio, the indulgent old man of Terence's comedy Adelphoe, brother of Demea and adoptive father of Aeschinus.

Micyllus.who: Micyllus, the poor cobbler of Lucian's dialogue The Dream, or the Cock (Gallus).

Middendorpius.who: Jacob Middendorp (d. 1611), Dutch Catholic theologian at Cologne, author of a work on the academies of the world.

Midianites.who: The Midianites, a desert people of the Old Testament whom Gideon routed (Judges 7).

Milan.who: Milan, city of Lombardy, northern Italy.

Milesian.who: The Milesians, people of Miletus, Greek city in Asia Minor, whose maidens' suicide epidemic Plutarch records.

Milford.who: Milford Haven, natural harbour in Pembrokeshire, south-west Wales.

Milles.basis: marginal citation on ancient combats; this English author fits the subject but the reference is bare
Milles.who: Thomas Milles (c. 1550–1627), English antiquary, author of The Catalogue of Honor (1610), which treats of combats and ceremonies of chivalry.

Miltiades.who: Miltiades (c. 550–489 BC), Athenian general who won the Battle of Marathon.

Mimner.who: Mimnermus of Colophon (fl. c. 630 BC), Greek elegiac poet of love and youth.

Mimnermus.who: Mimnermus of Colophon (fl. c. 630 BC), Greek elegiac poet of love, pleasure and the miseries of old age.

Minerva.who: Minerva, Roman goddess of wisdom and the arts, identified with the Greek Pallas Athena; a virgin goddess.

Minorites.who: The Minorites (Friars Minor), the Franciscan order of friars founded by St Francis of Assisi.

Minos.who: Minos, legendary king and lawgiver of Crete, husband of Pasiphae, said to have received his laws from Zeus.

Minotaur.who: The Minotaur, the bull-headed monster of the Cretan labyrinth, killed by Theseus.

Minuc.basis: The abbreviation and the attack on pagan festivals and priests fit the Octavius.
Minuc.who: Marcus Minucius Felix (fl. c. 200), Christian apologist, whose dialogue *Octavius* attacks pagan rites and priests.

Minucius Felix.basis: The first passage is the apologist; the second is a Roman consul Minucius in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 8.
Minucius Felix.who: Marcus Minucius Felix (fl. c. 200), Christian apologist, author of *Octavius*; the second passage wrongly applies the name to the consul Minucius who addressed Coriolanus in Dionysius.

Minucius Octaviano.who: Minucius Felix's *Octavius*, a Christian apologetic dialogue in which Caecilius speaks for paganism.

Mirach.who: Mirach, a term from Arabic medicine for the abdominal wall, especially the upper belly (epigastrium).

Mirachial.who: Mirachial, i.e. hypochondriacal or 'windy' melancholy seated in the mirach (the upper abdomen), from Arabic medical terminology.

Misnia.who: Misnia, Meissen, the margraviate in Saxony, eastern Germany, which contained Dresden.

Misopogon.who: *Misopogon* ('Beard-Hater'), the Emperor Julian's satirical self-defence addressed to the people of Antioch (363).

Mistress.who: A title of courtesy (Mrs), here before the name of Burton's mother, Dorothy Burton.

Mistylus.who: Mistylus, the pirate chief in Theodore Prodromos's twelfth-century Byzantine verse romance *Rhodanthe and Dosicles*.

Mithridate.who: Mithridate, a famous antidote made of many ingredients and named after Mithridates VI of Pontus.

Mithridates.who: Mithridates VI Eupator (132–63 BC), king of Pontus and enemy of Rome, famous for making himself immune to poisons and for his study of drugs.

Mizaldum.who: Antoine Mizauld (Mizaldus) (1510–1578), French physician and astrologer who compiled popular books of medical secrets and natural marvels.

Mizaldus.who: Antoine Mizauld (Mizaldus) (1510–1578), French physician and astrologer who compiled popular books of medical secrets and natural marvels.

Mizaldus. Nicander.basis: The form combines two separate names.
Mizaldus. Nicander.who: Two names run together: Antoine Mizauld (1510–1578), French physician, and Nicander of Colophon (2nd century BC), Greek author of poems on poisons and antidotes.

Moabar.who: Moabar (Ma'bar), the medieval name for the Coromandel coast of south-east India, known from Marco Polo.

Moabites.who: The Moabites, an ancient people east of the Dead Sea and neighbours and frequent enemies of Israel.

Moderator.who: Moderator, the person presiding over a disputation.

Moeris.who: Moeris, a legendary Egyptian king who, according to Herodotus, dug the great lake named after him.

Mogul.who: The Great Mogul, the Mughal emperor of northern India (in Burton's day Jahangir, then Shah Jahan).

Mogullians.who: The Mughals, the Muslim rulers of the Mughal empire in India, and their subjects.

Moll.who: Moll, a familiar form of Mary, used here as a stock girl's name.

Moloch.who: Moloch, a Canaanite god condemned in the Bible, to whom children were sacrificed by fire.

Mombasa.who: Mombasa, a port on the coast of East Africa, now in Kenya, held by the Portuguese in Burton's day.

Momus.who: Momus, the Greek god of mockery and censure, who found fault even with the gods.

Monardus.who: Nicolás Monardes (c. 1493–1588), physician of Seville, who wrote on New World remedies such as sassafras, guaiacum and tobacco.

Monavius.basis: His letters to Scholz and Dudith fit, but his brother Peter Monau, a physician, is also possible.
Monavius.who: Jacob Monau (Monavius) (1546–1603), humanist of Breslau whose letters appear in Lorenz Scholz's collections of medical epistles.

Monica.who: St Monica (c. 331–387), mother of St Augustine, whose death he mourns in the *Confessions*.

Mons Atlas.who: The Atlas mountains of north-west Africa.

Mons Draconis.who: Mondragone, a town in Campania, southern Italy, north-west of Naples.

Mons Hecla.who: Hekla, the volcano in southern Iceland, popularly thought to be a mouth of hell.

Mons Sloto.basis: A supposed Arctic mountain on early maps that I cannot identify with confidence.

Mont.basis: The second passage clearly means Montanus; the first abbreviation could also be Montaltus.
Mont.who: Giovanni Battista Da Monte (Montanus) (1498–1551), Paduan physician known for his *Consilia*.

Montagnana.who: Bartolomeo Montagnana (d. c. 1460), physician and professor at Padua, known for his *Consilia* and writings on compound medicines.

Montagu.who: Richard Montagu (1577–1641), English divine and later bishop, whose *Diatribae* (1621) defended clergy's right to tithes against Selden.

Montaigne.who: Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592), French essayist, author of the *Essais*.

Montaltum.who: Filipe Montalto (Philotheus Elianus Montaltus, d. 1616), Portuguese Jewish physician, whose *Archipathologia* (1614) on diseases of the head covers love-melancholy.

Montanists.who: Montanists, 2nd-century ascetic Christian sect, followers of the Phrygian prophet Montanus, condemned as heretics.

Montezuma.who: Moctezuma II (c. 1466–1520), Aztec emperor of Mexico at the time of the Spanish conquest under Cortés.

Montfort.basis: The Montano consilium is addressed to a 'Comes de Monteforti'; which count is meant is not settled.
Montfort.who: A count of Montfort, of the Swabian noble family (Tettnang, Bregenz), who was a patient of the Paduan physician Giovanni Battista Montano.

Montpellier.who: Montpellier in Languedoc, southern France, seat of a famous medical school.

Moon.who: The Moon, treated as an astrological planet.

Moons.who: Satellites of the planets, e.g. Jupiter's moons discovered by Galileo.

Moors.who: The Moors, Muslim peoples of North Africa and of medieval Spain.

Mopsus.basis: First passage lists prophets beside Manto; second uses the name generically for a beloved.
Mopsus.who: Mopsus, mythical Greek seer, son of Manto; in the second passage it is a stock lover's name taken from pastoral poetry (Virgil, Eclogue 8).

Moral Philosophy.who: Ethics as a branch of learning.

Morals.who: Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, whose books 8 and 9 treat friendship.

Moravian.who: A native of Moravia; Jan Dubravius (d. 1553), bishop of Olomouc, wrote a treatise on fishponds.

Mordecai.who: Mordecai, Jewish cousin and guardian of Esther in the Book of Esther, raised up when his enemy Haman was hanged.

Mordred.who: Mordred, King Arthur's treacherous nephew (or son) in Arthurian legend, who seized his kingdom and queen.

Morea.who: The Morea, the medieval and early modern name of the Peloponnese in southern Greece.

Mornay.who: Philippe de Mornay, seigneur du Plessis-Marly (1549–1623), Huguenot statesman, author of *De la vérité de la religion chrétienne* (1581).

Morocco.who: Morocco, city and kingdom (Marrakesh) in north-west Africa.

Moronia Foelix.basis: Hall's Moronia is divided into named provinces; Burton knew the work.
Moronia Foelix.who: An imaginary province of Moronia, the land of fools, in Joseph Hall's satirical *Mundus alter et idem* (c. 1605).

Moronia Pia.basis: Hall's Moronia is divided into named provinces; Burton knew the work.
Moronia Pia.who: An imaginary province of Moronia, the land of fools, in Joseph Hall's satirical *Mundus alter et idem* (c. 1605).

Morpheus.who: Morpheus, Greek god of dreams, son of Sleep (Hypnos).

Moschion.who: Muscio (Moschion), late-antique author of a Latin gynaecological manual adapted from Soranus.

Moses.who: Moses, Hebrew lawgiver and leader of the Exodus, traditional author of the Pentateuch.

Mossella.who: The Moselle (Latin Mosella), river of north-east France and western Germany, flowing into the Rhine.

Moving.who: The motive power of the sensible soul, in faculty psychology.

Moving Appetite.who: The appetite that sets the body in motion, in faculty psychology.

Moving Faculty.who: The motive faculty of the sensitive soul, in faculty psychology.

Muleasses.who: Mulay Hassan (Muleasses), Hafsid king of Tunis (r. 1526–1543), restored by Charles V and later blinded by his son.

Mully-Hamet.basis: Several rulers of Fez and Morocco bore this name; the passage does not settle which.

Mummias.who: Mummy, i.e. embalmed flesh used as a drug.

Mundi.who: Decius Mundus, Roman knight under Tiberius who seduced the matron Paulina in the temple of Isis by posing as the god Anubis (Josephus, Hegesippus).

Murcia.who: Murcia, city and region in south-eastern Spain.

Musarium.who: Musarion, a fictional courtesan who writes one of the love letters of Aristaenetus (c. 5th–6th century).

Muscovia.who: Muscovy, the Grand Duchy (later Tsardom) of Moscow, i.e. Russia.

Muscovian.who: Muscovite, i.e. Russian: of the Grand Duchy (later Tsardom) of Muscovy, whose rulers then included Ivan IV ("Jo. Basilius").

Muscovites.who: The Russians, subjects of the Grand Duchy (later Tsardom) of Muscovy.

Muscovy.who: Muscovy, the Grand Duchy and later Tsardom of Moscow, i.e. Russia.

Musculus.who: Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), German Reformed theologian at Augsburg and Bern, author of biblical commentaries, including one on the Psalms, and of the Loci communes.

Muses.who: The Muses, the nine Greek goddesses of poetry, music and learning, daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne.

Muses. Socrates.basis: Two separate names (the Muses; Socrates) run together across a sentence break.

Music.basis: The name of a field of study.

Musicles.basis: Plutarch's Life of Pericles names Mnesicles among the builders. Burton seems to have garbled both the name and the building.
Musicles.who: Mnesicles (fl. 430s BC), Athenian architect of the Propylaea on the Acropolis under Pericles.

Musonius.who: Gaius Musonius Rufus (1st century AD), Roman Stoic philosopher whose discourses on marriage are preserved in Stobaeus.

Mussulman.who: An older word for a Muslim.

Mustapha.basis: Selim I put to death a vizier of this name, and the passage gives the same context.
Mustapha.who: Koca Mustafa Pasha, Ottoman grand vizier under Bayezid II, executed by Selim I in 1512.

Mustapha Bassa.basis: Selim I put to death a vizier of this name, and the passage gives the same context.
Mustapha Bassa.who: Koca Mustafa Pasha, Ottoman grand vizier under Bayezid II, executed by Selim I in 1512.

Mycale.who: Mycale, a promontory in Ionia opposite Samos, where the Greeks defeated the Persians in 479 BC.

Mycenae.who: Mycenae, ancient city in the Argolid, Greece, seat of Agamemnon and the leading Greek power of the Bronze Age.

Mydorgius.who: Claude Mydorge (1585–1647), French mathematician and friend of Descartes, who worked on optics and the grinding of lenses.

Myndus.who: Myndus, an ancient Greek town in Caria near Halicarnassus, on the south-west coast of Asia Minor (modern Gümüşlük, Turkey).

Myrilla.basis: Probably a character in a late-Greek anecdote or letter collection, but the source is not certain.

Myrobalans.who: Myrobalans, dried plum-like fruits of East Indian trees (chiefly Terminalia), used as gentle purges.

Myrsine.who: Myrsine, a legendary Attic maiden in the Byzantine Geoponica; killed by envious companions, she was turned into the myrtle.

Myrta.basis: Burton's source is Nicholas Bellus; the mistress of Dionysius is otherwise unknown to me.

Myrtala.who: Myrtala, a fictional lover of Pamphilus in the Love Letters of Aristaenetus (5th–6th century AD).

Mysia.who: Mysia, a region of north-western Asia Minor (now Turkey) that included Pergamum.

Mytilene.who: Mytilene, the chief city of the island of Lesbos in the Aegean.

Mytilenean.who: The people of Mytilene on Lesbos.

Myunte.who: Myus, an ancient Ionian city near Miletus in Asia Minor; Xerxes gave its revenues to Themistocles.

Nabal.who: Nabal, the churlish rich man of 1 Samuel 25, husband of Abigail; his name means 'fool'.

Naiades.who: The Naiads, Greek nymphs of springs, rivers and fresh water.

Name.basis: An ordinary word in a heading.

Nancy.who: In the first passage, Nancy, the capital of the duchy of Lorraine, north-eastern France; in the second, a girl's name.

Naomi.who: Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law in the biblical Book of Ruth.

Napier’s Logarithms.who: The logarithm tables of John Napier (1550–1617), Scottish mathematician, first published as Mirifici logarithmorum canonis descriptio (1614).

Naples.who: Naples, city and kingdom of southern Italy.

Narbonne.who: Narbonne, a city in Languedoc, southern France.

Narcissus.who: Narcissus, the freedman and powerful favourite of Emperor Claudius; elsewhere, the mythical youth who loved his reflection, and the flower named after him.

Narsetes.who: Narses (c. 478–573), Byzantine eunuch general under Justinian who completed the reconquest of Italy from the Goths.

Narsinga.who: Narsinga, the European name for the Hindu kingdom of Vijayanagara in southern India.

Nasonem.who: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso, 43 BC–AD 17/18), Roman poet, author of the Remedia amoris.

Nat. Comes.who: Natale Conti (Natalis Comes, c.1520–1582), Italian humanist and mythographer, author of the *Mythologiae*, a standard handbook of classical myth.

Natalis.who: Jerónimo Nadal (Hieronymus Natalis, 1507–1580), Spanish Jesuit whose engraved meditations on the Sunday and feast-day Gospels were published at Antwerp.

Natural.basis: term of art (natural spirits, natural dreams)

Naupactus.who: Naupactus, ancient port on the north shore of the Gulf of Corinth; modern Nafpaktos (Italian Lepanto), Greece.

Nausicaa.who: Nausicaa, Phaeacian princess in Homer's *Odyssey*, daughter of King Alcinous, who plays at ball with her maids when she finds Odysseus.

Navarra.basis: a physician consulted alongside Montanus; not otherwise known to me

Navarre.who: Navarre, kingdom in the western Pyrenees, now a region of northern Spain, with its capital at Pamplona.

Navarrus.who: Martín de Azpilcueta, 'Doctor Navarrus' (1492–1586), Spanish canon lawyer and moral theologian, author of a widely used manual for confessors on cases of conscience.

Nazianzen.who: Gregory of Nazianzus (c.329–390), Cappadocian Church Father, bishop and theologian.

Neaera.basis: both passages use the conventional poetic name, but in poems by different authors
Neaera.who: Neaera, a stock name for a poet's mistress in Latin love poetry, used here by Renaissance Latin poets, among them George Buchanan.

Neander.basis: the Orbis terrae description fits Michael Neander; Jocoseria is a known jest-book by Melander, so Burton has probably confused the names
Neander.who: In the geographical note: Michael Neander (1525–1595), German schoolmaster and geographer; the jest-book 'de Jocoseriis' seems to be Otto Melander's *Jocoseria*.

Neander de Jocoseriis.basis: the title matches Melander's well-known jest-book; Neander and Melander are easily confused
Neander de Jocoseriis.who: Probably the *Jocoseria*, a Latin collection of jests and comic tales by the German jurist Otto Melander, here credited to 'Neander'.

Nebuchadnezzar.who: Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 605–562 BC), king of Babylon; the Book of Daniel says he was driven out to eat grass like an ox.

Nebuchadnezzars.who: Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon, who in the Book of Daniel lived like a beast. Burton uses the plural for men who shun human company.

Neckar.who: The Neckar, a river of south-west Germany that flows through Heidelberg to join the Rhine at Mannheim.

Necker.who: The Neckar, a river of south-west Germany and a tributary of the Rhine.

Nectar.basis: common noun, the drink of the gods

Negro.who: Black Africans, in the period's usage.

Negroes.who: Black Africans, in the period's usage.

Nell.basis: generic girl's name in an alliterative list

Nemean.who: The Nemean Games, one of the four Panhellenic festivals, held at Nemea in the north-eastern Peloponnese.

Nemesis.who: Nemesis, Greek goddess of retribution, who punishes arrogance and wrongdoing.

Neoptolemus.who: Neoptolemus (Pyrrhus), son of Achilles, whom Priam calls 'degenerate' in Virgil's *Aeneid* II for killing him at the altar.

Nepenthes.who: Nepenthes, the drug that banishes grief, which Helen mixes into the wine in Homer's *Odyssey* IV; she had it from Polydamna, wife of Thon of Egypt.

Nepotian.who: Nepotian (d. 396), priest and nephew of Bishop Heliodorus; Jerome sent him a letter on the clerical life and later wrote his memorial letter.

Neptune.who: Neptune, Roman god of the sea, identified with the Greek Poseidon.

Neptunia Doris.who: Doris, sea-nymph, daughter of Oceanus, wife of Nereus and mother of the Nereids.

Nequir.who: Nakir, who with Munkar makes up the pair of angels that in Islamic belief question the dead in the grave.

Nero.who: Nero (37–68), Roman emperor 54–68, notorious for cruelty and extravagance.

Nero Sporus.who: Sporus, the youth whom the emperor Nero (37–68) had castrated and then 'married'.

Neros.who: Nero (37–68), Roman emperor; the plural means tyrants like him.

Nero’s Massa.basis: the identity of Nero's favourite Massa is uncertain

Nero’s Poppaea.who: Poppaea Sabina (d. 65), Nero's second wife, famous for her luxury and care for her beauty.

Nessus.who: Nessus, the centaur killed by Hercules for assaulting Deianira; his poisoned blood later caused Hercules' death.

Nestor.who: Nestor, the aged king of Pylos in Homer, a byword for long life and wise counsel.

Nestorians.who: The Nestorians, Eastern Christians of the Church of the East, named after the condemned patriarch Nestorius (5th century).

Neuberg.basis: Several German towns are called Neuburg; the passage does not settle which one.

Neuhusius.basis: The Rosicrucian context and the name fit his tract on the brethren of the Rosy Cross.
Neuhusius.who: Henricus Neuhusius (Heinrich Neuhaus), German writer whose 1618 admonition on the Rosicrucians questioned whether the brotherhood existed.

Neuwaldus.basis: He is the Neuwaldus usually listed among sceptical writers on witches, alongside Ewich.
Neuwaldus.who: Hermann Neuwaldt, German author of a 1584 tract against the cold-water ordeal for witches.

Nevisanus.who: Giovanni Nevizzano (d. 1540), Italian jurist of Asti, author of the *Sylva nuptialis*, a satirical treatise on marriage.

New England.who: New England, the region of north-eastern North America named by John Smith in 1616.

Newark.who: Newark-on-Trent in Nottinghamshire, where Bishop Alexander of Lincoln built a castle.

Nic. Biesius.who: Nicolaus Biesius (1516–1572), Flemish physician and philosopher of Ghent who taught at Louvain and wrote *De republica*.

Nic. Gerbelius.who: Nikolaus Gerbel (c. 1485–1560), Strasbourg humanist and jurist, author of a description of Greece written to accompany Nikolaos Sophianos's map.

Nic. Harpsfield.who: Nicholas Harpsfield (c. 1519–1575), English Catholic archdeacon of Canterbury, author of a Latin ecclesiastical history of England.

Nic. Piso.who: Nicolas Le Pois (Piso) (1527–1587), physician of Lorraine, author of a widely used practical handbook of diseases and their cure.

Nicanor.basis: Several ancient men named Nicanor; it is not clear which one was killed by his wife.

Nicedia.who: Nicedia, one of the courtesans whom Plutarch names among Epicurus's associates.

Niceratus.who: Niceratus, son of the Athenian general Nicias; in Xenophon's *Symposium* he says his father made him learn all of Homer.

Nich. de Lynna.who: Nicholas of Lynn (fl. 14th century), Carmelite friar of King's Lynn, said to have described the Arctic regions in the lost *Inventio fortunata* that Mercator cited.

Nicholaites.who: The Nicolaitans, an early Christian sect condemned in Revelation, traditionally traced to Nicholas the Deacon of Acts 6.

Nicholas.who: Different bearers: Pope Nicholas III (r. 1277–1280); Niccolò Cabeo, Jesuit writer on magnetism; and Nicholas the Deacon (Acts 6), reputed founder of the Nicolaitans.

Nicholas Cabeus.who: Niccolò Cabeo (1586–1650), Jesuit natural philosopher of Ferrara, author of *Philosophia magnetica* (1629).

Nicholas Carr.who: Nicholas Carr (1524–1568), Regius Professor of Greek at Cambridge, whose oration on the scarcity of British writers was published in 1576.

Nicholas Damascen.who: Nicolaus of Damascus (1st century BC), Greek historian and philosopher, friend and adviser of Herod the Great.

Nicholas Gerbelius.who: Nikolaus Gerbel (c. 1485–1560), Strasbourg humanist and jurist, author of a description of Greece in which he praises recovered Greek authors.

Nicholas Laurentius.basis: A Protestant writer of consolations; I cannot tell which one is meant.

Nicholas Leonicus.who: Niccolò Leonico Tomeo (1456–1531), Venetian humanist and professor at Padua, author of *De varia historia*.

Nicholas Myrepsus.who: Nicholas Myrepsus (fl. 13th century), Byzantine physician whose large compilation of remedies was used in the West as an antidotarium.

Nicholas Nemo.who: A joke figure, 'Mr Nobody', built from proverbial Latin sayings that begin with *nemo* ('nobody').

Nicholas Piso.who: Nicolas Le Pois (Piso) (1527–1587), physician of Lorraine, author of a widely used practical handbook of diseases and their cure.

Nicholas Raimarus.who: Nicolaus Reimers Ursus (1551–1600), astronomer from Dithmarschen whose geoheliocentric system led to a priority quarrel with Tycho Brahe.

Nicholas Sanders.who: Nicholas Sander (c. 1530–1581), English Catholic polemicist, author of *De origine ac progressu schismatis Anglicani*, a hostile account of Henry VIII.

Nicholas’ Bourges.basis: The form looks corrupt; I cannot be sure which shrine of St Nicholas is meant.

Nicias.who: Nicias (d. 413 BC), Athenian general and statesman whose superstitious delay brought disaster on the Sicilian expedition.

Nicomachus.basis: Aelian gives this anecdote about the painter Nicomachus.
Nicomachus.who: Nicomachus (4th century BC), Greek painter who told a man criticising Zeuxis's Helen to take his eyes and see a goddess.

Nicostrata.who: Nicostrata, the Arcadian prophetess also called Carmenta, mother of Evander.

Nicostratus.basis: Stobaeus's marriage sections quote long prose passages under this name; it is not the comic poet.
Nicostratus.who: Nicostratus, Greek moralist of the Roman period whose prose sayings on marriage are preserved in Stobaeus.

Nidrose.who: Nidaros, the medieval name of Trondheim in Norway; the temple is its cathedral, the shrine of St Olaf.

Niger.who: Different bearers: first Domenico Mario Negri (Dominicus Marius Niger), Venetian geographer of the 16th century; second the river Niger in West Africa.

Nigidius Figulus.who: Publius Nigidius Figulus (d. 45 BC), Roman scholar and Neopythagorean, famous for astrology and occult learning.

Niklashausen.who: Niklashausen, a village in the Tauber valley in Franconia, where the herdsman Hans Böhm drew great crowds of pilgrims with his preaching in 1476.

Ninus.who: Ninus, legendary founder of Nineveh and the Assyrian empire, husband of Semiramis; to the ancients the first great conqueror.

Niobe.who: Niobe, in Greek myth the queen of Thebes whose children Apollo and Artemis killed; weeping for them, she was turned to stone.

Nireus.who: Nireus, king of Syme, called in Homer's Iliad (book 2) the handsomest Greek at Troy after Achilles.

Nisus.who: Nisus, Trojan companion of Aeneas whose devoted friendship with Euryalus, and death beside him, Virgil tells in Aeneid 9.

Noah.who: Noah, the biblical patriarch of the Flood, who got drunk and lay uncovered (Genesis 9).

Nodina.who: Nodina (Nodutus), minor Roman deity of the knots or joints of growing corn stalks, mocked by Augustine in the City of God.

Nokow.basis: Polish place near Pałuki in Münster's Cosmographia; could not identify it with confidence

Nomades.who: The Nomads, the wandering herding peoples (especially Scythians) whom classical writers describe living on mare's milk and blood.

Nombre de Dios.who: Nombre de Dios, Spanish port on the Caribbean coast of Panama, the Atlantic end of the route across the isthmus.

Nominals.who: The Nominalists, scholastic philosophers (e.g. Ockham's followers) who held universals to be mere names, opposed to the Realists.

Nonius.basis: different bearers: Pedro Nunes (Nonius Salaciensis), the mathematician; Nonius the senator in Pliny, owner of the opal; and an unclear marginal citation

Nordeling.who: Nördlingen, town in Swabia (now Bavaria, Germany), known for its annual fair.

Norman.who: The Normans, who conquered England in 1066 and built its great castles and abbeys.

Normandy.who: Normandy, region and former duchy in north-west France.

Northamptonshire.who: Northamptonshire, county in the English Midlands.

Norumbega.who: Norumbega, a half-legendary region on early maps of north-east America, roughly present-day Maine and New England.

Norway.who: Norway, the Scandinavian kingdom, ruled from Denmark in Burton's time.

Norwegians.who: The Norwegians, the people of Norway.

Norwich.who: Norwich, cathedral city and county town of Norfolk, England.

Nottinghamshire.who: Nottinghamshire, county in the English Midlands.

Nova Albion.who: Nova Albion ('New Albion'), the name Francis Drake gave in 1579 to the Pacific coast of North America he claimed, in present-day California.

Nova Francia.who: Nova Francia, New France: French North America, chiefly Canada.

Nova Hispania.who: Nova Hispania, New Spain: the Spanish viceroyalty centred on Mexico.

Nova Zembla.who: Nova Zembla, Novaya Zemlya, Arctic archipelago north of Russia where Barentsz's Dutch crew wintered in 1596–97.

Novem Judices.who: The Liber novem iudicum ('Book of the Nine Judges'), a medieval Latin compilation of Arabic astrological judgements.

Nubia.who: Nubia, region of the Nile valley south of Egypt, in modern Sudan.

Nubian Geography.who: The Geographia Nubiensis (Paris, 1619), a Latin translation of an abridged Arabic geography by al-Idrisi, then wrongly thought to be by a Nubian.

Nubrigensis.who: William of Newburgh (1136–c.1198), Augustinian canon and English chronicler, author of the Historia rerum Anglicarum.

Numa.who: Numa Pompilius, legendary second king of Rome and founder of its religious institutions, said to be advised by the nymph Egeria.

Numbers.who: Numbers, the fourth book of the Old Testament.

Numidia.who: Numidia, ancient kingdom of North Africa, roughly modern Algeria, ruled by Masinissa.

Nunquir.who: Munkar, one of the two angels (Munkar and Nakir) who in Islamic tradition question and punish the dead in the grave.

Nuremberg.who: Nuremberg, free imperial city in Franconia, southern Germany, famed for its craftsmen and trade.

Nuremburg.who: Nuremberg, imperial city in Franconia, Germany, home of Basilius Besler, whose Hortus Eystettensis (1613) is the herbal meant.

Nymannus.who: Gregor Nymann (1594–1638), Wittenberg physician, author of an oration on the imagination (De imaginatione) and of a treatise on the life of the foetus.

Nymphs.who: The nymphs, female nature spirits of classical myth who live in woods, waters and mountains.

Nysa.who: Nysa, a shepherdess in Virgil's eighth Eclogue who is married to Mopsus; afterwards a stock name in pastoral poetry.

Nyssa.who: Nysa, an ancient city in Caria near Tralles in the Maeander valley, now ruins near Sultanhisar in western Turkey.

O Clotho.who: Clotho, one of the three Fates (Moirai), the one who spins the thread of life.

O Egypt.who: Egypt, addressed in the lament of the Hermetic Asclepius.

O Tantalus.who: Tantalus, the mythical king punished in Hades with endless hunger and thirst.

Oby.who: The Ob, a great river of western Siberia that flows north into the Arctic Ocean (Gulf of Ob).

Ocean Decades.who: De orbe novo decades by Peter Martyr d'Anghiera (1457–1526), an early history of the Spanish discoveries in the New World, translated into English by Richard Eden.

Ochim.who: The ochim, Hebrew name of creatures haunting ruined Babylon in Isaiah 13:21 ('doleful creatures' in the King James Version), often read as demons.
