Ockham.who: William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347), English Franciscan scholastic philosopher and theologian, leader of the nominalists.

Octavia.who: First passage: Claudia Octavia (d. 62), Nero's wife, whom he divorced and had killed; second: Octavia the Younger, Augustus's sister and Mark Antony's wife.

Octaviano.who: Octavius, a Latin Christian apologetic dialogue by Minucius Felix (2nd or 3rd century).

Octavianus.who: Octavian, later the emperor Augustus (63 BC–AD 14), Julius Caesar's adopted heir.

Octavius Horatianus.who: Theodorus Priscianus (fl. c. 400), late Roman physician whose Latin medical books were printed in the 16th century under the name Octavius Horatianus.

Odyss.who: Homer's Odyssey; book Δ (4) describes Menelaus's palace and Helen's drug nepenthes.

Oenanthe.who: Oenanthe (late 3rd century BC), mother of Agathocles and Agathoclea, powerful at the court of Ptolemy IV Philopator of Egypt.

Oeneus.who: Oeneus, mythical king of Calydon in Aetolia and father of Meleager; Artemis sent the Calydonian boar to punish him.

Oenomaus.who: Oenomaus, mythical king of Pisa in Elis, who killed his daughter Hippodamia's suitors after chariot races until Pelops defeated him.

Oenone.who: Oenone, a nymph of Mount Ida and Paris's first wife, whom he abandoned for Helen.

Ofellius Bibulus.basis: the epitaph-drinker cannot be securely identified

Ogyges.who: Ogyges, a primeval mythical king of Boeotia or Attica, in whose reign the first great flood took place; a byword for remote antiquity.

Olaus Magnus.who: Olaus Magnus (1490–1557), Swedish Catholic archbishop of Uppsala in exile, author of the Historia de gentibus septentrionalibus (1555).

Oldbury.who: Oldbury, a hill with an Iron Age camp near Hartshill and Mancetter in north Warwickshire, close to Burton's birthplace at Lindley.

Oliver.who: Oliver, legendary paladin of Charlemagne and Roland's companion in the Song of Roland.

Oliver à Nort.who: Olivier van Noort (1558–1627), Dutch navigator and the first Dutchman to sail round the world (1598–1601).

Olympia.basis: Chrysostom's letters to Olympias in the first passage; Philip's queen in the second
Olympia.who: Two women named Olympias: the deaconess of Constantinople (d. c. 408) to whom Chrysostom wrote letters, and Olympias, wife of Philip II of Macedon and mother of Alexander.

Olympian.who: The Olympic games, held every four years at Olympia in Elis in honour of Zeus.

Olympics.who: The Olympic games, the ancient Greek athletic festival at Olympia in honour of Zeus.

Olympus.who: Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece, on the border of Macedonia and Thessaly.

Olynthian.who: The people of Olynthus, a Greek city in Chalcidice that Philip II of Macedon took and destroyed in 348 BC, enslaving its inhabitants.

Ombos.who: Ombos (Ombi), a town in Upper Egypt whose religious feud with neighbouring Tentyra (Dendera) is the subject of Juvenal's fifteenth satire.

Omphale.who: Omphale, mythical queen of Lydia, whom Hercules served as a slave, dressed as a woman and spinning wool.

Ophir.who: Ophir, the biblical land from which Solomon's fleet brought gold (1 Kings 9–10); its location is unknown and was much disputed.

Opimius.who: Lucius Opimius, Roman consul in 121 BC, who crushed Gaius Gracchus and Marcus Fulvius Flaccus and their followers.

Oppia.who: The Lex Oppia (215 BC), a Roman sumptuary law limiting women's gold and finery; it was repealed in 195 BC despite Cato's opposition.

Oppian.who: Oppian, Greek poet (early 3rd century AD) to whom the hunting poem *Cynegetica* is ascribed; he is now distinguished from the Cilician author of the *Halieutica*.

Orcades.who: The Orkney Islands, off the north coast of Scotland (Latin Orcades).

Orchomenian Strato.who: Strato of Orchomenus in Boeotia, the rich suitor of Aristocleia in the first of the Plutarchan *Love Stories* (Amatoriae narrationes).

Oreades.who: The Oreads, the mountain nymphs of Greek mythology.

Orenoque.who: The Orinoco, the great river of Venezuela in northern South America.

Orestes.who: Orestes, son of Agamemnon, who killed his mother Clytemnestra and was driven mad by the Furies.

Oribasius.who: Oribasius of Pergamum (c. 320–c. 400), Greek physician to the emperor Julian, who compiled the large *Collectiones medicae* largely from Galen.

Orientales.who: Latin: the 'eastern' peoples, which the passage glosses as Greeks, Italians, Africans and Asians.

Origan.who: David Origanus (David Tost, 1558–c. 1629), German astronomer and astrologer at Frankfurt an der Oder, author of *Ephemerides*.

Origanus.who: David Origanus (David Tost, 1558–c. 1629), professor at Frankfurt an der Oder, astrologer and author of *Ephemerides*; he accepted the earth's daily rotation.

Origen.who: Origen (c. 185–c. 254), Alexandrian Christian theologian and biblical commentator, author of a commentary and homilies on the Song of Songs.

Orion.basis: listed with Perseus among ancient royal astronomers; no historical astronomer-king of this name is known to me
Orion.who: Orion, the mythical hunter, here apparently treated as a royal astronomer of antiquity, as Perseus is in the same list.

Orlando.who: Orlando (Roland), hero of Ariosto's *Orlando furioso* (1516–32), who goes mad for love of Angelica.

Orleans.who: In the first passage, the house of Orléans (the Armagnac party), in a 15th-century feud with Burgundy; in the second, the city of Orléans on the Loire.

Ormus.who: Hormuz, an island trading port at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, held by the Portuguese from 1515 to 1622.

Orontius.who: Oronce Finé (Orontius Finaeus, 1494–1555), French mathematician and cartographer, professor at the Collège royal in Paris.

Orpheum Venus.basis: Latin construction 'apud Orpheum' followed by the subject Venus
Orpheum Venus.who: Not a single name: 'apud Orpheum… Venus' means Venus as she appears in the Orphic Hymns, which call her the companion of Bacchus.

Orpheus.who: Orpheus, the legendary Thracian singer and poet who went down to Hades for Eurydice; theological poems were later ascribed to him.

Orpheus Junior.who: William Vaughan (1575–1641), Welsh writer and promoter of the Cambriol colony in Newfoundland, who published *The Golden Fleece* (1626) as 'Orpheus Junior'.

Orson.who: Orson, the twin brother who is raised by a bear in the medieval French romance *Valentine and Orson*.

Ortelius Itinerario.who: The *Itinerarium per nonnullas Galliae Belgicae partes* (1584) by Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598), the Antwerp cartographer, an account of a journey through Lorraine and the Low Countries.

Ortelius. Egypt.who: Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598), Antwerp geographer and author of the atlas *Theatrum orbis terrarum*; 'Egypt' begins the next sentence.

Osiander.basis: He is named with the Protestant church historians (Magdeburg Centuriators, Chemnitz, Bale); Andreas Osiander cannot be ruled out for the first passage
Osiander.who: Lucas Osiander the Elder (1534–1604), Lutheran theologian of Württemberg and author of an *Epitome* of church history drawn from the Magdeburg Centuries.

Osiris.who: Osiris, the Egyptian god of the dead and husband of Isis.

Osorius.basis: The bare Latin name in a theological passage on the beatific vision fits Osório, Burton's usual 'Osorius'.
Osorius.who: Jerónimo Osório (1506–1580), Portuguese humanist and bishop of Silves, author of Latin moral and theological treatises.

Ostend.who: Ostend, port in Flanders (Belgium), besieged by the Spanish from 1601 to 1604 at enormous cost in lives.

Ostia.who: Ostia, the ancient port of Rome at the mouth of the Tiber.

Ostracism.who: Ostracism, the Athenian practice of banishing a citizen for ten years by popular vote.

Oswald. Crollius.who: Oswald Croll (c. 1560–1609), German Paracelsian physician and chemist, author of the *Basilica chymica*.

Osyris.who: Osiris, Egyptian god of the dead, said by euhemerist writers to have been a deified king.

Otacousticon.who: Otacousticon, a hypothetical ear-trumpet or instrument for magnifying hearing, the aural counterpart of the telescope.

Otacousticons.who: Otacousticons, hypothetical instruments for magnifying hearing, the aural counterpart of telescopes.

Otho.who: Otho (32–69), Roman emperor for three months in 69, who killed himself after his defeat by Vitellius.

Otho Nicholson.who: Otho Nicholson (d. 1622), Oxford benefactor who built the Carfax Conduit and the city's water supply and paid for refitting Christ Church library.

Otranto.who: Otranto, port town in Apulia at the heel of Italy.

Otto Herwardus.basis: Probably a member of the Herwart patrician family of Augsburg, but I cannot identify the individual.

Ottomans.who: The Ottomans, the ruling dynasty of the Turkish empire.

Otus.who: Otus, one of the Aloadae, giant sons of Poseidon who, with his brother Ephialtes, tried to storm heaven by piling Ossa on Olympus.

Ouse.basis: Several English rivers bear the name, and the passage does not say which is meant.
Ouse.who: The Ouse, an English river: probably the Great Ouse (through Bedford and Ely) or the Yorkshire Ouse (through York).

Outward.who: An anatomical heading word ('outward' parts and faculties), not a name.

Ovidium.who: Ovid (43 BC–AD 17/18), Roman poet; the Pygmalion story is in *Metamorphoses* 10.

Ovid’s Metamorphosis.who: Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, a Latin poem of mythological transformations.

Owen.who: Sir Owen (Owein), knight of the 12th-century legend of St Patrick's Purgatory, who went down into Purgatory and returned, as told by Matthew Paris and others.

Owen Tudor.who: Owen Tudor (c. 1400–1461), Welsh courtier who married Catherine of Valois, widow of Henry V; grandfather of Henry VII.

Oxford.who: Oxford, English university city, home of Burton's college, Christ Church.

Oxfordshire.who: Oxfordshire, the English county around Oxford.

Oxon.who: Oxon, Latin abbreviation (Oxonia, Oxoniensis) for Oxford, used for the city, its university and its diocese ('Bishop Oxon' = Bishop of Oxford).

Oxus.who: The Oxus, the modern Amu Darya, a great Central Asian river now flowing into the Aral Sea, thought in Burton's day to feed the Caspian.

Ozimen.who: Uthman ibn Affan (d. 656), third caliph after Muhammad.

P. Bayrus.who: Pietro Bairo (1468–1558), physician of Turin, author of the practical medical handbook *De medendis humani corporis malis*.

P. Cnemiander.basis: Cited from Hildesheim's Spicilegia; I know little else about him.
P. Cnemiander.who: Petrus Cnemiander, 16th-century physician whose consultations on melancholy are printed in Hildesheim's *Spicilegia*.

P. Cnemiandrus.basis: Cited from Hildesheim; same physician as the 'Cnemiander' form.
P. Cnemiandrus.who: Petrus Cnemiander, 16th-century physician whose consultations on melancholy are printed in Hildesheim's *Spicilegia*.

P. Comestor.who: Peter Comestor (d. c. 1178), French theologian, author of the *Historia scholastica*; legend made him a brother of Peter Lombard and Gratian, born out of wedlock.

P. Crescentius.who: Pietro de' Crescenzi (c. 1233–c. 1320), Bolognese jurist, author of the agricultural treatise *Ruralia commoda*.

P. Forestus.who: Pieter van Foreest (Forestus, 1521–1597), Dutch physician of Delft and Alkmaar, author of the many-volume *Observationes et curationes medicinales*.

P. Gillius.who: Pierre Gilles (1490–1555), French naturalist and topographer, author of descriptions of Constantinople and the Bosporus.

P. Jovius.who: Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), Italian historian and bishop of Nocera, whose works include a *Descriptio Britanniae*.

P. Lombard.who: Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), theologian and bishop of Paris, author of the *Sentences*; legend made him illegitimate.

P. Martyr.who: Peter Martyr Vermigli (1499–1562), Italian Protestant reformer and theologian, later Regius Professor of Divinity at Oxford.

P. Martyr Ocean. Decad.who: The *Decades de orbe novo* (Ocean Decades) of Peter Martyr d'Anghiera (1457–1526), the early history of the Spanish discovery of America.

P. Monavius.who: Peter Monau (Monavius, 1551–1588), Silesian physician of Breslau, whose medical letters appear in Scholz's collection of *Epistolae*.

P. Morales.basis: Burton calls him a Spanish Jesuit and cites a work on Jesus and Mary; I am unsure of the exact title and dates.
P. Morales.who: Pedro Morales, Spanish Jesuit theologian, author of a commentary on the opening of St Matthew treating Christ and the Virgin Mary.

P. Mutianus.who: Publius Licinius Crassus Dives Mucianus (consul 131 BC), Roman jurist and pontifex maximus, proverbial for his five chief blessings.

Padua.who: Padua, city in the Veneto, north-east Italy, seat of a famous university.

Padus.who: Padus, the Latin name of the Po, the great river of northern Italy.

Paetus.who: Caecina Paetus (d. 42), Roman consular ordered to die after Scribonianus' revolt; his wife Arria stabbed herself first, saying 'Paete, non dolet'.

Pagae.who: Pagae, ancient port of the Megarid on the Gulf of Corinth, near modern Alepochori, Greece.

Palaemon.who: Quintus Remmius Palaemon (1st century AD), Roman grammarian and teacher, notorious in Suetonius for his arrogance.

Palamon.who: Palamon, Theban knight in Chaucer's Knight's Tale, rival of Arcite for the love of Emily.

Palatinate.who: The Rhenish (Lower) Palatinate, the Elector Palatine's territory on the Rhine and Neckar around Heidelberg, Germany.

Palearius.who: Aonio Paleario (c. 1503–1570), Italian humanist, author of De animorum immortalitate; executed in Rome for heresy.

Paling.basis: Burton's usual abbreviated marginal citation of Palingenius
Paling.who: Marcellus Palingenius Stellatus (Pier Angelo Manzolli, d. c. 1543), Italian poet, author of the moralising Latin poem Zodiacus vitae.

Palladius.basis: Ammianus book 29 uses 'coagulum omnium aerumnarum' of Palladius
Palladius.who: Palladius, 4th-century imperial official whom Ammianus Marcellinus (book 29) shows caught up as informer in the treason and magic trials under Valens.

Pallas.who: Pallas Athena, virgin goddess of wisdom (Roman Minerva).

Pallas Palladium.basis: Phidias is credited; Burton's phrase is loose
Pallas Palladium.who: The Parthenon temple of Pallas Athena at Athens, or Phidias' great statue of Athena within it.

Pallor.who: Pallor, Roman personification of pallor or terror, to whom with Pavor Tullus Hostilius vowed shrines.

Pallukie.basis: form and pairing with Nokow (Nakło) fit
Pallukie.who: Pałuki, a district of Greater Poland around Żnin, near Nakło.

Palsy. Bodin.who: Jean Bodin (1530–1596), French jurist and political philosopher, author of Les six livres de la République.

Palumbus.who: Palumbus, priest and necromancer in William of Malmesbury's tale of the Roman youth who put a ring on a statue of Venus.

Pamphila.who: Pamphila, the girl loved by Chaerea in Terence's comedy Eunuchus.

Pamphilus.basis: stock lover's name: Terence's Andria (lover of Glycerium) and Aristaenetus' letters

Pamplona.who: Pamplona, capital of Navarre in northern Spain, besieged by the French in 1521.

Pan.who: Pan, Greek god of shepherds and flocks, son of Hermes.

Panacius.who: Panacius, physician in a love letter of Aristaenetus (1.13) who finds out Charicles' love from his pulse.

Panama.who: Panama, on the isthmus between the Caribbean and the Pacific.

Panareta.who: Panareta, young woman in one of Aristaenetus' love letters, loved by Speusippus after he saw her dance.

Panathenaeis.who: The Panathenaea, the great Athenian festival in honour of Athena.

Panciroli.who: Guido Panciroli (1523–1599), Italian jurist, author of Rerum memorabilium deperditarum et nuper inventarum, on lost and newly invented things.

Pancrates.who: Pancrates, Egyptian magician in Lucian's Philopseudes, source of the sorcerer's apprentice story.

Pandora.who: Pandora, first woman in Greek myth, given gifts by all the gods.

Pandulphus.who: Pandulf Verraccio (d. 1226), papal legate to England who received King John's submission in 1213; later Bishop of Norwich.

Panegyr.who: Pliny the Younger's Panegyricus, his speech in praise of the Emperor Trajan (AD 100).

Panthea.who: Panthea, beautiful and faithful wife of Abradatas in Xenophon's Cyropaedia, whom Cyrus refused to see.

Pantheon.basis: The second passage names Rome. The first, set in Athens and tied to a builder like Callicrates, points to the Parthenon.
Pantheon.who: The Pantheon at Rome, temple of all the gods built by Agrippa and rebuilt under Hadrian; the Athenian 'Pantheon' of the first passage seems to mean the Parthenon.

Panyasis.who: Panyassis of Halicarnassus (5th century BC), Greek epic poet and kinsman of Herodotus; Athenaeus quotes his verses on wine.

Papinius.who: Publius Papinius Statius (c. 45–c. 96), Roman poet, author of the *Thebaid* and the *Silvae*.

Papirius Massonius.who: Jean-Papire Masson (1544–1611), French historian who wrote lives of the popes.

Papists.who: Roman Catholics, so called by their Protestant opponents.

Paquin.who: Peking (modern Beijing), the capital of China, which Ricci identified with Marco Polo's Cambaluc.

Paracelsians.who: Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), the Swiss physician whose chemical medicine and spirit-filled cosmology challenged Galenic teaching.

Paradin.who: Claude Paradin (d. 1573), French cleric and author of the *Devises héroïques* (1551), a book of emblems and devices.

Paradise.who: Part of the common name 'birds of paradise'.

Parastatae.who: Parastatai, 'those who stand by': a Greek name for protecting or assisting tutelary gods.

Pariacaca.who: Pariacaca, a high snow-capped range in the Peruvian Andes east of Lima, famous from José de Acosta's account of mountain sickness.

Paridell.who: Paridell, a faithless knight in Books III and IV of Spenser's *The Faerie Queene*.

Paris. Frederick.basis: A mis-split form made from 'Paris' and 'Frederick', which belong to separate sentences.

Parma.who: Parma, a city in northern Italy.

Parmenio.who: Parmenion (c. 400–330 BC), Macedonian general under Philip II and Alexander the Great, put to death on Alexander's orders.

Parmeno.who: Parmeno, the slave of the young lover Phaedria in Terence's comedy *Eunuchus*.

Parnassus.who: Mount Parnassus, in Phocis above Delphi in central Greece.

Parrhasius.who: Parrhasius of Ephesus (fl. c. 400 BC), celebrated Greek painter who worked at Athens.

Parsons’ Resolution.who: *The First Book of the Christian Exercise, appertaining to Resolution* (1582), a devotional work by the Jesuit Robert Persons (1546–1610), widely read in Protestant versions.

Parthenis.who: Parthenis, a lovesick woman who appears as a letter-writer in the *Love Letters* of Aristaenetus (late antiquity).

Parthenopaeus.who: Parthenopaeus, son of Atalanta and one of the Seven against Thebes in Greek legend.

Parthian.who: Of the Parthians, the Iranian people whose empire was Rome's great eastern rival.

Parthians.who: The Parthians, an Iranian people whose empire (c. 247 BC–AD 224) defeated Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC.

Particular.who: An ordinary word, used here as a category in Burton's scheme of causes and cures.

Particular. Primary.who: Two ordinary words, used here as categories in Burton's scheme of causes.

Pasargada.who: Pasargadae, the royal city founded by Cyrus the Great in Fars, southern Iran, and the site of his tomb.

Paschalius.basis: Burton cites this author elsewhere, and the passage is a sententious moral quotation that suits him.
Paschalius.who: Carolus Paschalius (Charles Paschal, 1547–1625), Italian-born writer in French service, author of moral and political treatises such as *De coronis*.

Pasetes.who: Pases, a legendary magician in the Suda, whose magic half-obol always returned to his purse after it was spent.

Pasion.who: Pasion, a character in Lucian's *Dialogues of the Courtesans*.

Pasiphae.who: Pasiphaë, wife of King Minos of Crete, who coupled with a bull and bore the Minotaur.

Passible.who: A term of faculty psychology for the passive, receptive understanding.

Passus.basis: Aelian and Plutarch tell the same upside-down horse anecdote of Pauson.
Passus.who: Pauson (5th century BC), Greek painter; in the ancient anecdote he painted a horse galloping and turned the picture upside down to show it rolling.

Paternoster.who: The Lord's Prayer, from its Latin opening words *Pater noster*.

Paternosters.who: Recitations of the Lord's Prayer, often counted on rosary beads.

Patient.who: An ordinary word, used here as a term of faculty psychology and as a heading.

Patricians.who: The hereditary noble class (originally of ancient Rome, here of Venice and other states) from which plebeians were excluded.

Patrick.who: St Patrick (5th century), missionary bishop and patron saint of Ireland.

Patroclus.who: Patroclus, Homeric hero and beloved companion of Achilles, killed by Hector in the Iliad.

Paul.who: St Paul the Apostle (d. c. 64–67), tentmaker by trade and author of New Testament epistles.

Paula.who: St Paula (347–404), Roman noble widow, Jerome's disciple and correspondent, who followed him to Bethlehem.

Paulina.who: Pompeia Paulina, Seneca's wife (passages 1–2); in passage 3, Paulina, Roman matron deceived by Decius Mundus in Isis's temple, as told by Josephus.

Paulini.who: Paulina, Roman matron seduced by Decius Mundus disguised as the god Anubis in Isis's temple (AD 19), as told by Josephus and Hegesippus.

Pauls.who: St Paul of Thebes (d. c. 341), the 'first hermit' of the Egyptian desert, whose Life Jerome wrote.

Paulus.who: Paul of Aegina (fl. 7th century), Byzantine Greek physician, author of a seven-book medical epitome.

Paulus Aegineta.who: Paul of Aegina (fl. 7th century), Byzantine Greek physician, author of a seven-book medical epitome.

Paulus Aemilius.who: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus (c. 229–160 BC), Roman general who defeated Perseus of Macedon at Pydna (168 BC) and sacked Epirus.

Paulus Hentzner Itiner.who: Paul Hentzner (1558–1623), German jurist, author of a Latin Itinerarium of travels through Germany, France, England and Italy (1612).

Paulus Hentznerus.who: Paul Hentzner (1558–1623), German jurist, author of a Latin Itinerarium of travels through Germany, France, England and Italy (1612).

Paul’s Cross.who: Paul's Cross, the open-air pulpit in St Paul's churchyard, London, the chief public preaching place of the age.

Peg.who: Stock pet-form of Margaret in an alliterative list of typical wives; no particular person.

Pegasus.who: Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek myth; Burton uses it for al-Buraq, the steed of Muhammad's Night Journey.

Pegu.who: Pegu, kingdom of Lower Burma, named from its capital (modern Bago, Myanmar).

Pelagia.who: St Pelagia of Antioch (d. c. 311), virgin martyr who threw herself from a roof to preserve her chastity, praised by Ambrose.

Pelagians.who: Followers of Pelagius (c. 354–c. 418), whose denial of original sin was condemned as heresy.

Pelagius.basis: several saints Pelagius; which was invoked for oxen is unclear

Pelargus.basis: possibly Christoph Pelargus, Brandenburg theologian, but not certain

Peleca.basis: Burton glosses 'Aleacman now Peleca'; Aleacman fits Haliacmon
Peleca.who: Peleca, a later name given for the ancient river Haliacmon (modern Aliakmonas) in northern Greece.

Peleus.who: Peleus, father of Achilles, here as a hero of tragedy in exile and poverty, as in Horace's Ars Poetica.

Pelion.who: Mount Pelion, mountain in Magnesia, Thessaly, Greece.

Pelopidas.who: Pelopidas (d. 364 BC), Theban general and statesman, colleague and friend of Epaminondas.

Peloponnesians.who: The inhabitants of the Peloponnese, southern Greece.

Peloponnesus.who: The Peloponnese, the southern peninsula of Greece, called the Morea in Burton's day.

Pelops.who: Pelops, son of Tantalus, who won Hippodamia by defeating her father Oenomaus in a chariot race through the treachery of Myrtilus.

Pena.who: Jean Pena (1528–1558), French mathematician whose preface to Euclid's Optics and Catoptrics (1557) denied the sphere of fire.

Peneia.who: Daphne, daughter of the river-god Peneus, the nymph who fled Apollo.

Penelope.who: Penelope, faithful wife of Odysseus (Ulysses), who put off her suitors.

Peneus.who: The Peneus (modern Pineios), chief river of Thessaly, flowing through the vale of Tempe; also its river-god.

Penia.who: Penia, Poverty personified, who in Plato's Symposium conceives Eros by Poros.

Peninnah.who: Peninnah, Elkanah's second wife, who taunted the childless Hannah (1 Samuel 1).

Penottus.who: Bernard Georges Penot (c. 1519–1617), French Paracelsian physician and alchemist.

Pentheus.who: Pentheus, mythical king of Thebes who spurned Dionysus and was torn apart by the maenads, including his mother Agave.

Pera.who: Pera (Galata/Beyoğlu), the hillside quarter across the Golden Horn from Constantinople (Istanbul).

Pergamum.who: Pergamum, city of Mysia in north-west Asia Minor, Galen's birthplace (modern Bergama, Turkey).

Pergamus.who: Pergamum (Pergamon), Hellenistic kingdom and city in north-western Asia Minor, modern Bergama in Turkey; Eumenes II was its king.

Periander.who: Periander (d. c. 585 BC), tyrant of Corinth, counted among the Seven Sages of Greece but remembered as a harsh tyrant.

Pericles.who: Pericles (c. 495–429 BC), Athenian statesman who sponsored the great building programme of the Acropolis.

Perigeo.who: Perigee, the point of a planet's orbit nearest the earth; an astronomical term.

Perigord.who: Périgord, historic region of south-western France, roughly the modern département of Dordogne.

Perioeci.who: Perioeci, a geographers' term for peoples who live on the same latitude but on opposite meridians.

Peripatetics.who: The Peripatetics, the school of Aristotle and his followers.

Periplectomenes.who: Periplectomenus, the genial old bachelor in Plautus's comedy Miles Gloriosus, who explains why he will not marry.

Perithoonta.who: Pirithous (here in the Latin accusative), Lapith hero of Greek myth, friend of Theseus; listed by Giraldi among Hercules' favourites.

Perkins.who: William Perkins (1558–1602), Cambridge Puritan theologian whose Cases of Conscience was a standard work of practical divinity.

Perox.basis: The pearl earring of Peroz is reported by Procopius, and Zonaras repeats the story; 'Perox' fits as a variant spelling.
Perox.who: Peroz I, Sasanian king of Persia (r. 459–484), famous for the great pearl he wore in his ear.

Persepolis.who: Persepolis, ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian kings, near modern Shiraz in Iran; burned by Alexander in 330 BC.

Perseus.basis: The first and third passages are clear. In the astronomers' list Perseus is probably the mythical hero, credited with astronomical knowledge.
Perseus.who: In different passages: Perseus, the Greek hero who rescued Andromeda; and Perseus (c. 212–166 BC), last king of Macedon, defeated by Aemilius Paullus.

Perseus’ Pegasus.who: Pegasus, the winged horse that sprang from the Gorgon Medusa's blood when Perseus beheaded her.

Persia.who: Persia, modern Iran; in Burton's time ruled by the Safavid shahs.

Persian.who: Persian, of Persia (modern Iran), ancient or modern.

Persian Sophies.who: The Safavid shahs of Persia, called the 'Sophy' by Europeans.

Persian Xerxes.who: Xerxes I, Achaemenid king of Persia (r. 486–465 BC), who invaded Greece in 480 BC.

Persians.who: The Persians, people of ancient and modern Persia (Iran).

Persicis.who: Persica, the history of Persia by Ctesias of Cnidus (fl. c. 400 BC), Greek physician at the Persian court; it survives in fragments.

Persina.who: Persinna, the Ethiopian queen in Heliodorus's romance Aethiopica, mother of the white-skinned heroine Chariclea.

Perspective.who: Perspective, the science of optics and visual representation.

Perspectives.who: Perspectives, i.e. optics, the science of vision.

Pertinax.who: Pertinax, Roman emperor in AD 193, son of a freedman, who rose through the army and was murdered after three months.

Peru.who: Peru, the Spanish viceroyalty in South America, famous for its silver mines at Potosí.

Peruana.who: Peru, which some commentators proposed as the biblical Ophir.

Peruzium.who: Perugia (Latin Perusia), city in Umbria, central Italy, near Lake Trasimene.

Pet. Alcionius.who: Pietro Alcionio (c. 1487–1527), Venetian humanist, author of Medices legatus, sive de exsilio, a dialogue in two books on exile.

Pet. Aretine.who: Pietro Aretino (1492–1556), Italian satirist and author of scandalous dialogues about courtesans.

Pet. Blesensis.who: Peter of Blois (c. 1135–c. 1211), French-born cleric and letter-writer who served in England and declined higher preferment.

Pet. Martyr’s Decades.who: De orbe novo decades, Peter Martyr d'Anghiera's (1457–1526) Latin history of the Spanish discoveries in the New World.

Pet. Thyraeus.who: Petrus Thyraeus (1546–1601), German Jesuit theologian, author of De locis infestis, a treatise on haunted places.

Petavius.who: Denis Pétau (Dionysius Petavius, 1583–1652), French Jesuit chronologist who attacked Scaliger in his De doctrina temporum.

Peter Abelardus.who: Peter Abelard (1079–1142), French scholastic philosopher, lover of Héloïse, who told their story in his Historia calamitatum.

Peter Aretine’s Lucretia.basis: Barth's Latin version comes from a Spanish adaptation of Aretino in which Lucrecia is the courtesan who speaks.
Peter Aretine’s Lucretia.who: Lucretia, the courtesan speaker in Kaspar Barth's Latin Pornodidascalus (1623), a dialogue derived from Pietro Aretino's Ragionamenti.

Peter Bayrus.who: Pietro Bairo (1468–1558), physician of Turin, author of a treatise on the plague.

Peter Cnemiander.basis: Physician whose consultation is cited by way of Hildesheim's Spicilegia; I cannot identify him.

Peter Dunnius.who: Piotr Włostowic ('Dunin', d. 1153), Silesian magnate, blinded by Władysław II of Poland after a joke about their wives led to a quarrel.

Peter Forestus.who: Pieter van Foreest (Petrus Forestus, 1521–1597), Dutch physician of Alkmaar, author of the many-volume Observationes medicinales.

Peter Gillius.who: Pierre Gilles (Petrus Gyllius, 1490–1555), French naturalist and topographer, author of a description of Constantinople and a Latin version of Aelian's natural history.

Peter Godefridus.basis: The references to the second and third books of a work on love fit Godefridus's De amoribus.
Peter Godefridus.who: Petrus Godefridus (Pierre Godefroy), 16th-century French jurist, author of Latin dialogues on love (De amoribus) in three books.

Peter Mattheus.who: Pierre Matthieu (1563–1621), French royal historiographer, author of a history of Louis XI.

Peter Monavius.who: Peter Monau (Petrus Monavius, 1551–1588), Silesian physician and correspondent of Crato von Krafftheim.

Peter Morales.basis: The cited Latin work on the beauty of Jesus and Mary fits the Jesuit Morales, but I am not certain of the attribution.
Peter Morales.who: Pedro Morales, Spanish Jesuit theologian of the late 16th and early 17th centuries, who wrote on Christ and the Virgin Mary.

Peter Nonius.who: Pedro Nunes (1502–1578), Portuguese mathematician and cosmographer.

Petrarch’s Laura.who: Laura, the lady celebrated in Petrarch's Italian love poems, traditionally identified as Laura de Noves.

Petronel Flash.who: Sir Petronel Flash, a penniless, swaggering knight in the comedy Eastward Ho (1605) by Chapman, Jonson and Marston.

Petronella.who: St Petronilla, early Roman virgin martyr, invoked against fevers.

Petronii Catalect.who: The Catalecta, short poems ascribed to Petronius in Renaissance editions.

Petronio.who: Petronius (d. AD 66), Roman courtier under Nero and author of the Satyricon.

Petronius Arbiter.who: Petronius Arbiter (d. AD 66), Nero's courtier and author of the Satyricon.

Petronius Catal.who: The Catalecta, short poems ascribed to Petronius in Renaissance editions.

Petronius Catalec.who: The Catalecta, short poems ascribed to Petronius in Renaissance editions.

Petronius Catalect.who: The Catalecta, short poems ascribed to Petronius in Renaissance editions.

Petronius’ Catalects.who: The Catalecta, short poems ascribed to Petronius in Renaissance editions.

Petrus Thyraeus.who: Petrus Thyraeus (1546–1601), German Jesuit theologian who wrote treatises on demoniacs, haunted places and exorcism.

Peucer.who: Caspar Peucer (1525–1602), German physician and scholar, Melanchthon's son-in-law, author of a commentary on kinds of divination.

Phaeaces.who: The Phaeacians, the pleasure-loving people of Scheria in Homer's Odyssey, proverbial for luxury.

Phaeacia.who: Phaeacia (Scheria), the island of the Phaeacians in the Odyssey, often identified with Corfu.

Phaedon.who: Plato's Phaedo, the dialogue on the immortality of the soul and the death of Socrates.

Phaedra.who: Phaedra, mythical wife of Theseus, who fell in love with her stepson Hippolytus, as in Seneca's tragedy Phaedra (Hippolytus).

Phaedria.who: Phaedria, the young lover of the courtesan Thais in Terence's comedy Eunuchus.

Phaedro.who: Plato's Phaedrus, the dialogue whose myth of the soul's cycle speaks of a 10,000-year return.

Phaerus.who: Pheros, legendary king of Egypt and son of Sesostris in Herodotus (book 2), who was struck blind and cured by a faithful wife's urine.

Phalaris.who: Phalaris (fl. c. 570–554 BC), tyrant of Acragas in Sicily, notorious for his bronze bull, and the reputed author of spurious letters.

Phaon.basis: The second and third passages clearly mean the Lesbian Phaon. The first, which names him among the successors of Aesculapius, seems to mean a different bearer that I cannot identify.
Phaon.who: Phaon, legendary ferryman of Lesbos, given beauty by Venus and loved by Sappho.

Pharaoh.who: The Pharaoh of Exodus who oppressed the Israelites in Egypt.

Pharisee.who: The self-righteous Pharisee in Christ's parable of the Pharisee and the publican (Luke 18).

Pharisees.who: The Pharisees, a Jewish religious party of the Second Temple period known for strict observance of the Law.

Pharmacop.who: The Pharmacopoea dogmaticorum restituta (1607) of Joseph Du Chesne (Quercetanus), French iatrochemical physician.

Pharsalian.who: From Pharsalus in Thessaly, where Caesar defeated Pompey in 48 BC; Burton uses it to mean battlefields of civil war.

Phayllus.basis: The first passage describes the Delphic plunderer. The second, Phayllus of Argos and King Philip, seems to mean a different man.
Phayllus.who: Phayllus, Phocian general and tyrant in the Third Sacred War (d. c. 351 BC), who plundered the treasures of Delphi.

Phemius.who: Phemius, the minstrel who sings in Odysseus's palace on Ithaca in Homer's Odyssey.

Pherecydes Syrius.who: Pherecydes of Syros (fl. 6th century BC), Greek thinker and reputed teacher of Pythagoras, said to be the first to teach the soul's immortality.

Phidias.who: Phidias (c. 480–c. 430 BC), the most celebrated Athenian sculptor, maker of the Athena Parthenos and the Olympian Zeus.

Phiditiis.who: The phiditia (syssitia), the common public messes at which Spartan citizens dined together on plain fare.

Philaenis.who: Philaenis of Samos, Greek woman to whom antiquity ascribed a notorious manual on sexual positions, fragments of which survive on papyrus.

Philebus.who: The Philebus, a dialogue of Plato on pleasure and the good, with Socrates as chief speaker.

Philematium.basis: Burton's citations point to Aristaenetus and Lucian; two different fictional characters.
Philematium.who: Philematium, a courtesan's name in Greek fiction: a letter-writer in Aristaenetus's Epistles and an ageing courtesan in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans.

Philes.who: Manuel Philes (c. 1275–c. 1345), Byzantine court poet, author of a verse treatise On the Properties of Animals.

Philinna.who: Fictional women: Philinna, the courtesan quarrelling with her lover Diphilus in Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans, and a gossip addressed in Aristaenetus's Epistles.

Philinnium.who: Philinnion, the dead girl who returned at night to the young guest Machates, in Phlegon of Tralles' Book of Marvels.

Philip Melanchthon.who: Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), German humanist and Lutheran reformer, Luther's colleague at Wittenberg.

Philippinae.who: The Philippine Islands, then a Spanish possession.

Philippus.basis: The saying 'not all the suns have yet set' is Philip V's in Livy; the battle passage seems to come from Livy too.
Philippus.who: Philip II of Macedon (382–336 BC), Demosthenes' adversary, in the first passage; elsewhere Philip V of Macedon (238–179 BC), as reported by Livy.

Philippus Arabs.who: Philip the Arab (Marcus Julius Philippus), Roman emperor 244–249, who rose from the ranks.

Philippus Beroaldus.who: Filippo Beroaldo the Elder (1453–1505), humanist and professor of rhetoric at Bologna, who married late after writing against scholars marrying.

Philippus Bonus.who: Philip the Good (1396–1467), Duke of Burgundy, of whom the story of the drunken countryman made king for a day is told.

Philippus Faber Faventinus.basis: Latin name and Faenza origin fit; work cited as Venice 1627.
Philippus Faber Faventinus.who: Filippo Fabri (Philippus Faber) of Faenza (d. 1630), Franciscan Scotist philosopher who wrote disputations against atheists.

Philippus Lansbergius.who: Philip van Lansberge (1561–1632), Dutch astronomer and minister who defended Copernican theory.

Philistines.who: The Philistines, biblical people of the southern coast of Palestine, worshippers of Dagon.

Phillida.who: Phillida, the scornful shepherdess of the popular Elizabethan ballad 'Phillida flouts me'.

Philo.basis: The second passage names Leone Ebreo's interlocutors; the others fit Philo Judaeus.
Philo.who: Philo of Alexandria, the Jewish philosopher, in the first and third passages; in the second, Filone, the lover who speaks in Leone Ebreo's Dialoghi d'amore.

Philo Judaeus.who: Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC–c. AD 50), Hellenistic Jewish philosopher and allegorical interpreter of Scripture.

Philochorus.who: Philochorus, a fictional lover who writes in the love letters of Aristaenetus.

Philolaches.who: Philolaches, the spendthrift young man in Plautus's comedy Mostellaria, who compares a man to a house.

Philologia.who: Philologia, the allegorical bride of Mercury in Martianus Capella's On the Marriage of Philology and Mercury.

Philology.who: Philology, the study of language and literature.

Philonides.who: Philonides, the fictional lover to whom Chelidonium writes in Aristaenetus's love letters.

Philonium Romanum.who: Philonium, an ancient opiate electuary named after the physician Philo of Tarsus; 'Romanum' marks one version of the recipe.

Philonius.basis: Burton derives Philonium from its inventor; the Tilianus passage is unclear.
Philonius.who: In the medical passage, Philo of Tarsus (1st century AD), Greek physician who devised the opiate philonium; the other passage refers to a work not identified here.

Philopoemen.who: Philopoemen (c. 253–183 BC), general of the Achaean League; Plutarch tells how his plain dress got him set to chop wood.

Philostratus.basis: Lives of the Sophists and Imagines Book 1 are the Elder's; Orpheus appears in the Younger Philostratus's Imagines.
Philostratus.who: Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–c. 250), Greek sophist, author of the Lives of the Sophists and the Imagines; the Orpheus picture belongs to his grandson's later Imagines.

Philostratus Lemnius.basis: Burton cites his love epistles; the 'Lemnian' tag belongs to the Philostratus family.
Philostratus Lemnius.who: Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–c. 250), Greek sophist from Lemnos, to whom a collection of erotic Letters is attributed.

Philoxenus.who: Philoxenus of Cythera (c. 435–380 BC), dithyrambic poet at the court of Dionysius I of Syracuse, sent to the quarries for criticising the tyrant's verses.

Phlebotomy.who: Bloodletting, the opening of a vein.

Phlegethon.who: Phlegethon, the river of fire in the Greek underworld.

Phlegethons.who: Phlegethon, the river of fire in the Greek underworld; used here in the plural.

Phlegm.who: Phlegm (pituita), one of the four humours.

Phocicis.who: The Phocica, Book 10 of Pausanias's Description of Greece, covering Phocis and Delphi.

Phocion.who: Phocion (c. 402–318 BC), austere Athenian general and statesman, condemned to drink hemlock by the Athenians.

Phocis.who: Phocis, a region of central Greece around Delphi and Mount Parnassus; Anticyra, famous for its hellebore, lay on its coast.

Phoebus.who: Phoebus Apollo, the Greek god of light, music and prophecy, who pursued the nymph Daphne in Ovid's Metamorphoses, book 1.

Phoenicia.who: Phoenicia, the ancient coastal land of Tyre and Sidon, roughly modern Lebanon; Europa was a Phoenician princess.

Phoenician.who: A native of Phoenicia, the ancient coastal land of Tyre and Sidon, roughly modern Lebanon.

Phoenix.basis: The two passages mean different things: a bird and a dialogue speaker
Phoenix.who: First passage: the fabulous unique bird, used figuratively for a peerless woman; second: the Phoenician traveller who talks with the vinedresser in Philostratus's Heroicus.

Phornutus.who: Lucius Annaeus Cornutus (1st century AD), Stoic philosopher whose Greek compendium of theology gives allegorical explanations of the gods.

Photinians.who: Followers of Photinus, 4th-century bishop of Sirmium, who denied Christ's pre-existence; Burton uses the name for the antitrinitarians of his own day.

Photius’ Bibliotheca.who: The Bibliotheca (Myriobiblon) of Photius (c. 810–c. 893), patriarch of Constantinople, which summarises hundreds of books he had read, many now lost.

Phrenitis.who: Phrenitis, the ancient medical term for frenzy, an acute delirium accompanied by fever.

Phrygia.who: Phrygia, an ancient region of west-central Asia Minor (Anatolia); here it includes Troy, whose walls Apollo and Neptune built for Laomedon.

Phryne.who: Phryne (4th century BC), famous Athenian courtesan and model for Praxiteles; she offered to rebuild the walls of Thebes if they bore her name.

Phylarchus.who: Phylarchus (3rd century BC), Greek historian whose sensational histories are now lost; Parthenius drew stories from them.

Phyllis.basis: The mythical Phyllis in one passage; a generic name in the others
Phyllis.who: First passage: Phyllis, the Thracian princess deserted by Demophoon in Ovid's Heroides; in the other passages it is a stock pastoral name for a sweetheart.

Piacenza.who: Piacenza, a city on the Po in Emilia-Romagna, northern Italy.

Picardus.who: Picard, the heretical preacher said to have founded the Adamite sect in Bohemia in the early fifteenth century.

Picatrix.who: Picatrix, the Latin version of the Arabic Ghayat al-hakim, an 11th-century handbook of astral magic, translated into Latin at the court of Alfonso X.

Piccolomineus.who: Francesco Piccolomini (1520–1604), Aristotelian philosopher at Padua, author of a moral philosophy divided into 'grades', and Zabarella's opponent on the soul.

Pictorius.who: Georg Pictorius (c. 1500–1569), German physician of Villingen who wrote on demons and magic.

Picus Mirandula.who: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), Italian Renaissance philosopher, author of the Disputations against Divinatory Astrology.

Piedmont.who: Piedmont, a region of north-west Italy below the Alps, then ruled by the dukes of Savoy.

Pierleonus.who: Pierleone Leoni of Spoleto (d. 1492), physician to Lorenzo de' Medici and a friend of Marsilio Ficino.

Pigafetta.who: Filippo Pigafetta (1533–1604), Italian author of a 1591 account of the kingdom of Congo, based on the report of Duarte Lopes.

Pigmalionis.who: Pygmalion, the legendary sculptor who fell in love with his ivory statue, which came to life (Ovid, Metamorphoses 10).

Pil. Ind. Mesue.basis: name of a compound medicine (Mesue's Indian pills)

Pil. Indae.basis: name of a compound medicine (Indian pills)

Pilate.who: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judaea who sentenced Christ to death.

Pindarus.who: Pindar (c. 518–c. 438 BC), Greek lyric poet of Thebes, famous for his victory odes.

Pineda.who: Juan de Pineda (1558–1637), Spanish Jesuit who wrote a large commentary on the Book of Job.

Pineus.basis: The Geoponica (11.10) tells this tale with Pan and Boreas as rivals; Burton's 'Pineus' seems to be a garbled name
Pineus.who: Probably Pan, who in the Geoponica's tale was Boreas's rival for the nymph Pitys, later turned into a pine.

Pinzonus.basis: Listed among discovering voyagers; Vicente is the Pinzón known for his own expeditions, though his brother Martín Alonso is also possible
Pinzonus.who: Vicente Yáñez Pinzón, Spanish navigator who sailed with Columbus in 1492 and later explored the coast of Brazil.

Piraeus.who: Piraeus, the port of Athens, fortified as a harbour on the advice of Themistocles.

Pirithous.who: Pirithous, legendary king of the Lapiths and devoted friend of Theseus, whom he joined in the attempt to carry off Persephone from the underworld.

Pirovanus.basis: The name appears in a list of defenders of astrology, and the Latin form fits Pirovano.
Pirovanus.who: Gabriele Pirovano, Milanese physician of the early sixteenth century, who wrote a defence of astrology.

Pisa.who: Pisa, a city in Tuscany, Italy, whose marshy surroundings were notorious for unhealthy air.

Pisidice.who: Pisidice, legendary princess of Methymna on Lesbos, who betrayed the city to Achilles for love, as told in Parthenius's Erotica Pathemata.

Pisistratus.who: Peisistratus (d. 527 BC), tyrant of Athens who was twice driven into exile before establishing lasting rule.

Pistorius.basis: The initial J. and the occult context fit Pistorius's Cabalistic collection.
Pistorius.who: Johann Pistorius the Younger (1546–1608), German physician and controversialist, who edited the collection of Cabalistic writings Artis cabalisticae scriptores.

Pitho.basis: I cannot identify this courtesan or Burton's source with confidence.

Pituita.who: Pituita, the Latin term for phlegm, one of the four humours.

Pius Secundus.who: Pope Pius II, Enea Silvio Piccolomini (1405–1464), humanist who, before becoming pope, wrote the love story Historia de duobus amantibus (Euryalus and Lucretia).

Pizarro.who: Francisco Pizarro (c. 1478–1541), Spanish conqueror of Peru, made a marquess by the Emperor Charles V.

Plancus.basis: Several Romans named Plancus are possible, and Burton's source is unclear; it may be a confusion with one of Crassus's companions.

Plantagenet.who: The Plantagenets, the royal house that ruled England from 1154 to 1485.

Plat.basis: 'Plat.' is Burton's usual marginal abbreviation for Plato, who discusses love returned (anteros) in the Phaedrus.
Plat.who: Plato (c. 427–347 BC), the Athenian philosopher, cited here in abbreviated form.

Plataea.who: Plataea, a city in Boeotia, Greece, where the Greeks defeated the Persians in 479 BC.

Platina.who: Bartolomeo Sacchi, called Platina (1421–1481), Italian humanist who wrote the Lives of the Popes and a dialogue against love.

Plato Apologia Socratis.who: Plato's Apology, his account of Socrates's speech in his own defence at his trial in 399 BC.

Plato Phaedone.who: Plato's Phaedo, the dialogue on the immortality of the soul and the death of Socrates; the quoted sentiment is actually closer to the Phaedrus.

Plato. Aretaeus.who: Two names run together: Plato (c. 427–347 BC), who wrote on love as divine madness, and Aretaeus of Cappadocia, ancient Greek physician who wrote on melancholy and mania.

Platonic.who: Platonic love: love of the soul's beauty rather than the body, following Plato's teaching.

Platonist.who: A follower of Plato's philosophy; here describes Maximus of Tyre (2nd century AD).

Platonists.who: The Platonists, followers of Plato's philosophy, including the Neoplatonists such as Plotinus.

Plato’s Phaedon.who: Plato's Phaedo, the dialogue on the immortality of the soul that ends with the death of Socrates.

Plato’s Timaeus.who: Plato's Timaeus, the dialogue on the making of the cosmos, notoriously difficult to understand.

Plautus Asinar.who: Plautus's comedy Asinaria ('The Comedy of Asses').

Plautus Aulular.who: Plautus's comedy Aulularia ('The Pot of Gold'), about a miserly old man.

Plautus Menec.who: Plautus's comedy Menaechmi, about twin brothers who are mistaken for one another.

Plautus Menech.who: Plautus's comedy Menaechmi, about twin brothers who are mistaken for one another.

Plautus Menechmi.who: Plautus's comedy Menaechmi, about twin brothers who are mistaken for one another.

Pleasance.who: Pleasure; Burton's English rendering of the Latin Lubentia.

Pleasure.who: Pleasure as an allegorical figure in a fable about Opulentia (Wealth).

Pleiades.who: The Pleiades, the star cluster in Taurus, named after the seven daughters of Atlas.

Plethora.who: Plethora, a medical term for an excess of blood or humours.

Pleura.who: Pleura, the membrane that lines the chest cavity.

Pleusicles.who: Pleusicles, the young Athenian lover in Plautus' comedy *Miles Gloriosus*, guest of the old man Periplectomenus.

Plinius.basis: the villa passage means the Younger; the other two mean the Elder
Plinius.who: Usually Pliny the Elder (23–79), Roman author of the *Natural History*; the Laurentine villa belonged to his nephew Pliny the Younger (c. 61–c. 113).

Plinius Secundus.who: Pliny the Younger (Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus, c. 61–c. 113), Roman senator and letter-writer whose correspondence includes letters to Trajan.

Pliny.who: Pliny the Elder (23–79), Roman encyclopedist, author of the *Natural History*.

Plotinus.who: Plotinus (c. 205–270), Neoplatonist philosopher whose treatises were collected by Porphyry as the *Enneads*.

Plutar.who: Plutarch (c. 46–c. 120), Greek biographer and moralist; the advice to husbands comes from his *Conjugal Precepts*.

Plutarchum Gryllus Ulyssi.who: Plutarch's dialogue *Gryllus* (*Beasts are Rational*), in which Gryllus, a companion of Ulysses turned into a pig by Circe, argues with Ulysses.

Pluto.who: Pluto, Roman god of the underworld.

Plutus.basis: the abduction of Proserpina belongs to Pluto
Plutus.who: Plutus, Greek god of wealth; in the Proserpina passage Burton uses the name for Pluto, god of the underworld.

Pluvinel.who: Antoine de Pluvinel (1555–1620), French riding master to Louis XIII and author of a celebrated treatise on horsemanship.

Podagra.who: Podagra (Gout), personified as a goddess in the mock tragedy *Tragodopodagra* attributed to Lucian.

Podalirius.who: Podalirius, legendary physician and son of Asclepius, who served as a healer with the Greeks at Troy.

Podolians.who: Inhabitants of Podolia, a region of the old Polish kingdom, now in south-western Ukraine, exposed to Tatar raids.

Poet.basis: common noun; the margin refers to Theocritus

Poggius.who: Poggio Bracciolini (1380–1459), Florentine humanist, author of the jest-book *Facetiae* and of a famous letter describing the baths of Baden.

Poggius Florentinus.who: Poggio Bracciolini (1380–1459), Florentine humanist, author of the jest-book *Facetiae*.

Poitiers.who: Poitiers, city in west-central France, seat of St Hilary's church and site of the English victory of 1356.

Polemus.who: Polemon of Laodicea (c. 88–144), Greek sophist and author of a treatise on physiognomy that Adamantius later paraphrased.

Polesworth.who: Polesworth, village on the river Anker in north Warwickshire, near Tamworth.

Poliarchus.who: Poliarchus, hero of John Barclay's Latin romance *Argenis* (1621), lover of the princess Argenis.

Policy.basis: politics as a field of study

Politianus.who: Angelo Poliziano (Politian, 1454–1494), Florentine humanist scholar and poet.

Pollio Romilius.who: Romilius Pollio, Roman centenarian mentioned by Pliny the Elder, who told Augustus he owed his vigour to mead within and oil without.

Pollux.basis: the third passage pairs him with the grammarian Festus
Pollux.who: Pollux, one of the twin Dioscuri, brother of Castor; in the Festus passage, Julius Pollux (2nd c.), Greek grammarian, author of the *Onomasticon*.

Polonian Baron.basis: an unnamed Polish baron who was Claudinus's patient

Polus.who: Polus of Acragas (fl. late 5th c. BC), sophist and pupil of Gorgias, who argues with Socrates in Plato's *Gorgias*.

Polus Venetus.who: Marco Polo (1254–1324), Venetian traveller to China.

Polyaenus.who: Polyaenus, the fictional person to whom one of Aristaenetus' Greek *Love Letters* is addressed.

Polyanthean.who: From the *Polyanthea*, a popular Renaissance compilation of quotations by Domenico Nani Mirabelli, first printed 1503.

Polycles.who: Polycles, the fictional father of Charicles in a letter of Aristaenetus' *Love Letters*.

Polycletum.basis: one of Hercules' minor favourites in Giraldi's list; cannot pin down

Polycrates.who: Polycrates (d. c. 522 BC), tyrant of Samos, famous for his good fortune and a patron of the poet Anacreon.

Polycrates Samius.who: Polycrates (d. c. 522 BC), tyrant of Samos, whose ring was thrown into the sea and found again in a fish, as Herodotus tells.

Polycrita.who: Polycrite of Naxos, legendary heroine; in Parthenius' *Erotika Pathemata* the enemy commander Diognetus, in love with her, betrayed his side.

Polydore.who: Polydore Vergil (c. 1470–1555), Italian humanist who settled in England and wrote the *Anglica Historia*.

Polydore Vergil.who: Polydore Vergil (c. 1470–1555), Italian humanist who settled in England and wrote the *Anglica Historia*.

Polymaths.basis: common noun: people of wide learning

Polynices.who: Polynices, in Greek legend a son of Oedipus and Jocasta, exiled from Thebes; he and his brother Eteocles killed each other fighting over the throne.

Polyphemus.who: Polyphemus, the one-eyed Cyclops of Greek myth who courts the sea-nymph Galatea in Ovid's Metamorphoses, book 13.

Polypody.basis: a fern used as a purge

Polyxena.who: Polyxena, in Greek legend a daughter of Priam of Troy, loved by Achilles and sacrificed at his tomb.

Pomerland.who: Pomerania, a region on the southern Baltic coast, now divided between Germany and Poland; Stettin is modern Szczecin.

Pompeius.who: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, Pompey the Great (106–48 BC), Roman general and Caesar's rival, who took Jerusalem in 63 BC.

Pompey.who: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, Pompey the Great (106–48 BC), Roman general and Caesar's rival in the civil war.

Pomponatius.who: Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), Aristotelian philosopher at Padua, who argued in De immortalitate animae that the soul's immortality cannot be proved by reason; also wrote De incantationibus.

Pomponius Atticus.who: Titus Pomponius Atticus (110–32 BC), wealthy Roman knight, Cicero's close friend and the recipient of his letters Ad Atticum.

Pomponius Columna.who: Pompeo Colonna (1479–1532), Roman nobleman, soldier and cardinal, whose life was written by Paolo Giovio.

Pomponius Laetus.who: Giulio Pomponio Leto (1428–1498), Roman humanist and antiquary who studied and described the ancient remains of Rome.

Pomponius Mela.who: Pomponius Mela (fl. c. AD 43), Roman geographer, author of De chorographia, the earliest surviving Latin geography.

Pont.basis: abbreviation in a marginal note, followed by 'Heuter'
Pont.who: Pontus Heuterus (Pontus de Huyter, 1535–1602), Netherlandish historian, author of Rerum Burgundicarum libri, a history of the dukes of Burgundy.

Pontanus.who: Giovanni Gioviano Pontano (1429–1503), Neapolitan humanist, poet, astrological writer and secretary to the Aragonese kings of Naples.

Pontus.who: Pontus, ancient region on the southern shore of the Black Sea in northern Anatolia, kingdom of Mithridates; Ovid's exile was at Tomis on the Pontic coast.

Pontus Heuter.who: Pontus Heuterus (Pontus de Huyter, 1535–1602), Netherlandish historian, author of Rerum Burgundicarum libri, a history of the dukes of Burgundy.

Popelius.who: Popiel II, legendary early king of Poland who, according to the chronicles, was devoured by mice.

Porcius Latro.who: Marcus Porcius Latro (d. 4 BC), Augustan rhetorician and declaimer, often quoted in the Elder Seneca's Controversiae.

Porphyrius.who: Porphyry (c. 234–c. 305), Neoplatonist philosopher, pupil and biographer of Plotinus, who talked him out of suicide.

Porphyry.who: Porphyry (c. 234–c. 305), Neoplatonist philosopher, pupil of Plotinus, author of De abstinentia, which argues for abstaining from meat.

Porrectan.who: The baths of Porretta (Porretta Terme), mineral springs in the Apennines south of Bologna.

Portsmouth.who: Portsmouth, naval port on the Hampshire coast of southern England.

Portugal.who: Portugal, kingdom of the western Iberian peninsula.

Porus.who: In the first two passages, Porus, Indian king defeated by Alexander at the Hydaspes in 326 BC; in the third, Poros (Plenty), father of Love in Plato's Symposium.

Postellus.who: Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), French orientalist and visionary, author of De orbis terrae concordia (1544).

Postumia.who: Postumia, wife of the Roman jurist Servius Sulpicius Rufus, named by Suetonius as one of Julius Caesar's mistresses.

Postvorta.who: Postverta, Roman goddess of childbirth and of the past, paired with Antevorta, who looked to the future.

Potina.who: Potina, minor Roman goddess who presided over children's drink.

Potosa.who: Potosí, silver-mining city in the Andes, then in Spanish Peru, now in Bolivia.

Practics.basis: generic term for a medical practice-book

Praestites.who: The Lares Praestites, Roman guardian spirits, protectors of the city and of individuals, as named by Martianus Capella.

Praetextatus.basis: may render a Latin description rather than a name; source in Plutarch not certain

Prague.who: Prague, capital of Bohemia, now of the Czech Republic.

Pratum.who: Prato, Tuscan town near Florence, famous for its relic of the Virgin's girdle.

Praxinoe.who: Praxinoa, one of the two Syracusan housewives in Theocritus' Idyll 15, who push through the crowd to see the Adonis festival at Alexandria.

Praxiteles.who: Praxiteles (fl. 4th century BC), Athenian sculptor famed for his Aphrodite of Cnidus and his Eros; Phryne was said to have been his model and mistress.

Prema.who: Prema, a minor Roman goddess of the wedding night, mocked by Augustine (City of God 6.9) among the deities invoked at a consummation.

Premunda.basis: Burton pairs it with Prema as in Augustine's list; the form Premunda itself is not standard.
Premunda.who: Apparently a minor Roman goddess of the wedding night, probably a corrupt form of Pertunda, named with Prema by Augustine (City of God 6.9).

Presbyter John.who: Prester John, the legendary Christian priest-king first placed in Asia and later identified with the Emperor of Ethiopia.

Priamus.who: Priam, the legendary last king of Troy and father of Hector, Paris and many other sons.

Priapeiis.who: The Priapea, a collection of obscene Latin poems on Priapus, once partly ascribed to Virgil; Kaspar Schoppe (Scioppius) published an edition with commentary.

Priapo.who: Priapus, the Greek and Roman fertility god of gardens, especially worshipped at Lampsacus on the Hellespont.

Priapus.who: Priapus, the Greek and Roman ithyphallic god of fertility and gardens.

Prideaux.who: John Prideaux (1578–1650), Regius Professor of Divinity at Oxford and Rector of Exeter College, later Bishop of Worcester.

Primerius.basis: friend to whom Daniel Heinsius addressed an epistle on whether a scholar should marry; not securely identifiable

Priscilianists.who: Priscillianists, followers of Priscillian of Ávila (executed 385), a heretical sect accused of astrological fatalism and attacked by Augustine.

Proclus.basis: Passages 1–2 clearly mean the philosopher; passage 3 (burning-glasses) follows a tradition about a different Proclus, often confused with the philosopher.
Proclus.who: Proclus (412–485), Neoplatonist philosopher and head of the Academy at Athens; the burning-glass story belongs to another Proclus, a mechanician under Emperor Anastasius.

Procris.who: Procris, in Greek myth the wife of Cephalus, who jealously spied on him while he hunted and was killed by his javelin by mistake.

Procrustes.who: Procrustes, mythical Attic robber who stretched or cut his victims to fit his bed, killed by Theseus.

Proculus.who: Proculus (d. c. 281), Roman usurper under Probus; the Historia Augusta quotes his letter boasting of deflowering a hundred Sarmatian virgins.

Proetus.who: Proetus, mythical king of Tiryns whose wife Stheneboea (Anteia) falsely accused Bellerophon after he rejected her.

Promethei.who: Prometheus (Latin plural), the Titan who stole fire from heaven for mankind.

Prometheus.who: Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire from heaven and was chained to the Caucasus, where an eagle fed on his liver.

Proserpina.who: Proserpina (Persephone), daughter of Ceres, carried off by Pluto to be queen of the underworld.

Prosper.basis: the first passage may be Prosper of Aquitaine (epigrams); the second sits with a citation to Ficino's De vita coelitus comparanda; bearers unclear

Prosper Alpinus.who: Prospero Alpini (1553–1617), Venetian physician and botanist, author of works on Egyptian medicine and Egyptian plants.

Prosper Calanius.who: Prospero Calani (Calanius), 16th-century Italian physician and Galenist, author of a treatise De atra bile on black bile.

Protagoras.who: Protagoras of Abdera (c. 490–c. 420 BC), Greek sophist; in the second passage it is the title of Plato's dialogue named after him.

Protela.basis: Strabo (10.2.9) tells of Cephalus, son of Deioneus, leaping from Leucas for love of Pterelas; Burton's 'Degonetus' corresponds to Deioneus.
Protela.who: Pterelas, in Strabo's account the beloved for whose sake Cephalus leapt from the Leucadian cliff; Burton garbles both names.

Protervia.who: Protervia, personification of wantonness or impudence, listed among minor Roman deities.

Protesilaus.who: Protesilaus, Greek hero and first Greek killed at Troy, whose grieving wife Laodamia kept an image of him.

Protestants.who: Protestants, the adherents of the reformed churches.

Proteus.who: Proteus, the prophetic old man of the sea in Greek myth, who changed shape endlessly to avoid capture.

Proteus Poeticus.basis: title of a work of verse permutations; author and edition not securely known

Provence.who: Provence, region of south-eastern France on the Mediterranean.

Prudentius.who: Aurelius Prudentius Clemens (348–after 405), Latin Christian poet from Spain who attacked pagan cults in works such as Contra Symmachum.

Prudentius. Cuna.basis: the form runs the name into the next word, Cuna
Prudentius. Cuna.who: Aurelius Prudentius Clemens (348–after 405), Latin Christian poet, quoted from his attack on pagan gods in Contra Symmachum.

Prytanaeo.who: The Prytaneum, the town hall of Athens, where honoured citizens and guests were given public meals.

Psalmist.who: The Psalmist, i.e. King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.

Psammetichus.who: Psammetichus (Psamtik), Saite king of Egypt; Aelian makes him the king in the slipper story who married the courtesan Rhodopis.

Pseudo-Christians.who: Burton's term for false or superstitious Christians, chiefly Roman Catholics, in his survey of religious melancholy.

Psophidians.who: The people of Psophis in Arcadia, whose Aglaus was declared by the Delphic oracle to be happier than King Gyges.

Psyche.who: Psyche, the mortal girl loved by Cupid in the tale told by the old woman in Apuleius's Golden Ass, books 4–6.

Ptolemaeus.who: Usually Claudius Ptolemy (fl. c. 150 AD), Alexandrian astronomer; in the Valerius passage, Ptolemy, king of Cyprus (d. 58 BC), a notorious miser.

Ptolemaeus Philadelphus.who: Ptolemy II Philadelphus (r. 285–246 BC), king of Egypt, who married his daughter Berenice to the Seleucid king Antiochus II.

Ptolemy.who: In Diodorus's account of the canal, Ptolemy II Philadelphus, king of Egypt; elsewhere Claudius Ptolemy (fl. c. 150 AD), Alexandrian astronomer and astrologer (Tetrabiblos).

Ptolemys.who: The Ptolemies, Macedonian kings of Egypt, proverbial patrons of learning as founders of the Alexandrian Library and Museum.

Ptolemy’s Hieralogodion.basis: the name matches the known compound; why Burton credits it to Ptolemy is unclear
Ptolemy’s Hieralogodion.who: Hiera logadii, a bitter purgative electuary of the 'hiera' family in the old pharmacopoeia.

Publius Cornutus.basis: seems to be a pun (Tacitus 'silent' against Cornutus 'horned'); no certain bearer

Puck.who: Puck, the mischievous English folk sprite who leads night travellers astray, like a will-o'-the-wisp.

Pucks.who: Pucks, English folk sprites who mislead night travellers, like the will-o'-the-wisp.

Pudentilla.who: Aemilia Pudentilla, wealthy widow of Oea in North Africa who married Apuleius (2nd century AD), which led to his trial for magic.

Pulcheria.who: First, Pulcheria, the young daughter of Theodosius I, mourned in a funeral oration by Gregory of Nyssa; second, Aelia Pulcheria (399–453), sister of Theodosius II.

Purbachius.who: Georg von Peuerbach (1423–1461), Austrian astronomer, author of the Theoricae novae planetarum, which taught the Ptolemaic system of orbs.

Purgatory.who: Purgatory, in Catholic doctrine the state or place where souls are cleansed by suffering before entering heaven.

Puteoli.who: Puteoli, Roman port on the Bay of Naples, now Pozzuoli.

Pylades.who: Mostly Pylades, the faithful friend of Orestes in Greek legend; in the Galen story, Pylades, a pantomime dancer at Rome.

Pyramus.who: Pyramus, the Babylonian lover of Thisbe; in Ovid's Metamorphosis 4, both kill themselves.

Pyrenean.who: The Pyrenees, the mountains between France and Spain.

Pyrrhus.who: Pyrrhus (319/318–272 BC), king of Epirus, whose dreams of conquest his adviser Cineas questioned in Plutarch's Life of Pyrrhus.

Pythagoras.who: Pythagoras of Samos (6th century BC), Greek philosopher who taught the transmigration of souls and abstinence from beans.

Pythagoreans.who: The followers of Pythagoras, known for teaching metempsychosis and for abstaining from meat.

Pythian.who: The Pythian Games, held at Delphi in honour of Apollo.

Pythias.who: Pythias (properly Phintias), Pythagorean of Syracuse, whose friend Damon offered his life as surety for him to the tyrant Dionysius.

Q. Fabius Maximus.who: Quintus Fabius Maximus Allobrogicus, consul 121 BC, who defeated the Allobroges and Arverni near the Isère (Isara).

Quartilla.who: Quartilla, a lustful priestess of Priapus in Petronius's Satyricon.

Queen Katherine.who: Catherine of Aragon (1485–1536), first wife of Henry VIII and patron of Juan Luis Vives.

Quercetan.who: Joseph Du Chesne (Quercetanus) (c. 1544–1609), French Paracelsian physician and author on chemical (spagyric) pharmacy.

Quiloa.who: Kilwa (Kilwa Kisiwani), island port and trading city on the coast of East Africa, now in Tanzania.

Quincia.who: Quincia, the dead mistress mourned in a Latin epitaph that Celio Calcagnini wrote in a lover's voice.

Quinctius.who: Titus Quinctius Flamininus (c. 229–174 BC), Roman general who freed Greece from Macedon; Livy gives him the tortoise simile about the Peloponnese.

Quinsay.who: Quinsay (Kinsay), Marco Polo's name for Hangzhou, the great city of southern China.

Quintus.who: Quintus Tullius Cicero (102–43 BC), Cicero's younger brother, who served under Caesar in Britain and wrote to him from there.

Quintus Catulus.who: Quintus Lutatius Catulus (c. 149–87 BC), Roman consul and minor poet who wrote an epigram admiring the actor Roscius.

Quintus Fabius.basis: the well-known Papirius–Fabius quarrel in Livy; Burton's 'Gnaeus' does not fit exactly
Quintus Fabius.who: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus, master of horse whose quarrel with the dictator Lucius Papirius Cursor in 325 BC nearly cost him his life.

Quintus Metellus.who: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus (d. 115 BC), Roman general whom Velleius Paterculus praises as the most fortunate of men.

Quivira.who: Quivira, a legendary rich land in North America sought by Coronado (1541); old maps put it on the Pacific coast near Drake's Nova Albion.

R. T.who: Robert Tofte (c. 1561–1620), English poet and translator of Benedetto Varchi as The Blazon of Jealousie (1615), source of these verses.

Rabbi Achiba.who: Rabbi Akiva ben Joseph (c. 50–135), leading Mishnaic sage, to whom kabbalistic tradition attributed esoteric writings.

Rabbi Azariel.basis: the only well-known kabbalist Azriel; he is cited alongside other Jewish esoteric authorities
Rabbi Azariel.who: Azriel of Gerona (13th century), Catalan kabbalist who wrote on the divine emanations.

Rabbins.who: The rabbis: Jewish teachers and commentators on Scripture and the Talmud.

Rabelais.who: François Rabelais (c. 1494–1553), French physician and comic satirist, author of Gargantua and Pantagruel.

Rabshakeh.who: Rabshakeh, the Assyrian official Sennacherib sent to taunt besieged Jerusalem (2 Kings 18–19; Isaiah 36).

Rachel.who: Rachel, Jacob's beloved wife and Leah's sister, mother of Joseph and Benjamin (Genesis 29–30).

Radnor.who: Radnor (New Radnor), a town and lordship in Radnorshire, Wales, now in Powys.

Radway Grange.who: Radway Grange, a house below Edgehill in south Warwickshire, known for its wide prospect.

Radzivilius.who: Mikołaj Krzysztof Radziwiłł 'Sierotka' (1549–1616), Polish-Lithuanian prince whose account of his pilgrimage to Jerusalem and Egypt was published in Latin.

Ragusa.who: Ragusa, now Dubrovnik in Croatia, then an independent merchant republic on the Adriatic.

Ragusian.who: The Republic of Ragusa (now Dubrovnik, Croatia), an aristocratic merchant republic on the Adriatic.

Rahab.who: Rahab, the harlot of Jericho who hid Joshua's spies (Joshua 2).

Raimarus.who: Nicolaus Reimers Ursus (1551–1600), German astronomer whose geo-heliocentric world system led to a priority dispute with Tycho Brahe.

Raimundus Lullius.who: Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), Majorcan philosopher and mystic, falsely credited with alchemical works; legend has his conversion follow sight of his mistress's diseased breast.

Rakow.who: Raków, a town in southern Poland and centre of the Socinians, home of the Racovian Catechism (1605).

Ralph Burton.basis: the passages name the father and the brother
Ralph Burton.who: In the first passage, Ralph Burton of Lindley, Leicestershire, Robert Burton's father; in the second, Ralph Burton, Robert's younger brother.

Rameh.who: Ramah, the name of several hill-towns in biblical Palestine.

Ranzovius.who: Heinrich Rantzau (1526–1598), Danish royal governor in Schleswig-Holstein and humanist, who wrote on astrology and on keeping health (De conservanda valetudine).

Rasceburg.who: Raseborg (Finnish Raasepori), a castle and district on the south coast of Finland.

Rascia.who: Rascia (Raška), the medieval heartland of Serbia; the name was often used for Serbia itself.

Ratholde.who: Radbod, king of the Frisians (d. 719), who refused baptism rather than be parted from his ancestors in hell.

Razis.who: Razis, an elder of Jerusalem who killed himself rather than fall into Nicanor's hands (2 Maccabees 14).

Reals.who: The Realists, scholastic philosophers who held that universals really exist, opposed to the Nominalists.

Recorder.basis: civic office (the town's legal officer), not a proper name

Red Sea.who: The Red Sea, the arm of the Indian Ocean between Africa and Arabia.

Rednitz.who: The Rednitz, a river in Franconia, Bavaria; Charlemagne's canal (Fossa Carolina) near Weissenburg linked its headwaters to the Altmühl.

Redshanks.who: Redshanks, an English nickname for the Scottish Highlanders (and Irish), from their bare legs.

Regium.basis: could be Reggio Emilia or Reggio Calabria; the passage does not settle which

Regulus.who: Marcus Atilius Regulus (fl. 3rd century BC), Roman consul captured by Carthage in the First Punic War, who kept his oath and returned to captivity.

Reinerus Solenander.who: Reiner Solenander (1524–1601), German physician to the Dukes of Cleves, author of a collection of medical consultations (Consilia).

Religious Melancholy.basis: cross-reference to Burton's own section heading

Remelinus.who: Johann Remmelin (1583–1632), German physician of Ulm, author of the anatomical flap-book Catoptrum microcosmicum.

Remora.basis: the sucking-fish, believed to stop ships

Renagolosa.who: Penyagolosa (Peñagolosa), a mountain in Castellón province in the old kingdom of Valencia, Spain.

Renodaeus.who: Jean de Renou (Johannes Renodaeus), French physician of Paris, author of a much-used Dispensatorium medicum (1608).

Resolutus.who: 'Doctor Resolutus', the scholastic title of John Baconthorpe (c. 1290–1346), English Carmelite theologian named just before it.

Reuben.who: Reuben, Jacob's eldest son, who lay with his father's concubine Bilhah (Genesis 35).

Reuchlin.who: Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), German humanist and Hebraist, whose quarrel with the Cologne Dominicans prompted the satirical Epistolae obscurorum virorum, written by his supporters.

Rhadamanthus.who: Rhadamanthus, son of Zeus and Europa, one of the judges of the dead in the underworld in Greek myth.

Rhasin.who: Rhazes (Abu Bakr al-Razi, c. 865–925), Persian physician whose medical works were widely read in Latin.

Rhegium Lepidi.who: Regium Lepidi, the Roman name of Reggio Emilia in northern Italy.

Rheti.who: The Rhaetians, ancient Alpine people of Rhaetia, roughly the modern Grisons, Tyrol and neighbouring regions.

Rhetoric.who: Aristotle's Rhetoric, whose second book treats the emotions.

Rhodanthe.who: Rhodanthe, heroine of Theodore Prodromos's 12th-century Byzantine verse romance Rhodanthe and Dosicles.

Rhodanus.who: Rhodanus, the Latin name of the river Rhône.

Rhodes.who: Rhodes, Aegean island, besieged and taken from the Knights Hospitaller by Suleiman the Magnificent in 1522.

Rhodian Colossus.who: The Colossus of Rhodes, giant bronze statue of Helios at Rhodes (c. 280 BC), one of the Seven Wonders.

Ribadeneira.who: Pedro de Ribadeneira (1526–1611), Spanish Jesuit, biographer of Ignatius Loyola and compiler of the saints' lives Flos sanctorum.

Rich. Argentine.who: Richard Argentine, 16th-century English physician and cleric, author of De praestigiis et incantationibus daemonum (1568).

Rich. Dinoth.who: Richard Dinoth (Dinothus), 16th-century French Protestant historian, author of De bello civili Gallico religionis causa suscepto (1582).

Richard.who: Different bearers: Richard Dinoth, French historian; Richard I of England (1157–1199) at the siege of Acre; Richard II (1367–1400), deposed and imprisoned.

Richard Dinoth.who: Richard Dinoth (Dinothus) of Coutances (fl. later 16th century), French Protestant historian, author of De bello civili Gallico on the French Wars of Religion.

Richard Hawkins.who: Sir Richard Hawkins (c.1560–1622), English seaman, author of the Observations of his voyage into the South Sea (1622).

Richarda.who: Richardis (St Richardis, d. c.896), wife of Emperor Charles III the Fat; accused of adultery in 887, she was said to have cleared herself by ordeal.

Rim.who: The 'rim': an old anatomical term for the membrane lining the belly.

Rivet.who: André Rivet (1572–1651), French Huguenot theologian and professor at Leiden, author of an Isagoge to Holy Scripture.

Robert.basis: The Falaise and Arlette story belongs to Robert I, William's father.
Robert.who: In two passages Robert Curthose (c.1051–1134), William the Conqueror's eldest son, imprisoned by Henry I; at Falaise, Robert I of Normandy, father of William by Arlette.

Robert Bradshaw.basis: Known only as the owner of an estate named in Burton's note.

Robert Constantine.basis: The name and period fit, but I cannot confirm his work on the music of the spheres.
Robert Constantine.who: Robert Constantin (c.1530–1605), French physician and scholar of Caen, known for his Greek lexicon.

Robin Goodfellows.who: Robin Goodfellow, or Puck, the mischievous household sprite of English folklore.

Robin Hood.who: Robin Hood, the legendary English outlaw of Sherwood Forest.

Rod. à Castro.who: Rodrigo de Castro (1546–1627), Portuguese Jewish physician at Hamburg, author of De universa mulierum medicina (1603).

Rodericus.basis: Two passages name him outright; the passage on choosing a nurse fits his treatise on women's medicine.
Rodericus.who: Rodrigo de Castro (1546–1627), Portuguese Jewish physician at Hamburg, author of De universa mulierum medicina (1603).

Rodericus à Castro.who: Rodrigo de Castro (1546–1627), Portuguese Jewish physician at Hamburg, author of De universa mulierum medicina (1603).

Rodericus à Castro Lusitanus.who: Rodrigo de Castro (1546–1627), Portuguese Jewish physician at Hamburg, author of De universa mulierum medicina (1603).

Rodericus à Fonseca.who: Rodrigo da Fonseca (d. 1622), Portuguese physician who taught at Pisa and Padua, author of Consultationes medicae.

Rodericus à Vega.basis: The Latin form 'Rodericus a Vega' and the Galen commentary fit him.
Rodericus à Vega.who: Tomás Rodrigues da Veiga (1513–1579), Portuguese physician at Coimbra who wrote commentaries on Galen, including De locis affectis.

Rodomont.who: Rodomonte, the boastful Saracen king of Algiers in Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, who woos Isabella.

Rodomonts.who: Braggarts named after Rodomonte, the boastful Saracen king in Ariosto's Orlando Furioso.

Rodophe.who: Rhodopis, Greek courtesan in Egypt; in Aelian an eagle carried her sandal to the king, who then married her.

Rodopheian Phyllis.who: Phyllis, Thracian princess of the Rhodope region who loved Demophon and died when he did not return.

Roeslin.who: Helisaeus Röslin (1545–1616), Alsatian physician and astrologer who wrote on the comet of 1577 (Theoria nova coelestium meteoron, 1578).

Roeslinus.who: Helisaeus Röslin (1545–1616), Alsatian physician and astrologer who wrote on cosmology and the comet of 1577.

Rog. Bacon.who: Roger Bacon (c.1219–c.1292), English Franciscan philosopher; a tract on the degrees of medicines was attributed to him.

Roger.who: Roger of Salisbury (d. 1139), bishop and chief minister of Henry I, builder of castles, arrested and stripped of his goods by King Stephen.

Roger Bacon.who: Roger Bacon (c.1219–c.1292), English Franciscan philosopher who wrote on optics (perspectiva) and the secrets of art and nature.

Rogers.basis: Several English writers named Rogers fit; the passage does not settle which.

Roland.who: Roland, legendary paladin of Charlemagne and hero of the Chanson de Roland, paired with Oliver.

Rollo.who: Rollo (c.860–c.930), Viking leader who founded the duchy of Normandy.

Roman Saturnals.who: The Saturnalia, the Roman December festival when servants were allowed licence.

Romanus.basis: Pliny's letter on Verginius is addressed to Romanus; I cannot settle which saint is meant.
Romanus.who: In the Pliny passage, Voconius Romanus, Pliny the Younger's friend; in the other, a St Romanus invoked for the possessed.

Romeo.who: Romeo, the lover in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet.

Romney.who: Romney Marsh, low-lying marshland in south-east Kent, known for unhealthy air.

Romulus.who: Romulus, legendary founder and first king of Rome.

Romulus Amaseus.who: Romolo Amaseo (1489–1552), Italian humanist of Udine who taught at Bologna and translated Pausanias and Xenophon.

Rondoletius.who: Guillaume Rondelet (1507–1566), professor of medicine at Montpellier and writer on fishes.

Ros.who: Ros ('dew'), a term in old physiology for one of the secondary humours that nourish the body.

Rosamond.who: Rosamond Clifford (d. c.1176), mistress of Henry II, said to have been kept at Woodstock; subject of Daniel's Complaint of Rosamond.

Rosamund.who: The Complaint of Rosamond (1592), Samuel Daniel's poem on Henry II's mistress.

Roscius.who: Quintus Roscius Gallus (d. c. 62 BC), the celebrated Roman comic actor, whose beauty Quintus Lutatius Catulus praised in verse despite his squint.

Rostock.who: Rostock, Hanseatic port and university town on the Baltic in Mecklenburg, northern Germany.

Rosy Cross.who: The Rosicrucians, a supposed secret brotherhood announced in German manifestos of 1614–16, promising a universal reformation of learning and religion.
