Rotman.basis: The second passage clearly means Christoph Rothmann. The Chiromancy in the first passage is probably by Johannes Rothmann, a different man, whom Burton seems to conflate with him.
Rotman.who: Christoph Rothmann (d. c. 1600), mathematician to Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel, who debated cosmology with Tycho Brahe in their published astronomical letters.

Rowena.who: Rowena (Renwein), legendary daughter of the Saxon leader Hengist, married to the British king Vortigern in Geoffrey of Monmouth's account.

Roxane.who: Roxane (d. c. 310 BC), Bactrian noblewoman whom Alexander the Great married in 327 BC.

Roxolana.who: Roxelana (Hürrem Sultan, c. 1502–1558), slave-concubine who became the wife and powerful favourite of the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent.

Rubenius Celer.basis: Known only from an ancient inscription collected by Renaissance antiquaries; nothing else is recorded of him.
Rubenius Celer.who: Rubenius Celer, a Roman known only from a funerary inscription that he set up commemorating his wife Ennia.

Rubeus.basis: The distilled 'compound water' and the medical setting fit Rossi's treatise on distillation.
Rubeus.who: Girolamo Rossi (Hieronymus Rubeus, 1539–1607), physician of Ravenna, author of a treatise on distillation (De destillatione).

Rucke.who: The roc (rukh), the gigantic bird of Arabian legend, which Marco Polo reported from Madagascar.

Ruellius.who: Jean Ruel (Ruellius, 1474–1537), French physician and botanist, translator of Dioscorides and author of De natura stirpium.

Rueus.who: François de la Rue (Franciscus Rueus), sixteenth-century Flemish physician, author of De gemmis, a treatise on precious stones.

Rufus.who: Rufus of Ephesus (fl. c. AD 100), Greek physician whose treatise on melancholy was a principal ancient source on the disease.

Rufus Ephesius.who: Rufus of Ephesus (fl. c. AD 100), Greek physician whose treatise on melancholy was a principal ancient source on the disease.

Rulandus.basis: The medical and remedy context and the Latin form fit Ruland the Elder; his son, also Martin, is less likely.
Rulandus.who: Martin Ruland the Elder (1532–1602), German physician, author of popular collections of empirical cures and remedies.

Rumina.who: Rumina, Roman goddess of suckling and nursing, whom Burton lists among minor deities of eating and drinking.

Rusca.who: Antonio Rusca, Milanese priest and doctor of the Ambrosian College, author of De inferno et statu daemonum (1621).

Russia.who: Russia, i.e. Muscovy, the realm of the Grand Duke or Tsar of Moscow.

Russians.who: The Russians, subjects of the Grand Duke of Muscovy, Orthodox Christians of the Greek Church.

Rustan Bassa.who: Rüstem Pasha (d. 1561), grand vizier and son-in-law of Suleiman the Magnificent.

Rusticity.who: Rusticity, a common noun (boorishness), here the vice opposed to scurrility.

Rye.who: Rye, one of the Cinque Ports in East Sussex, whose harbour silted up.

Sabea.basis: Burton's 'Sabea' presumably reflects a variant of the Golden Legend's setting; the form itself is uncertain.
Sabea.who: The kingdom of the princess rescued by St George in the Golden Legend, usually given there as Silene in Libya.

Sabina Poppaea.who: Poppaea Sabina (d. AD 65), second wife of the emperor Nero, famous for her beauty and luxury.

Sabine.who: St Sabinus, early martyr-bishop venerated at Spoleto, whom the Lombard duke Ariulf of Spoleto reportedly saw defending him in battle.

Sacroboscus.who: Johannes de Sacrobosco (John of Holywood, c. 1195–c. 1256), whose astronomical textbook De sphaera was much commented on, including by Barocius.

Sadael.who: Antoine de la Roche Chandieu (1534–1591), learned French Huguenot nobleman and divine who wrote under the name Sadeel.

Sadducees.who: The Sadducees, Jewish priestly party of the Second Temple period who denied resurrection, angels and spirits.

Sadeler.who: Aegidius Sadeler (c. 1570–1629), Flemish engraver at the imperial court of Rudolf II in Prague.

Sadoletus.who: Jacopo Sadoleto (1477–1547), Italian humanist cardinal and bishop of Carpentras, author of moral and consolatory writings.

Sagittarius.who: Sagittarius, the zodiac sign and constellation of the Archer.

Saint John de Ullua.who: San Juan de Ulúa, island fortress and harbour off Veracruz in Mexico (New Spain).

Saints.who: Saints, a common noun for the canonised saints of the Roman Church.

Salamanca.who: Salamanca, university city in Castile, western Spain.

Salamina.who: Salamis, Greek island near Athens, scene of the Greek naval victory over Persia in 480 BC.

Saldanian.who: Inhabitants of Saldanha Bay near the Cape of Good Hope, i.e. the Khoikhoi people met by early English voyagers.

Salernitan.who: Of Salerno, the medieval medical school whose verse Regimen sanitatis Salernitanum names the three doctors Merryman, Diet and Quiet.

Salerno.who: Salerno, city and principality south of Naples, setting of Boccaccio's tale of Tancredi and Ghismonda.

Salisbury.who: Salisbury, cathedral city and bishopric in Wiltshire, England.

Salmacis.basis: Passage 1 means the fountain; passage 2 means the nymph.
Salmacis.who: Salmacis, nymph of a fountain near Halicarnassus in Caria whose waters were said to make men soft; in Ovid, Metamorphoses 4, she woos Hermaphroditus.

Salmoneus.who: Salmoneus, mythical king in Elis who imitated Zeus's thunder and lightning and was struck down by Zeus's thunderbolt.

Salust. Salvianus.who: Sallustio Salviani (Sallustius Salvianus), Italian physician at Rome, son of Ippolito Salviani, author of a work on medicine (De re medica).

Salustius Salvianus.who: Sallustio Salviani (Sallustius Salvianus), Italian physician at Rome, son of Ippolito Salviani, author of a work on medicine (De re medica).

Salvianus.who: Sallustio Salviani (Sallustius Salvianus), Italian physician at Rome, son of Ippolito Salviani, author of a work on medicine (De re medica).

Salzburg.who: Salzburg, city in Austria, seat of a powerful prince-archbishopric.

Sam. Neander.basis: Cannot securely identify which Samuel Neander is meant.

Samaritan.who: The Samaritan woman who gave Jesus water at Jacob's well (John 4).

Samaritans.who: The Samaritans, the people of Samaria in central Palestine.

Sambucus.who: Johannes Sambucus (János Zsámboky, 1531–1584), Hungarian humanist, physician and historian, known especially for his Emblemata (1564).

Samian.who: Of Samos, the Greek island in the eastern Aegean.

Samos.who: Samos, Greek island in the eastern Aegean off the coast of Asia Minor, ruled by the tyrant Polycrates in the 6th century BC.

Samosetans.who: Samosatenians, anti-Trinitarians named after Paul of Samosata (3rd-century bishop of Antioch), who denied Christ's divinity before his human birth.

Samson.who: Samson, Israelite judge of great strength (Judges 13–16).

Sanguification.who: Sanguification, the making of blood from chyle in the liver, as old physiology taught.

Sansovinus.who: Francesco Sansovino (1521–1586), Venetian man of letters who wrote widely on the governments and customs of states.

Sapor.basis: Passage 1 matches Shapur II's title; the physician king and the syrup 'of King Sapor' from the Arabic pharmacopoeia may refer to another Sapor.
Sapor.who: Shapur (Sapor), name of several Sasanian kings of Persia; Shapur II (309–379) styled himself brother of the Sun and Moon.

Sappho.who: Sappho (fl. c. 600 BC), Greek lyric poet of Lesbos, said in legend to have loved the ferryman Phaon.

Saracen.who: A Saracen, a European name for an Arab or Muslim.

Sarah.who: Sarah, wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac (Genesis).

Sarapion.basis: The context is Arabic medicine, but the passages do not settle which Serapion is meant.
Sarapion.who: Serapion, Arabic medical authority read in Latin translation: either Yuhanna ibn Sarabiyun, a 9th-century Syriac physician, or the later 'Serapion the Younger', who wrote on simples.

Sarcasmus.who: Sarcasm, as a figure of speech.

Sardanapalus.who: Sardanapalus, legendary last king of Assyria, a byword for luxury and effeminacy, said to have burned himself with his palace.

Sardis.who: Sardis, ancient capital of Lydia in western Asia Minor, near modern Sart, Turkey.

Sardus.who: Alessandro Sardi (Alexander Sardus, c. 1520–1588), Ferrarese humanist, author of De moribus ac ritibus gentium on the customs of nations.

Sarmatia.who: Sarmatia, ancient name for the lands of eastern Europe between the Vistula and the Don (roughly Poland and western Russia).

Sarmiento.who: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa (c. 1532–1592), Spanish navigator sent by the viceroy of Peru to explore the Strait of Magellan (1579–80).

Sarpedon.who: Sarpedon, son of Zeus and Lycian ally of Troy in the Iliad, killed by Patroclus; Glaucus was his companion-in-arms.

Sarsaparilla.who: Sarsaparilla, a root from the New World used as a medicine.

Sassafras.who: Sassafras, the bark and root of a North American tree used as a medicine.

Satirist.basis: Refers to Petronius in passage 1 and to Juvenal in passage 2.

Saturn.who: Saturn, the planet in its astrological role, thought to cause melancholy.

Saturnal.who: Of the Saturnalia, the Roman December festival of license.

Saturnalian.who: Of the Saturnalia, the Roman December festival when slaves could speak freely.

Saturnals.who: The Saturnalia, the Roman December festival of license.

Saturnine.who: Under the influence of the planet Saturn, so melancholy by nature.

Saturninus.who: Not a person here: a 'Saturnine' man, born under the planet Saturn and so of gloomy, unlucky temperament.

Satyram Menippeam.who: Varro's Menippean Satires (1st century BC), now lost except for fragments; Aulus Gellius quotes the one on a husband's duties.

Satyricon.who: John Barclay's Euphormionis Lusinini Satyricon (1603–07), a satirical Latin novel whose hero Euphormio serves as a dependant in great households.

Satyrs.who: Satyrs, the lustful goat-like woodland spirits of Greek myth, companions of Dionysus.

Satyrus Lyda.who: From an epigram of Moschus: Pan loved Echo, Echo loved a skipping Satyr, and the Satyr loved Lyde, so each lover was spurned in turn.

Saul.who: Saul, first king of Israel, troubled by an evil spirit and jealous of David (1 Samuel).

Savonarolum.who: Michele Savonarola (c. 1385–1466), Paduan physician and author of a widely used Practica of medicine; grandfather of Girolamo Savonarola.

Savoy.who: Savoy, Alpine duchy between France and Italy, now divided between south-eastern France and Piedmont.

Saxo Grammaticus.who: Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1150–after 1208), Danish historian whose Gesta Danorum tells of northern kings, magic and wonders.

Saxola.basis: Filelfo's letters include ones to Saxolus Pratensis; the form fits
Saxola.who: Probably Sassolo da Prato (Saxolus Pratensis), Italian humanist, pupil of Vittorino da Feltre and correspondent of Francesco Filelfo.

Saxon.who: The Saxons, the Germanic people whose leader Hengist settled in Kent in the 5th century.

Saxon Heptarchy.who: The 'Heptarchy', the seven Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of early medieval England (Kent, Sussex, Wessex, Essex, East Anglia, Mercia, Northumbria).

Saxons.who: The Saxons of Germany, inhabitants of Saxony, as described in Sebastian Münster's Cosmographia.

Saxony.who: Saxony, electorate and duchy in eastern Germany, with mining country around Mansfield.

Sayrus.who: Gregory Sayer (Gregorius Sayrus, 1560–1602), English Benedictine casuist, author of the Thesaurus casuum conscientiae.

Scaean.who: The Scaean Gate, the main western gate of Troy in the Iliad.

Scaeva.who: Cassius Scaeva, Caesar's centurion, famed for holding a fort at Dyrrachium (48 BC) despite many wounds and a shield pierced by arrows.

Scaevola.who: First, Gaius Mucius Scaevola, legendary Roman who burned his right hand before Porsenna; second, Quintus Mucius Scaevola (d. 82 BC), pontifex and jurist, criticised by Augustine.

Scaliger.who: Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), Italian-French physician and scholar, author of the Exotericae exercitationes against Cardano.

Scaligers.who: Men like Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), the learned physician and philosopher who wrote against Cardano.

Scandaroon.who: Scanderoon, i.e. Alexandretta, now İskenderun, a port in south-eastern Turkey that was notorious for unhealthy air.

Scanderbeg.who: George Kastrioti Skanderbeg (1405–1468), Albanian prince who led resistance against the Ottoman Turks; his life was written by Marin Barleti.

Scanderoon.who: Scanderoon, i.e. Alexandretta, now İskenderun, a port in south-eastern Turkey and the harbour for Aleppo.

Scandia.who: Scandia, the Latin name for Scandinavia.

Schaffhausen.who: Schaffhausen, Swiss town on the Rhine near the Rhine Falls.

Scherertzius.who: Sigismund Scherertz, German Lutheran divine, author of a Libellus consolatorius de spectris on ghosts and apparitions.

Schismatics.who: Schismatics: those who break away from the unity of the Church.

Schoeneus.who: Schoeneus, mythical Boeotian king, father of Atalanta in the version where Hippomenes wins her in a footrace.

Schoenunte.who: Schoenus, a harbour on the Isthmus of Corinth near the Isthmian sanctuary of Poseidon.

Schola Salern.who: The Regimen sanitatis Salernitanum, a medieval Latin verse guide to health from the medical school of Salerno.

Schola Salernitana.who: The Regimen sanitatis Salernitanum, a medieval Latin verse guide to health from the medical school of Salerno, later commented on by Johannes Curio.

Schonbornerus.basis: the Latin form fits, and his Politica discusses household and marriage
Schonbornerus.who: Georg Schönborner, German jurist and political writer, author of Politicorum libri septem.

Schoner.who: Johannes Schöner (1477–1547), Nuremberg mathematician and astrologer who wrote on judging nativities.

Schottus.basis: the Itinerarium Italiae citation fixes the second passage; the first Schottus may be someone else
Schottus.who: In the second passage, François Schott (1548–1622) of Antwerp, author of the Itinerarium Italiae; the learned gentleman in the first passage is uncertain.

Schouten.who: Willem Cornelisz Schouten (c. 1567–1625), Dutch navigator who rounded and named Cape Horn in 1616.

Science.who: Not a name: 'science' in the scholastic sense of demonstrated knowledge.

Scilla.who: Not a name: squill or sea onion (Scilla/Urginea maritima), used as a purge and emetic.

Scioppius.who: Caspar Schoppe (Scioppius, 1576–1649), German scholar and controversialist who edited the Priapeia and wrote Suspectae lectiones; he was first praised, later attacked by Scaliger.

Scipio.who: First, Scipio Africanus the Elder (236–183 BC), who beat Hannibal; later passages, Scipio Aemilianus (d. 129 BC), Terence's patron, possibly murdered.

Scipio Africanus.who: Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus the Elder (236–183 BC), Roman general who defeated Hannibal at Zama and was patron of the poet Ennius.

Scipios.who: The Scipios, Roman family of generals, chiefly Scipio Africanus the Elder, who beat Hannibal, and Scipio Aemilianus, who destroyed Carthage: Virgil's 'two thunderbolts of war'.

Sciron.who: Sciron, mythical robber on the Isthmus road near Megara who kicked travellers off the cliffs; Theseus killed him.

Scot.basis: In the third passage 'Scot. hist.' is short for Hector Boece's *Scotorum historia*, not Reginald Scot.
Scot.who: Reginald Scot (c.1538–1599), English writer whose *Discoverie of Witchcraft* (1584) argued sceptically against belief in witches.

Scotists.who: Scotists, scholastic followers of the Franciscan theologian John Duns Scotus, rivals of the Thomists.

Scotland.who: Scotland, the northern kingdom of Britain, joined in a personal union with England under James I in 1603.

Scotus.who: John Duns Scotus (c.1266–1308), Scottish Franciscan scholastic theologian and philosopher.

Scribes.who: The Scribes, Jewish scholars and teachers of the Law, often named in the Gospels alongside the Pharisees.

Scylla.who: Scylla, mythical sea monster in the Strait of Messina, set opposite the whirlpool Charybdis.

Scyros.who: Scyros (modern Skyros), Aegean island off Euboea, where Achilles was hidden among the daughters of King Lycomedes.

Scytala Laconica.basis: the Spartan scytale, a staff used for coded dispatches

Scythia.who: Scythia, the ancient name for the steppe lands north of the Black Sea and beyond.

Scythian.who: Scythian: of Scythia, the steppe region north of the Black Sea, home in legend of the gold-guarding griffins.

Scythians.who: The Scythians, ancient nomadic peoples of the steppes north of the Black Sea.

Seagrave.who: Seagrave, a village in Leicestershire where Burton was rector from 1632.

Sebastian.who: Saint Sebastian (d. c.288), Roman martyr shot with arrows, invoked as patron against the plague.

Sebastian Foscarinus.basis: There was no doge of Venice named Sebastian Foscarini; the epitaph may belong to another Venetian, and I cannot settle who.

Secundus.who: Johannes Secundus (Jan Everaerts, 1511–1536), Dutch neo-Latin poet famous for his *Basia* (Kisses).

Segovia.who: Segovia, city in Old Castile, central Spain.

Segovian.who: The Roman aqueduct of Segovia in Castile, Spain, still standing.

Seine.who: The Seine, the river of northern France that flows through Paris.

Seius.who: Seius, a stock Roman name for an anybody, used like Titius in legal examples and satire.

Sejani.who: Lucius Aelius Sejanus (d. AD 31), Tiberius's all-powerful praetorian prefect, who fell suddenly and was executed, his body thrown down the Gemonian stairs.

Sejanus.who: Lucius Aelius Sejanus (d. AD 31), Tiberius's all-powerful praetorian prefect, who fell suddenly and was executed, his body thrown down the Gemonian stairs.

Seleucus.basis: The first and third passages mean Seleucus I; the second, a Syrian king who would only contend with Rome, is a later Seleucid (in Plutarch's Cato apparently Antiochus III).
Seleucus.who: Seleucus I Nicator (c.358–281 BC), general of Alexander the Great and founder of the Seleucid kingdom of Syria.

Selim.who: Selim I (1470–1520), Ottoman sultan who took Tabriz in 1514 and carried its craftsmen off to Constantinople.

Selimus.who: Selim I (1470–1520), Ottoman sultan who had his brothers, including Korkut, and his nephews put to death to secure the throne.

Selius.who: Selius, a character satirised in Martial's *Epigrams*.

Semidei.who: Latin term 'semidei', half-gods or demigods, a class of spirits.

Semierus.basis: Camden's Annals for 1578 and the description of a master of courtship fit Simier's embassy.
Semierus.who: Jean de Simier, French courtier sent by François, Duke of Anjou, to woo Queen Elizabeth I on his master's behalf.

Semiramis.who: Semiramis, legendary queen of Assyria, famed for conquests, building Babylon, and lurid tales of vice.

Semiustulation.who: Semiustulation: half-burning or scorching, a term of old physiology.

Semonides.basis: Fits the women-haters passage; the passage on hope may refer to Simonides of Ceos instead.
Semonides.who: Semonides of Amorgos (fl. 7th century BC), Greek iambic poet whose satire compares types of women to animals.

Sempronia.who: Sempronia, Roman noblewoman portrayed by Sallust in the Catiline as an accomplished but dissolute supporter of Catiline's conspiracy.

Sempronius.who: Sempronio, Calisto's servant in Fernando de Rojas's Celestina, which Caspar Barth translated into Latin.

Sen.who: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC–AD 65), Roman Stoic philosopher and moralist.

Senae.who: Siena, city in Tuscany, setting of Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini's tale of Euryalus and Lucretia.

Senec.who: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC–AD 65), Roman Stoic philosopher; the quotation is from his lost work on superstition, preserved by Augustine.

Seneca.who: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC–AD 65), Roman Stoic philosopher, author of moral epistles and the satire on Claudius's death.

Seneca Hipp.who: Seneca's tragedy Phaedra, also called Hippolytus, about Phaedra's passion for her stepson.

Seneca Hippol.who: Seneca's tragedy Phaedra, also called Hippolytus, about Phaedra's passion for her stepson.

Senecio.basis: The anecdote matches the elder Seneca's account of the man obsessed with greatness.
Senecio.who: Senecio, a declaimer described by Seneca the Elder (Suasoriae 2.17) as nicknamed 'Grandio' for his mania for everything big.

Senega.who: The Senegal River in West Africa.

Senelus.who: Selemnus, a river in Achaea near Patrae; Pausanias says bathing in it cured lovers of love.

Sense.who: Sense, a kind of knowledge in scholastic psychology.

Sensible.who: Sensible, i.e. pertaining to the senses; a term of faculty psychology.

Sensible Faculty.who: The sensible faculty of the soul, a term of faculty psychology.

Sensible Soul.who: The sensible soul, a term of faculty psychology.

Sensitive.who: The sensitive faculty of the soul, a term of faculty psychology.

Sensitive Appetite.who: The sensitive appetite, a term of faculty psychology.

Sensitive Soul.who: The sensitive soul, a term of faculty psychology.

Separatists.who: English Protestant Separatists (Brownists and others) who left the Church of England, many settling in congregations at Amsterdam.

Septalius.who: Ludovico Settala (1552–1633), Milanese physician, author of a commentary on the pseudo-Aristotelian Problems.

Seraglio.who: The Seraglio, the Ottoman sultan's palace (Topkapı) at Constantinople, including its harem and gardens.

Serapeum.who: The Serapeum, the great temple of Serapis at Alexandria, destroyed in AD 391.

Serarius.who: Nicolaus Serarius (1555–1609), Jesuit biblical commentator at Mainz, author of commentaries on Joshua and a history of Mainz.

Serbia.who: Serbia, Balkan country then under Ottoman rule.

Serbian.who: Serbian, of Serbia; the 'Crales' (kral, king) here is the Serbian king Stefan Uroš II Milutin.

Serena.basis: The legendary tradition names Diocletian's wife Serena.
Serena.who: Serena, in Christian legend the wife of the emperor Diocletian, venerated as a saint; his historical wife was Prisca.

Serm.who: Abbreviation of 'sermo', a sermon (here of St Bernard).

Serranus.basis: Spinola's attempt to relieve Sluis in 1604 and the Spanish governor's name fit.
Serranus.who: Mateo Serrano, Spanish governor of Sluis (Sluys) during its siege by Maurice of Nassau in 1604.

Serres.who: Jean de Serres (c. 1540–1598), French Huguenot historian, author of the Inventaire général de l'histoire de France.

Sertorius.who: Quintus Sertorius (c. 123–72 BC), Roman general who led a revolt in Spain and claimed his white hind brought divine counsel.

Servetus.who: Michael Servetus (c. 1511–1553), Spanish physician and anti-Trinitarian theologian burned for heresy at Geneva.

Servius.who: Maurus Servius Honoratus (fl. c. 400 AD), Latin grammarian whose commentary on Virgil's works was standard throughout the Middle Ages and Renaissance.

Servius Sulpicius.who: Servius Sulpicius Rufus (c. 106–43 BC), Roman jurist and consul; he wrote Cicero a famous letter of consolation on the death of Tullia (Ad familiares 4.5).

Sesellio.who: Claude de Seyssel (c. 1450–1520), French statesman and bishop, author of La Grande Monarchie de France, known in Latin as De republica Galliae.

Sesostris.who: Sesostris, a legendary Egyptian king and conqueror described by Herodotus and Diodorus; the figure is partly based on the pharaohs called Senusret.

Sestos.who: Sestos, an ancient town on the European shore of the Hellespont (Dardanelles); in the legend, Hero lived there and Leander swam across to her from Abydos.

Severians.who: The Severians, a 2nd-century Encratite sect named after one Severus; they rejected wine and marriage.

Severinus.who: Petrus Severinus (Peder Sørensen, c. 1540–1602), Danish physician and leading interpreter of Paracelsus, author of the Idea medicinae philosophicae (1571).

Severn.who: The Severn, Britain's longest river, which flows through Wales and western England into the Bristol Channel; Aust is on its estuary in Gloucestershire.

Severus.who: Septimius Severus (145–211), Roman emperor from 193; he died at York, and ancient writers mention his reliance on astrology.

Sextus Empiricus.who: Sextus Empiricus (fl. c. 200 AD), Greek physician and Pyrrhonist sceptic, author of the Outlines of Pyrrhonism and Against the Professors (Adversus mathematicos).

Shame.who: Not a name: a personified abstraction in an allegory.

Sheba.who: Sheba (Saba), an ancient kingdom in south-west Arabia, roughly modern Yemen; its queen visited Solomon (1 Kings 10).

Shechem.who: Shechem, son of Hamor, a Hivite prince who seized and defiled Jacob's daughter Dinah (Genesis 34).

Sherborne.who: Sherborne, a town in Dorset, England; Bishop Roger of Salisbury built its castle in the early 12th century.

Shereefs.who: The Sharifs, the Saadian dynasty that ruled Morocco (Fez, Marrakesh, Sus) in the 16th and 17th centuries, claiming descent from the Prophet.

Sherwood.who: Sherwood Forest in Nottinghamshire, England, the legendary haunt of Robin Hood.

Shetland.who: The Shetland Islands, an archipelago north-east of mainland Scotland.

Shimei.who: Shimei, son of Gera, a Benjaminite who cursed and stoned King David as he fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 16).

Shoemakers.who: Not a name: a trade, shoemakers, of which St Crispin is the patron saint.

Shrine.basis: Peter Dunin (Piotr Włostowic) is meant, but which Polish lordship 'Shrine' stands for is uncertain.

Siam.who: Siam, the kingdom in South-East Asia now called Thailand.

Sib.who: Sib, a pet form of Sibyl, used here as a stock name for a country girl.

Sibylla Cumea.who: The Cumaean Sibyl, the prophetess of Apollo at Cumae near Naples; Christians read prophecies of Christ into oracles attributed to her.

Sibylline.who: An adjective from the Sibyls, prophetesses of antiquity; it refers to the oracles ascribed to them, including the forged Christian 'Sibylline Oracles' that Casaubon exposed.

Sibylline Prophets.who: Prophets of the Sibyls' kind: inspired prophetesses of antiquity, such as the Cumaean and Delphic Sibyls.

Sibyls.who: The Sibyls, inspired prophetesses of Greek and Roman tradition, such as those of Cumae, Erythrae and Delphi.

Sichem.who: Scherpenheuvel (Montaigu) in Brabant, in modern Belgium, a Marian pilgrimage shrine famed for miracles; Lipsius wrote of it in Diva Sichemiensis (1605).

Sicilian.who: Of Sicily: the 'Sicilian Evensongs' are the Sicilian Vespers, the massacre of the French in 1282; the other passages mean Sicily's ancient tyrants.

Sicily.who: Sicily, the large Mediterranean island off the south-west tip of Italy.

Sicinius Aemilianus.who: Sicinius Aemilianus (2nd century AD), brother-in-law of Pudentilla; c. 158 he prosecuted Apuleius for magic, and Apuleius answered in his Apologia.

Sicinius Dentatus.who: Lucius Siccius (or Sicinius) Dentatus (5th century BC), legendary Roman soldier and tribune, called the 'Roman Achilles' for his many battles and wounds.

Sicyon.who: Sicyon, an ancient Greek city in the north-east Peloponnese, west of Corinth, famous for its school of painting and sculpture.

Sicyonian.who: Of Sicyon, the ancient Greek city near Corinth; Dibutades (Butades) of Sicyon was a potter whose daughter's outline drawing was said to be the origin of painting.

Sidonians.who: The people of Sidon, an ancient Phoenician city, now Saida in Lebanon; they worshipped Astarte.

Sidonius Apol.who: Sidonius Apollinaris (c. 430–c. 489), Gallo-Roman poet and letter-writer, bishop of Clermont.

Siena.who: Siena, a city in Tuscany, Italy, an independent republic until 1555.

Siennois.who: A man of Siena, in Tuscany.

Sierra de Cadarama.who: The Sierra de Guadarrama, the mountain range north-west of Madrid, beside El Escorial.

Sierras.basis: The passage pairs it with the Andes and 'Lanes' (llanos) and cites Spanish writers on America.
Sierras.who: The sierras, the highland zone of Peru and the Andes, as opposed to the coastal plains and the llanos (lowland plains).

Sight.who: Not a name: the sense of sight.

Sigismund.basis: The first passage means Emperor Sigismund (1368–1437); the second means a Polish King Sigismund in 1548, a different person.

Signior.basis: A title that refers to different sultans in the two passages.
Signior.who: The 'Grand Signior' was the usual European title for the Ottoman sultan: Suleiman I in Busbecq's time, and Mehmed II at the fall of Constantinople.

Sigonius.who: Carlo Sigonio (c.1524–1584), Italian humanist historian, author of *De regno Italiae*, a history of medieval Italy.

Silenus.who: Silenus, the aged satyr who tutored Dionysus; when captured by King Midas he declared it best never to be born, and next best to die soon.

Silesia.who: Silesia, a region on the upper Oder, now mostly in south-western Poland; its chief city is Breslau (Wrocław).

Silius.who: Gaius Silius (d. AD 24), Roman general who put down Sacrovir's revolt in Gaul, later prosecuted under Tiberius and driven to suicide (Tacitus, *Annals* 4).

Simeon.basis: Three different bearers: the Byzantine physician Simeon Seth, the old Simeon of Luke 2, and Simeon the son of Jacob.

Simeon Sethi.who: Symeon Seth (fl. late 11th century), Byzantine physician, author of a treatise on the properties of foods.

Similar.basis: An anatomical term (similar, i.e. homogeneous, parts).

Simlerus.who: Josias Simler (1530–1576), Swiss Reformed theologian of Zurich, author of *De republica Helvetiorum* (1576).

Simon.basis: The passage ascribes him to Lucian, but I am not sure which dialogue he appears in.
Simon.who: Simon, a fictional upstart in one of Lucian's satirical dialogues who became rich and renamed himself Simonides.

Simon Magus.who: Simon Magus, the Samaritan sorcerer of Acts 8, who in later legend (e.g. the Clementine *Recognitions*) became the archetypal magician and opponent of Peter.

Simonida.who: Simonida Palaiologina (c.1294–after 1336), daughter of the Byzantine emperor Andronikos II, married as a child to the Serbian king Stefan Uroš II Milutin.

Simonides.basis: The first two passages mean the poet Simonides of Ceos; the third is the new name Lucian's Simon took for himself.

Simple.basis: An ordinary word used as a term of classification.

Simplicius.who: Simplicius of Cilicia (c.490–c.560), Neoplatonist philosopher, commentator on Aristotle and on Epictetus' *Enchiridion*.

Sinalda.basis: The story matches Saxo's Swanhild (Svanhildr); Burton's spelling of the name is unusual.
Sinalda.who: Swanhild, a legendary queen in Saxo Grammaticus whose beauty held back the horses sent to trample her, until she was covered up.

Sinapismus.basis: A mustard plaster used to raise blisters.

Sion.who: Mount Zion, a hill in Jerusalem.

Sir Amorous La-Fool.who: Sir Amorous La-Foole, a foolish gallant in Ben Jonson's comedy *Epicoene, or The Silent Woman* (1609).

Sir Christopher Heydon.who: Sir Christopher Heydon (d. 1623), English writer on astrology, author of *A Defence of Judiciall Astrologie* (1603).

Sir Walter Mauny.who: Sir Walter Mauny (c.1310–1372), knight from Hainault who served Edward III and was celebrated by Froissart; founder of the London Charterhouse.

Siracides.who: Jesus ben Sira (fl. early 2nd century BC), Jewish sage and author of Ecclesiasticus (the Wisdom of Sirach).

Sirens.who: The Sirens, sea-creatures of Greek myth whose song lured sailors to their deaths.

Sisyphus.who: Sisyphus, the king of Corinth in Greek myth who was condemned in Hades to roll a stone uphill for ever.

Sitius.who: Francesco Sizzi (c.1585–1618), Florentine astronomer whose *Dianoia astronomica* (1611) attacked Galileo's discovery of Jupiter's moons.

Sixtus ab Hemminga.who: Sixtus ab Hemminga (1533–1586), Frisian writer who attacked judicial astrology by examining the horoscopes of famous people.

Slavonia.who: Slavonia, a region between the Drava and Sava rivers, now in eastern Croatia.

Sluce.who: Sluis, a fortified port town in Zeeland, the Netherlands, near Bruges; contested in the Dutch Revolt.

Sluis.who: Sluis, a port town in Zeeland, the Netherlands, linked to Bruges by a canal.

Smindyrides.who: Smindyrides of Sybaris (6th century BC), a byword for luxury and a suitor of Agariste of Sicyon according to Herodotus.

Sneezing.basis: a symptom in a list of diseases

Snellius.who: Willebrord Snellius (1580–1626), Dutch mathematician whose *Eratosthenes Batavus* (1617) measured the size of the earth by triangulation.

Socia.basis: a servant's name with Latin threat of the mill; it matches the comic slave name Sosia
Socia.who: Sosia, the stock name of a slave in Roman comedy (as in Plautus's *Amphitruo* and Terence's *Andria*), used here for any servant.

Socinians.who: The Socinians: antitrinitarian followers of Laelius and Faustus Socinus, organised as the Polish Brethren and centred on Raków in Poland.

Socinus.basis: Paired with Vorstius and linked to toleration; Faustus fits better than his uncle Laelius Socinus
Socinus.who: Faustus Socinus (Fausto Sozzini, 1539–1604), Italian antitrinitarian theologian who led the Polish Brethren and gave his name to Socinianism.

Socrates.who: Socrates (c. 470–399 BC), the Athenian philosopher, Plato's teacher.

Sodom.who: Sodom, the biblical city destroyed with Gomorrah for its wickedness (Genesis 19).

Sodomite.basis: a term of abuse applied to Socrates

Sodomites.basis: a common noun in a description of Bale's list

Solinander.who: Reiner Solenander (1524–1601), German physician to the Dukes of Cleves and author of *Consilia medicinalia*.

Solomon.who: Solomon, king of Israel, son of David, traditional author of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes.

Solomon’s Concubines.who: The concubines and foreign wives of King Solomon, who turned his heart to other gods (1 Kings 11).

Solon.who: Solon (c. 640–c. 560 BC), Athenian statesman, lawgiver and poet, counted among the Seven Sages.

Solon’s Areopagites.who: The Areopagites, members of the Council of the Areopagus at Athens, which Solon made the guardian of the laws and of public conduct.

Sols.basis: 'Obs and Sols', the objections and solutions of scholastic disputation

Soncinas.who: Paulus Soncinas (Paolo Barbò of Soncino, d. 1495), Italian Dominican Thomist philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.

Sophia.who: First passage: Empress Sophia, wife of Justin II (Burton says Justinian), who mocked Narses. Second: Sophia, an interlocutor in Leone Ebreo's *Dialoghi d'amore*.

Sophianus.who: Nicolaus Sophianus (fl. 1540s), Greek scholar from Corfu who made a map and description of Greece.

Sophies.who: The 'Sophies', the Safavid shahs of Persia.

Sophocles Antigone.who: Sophocles' tragedy *Antigone*; the line comes from its choral ode to Love.

Sophonisba.who: Sophonisba (d. 203 BC), Carthaginian noblewoman, wife of Syphax and then Masinissa, who took poison rather than be led captive to Rome.

Sophy.who: The Sophy, the Safavid shah of Persia, the title used in Burton's time.

Sorbonists.who: Sorbonists: the scholastic theologians of the Sorbonne, the theology faculty of Paris.

Sorites.basis: logical term: a chain of syllogisms

Sossius Sinesius.who: Quintus Sosius Senecio, Roman consul (99 and 107 AD) and friend of Pliny the Younger, who addressed *Letters* 1.13 to him.

Soteres.who: Soteres ('saviours'), Greek title for protecting gods, given especially to the Dioscuri.

Souda.who: Souda (Suda) Bay, a large natural harbour on the north-west coast of Crete near Chania.

Spagirica Pharmac.basis: Burton credits it to Quercetan; the exact title is uncertain
Spagirica Pharmac.who: A spagyric (chemical) pharmacopoeia by Joseph Duchesne (Quercetanus, c. 1544–1609), French Paracelsian physician.

Spahan.who: Spahan: Isfahan, the Safavid capital of Persia, in central Iran.

Spain Aragon.who: Aragon, a former kingdom and now a region in north-eastern Spain.

Spaniard.who: A Spaniard; a native of Spain.

Spaniards.who: The Spaniards, the people of Spain.

Spaniards. Schouten.basis: Form wrongly joins 'Spaniards' to 'Schouten'; identification is of Schouten.
Spaniards. Schouten.who: Willem Schouten (c.1567–1625), Dutch navigator who sailed with Jacob Le Maire round Cape Horn in 1616, finding a new route into the Pacific.

Sparta.who: Sparta (Lacedaemon), the ancient Greek city-state in the southern Peloponnese.

Spartan.who: Of Sparta (Lacedaemon), the ancient Greek city-state.

Speed.who: John Speed (1552–1629), English mapmaker and historian, author of the History of Great Britain (1611).

Speusippus.basis: Different bearers in the two passages
Speusippus.who: First, Speusippus (c.408–339 BC), Plato's nephew and successor at the Academy; second, a young lover in the fictional letters of Aristaenetus.

Speyer.who: Speyer, imperial city and bishopric on the Rhine in south-west Germany.

Spinola.who: Ambrogio Spinola (1569–1630), Genoese general who commanded the Spanish armies in the Netherlands.

Spintrias.basis: Latin term for sexual perverts (from Suetonius on Tiberius)

Spoleto.who: Spoleto, town in Umbria, central Italy, seat of a Lombard duchy in the early Middle Ages.

Spondanus.basis: Second passage cites his commentary on the Odyssey; the first (Circe-like metamorphoses) fits the same commentary, though his brother Henri de Sponde is also a 'Spondanus'.
Spondanus.who: Jean de Sponde (Spondanus, 1557–1595), French humanist and poet, editor of Homer with a Latin commentary (1583).

Sprenger.who: Jacob Sprenger (c.1436–1495), German Dominican inquisitor, named as co-author of the witch-hunting manual Malleus Maleficarum.

Springer.basis: The despairing man is Spiera; Scrimgeour's account of him is known and the name is a corruption.
Springer.who: Henry Scrimgeour (c.1506–1572), Scottish jurist and humanist at Geneva, who wrote an account of the despairing death of Francesco Spiera.

Spruce.who: Prussia ('Spruce' is the old English name), the Baltic region around Danzig.

St. George.who: St George, legendary soldier-martyr and patron saint of England, famed in the Golden Legend for slaying a dragon.

St. John de Ullua.who: San Juan de Ulúa, island fortress and harbour off Veracruz, Mexico, notoriously unhealthy.

Staffordshire.who: Staffordshire, county in the English Midlands.

Stanihurst.who: Richard Stanihurst (1547–1618), Dublin-born scholar, author of De rebus in Hibernia gestis (1584), a Latin history of Ireland.

Staphyla.who: Staphyla, the old servant-woman of the miser Euclio in Plautus's comedy Aulularia (Burton calls her his wife).

Stapleton.who: Thomas Stapleton (1535–1598), English Catholic theologian and controversialist in exile at Louvain and Douai.

Stentor.who: Stentor, the Greek herald in Homer's Iliad whose voice was as loud as fifty men's.

Stentorian Democritus.basis: figurative phrase: a loud-voiced Democritus, the laughing philosopher of Abdera

Stephan.basis: The Avignon anecdote of papal luxury fits Estienne's Apologie; the second passage names a different person.
Stephan.who: First, probably Henri Estienne (Stephanus, 1531–1598), French scholar-printer, author of the satirical Apologie pour Hérodote; second, a Neapolitan knight in Panormita's account.

Stephanus.basis: Third passage cites Praedium rusticum (Charles Estienne); the first concerns Greek cities (Stephanus of Byzantium); the second probably refers to Henri Estienne's anecdote.
Stephanus.who: Different men: Stephanus of Byzantium, Greek geographer (Ethnica); Henri Estienne, French scholar (Apologie pour Hérodote); Charles Estienne (1504–1564), French physician, author of Praedium rusticum.

Stephanus Bathorius.who: Stephen Báthory (1533–1586), prince of Transylvania and king of Poland from 1576.

Stercutius.who: Stercutius (Sterculius), minor Roman god of manuring the fields.

Stesichorus.who: Stesichorus (fl. 6th century BC), Greek lyric poet of Himera, said to have been struck blind for slandering Helen until he recanted in his Palinode.

Stetein.who: Stettin in Pomerania, now Szczecin, Poland.

Stheneboea.who: Stheneboea (also called Anteia), in Greek myth the wife of King Proetus of Tiryns, who falsely accused Bellerophon after he rejected her.

Stimula.who: Stimula, a minor Roman goddess who stirred people to action, later identified with Semele.

Stockerus.basis: Burton cites a medical recipe collection, and the Latin form fits Stocker.
Stockerus.who: Johann Stocker (Stockerus), physician of Ulm, whose collection of medical recipes, the *Praxis aurea*, was published after his death.

Stoic.who: A member of the Stoic school founded by Zeno of Citium; in the first passage the word is part of a citation of Lipsius's *Manuductio ad Stoicam philosophiam*.

Stoical.who: Belonging to the Stoics, the philosophical school founded by Zeno of Citium.

Stoics.who: The Stoics, the Greek philosophical school founded by Zeno of Citium (c. 300 BC).

Strasbourg.who: Strasbourg in Alsace, famous for its cathedral spire and astronomical clock.

Stratocles.who: Stratocles, the old physician who marries in Theodore Prodromus's twelfth-century Byzantine satirical dialogue *Amarantus*.

Stratonice.who: Stratonice, daughter of Demetrius Poliorcetes, wife of Seleucus I and then of his son Antiochus I; the second passage means a different Stratonice, wife of the Galatian king Deiotarus.

Strode.who: Ralph Strode (fl. c. 1350–1400), Oxford logician and Merton fellow, a writer of scholastic logical treatises.

Stroza.basis: The citations 'Stroza fil.' and 'Erot. lib. 2' point to the son and the father respectively; the first passage could be either.
Stroza.who: The Strozzi of Ferrara, Latin poets: Tito Vespasiano Strozzi (author of the *Eroticon* books) and his son Ercole Strozzi ('Stroza filius').

Stroza Filius.who: Ercole Strozzi (1473–1508), Ferrarese Latin poet, son of Tito Vespasiano Strozzi, whose death he mourned in an epicedium.

Stroza’s Gargiliana.basis: Burton attributes the poem to 'Stroza'; it is unclear whether the father or the son wrote it.
Stroza’s Gargiliana.who: Gargiliana, a scorned ageing beauty addressed in a Latin poem by one of the Strozzi poets of Ferrara.

Struthius.who: Józef Struś (Josephus Struthius, 1510–1568), Polish physician, author of the *Sphygmicae artis libri V*, a treatise on the pulse.

Stuckius.who: Johann Wilhelm Stucki (1542–1607), Zurich theologian and antiquary, author of a description of pagan sacrifices (*Sacrorum sacrificiorumque gentilium descriptio*).

Stygian.who: Belonging to the Styx, the river of the classical underworld; hence hellish.

Stymphalus.who: Stymphalus, an ancient town in north-eastern Arcadia in the Peloponnese, Greece.

Styrians.who: The Styrians, inhabitants of Styria, an Alpine duchy now a province of south-eastern Austria.

Styx.who: The Styx, the chief river of the underworld in Greek myth.

Suadela.who: Suadela, the Roman goddess of persuasion, the counterpart of the Greek Peitho, often attending Venus.

Subtleties.who: Girolamo Cardano's *De subtilitate* (1550), an encyclopaedic work of natural philosophy.

Succuba.basis: Succubus, a kind of demon, not a proper name.

Succubi.basis: Succubi, a kind of demon, not a proper name.

Succubus.basis: Succubus, a kind of demon, not a proper name.

Suetonio.who: Suetonius (c. 70–after 122), Roman biographer, author of the *Lives of the Caesars*.

Suffenus.who: Suffenus, a bad poet mocked by Catullus (poem 22) for being blindly pleased with his own verses.

Suisset.who: Richard Swineshead (fl. c. 1340–1355), Merton College mathematician known as 'the Calculator', author of the *Liber calculationum*.

Suleyman.who: Suleiman the Magnificent (reigned 1520–1566), Ottoman sultan, who took Rhodes (1522), besieged Vienna (1529), and married Roxelana.

Sulla.who: Lucius Cornelius Sulla (c. 138–78 BC), Roman general and dictator.

Sulpicia.who: In the first passage, the Augustan Roman poet Sulpicia, beloved of Cerinthus, whose poems survive among Tibullus's; in the second, a later Sulpicia, wife of Calenus.

Sulpicius Gallus.who: Gaius Sulpicius Gallus, Roman officer under Aemilius Paullus in the Third Macedonian War (168 BC), later consul (166 BC), known for predicting an eclipse.

Sultan.who: A title of Muslim rulers: in the first passage the Ottoman sultan reigning when Sandys travelled; in the second, the ruler of Sana'a in Yemen.

Sultans.who: The Ottoman sultans, rulers of the Turkish empire.

Sun.who: The sun, as a heavenly body and astrological planet.

Sunian.who: Cape Sounion, the southern tip of Attica in Greece.

Suppatius.who: Suppatius, a speaker in the humanist Giovanni Pontano's dialogue *Antonius*.

Surat.who: Surat, a port city in Gujarat, western India.

Surenas.who: Surena (d. 52 BC), the Parthian general who defeated Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC.

Surius.who: Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), Carthusian monk of Cologne, hagiographer and author of a chronicle of the events of his own time.

Surrey.who: Surrey, a county in southern England.

Sus.who: Sous, a region of southern Morocco.

Susa.who: Susa (biblical Shushan, modern Shush in south-west Iran), a royal capital of the Persian kings.

Susan.who: A common girl's name in Burton's alliterative list of sweethearts; no particular person is meant.

Susanna.who: Susanna, the virtuous wife in the apocryphal addition to Daniel, spied on while bathing and falsely accused by two elders.

Susarion.who: Susarion (6th century BC), Megarian poet, traditionally the founder of Greek comedy.

Sussex.who: Sussex, a county in southern England.

Sutton Coldfield.who: Sutton Coldfield, a town in Warwickshire, now part of Birmingham, where Burton went to the grammar school.

Swabian.who: Of Swabia, the south-west German duchy; the prince is Conradin (1252–1268), the last Hohenstaufen, beheaded at Naples by Charles of Anjou.

Swarston.who: Swarkestone, Derbyshire, on the Trent, where the Harpur family had their seat.

Swiss.who: The Swiss, here as mercenary soldiers.

Switzers.who: The Swiss, including Swiss mercenary soldiers.

Sybaris.who: Sybaris, a Greek city in southern Italy that was proverbial for luxury and was destroyed in 510 BC.

Sybarite.who: An inhabitant of Sybaris, the Greek city in southern Italy proverbial for luxury.

Sybarites.who: The people of Sybaris, proverbial for luxury and soft living.

Syllogism.who: A syllogism, a term of logic.

Sylvaducis.who: 's-Hertogenbosch (Bois-le-Duc), a town in North Brabant in the Netherlands.

Sylvanus.who: Silvanus, the Roman god of woods and fields.

Sylvius.basis: Medical context and the date make him the likeliest Sylvius; Franciscus Sylvius came too late for Burton.
Sylvius.who: Jacobus Sylvius (Jacques Dubois, 1478–1555), Paris physician and anatomist who wrote on Galenic medicine.

Symmachus.who: In the first passage, Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 345–402), pagan orator; in the second, his descendant Memmius Symmachus (d. c. 526), Boethius's father-in-law, executed by Theodoric.

Sympos.who: Xenophon's *Symposium*, a dialogue set at a banquet where Socrates is a principal speaker.

Symposio.who: Xenophon's *Symposium* (*Banquet*), a dialogue on love in which Critobulus and Socrates speak.

Syncope.who: Syncope, a medical term for fainting.

Synteresis.who: Synteresis, a scholastic term for the innate knowledge of moral principles in the conscience.

Syracuse.who: Syracuse, the chief Greek city of Sicily.

Syracusian.who: A man of Syracuse in Sicily.

Syrian.who: A Syrian, here Naaman, the Aramaean army commander healed of leprosy by Elisha (2 Kings 5).

Syrian Pherecydes.who: Pherecydes of Syros (fl. 6th century BC), Greek mythographer and cosmologist, traditionally Pythagoras's teacher and said to have first taught the soul's immortality.

Syrians.who: The ancient Syrians, the peoples of Syria and Aram.

Syrophanes.who: Syrophanes of Egypt, a figure in Fulgentius's Mythologies whose statue of his dead son is given as the origin of idolatry.

T. B.who: Timothy Bright (c. 1551–1615), English physician, author of a treatise on the sufficiency of English medicines (1580; reissued 1615).

T. Bright.who: Timothy Bright (c. 1551–1615), English physician and clergyman, author of A Treatise of Melancholie (1586).

T. H.basis: initials of an unidentified translator or source

T. Linacre.who: Thomas Linacre (c. 1460–1524), English humanist physician, founder of the College of Physicians, who took holy orders late in life.

Tabin.who: Tabin (Pliny's Tabis), a promontory placed by ancient geographers and sixteenth-century maps at the north-eastern tip of Asia.

Tables.who: Tables, the old name for backgammon and similar board games.

Tac.who: Tacitus (c. 56–c. 120), Roman historian; the quoted sentence comes from his Annals.

Taisnier.who: Jean Taisnier (1508–c. 1562), Hainaut mathematician and writer on the magnet, perpetual motion, chiromancy and physiognomy.

Tales (Galen.who: Latin 'tales', meaning 'such people', not a name.

Talmudists.who: The rabbinic scholars and commentators of the Talmud.

Tamar.who: In the first passage, Tamar, Judah's daughter-in-law (Genesis 38); in the second, Tamar, David's daughter, raped by her half-brother Amnon (2 Samuel 13).

Tamburlaine.who: Timur, or Tamerlane (1336–1405), Turco-Mongol conqueror of Central Asia, Persia and beyond.

Tancredus.who: Tancredi, prince of Salerno in Boccaccio's Decameron (IV.1), who killed his daughter Ghismonda's lover Guiscardo.

Tandlerus.who: Tobias Tandler (1571–1617), Wittenberg physician and mathematician, author of a dissertation on fascination and enchantment (1606).

Tangents.who: Tangents, trigonometric tables, not a name.

Tarantula.who: Tarantula, the Apulian wolf spider whose bite was thought to cause tarantism.

Tarasconus.who: Tarascon of Parma, a musician mocked as a butt at Pope Leo X's court, as recounted by Paolo Giovio.

Taratantara.who: Taratantara, a Latin word imitating the sound of a trumpet (from Ennius).

Tarentum.who: Tarentum, a Greek city of southern Italy, now Taranto in Apulia.

Tarquin.who: Sextus Tarquinius, son of Tarquin the Proud, whose rape of Lucretia, Collatinus's wife, led to the fall of the Roman monarchy.

Tarquinius.who: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, the last king of Rome, a tyrant expelled c. 509 BC.

Tarquins.who: Men like Sextus Tarquinius, the ravisher of Lucretia, used generically for lustful seducers.

Tarquin’s Tanaquil.who: Tanaquil, Etruscan wife of Tarquinius Priscus, fifth king of Rome, famed in Livy for her shrewdness.

Tartalea.who: Niccolò Tartaglia (c. 1500–1557), Italian mathematician who wrote on ballistics, gunnery and fireworks.

Tartar.who: Tartar: of the Tatars or Tartary; the 'Tartar lamb' is the fabled vegetable lamb; 'the Tartar' means the Tatar khan and his people.

Tartari Zamolhenses.basis: Burton's form seems a corruption of 'Zavolhenses', a term used in sixteenth-century accounts of Muscovy
Tartari Zamolhenses.who: The 'Zavolhensian' Tatars, the nomadic hordes living beyond the Volga.

Tartaria.who: Tartary, the early-modern European name for the vast region of Central and Northern Asia ruled by the Tatar and Mongol khans.

Tartarian Chams.who: The Tatar khans, the Mongol and Tatar rulers of Central Asia.

Tartarian Moguls.basis: the 'great Mogul' is linked with the Tartars elsewhere in Burton
Tartarian Moguls.who: The Mughal emperors of India, a Timurid line seen by Europeans as Tartars.

Tartars.who: The Tatars, Turkic-Mongol peoples of the steppes, including the Crimean Tatars who raided Podolia.

Tartary.who: Usually Tartary, Central and North-East Asia; in the third passage, Tartak, idol of the Avvites (2 Kings 17:31).

Taste.who: Taste, one of the five senses.

Tasting.who: Tasting, one of the five senses.

Tatia.basis: the sieve story belongs to Tuccia in Valerius Maximus and Pliny
Tatia.who: Tuccia, a Roman Vestal Virgin who proved her chastity by carrying water from the Tiber in a sieve.

Tatians.who: Followers of Tatian (2nd century), the Syrian Christian apologist who founded the ascetic Encratites, who rejected marriage, meat and wine.

Tatium.who: Achilles Tatius (fl. 2nd century AD), Greek novelist, author of Leucippe and Clitophon, which includes a debate on love of boys and of women.

Tatius’ Leucippe.who: Leucippe and Clitophon, Greek prose romance by Achilles Tatius (2nd century AD).

Taurellus.who: Nicolaus Taurellus (1547–1606), German philosopher and physician at Altdorf, author of De vita et morte.

Taurellus. Leo Suavius.who: Two names run together: Nicolaus Taurellus (1547–1606), German philosopher; and Leo Suavius, pen-name of Jacques Gohory (1520–1576), French commentator on Paracelsus.

Tauris.who: Tabriz, city in north-western Iran, taken by Selim I in 1514.

Taygetus.who: Taygetus, the mountain range of Laconia in the southern Peloponnese, above Sparta.

Tecmessa.who: Tecmessa, Phrygian princess taken captive by Ajax, who became his concubine, as in Sophocles' Ajax.

Telchine.who: One of the Telchines, mythical spirits of Rhodes, sorcerers known for the evil eye and malignant magic.

Telchines.who: The Telchines, mythical spirits of Rhodes, sorcerers and smiths; Burton uses the name for demons and household spirits.

Telemachus.who: Telemachus, son of Odysseus and Penelope in Homer's Odyssey.

Telephus.who: Telephus, mythical king of Mysia and son of Heracles; with Peleus, Horace cites him as a hero of tragedy in the Ars Poetica.

Telesius.who: Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588), natural philosopher of Cosenza who wrote on the sea and the tides.

Telia Juno.who: Hera Teleia (Juno 'the Fulfiller'), Juno as goddess of marriage, worshipped on Mount Thornax (Cuckoo Mountain) in the Argolid.

Temanite.who: A man of Teman in Edom; the epithet of Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends.

Temenus.who: Temenus, a son of Phegeus of Psophis; with Axion he dedicated Harmonia's necklace at Delphi, as Pausanias tells it.

Tenedos.who: Tenedos, Aegean island off the Trojan coast, now Bozcaada, Turkey; a seat of Apollo's cult.

Tenerife.who: Tenerife, largest of the Canary Islands, whose volcanic peak (Teide) was thought one of the world's highest mountains.

Tentyra.who: Tentyra, modern Dendera in Upper Egypt, whose feud with nearby Ombos Juvenal describes in Satire 15.

Terapeia.basis: Acosta describes this round hot pool in a cold valley in Peru, and the name and description fit Tarapaya
Terapeia.who: Tarapaya, near Potosí in Bolivia, where a circular hot lake (the Ojo del Inca) lies.

Terentia.who: Terentia, wife of Marcus Tullius Cicero.

Tereus.who: Tereus, mythical king of Thrace who raped Philomela and was turned into a hoopoe (Burton says lapwing).

Terra Australis Incognita.who: The 'unknown southern land', a supposed great southern continent; Pedro Fernández de Quirós claimed to have found it in 1606.

Terracina.who: Terracina (ancient Tarracina), coastal town in southern Latium, Italy.

Tertulla.who: Tertulla, wife of the triumvir Marcus Licinius Crassus; Suetonius names her as one of Caesar's mistresses.

Tetrabiblos.who: The Tetrabiblos (or Tetrabiblon), the sixteen-book medical compilation of Aetius of Amida (6th century), arranged in four groups.

Teuchedy.basis: Japanese idol named in Purchas; cannot be matched with confidence

Th. Aquinas.who: St Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), Dominican theologian; the story is of his dinner with Louis IX of France.

Th. Burdett.who: Sir Thomas Burdett, 1st Baronet (d. 1647), whose seat was Foremark (Formark), Derbyshire, near the Trent.

Th. Erastus.who: Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), Swiss physician and theologian at Heidelberg, an opponent of Paracelsus.

Thaddeus Hagecius.who: Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku (1525–1600), Bohemian physician and astronomer who wrote on the new star of 1572.

Thais.who: Thais, stock name of a courtesan: the famous Athenian hetaera, a courtesan in Lucian's dialogues, and the courtesan in Terence's Eunuchus.

Thales.who: Thales of Miletus (c. 624–c. 546 BC), first Greek philosopher and one of the Seven Sages.

Thame.who: River Thame, which joins the Isis (Thames) near Dorchester-on-Thames in Oxfordshire.

Thamus.who: Thamus, the Egyptian pilot in Plutarch's On the Obsolescence of Oracles who was told to announce that 'Great Pan is dead'.

Theagenes.basis: First two passages are certainly the romance hero; the philosopher cited from Lucian is probably Theagenes the Cynic, but this is not certain
Theagenes.who: Mainly Theagenes, hero of Heliodorus' Aethiopica who loves Chariclea; the third passage cites a different Theagenes, a philosopher in Lucian.

Theban.who: The people of Thebes in Boeotia, Greece.

Theban Crates.who: Crates of Thebes (c. 365–c. 285 BC), Cynic philosopher who gave away his wealth; Athenians honoured him as a peacemaker.

Theban Lysias.basis: Burton is following Ficino's Symposium commentary, where Phaedrus is paired with Lysias; 'Theban' is Ficino's error
Theban Lysias.who: Lysias (c.445–c.380 BC), Athenian orator whose speech on love opens Plato's Phaedrus; Ficino wrongly calls him a Theban.

Thebes.who: Thebes, the chief city of Boeotia in ancient Greece.

Thebit Benchorat.who: Thabit ibn Qurra (c.826–901), mathematician and astronomer of Baghdad, known for his theory of the trepidation of the equinoxes (the motion of the eighth sphere).

Themison.who: Themison of Laodicea (1st century BC), Greek physician, pupil of Asclepiades and founder of the Methodist school of medicine.

Themistocles.who: Themistocles (c.524–c.459 BC), Athenian statesman and general, victor at Salamis, who fortified the Piraeus.

Themistocles Lampsacus.basis: Two names run together: Themistocles and the city of Lampsacus
Themistocles Lampsacus.who: Themistocles (c.524–c.459 BC), the exiled Athenian statesman, given the revenues of Lampsacus, a city on the Hellespont, by the Persian king.

Theo.who: The Greek name-prefix 'Theo-', which the diviners' oracle gave as the first letters of Valens's successor.

Theocles.who: Theocles, a lovesick letter-writer in the fictional love letters of Aristaenetus (c. 5th century AD).

Theod. Cyrensis.who: Theodoret of Cyrrhus (c.393–c.458), Syrian bishop and theologian, author of the Graecarum affectionum curatio, an apology against pagan philosophy.

Theodora.who: Theodora (d. after 867), Byzantine empress, wife of the iconoclast emperor Theophilus; she later restored the veneration of icons.

Theodoret.who: Theodoret of Cyrrhus (c.393–c.458), Syrian bishop, theologian and church historian, author of the Graecarum affectionum curatio.

Theodoricus.who: Theodoric the Great (454–526), Ostrogothic king of Italy, who had Boethius and his father-in-law Symmachus put to death.

Theodorus Prodromus.who: Theodore Prodromos (c.1100–c.1170), Byzantine poet, author of the verse romance Rhodanthe and Dosicles, edited with other pieces by Gilbert Gaulmin.

Theodosii.who: Latin plural: men named Theodosius, among those Valens had killed because a divination foretold a successor whose name began 'Theod-'.

Theodosius.who: In the first passage, Theodosius I (r. 379–395), in whose reign John of Lycopolis lived; elsewhere, Theodosius II (401–450), Eastern emperor who married Eudocia.

Theodoti.who: Latin plural: men named Theodotus, among those Valens had killed because of a divination about a successor named 'Theod-'.

Theoduli.who: Latin plural: men named Theodulus, among those Valens had killed because of a divination about a successor named 'Theod-'.

Theog.who: Theognis of Megara (6th century BC), Greek elegiac poet, whose line says that wealth brings folly to mortals.

Theognosti.who: Latin plural: men named Theognostus, among those Valens had killed because of a divination about a successor whose name began 'Theo-'.

Theomestus.who: Theomnestus, an amorous speaker in the Amores (Affairs of the Heart), a dialogue attributed to Lucian.

Theophanes.who: Theophanes, father of Aristoclea, in Plutarch's Love Stories (Amatoriae narrationes).

Theophilus.who: Theophilus (r. 829–842), Byzantine emperor, husband of Theodora, who chose his bride at a bride-show arranged by his stepmother Euphrosyne.

Theophrastian.who: Paracelsian: from Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), Swiss physician and alchemist whom the Rosicrucians revered.

Theophrastus.who: Theophrastus of Eresus (c.371–c.287 BC), Aristotle's successor, author of the Characters and of works on plants.

Theophylact.basis: Could be Theophylact Simocatta or Theophylact of Ohrid; the passage does not settle which

Theriacum Andromachi.who: Theriac of Andromachus: the antidote compounded by Andromachus of Crete, physician to Nero, the standard theriac of later pharmacy.

Thermopylae.who: Thermopylae, the pass in central Greece where Leonidas's Spartans fell fighting the Persians in 480 BC.

Thersites.who: Thersites, the ugliest and most abusive Greek at Troy in Homer's Iliad, who railed at Achilles and Agamemnon.

Theseus.who: Theseus, legendary king and hero of Athens, slayer of the Minotaur, who was later driven from Athens.

Thesmopheries.who: The Thesmophoria, an Athenian festival of Demeter kept by married women only.

Thesperiis.basis: apparently a Greek festival name, possibly corrupt; cannot be settled

Thesprio.who: Thesprio, a slave in Plautus's comedy Epidicus.

Thessala Tempe.who: Vale of Tempe, the gorge of the river Peneus in Thessaly, proverbial for its beauty.

Thessalian.who: Of Thessaly, the region of northern Greece.

Thessalian Thero.who: Thero of Thessaly, a lover in Plutarch's Amatorius who cut off his own thumb to challenge his rival.

Thessalian Tyro.who: Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus, who loved the river Enipeus and was seduced by Poseidon disguised as him.

Thessalonica.who: Thessalonica, modern Thessaloniki, the chief city of Macedonia in northern Greece.

Thessalus.who: Thessalus of Tralles (1st century AD), Methodist physician at Nero's court who boasted that he surpassed all earlier physicians; Galen attacked him.

Thetis.who: Thetis, sea-nymph (Nereid) of Greek myth, wife of Peleus and mother of Achilles.

Theutus.who: Theuth (Thoth), Egyptian god credited in Plato's Phaedrus with inventing letters, numbers and games such as dice.

Thibault.who: Girard Thibault (d. c.1629), Antwerp fencing master, author of the lavishly illustrated fencing treatise Académie de l'espée.

Thisbe.who: Thisbe, Babylonian girl in Ovid's Metamorphoses (book 4) who killed herself over the body of her lover Pyramus.

Tholosanus.who: Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse (Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus, c.1540–1597), French jurist, author of the encyclopaedic Syntaxes artis mirabilis.

Thomas.who: St Thomas Aquinas (c.1225–1274), Dominican theologian and schoolman, author of the Summa theologiae.

Thomas Boderius.basis: The context is astrology in medicine, and the Latin form fits Bodier's treatise on critical days.
Thomas Boderius.who: Thomas Bodier, 16th-century French physician who wrote on critical days and their astrological reckoning (De ratione et usu dierum criticorum, 1555).

Thomas Bodley.who: Sir Thomas Bodley (1545–1613), diplomat and scholar who refounded Oxford University's library, the Bodleian.

Thomas Bozius.who: Tommaso Bozio (1548–1610), Italian Oratorian of Gubbio who wrote against Machiavelli, including De ruinis gentium et regnorum.

Thomas Campanella.who: Tommaso Campanella (1568–1639), Calabrian Dominican philosopher, author of De sensu rerum and The City of the Sun.

Thomas Didymus.who: St Thomas the Apostle ('Didymus', the twin), the traditional evangelist of India, venerated by the St Thomas Christians there.

Thomas Erastus.who: Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), Swiss physician and theologian at Heidelberg, chief opponent of Paracelsus and his medicine.

Thomas Gianinius.basis: His work on the soul after death fits the list of writers on immortality.
Thomas Gianinius.who: Tommaso Giannini of Ferrara (1556–1638), Italian philosopher who wrote on the state of the human mind after death.

Thomas Jackson.who: Thomas Jackson (1579–1640), Oxford divine and President of Corpus Christi College, author of the multi-volume Commentaries upon the Creed.

Thomas Nickell.basis: Known only from Garcaeus's anecdote; the passage says enough

Thomas Philol. Ravennas.who: Tommaso Rangone of Ravenna (1493–1577), physician at Venice, author of a treatise on prolonging human life beyond 120 years.

Thomas’ Shrine.who: The shrine of St Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral, a major pilgrimage site until Henry VIII destroyed it in 1538.

Thomists.who: Thomists, followers of the theology and philosophy of St Thomas Aquinas.

Thornax.who: Mount Thornax near Hermione in the Argolid, Greece, later called Kokkygion (Cuckoo Mountain), where Zeus courted Hera as a cuckoo.

Thrace.who: Thrace, the ancient region north of the Aegean, now divided between Greece, Bulgaria and European Turkey.

Thrace (Andromeda.basis: the form includes a broken parenthesis; the name is Thrace
Thrace (Andromeda.who: Thrace, the ancient region north of the Aegean in which Abdera lay.

Thracian Bosphorus.who: The Thracian Bosporus, the strait at Constantinople (Istanbul) linking the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara.

Thracian Rodophe.who: Rhodopis, the Thracian courtesan at Memphis in Heliodorus's romance Aethiopica, whose beauty tempted the priest Calasiris.

Thracians.who: The Thracians, ancient people of Thrace, north of the Aegean.

Thraso.who: Thraso, the boastful soldier who is Phaedria's rival for the courtesan Thais in Terence's comedy Eunuchus.

Thrasumene.who: Lake Trasimene (Lago Trasimeno), near Perugia in Umbria, Italy.

Thrasymachus.who: Thrasymachus of Chalcedon (fl. late 5th century BC), Greek sophist, Socrates' opponent in Plato's Republic.

Thuanus.who: Jacques-Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), French magistrate and historian, author of the Latin Historia sui temporis.

Thuringia.who: Thuringia, a region of central Germany.

Thurneisserus.who: Leonhard Thurneysser (1531–1596), Basel-born Paracelsian physician, alchemist and astrologer at the Brandenburg court.

Thyamis.who: Thyamis, the Egyptian brigand chief, son of the priest Calasiris, in Heliodorus's romance Aethiopica.

Thyestes.who: Thyestes, brother and rival of Atreus in Greek myth; he seduced Atreus's wife Aerope, and Atreus served him his own sons.

Thyra.who: Thyra (Thyra Danebod, 10th century), queen of Denmark and wife of King Gorm the Old.

Thyraeus.who: Petrus Thyraeus (1546–1601), German Jesuit theologian, author of De locis infestis on haunted places.

Tib.who: Tib, a stock pet-name for a country girl (short for Isabel), used in a list of alliterative nicknames.

Tibareni.who: The Tibareni, an ancient people on the Black Sea coast of Pontus, said to practise the couvade, the husband lying in at childbirth.

Tiber.who: The Tiber, the river flowing through Rome.

Tiberius.who: Tiberius (42 BC–AD 37), second Roman emperor and successor of Augustus.

Tibris.who: The Tiber (Latin Tiberis), the river flowing through Rome.

Tibullus Epig.who: Albius Tibullus (c.55–19 BC), Roman elegiac poet; the Sulpicia–Cerinthus poems survive in the collection under his name.

Ticinum.who: Ticinum, the Roman name of Pavia in Lombardy, northern Italy.

Tidore.who: Tidore, a spice island in the Moluccas, in present-day eastern Indonesia.

Tigillinus.who: Ofonius Tigellinus (d. 69 AD), Nero's praetorian prefect and notorious companion in his debaucheries.

Tigranes.who: Tigranes, son of the Armenian king in Xenophon's Cyropaedia, whose wife praised only him and not Cyrus.

Tigris.who: The Tigris, the great river of Mesopotamia.

Tillesley.who: Richard Tillesley (1582–1621), Archdeacon of Rochester, who wrote Animadversions (1619) against Selden's History of Tithes.

Tim. Bright.who: Timothy Bright (c. 1551–1615), English physician, author of A Treatise of Melancholie (1586).

Timaea.who: Timaea, wife of the Spartan king Agis II, who was seduced by Alcibiades during his exile in Sparta.

Timaeus.who: Plato's Timaeus, his dialogue on cosmology and the world-soul.

Timanthes.who: Timanthes (fl. c. 400 BC), Greek painter, famous for his Sacrifice of Iphigenia, in which Agamemnon's face was veiled.

Timocreon.who: Timocreon of Rhodes (5th century BC), Greek lyric poet, famous as a glutton and heavy drinker.

Timolaus.who: Timolaus, a speaker in Lucian's dialogue The Ship, or The Wishes, who wishes for magic rings giving strength and invisibility.

Timoleon.who: Timoleon (d. c. 337 BC), Corinthian general who freed Syracuse from its tyrants and went blind in old age.

Timon.who: Timon of Athens (5th century BC), the proverbial misanthrope and subject of Lucian's dialogue Timon.

Timon Misanthropus.who: Timon of Athens (5th century BC), the proverbial misanthrope.

Timons.who: Timon of Athens (5th century BC), the proverbial misanthrope.

Timotheus.who: Timotheus, an aulos-player at the court of Alexander the Great, whose music was said to rouse the king to arms.

Timothy.who: Timothy, St Paul's disciple, to whom Paul wrote 'use a little wine for thy stomach's sake' (1 Timothy 5:23).

Tiraquellus.who: André Tiraqueau (1488–1558), French jurist, author of De legibus connubialibus, a treatise on marriage laws.

Tiresias.who: Tiresias, the blind Theban seer of Greek myth, whom Menippus consults in the underworld in Lucian's Necyomantia.

Tiridates.who: Tiridates III, king of Armenia (d. c. 330), said to have been struck mad for martyring Rhipsime and her nuns, then converted by Gregory the Illuminator.

Tiro.who: Calestrius Tiro, Roman senator and friend of the younger Pliny, who addressed letters to him.

Titicacan.who: Lake Titicaca, the great lake of the Andes, on the border of present-day Peru and Bolivia.

Titus Pomponius Atticus.who: Titus Pomponius Atticus (110–32 BC), Roman knight and Cicero's friend, who starved himself to death when incurably ill.

Tityus.who: Tityus, the giant of Greek myth punished in Tartarus by vultures that fed on his liver.

Toledo.who: Toledo, city in central Spain, seat of the primate archbishops of Spain.

Tolet.who: Francisco de Toledo (Toletus) (1532–1596), Spanish Jesuit cardinal, author of commentaries on Aristotle, including De anima.

Tom Straw.basis: He is named beside Jack Cade and Kett as an English rebel; Burton seems to mean Jack Straw.
Tom Straw.who: Jack Straw (d. 1381), a leader of the English Peasants' Revolt with Wat Tyler.

Tontonteac.basis: The spelling and the barbarous New World context fit the Spanish accounts.
Tontonteac.who: Totonteac, a legendary kingdom of the American Southwest named in Spanish reports of the Cibola expeditions, such as that of Marcos de Niza.

Tophas.basis: The verse quoted is pastoral, and the name appears to derive from Chaucer's Sir Thopas.
Tophas.who: Sir Thopas, Chaucer's burlesque knight, whose name pastoral poets borrowed for a rustic swain.

Torlaquis.who: Torlaks, an order of wandering Turkish dervishes known for their extreme asceticism.

Torquati.who: The Manlii Torquati, a Roman family named after Titus Manlius Torquatus, who killed a Gaulish champion in single combat (Livy, Book 7).

Tostatus.who: Alonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), Bishop of Ávila, Spanish theologian and voluminous biblical commentator, here on the Books of Kings.

Toulouse.who: Toulouse, city in south-western France, seat of a parlement; Vanini was burned there in 1619.

Trajan.who: Trajan (53–117), Roman emperor from 98, correspondent of the younger Pliny and builder of the great bridge over the Danube.

Tralles.who: Tralles, ancient city of western Asia Minor in the Maeander valley, at modern Aydın, Turkey.

Trallianus.who: Alexander of Tralles (6th century), Byzantine physician whose twelve books on medicine treat melancholy at length.

Tranio.who: Tranio, the scheming slave in Plautus's comedy Mostellaria.

Transalpines.who: Peoples beyond the Alps, as seen from Italy; here the English.

Transylvania.who: Transylvania, principality in the eastern Carpathian region, now in Romania, known for its mines and its toleration of Unitarians.

Treacle.who: Theriac, a compound antidote of many ingredients.

Trebatius.who: Gaius Trebatius Testa (1st century BC), Roman jurist, protégé of Cicero and legal adviser to Augustus.

Trebellius Pollio.who: Trebellius Pollio, one of the supposed authors of the late Roman imperial biographies, the Historia Augusta.

Trebius.basis: Unclear whether a slip for Horace's lawyer Trebatius or some other figure.

Trent.who: In the first two passages the River Trent in the English Midlands; in the third Trento (Trent), city in northern Italy.

Tribadas.who: Tribades: women who have sex with women.

Tricassus.who: Patrizio Tricasso (fl. early 16th century), Mantuan writer on chiromancy (palmistry).

Trigautius.who: Nicolas Trigault (1577–1628), Flemish Jesuit missionary to China, who edited Matteo Ricci's account of the China mission (1615).

Trimalchionis Topanta.basis: In the Satyricon the phrase 'Trimalchionis topanta' and the bread and money-measure details are used of Fortunata.
Trimalchionis Topanta.who: Fortunata, the low-born wife of Trimalchio in Petronius's Satyricon, called Trimalchio's 'topanta' (his all-in-all).

Tripos.who: Tripod; the golden tripod of the Seven Sages story.

Trismegistus.who: Hermes Trismegistus, legendary Egyptian sage to whom the Hermetic writings on theology and philosophy were attributed.

Tristram.who: Sir Tristram (Tristan), knight of Arthurian romance and lover of Iseult.

Trithemius.who: Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), German Benedictine abbot of Sponheim, bibliographer and occultist, author of Steganographia and Polygraphia.

Triton.who: In the first passage a triton or merman; in the others the sea-god Triton, son of Poseidon, a speaker in Celio Calcagnini's dialogues.

Tritons.who: Tritons, mermen of Greek myth who attend Poseidon (Neptune).

Troezenian Anaxo.who: Anaxo of Troezen, a woman whom Theseus carried off, according to Plutarch's Life of Theseus.

Trogus.who: Pompeius Trogus (1st century BC), Roman historian whose Philippic Histories survive in Justin's epitome.

Troilus.who: Troilus, Trojan prince and son of Priam, killed by Achilles; hero of Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde.

Troja.who: Troy, the city of Priam besieged by the Greeks.

Trojans.who: The people of Troy; in the third passage used in the proverbial sense of 'true Trojans'.

Trolli.who: Trolls, household spirits of Scandinavian folklore.

Trolly Lolly.basis: A comic name in a mock love letter.

Tropics.who: The tropics: the torrid zone between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.

Troy.who: Troy, the city of Priam besieged by the Greeks, in north-western Asia Minor.

Tryphaena.who: Tryphaena, a courtesan in one of Lucian's Dialogues of the Courtesans.

Tubery.basis: The French form 'Tubery' and the marginal note 'In Gallia Narbonensi' fit Saint-Thibéry.
Tubery.who: St Tiberius (Thibéry), early martyr venerated at Saint-Thibéry near Agde in Languedoc.

Tullies.who: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Roman orator and philosopher; the plural means men learned like him.

Tulliola.who: Tullia (c. 79–45 BC), Cicero's beloved daughter; after her death he planned a shrine to deify her.

Tully’s Tusculan.who: Cicero's country villa at Tusculum, in the Alban Hills near modern Frascati, his retreat for study.

Tully’s Tusculans.who: Cicero's Tusculan Disputations (45 BC), philosophical dialogues on death, pain, grief, the passions and happiness.

Tunis.who: Tunis, city and kingdom in North Africa, now the capital of Tunisia.

Turbervile.who: George Turberville (c. 1540–c. 1597), English poet and translator, under whose name The Noble Art of Venerie or Hunting (1575) appeared.

Turcas.who: The Turks (Latin accusative), i.e. the Ottoman Turks.

Turcia.who: Turkey, i.e. the Ottoman Empire (Latin form).

Turditans.who: The Turdetani, an ancient people of southern Spain in the Guadalquivir valley (Roman Baetica).

Turk.who: An Ottoman Turk; Burton applies it to Sultan Mehmed II, Sultan Bayezid I, and an anonymous man of Constantinople in Busbecq.

Turkey Paradise.who: The paradise of Islam as described in the Qur'an.

Turkish History.who: Richard Knolles's The Generall Historie of the Turkes (1603), the standard English history of the Ottomans.

Turks’ Alcoran.who: The Qur'an, the holy book of Islam.

Turner.who: William Turner (c. 1508–1568), English physician, divine and botanist, author of A New Herball and a book on English baths.

Turnus.who: Turnus, king of the Rutulians in Virgil's Aeneid, Aeneas's rival for Lavinia.

Turri Babel.who: Turris Babel (1619), Johann Valentin Andreae's satirical tract on the controversy about the Rosicrucian fraternity.

Tursellinus.who: Orazio Torsellino (1545–1599), Italian Jesuit, author of a Life of St Francis Xavier.

Tuscan.who: Etruscan; the soothsayer is an Etruscan haruspex, friend of Fulvius Flaccus (121 BC).

Tuscans.who: The ancient Etruscans of central Italy.

Tuscany.who: Tuscany, the grand duchy in central Italy ruled by the Medici.

Tusculan.who: Cicero's villa at Tusculum (first passage); in the second, his Tusculan Disputations.

Tusculans.who: Cicero's Tusculan Disputations (45 BC); Book 4 treats the passions of the mind.

Tusser.who: Thomas Tusser (c. 1524–1580), English poet and farmer, author of Five Hundred Points of Good Husbandry.

Tycho.who: Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), Danish astronomer, author of the Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata.

Tycho Brahe.who: Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), Danish astronomer, who built his observatory Uraniborg on the island of Hven.

Tyrtaeus.who: Tyrtaeus (fl. 7th century BC), Spartan elegiac poet of martial verse.

Udalricus.who: Ulrich II, Count of Celje (Cilli) (1406–1456), Hungarian magnate and rival of the Hunyadi family.

Ulfo.basis: Saxo is cited and the Danish royal line descends from Ulf through Sweyn Estridsen
Ulfo.who: Ulf Jarl (d. 1026), Danish earl, father of King Sweyn II Estridsen; Saxo tells a legend of his family's descent from a bear.

Ulmus.basis: Latin form fits, and he appears in a list of 16th-century medical writers
Ulmus.who: Franciscus Ulmus (François Orme), 16th-century French physician and medical author.

Ulricus.who: St Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg (c. 890–973), to whom a spurious letter against clerical celibacy, telling of Pope Gregory and infants' skulls, was attributed.

Ulricus Huttenus.who: Ulrich von Hutten (1488–1523), German humanist and satirist, author of the poem Nemo.

Ulricus Molitor.who: Ulrich Molitor (c. 1442–1507), German jurist, author of De lamiis et phitonicis mulieribus (1489) on witches.

Ulysses.who: Ulysses (Odysseus), the hero of Homer's Odyssey.

Ulysses Aldrovandus.who: Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605), naturalist of Bologna, author of large illustrated natural histories, including the Ornithologia.

Understanding.who: The faculty of understanding: a heading, not a name.

Urania.who: *The Countess of Montgomery's Urania* (1621), prose romance by Lady Mary Wroth, modelled on Sidney's *Arcadia*.

Uraniborg.who: Uraniborg, Tycho Brahe's observatory-castle, built from 1576 on the island of Hven (now Ven) in the Øresund, now part of Sweden.

Ursula.who: St Ursula, legendary virgin martyr said to have been killed at Cologne with eleven thousand companions; in the first passage simply a girl's name.

Ussher.who: James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh, whose *De Christianarum ecclesiarum successione et statu* (1613) traced the corruption of the Church under the papacy.

Utopia.who: Utopia, the imaginary island commonwealth of Sir Thomas More's *Utopia* (1516).

Utopian.who: Of Utopia, the ideal commonwealth described in Sir Thomas More's *Utopia* (1516).

Vacuna.who: Vacuna, ancient Sabine goddess of leisure and rest, to whom farmers sacrificed after their labours.

Vacunal.who: Of Vacuna, Sabine goddess of leisure, whose festival fires Ovid mentions in the *Fasti*.

Valence.who: Valencia, the kingdom and region on the east coast of Spain (not Valence in France).

Valencia.who: Valencia, the kingdom and region on the Mediterranean coast of eastern Spain.

Valens.who: Valens (r. 364–378), Roman emperor of the East, an Arian, killed at the battle of Adrianople.

Valentine.who: St Valentine, early Roman martyr, invoked against epilepsy; in the second passage the hero of the romance *Valentine and Orson*.
