Valentinian.basis: The pairing with Theodosius fits the joint divorce legislation; the heretics are clearly the Gnostic sect.
Valentinian.who: Valentinian III (419–455), Western Roman emperor, joint issuer with Theodosius II of laws on divorce; in the second passage the Valentinians, followers of the Gnostic Valentinus.

Valentinius.who: Valentinus (fl. c. 140), Gnostic teacher at Rome, whose followers Irenaeus attacks in *Against Heresies*.

Valentinus Andreas.who: Johann Valentin Andreae (1586–1654), Lutheran theologian of Württemberg, associated with the Rosicrucian manifestos, author of *Turris Babel* and *Christianopolis*.

Valerian.who: Valerian (r. 253–260), Roman emperor captured by the Persian king Shapur I, who died in captivity.

Valerianus.who: Valerian (r. 253–260), Roman emperor who persecuted the Christians, following Decius.

Valerius Flaccus.who: Gaius Valerius Flaccus (d. c. 90), Roman poet, author of the epic *Argonautica*.

Valescum.who: Valescus de Taranta (fl. 1382–1418), physician at Montpellier, author of the medical compendium *Philonium*.

Valescus.who: Valescus de Taranta (fl. 1382–1418), physician at Montpellier, author of the medical compendium *Philonium*.

Valescus de Taranta.who: Valescus de Taranta (fl. 1382–1418), physician at Montpellier, author of the medical compendium *Philonium*.

Valesians.who: The people of the Valais (Wallis), the Alpine valley of the upper Rhône in Switzerland, noted for goitre.

Valleriolam.who: François Valleriole (1504–1580), French physician of Arles, later professor at Turin, author of medical *Observationes*.

Vandals.who: The Vandals, Germanic people who overran Gaul, Spain and Roman Africa in the fifth century.

Varronists.who: Satirists in the manner of Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), whose Menippean satires mixed prose and verse.

Vascus Gama.who: Vasco da Gama (c. 1460–1524), Portuguese navigator who first sailed from Europe round Africa to India (1497–99).

Vaticanus.basis: Castellio's anti-Calvin tract on Servetus is cast as a dialogue with a speaker named Vaticanus; Castellio and Bellius are named next.
Vaticanus.who: 'Vaticanus', the speaker who answers Calvin in Sebastian Castellio's dialogue *Contra libellum Calvini*, attacking Calvin's defence of Servetus's execution.

Vatinian.who: Publius Vatinius, Roman politician of Caesar's party, so detested that 'Vatinian hatred' (odium Vatinianum) became proverbial.

Vatinius.who: Publius Vatinius, Caesarian politician who was elected praetor for 55 BC over Cato the Younger, a byword for the unworthy preferred.

Vaughan.who: William Vaughan (1575–1641), Welsh writer on health and promoter of a Newfoundland colony (Cambriol), author of *The Golden Fleece* (1626).

Vegetius.who: Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus (late 4th century), Roman writer of the military handbook *Epitoma rei militaris*.

Veientes.who: The Veientes, people of Veii, Etruscan city north of Rome and Rome's persistent early enemy, taken in 396 BC.

Veneranda Pales.who: Pales, Roman deity of shepherds and flocks, honoured at the Parilia festival.

Venerem.basis: Latin 'ad Venerem', i.e. to sexual intercourse

Veneres.who: The two Venuses of Plato's Symposium, heavenly (Urania) and common (Pandemos); in the third passage 'Veneres' means charms or graces.

Venetian.who: Of Venice; used of Barocius, Marco Polo and Venetian women.

Venetian Palma.who: Palmanova, star-shaped fortress town in Friuli, north-east Italy, built by Venice from 1593 on a regular plan.

Venetians.who: The people and republic of Venice.

Venice.who: Venice, city and republic in north-east Italy.

Venner.who: Tobias Venner (1577–1660), English physician at Bath, author of the dietary work Via recta ad vitam longam (1620).

Ventidius.basis: Burton's note cites Horace, and the story matches Satires 1.1; the name form varies between texts
Ventidius.who: The miser in Horace's Satires 1.1 who feared dying in want; modern texts name him Ummidius.

Venus.who: Venus, Roman goddess of love; Burton also uses the name for sexual intercourse and for the planet.

Venus Barbata.basis: Burton's hair story fits Venus Calva better, so he may have confused the two cults
Venus Barbata.who: The 'bearded Venus', an androgynous form of the goddess worshipped in Cyprus and mentioned by ancient mythographers.

Venus’ Vigil.who: The Pervigilium Veneris, anonymous late Latin poem on Venus' spring festival, with the refrain 'Cras amet qui nunquam amavit'.

Verderius.who: Antoine du Verdier (1544–1600), French bibliographer, who produced the Latin edition of Vincenzo Cartari's Imagines deorum (1581).

Verduri.who: The Vardar (ancient Axios), the main river of Macedonia, flowing into the Aegean near Thessaloniki.

Verona.who: Verona, city in north-east Italy, then under Venice, famous for its Roman amphitheatre.

Verres.who: Gaius Verres (d. 43 BC), corrupt Roman governor of Sicily, prosecuted by Cicero in the Verrine orations.

Verulam.who: Francis Bacon (1561–1626), Baron Verulam and Viscount St Albans, author of the Historia vitae et mortis.

Verulamium.who: Verulamium, the Roman town beside modern St Albans, Hertfordshire.

Vesalius.who: Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564), Flemish anatomist, author of De humani corporis fabrica (1543).

Vespasian.who: Vespasian, Roman emperor AD 69–79, proverbial for his avarice.

Vesper.who: Vesper, the evening star (the planet Venus), personified.

Vesta.who: Vesta, Roman virgin goddess of the hearth.

Vestal.basis: Burton's note cites Seneca, and the quoted verse belongs to that controversia
Vestal.who: The unnamed Vestal virgin in the elder Seneca's Controversiae (6.8), accused of writing the line 'Felices nuptae! moriar nisi nubere dulce est'.

Vesuvius.who: Vesuvius, the volcano near Naples, whose eruption of AD 79 killed the elder Pliny.

Vettius.who: Vettius Agorius Praetextatus (d. 384), pagan Roman senator, a leading speaker in Macrobius' Saturnalia.

Vetustina.basis: the quoted verses are from Martial's epigram addressed to Vetustilla
Vetustina.who: Vetustilla, the decrepit old woman mocked in Martial, Epigrams 3.93.

Vibius.who: Vibius Paciaecus, Spaniard who hid the young Marcus Crassus in a seaside cave, as Plutarch relates in his life of Crassus.

Vibius Virrius.who: Vibius Virrius, Capuan leader who poisoned himself with other senators when Rome retook Capua in 211 BC (Livy book 26).

Vicenza.who: Vicenza, city in the Veneto, north-east Italy.

Victorina.basis: one of a list of generic names for a mistress

Victorinus.basis: Jerome's letter on Nepotian lists him with Cyprian, Lactantius, Hilary and Arnobius; Marius Victorinus is the other candidate
Victorinus.who: Victorinus of Pettau (Poetovio) (d. c. 304), bishop and early Latin biblical commentator, named in Jerome's list of Latin Christian writers.

Victorius Faventinus.who: Leonello Vittori (Leonellus Faventinus de Victoriis), Italian physician of Faenza, early 16th century, author of a Practica medicinalis.

Victorius Faventinus Emper.who: Leonello Vittori of Faenza, early-16th-century Italian physician; 'Emper.' refers to his empirica, his practical medical writings.

Vidus Vidius.who: Guido Guidi (Vidus Vidius, 1509–1569), Florentine physician and anatomist, royal physician in Paris and later professor at Pisa; Burton wrongly calls him Dutch.

Vienna.who: Vienna, capital of Austria, besieged by Suleiman the Magnificent in 1529.

Villalpandus.who: Juan Bautista Villalpando (1552–1608), Spanish Jesuit whose commentary on Ezekiel contains a celebrated reconstruction of Solomon's Temple.

Villanovanus.who: Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), Catalan physician and alchemist, author of the Breviarium practicae and a treatise on wines.

Vincent.basis: different bearers in the two passages
Vincent.who: In one passage a currier, father of a girl treated by Amatus Lusitanus; in the other Vicente de Valverde, Dominican friar who confronted Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532.

Vinitor.who: The vinedresser who talks with a Phoenician in Philostratus's Heroicus; Burton takes 'Phoenix' (the Phoenician) for a proper name.

Violanta.who: Violante Visconti (1354–1386), daughter of Galeazzo II Visconti of Milan, married in 1368 to Lionel of Antwerp, Duke of Clarence.

Virg.who: Virgil (70–19 BC), Roman poet of the Aeneid, Eclogues and Georgics; abbreviation used in citations.

Virgilius Alexin.who: Virgil and Alexis, the beautiful boy loved by the shepherd Corydon in Virgil's second Eclogue, traditionally read as the poet's own love.

Virgin Mary.who: Mary, mother of Jesus, venerated by Catholics as patron and intercessor.

Virginia.who: Virginia, the English colony in North America founded at Jamestown in 1607.

Virginian.who: The native Algonquian inhabitants of Virginia; Dasamonquepeuc was a village on the mainland opposite Roanoke Island.

Viriplaca.who: Viriplaca, Roman goddess who reconciled quarrelling husbands and wives, with a shrine on the Palatine.

Viriplaca Dea.who: Viriplaca, Roman goddess who reconciled quarrelling husbands and wives, with a shrine on the Palatine.

Virtue.who: Virtus, Roman personification and goddess of virtue; in one passage simply the moral habit opposed to vice.

Vitellio.who: Witelo (c. 1230–after 1275), Silesian scholar whose Perspectiva was the standard medieval Latin treatise on optics.

Vitellius.who: Aulus Vitellius (15–69), Roman emperor for part of 69, the Year of the Four Emperors, notorious for gluttony.

Viterbium.who: Viterbo, town in northern Lazio, central Italy.

Vitry.basis: Coubert was a seat of the L'Hospital-Vitry family in Renou's time; which member is meant is uncertain
Vitry.who: Probably Louis de L'Hospital, seigneur de Vitry, French nobleman whose family held the château of Coubert in Brie.

Vitus.who: St Vitus, early Christian martyr, invoked against the dancing mania called St Vitus' dance; his shrines drew sufferers.

Vladislaus.who: First, Władysław II the Exile (1105–1159), ruler of Poland, with Piotr Włostowic; second, Jogaila of Lithuania, baptised Władysław II Jagiełło (d. 1434).

Vladislaus Cubitalis.who: Władysław I the Elbow-high (Łokietek, 1260–1333), diminutive king of Poland who reunited the kingdom.

Volateran.who: Raffaele Maffei of Volterra (Volaterranus, 1451–1522), Italian humanist, author of the encyclopaedic Commentaria urbana.

Volga.who: The Volga, Europe's longest river, flowing into the Caspian Sea.

Volkelius.who: Johannes Völkel (d. 1618), German Socinian theologian at Raków, author of De vera religione.

Volpone.who: Volpone, the cunning Venetian magnifico in Ben Jonson's comedy Volpone, or the Fox (1606).

Volupia.who: Volupia, Roman goddess of pleasure and delight.

Vopiscus.who: Flavius Vopiscus, one of the purported authors of the Historia Augusta, credited with the Life of Aurelian.

Vopiscus Aureliano.who: Flavius Vopiscus, purported Historia Augusta author, cited for his Life of Aurelian.

Vorstius.who: Conrad Vorstius (1569–1622), German Remonstrant theologian at Leiden, attacked by James I for allegedly Socinian views of God.

Vortigern.who: Vortigern, 5th-century British king who invited the Saxons Hengist and Horsa into Britain and, in legend, married Rowena.

Voscius.basis: cited among scholastics on hell-fire; cannot be securely identified

Vrients.basis: Possibly the Antwerp print publisher Jan Baptist Vrients, but not certain.

Vulcan.who: Vulcan (Hephaestus), Roman god of fire and smithing, who made Achilles' shield and was thrown from heaven onto Lemnos.

Vulcanian.who: The volcanic Aeolian or Lipari Islands north of Sicily, anciently called the Vulcanian islands.

Wadley.who: Wadley House, near Faringdon in the Vale of White Horse, then in Berkshire (now Oxfordshire), seat of the Purefoy family.

Waking.who: Not a name: waking, the state opposed to sleep.

Walesby.who: Walesby, a village in Lincolnshire; Burton held its living for a time through the Countess of Exeter's patronage and later resigned it.

Wallachia.who: Wallachia, the principality between the Carpathians and the Danube, now southern Romania.

Walloons.who: The Walloons, French-speaking people of the southern Low Countries, now southern Belgium; Burton loosely equates them with Swiss mercenaries.

Walsingham.who: Walsingham in Norfolk, site of the great medieval pilgrimage shrine of Our Lady, destroyed at the Reformation.

Ware.who: Ware, a Hertfordshire town on the River Lea, from which the Lea was made navigable to London.

Watery.who: Not a name: watery (excrements), a humoral term.

Wecker’s Electuary de Epithymo.who: A purging electuary of epithyme (dodder of thyme) in the formula of Johann Jacob Wecker (1528–1586), physician of Colmar and pharmacological compiler.

Weddington.who: Weddington, a village on the River Anker near Nuneaton, Warwickshire.

Weever.who: John Weever (1576–1632), English antiquary and poet, author of Ancient Funerall Monuments (1631).

Weissenberg.who: Weissenburg in Bavaria, near which lie the remains of Charlemagne's canal (Fossa Carolina) between the Rezat and the Altmühl.

Wenceslaus.basis: The form names him, but the patronage of sheep usually belongs to St Wendelin, so Burton or his source may have confused the two.
Wenceslaus.who: St Wenceslaus (d. 935), duke of Bohemia and martyr, here cited as a patron saint of sheep.

Wernerus.basis: The Latin form and the subject, marvellous waters of central Europe, fit him.
Wernerus.who: Georg Werner (Wernher), 16th-century Silesian author of a Latin treatise on the remarkable waters of Hungary.

Westchester.who: Chester, then often called Westchester, famous for its Rows, covered galleries along the streets.

Westminster.who: Westminster, where John Williams, as Dean, fitted out the Abbey library.

Westmonasteriensis.who: 'Matthew of Westminster', the supposed author of the medieval chronicle Flores Historiarum, really a compilation from Matthew Paris and later continuators.

Whitbourne.who: Sir Richard Whitbourne (1561–1635), English mariner and promoter of colonising Newfoundland, author of A Discourse and Discovery of New-found-land (1620).

White Hellebore.who: Not a name: white hellebore (Veratrum album), a violent emetic drug.

William.who: William the Conqueror (c. 1028–1087), duke of Normandy and king of England, illegitimate son of Duke Robert and Arlette of Falaise.

William Burton.who: William Burton (1575–1645), Robert Burton's elder brother, antiquary and author of The Description of Leicestershire (1622).

William Jones.who: William Jones, London printer who printed Edmund Gunter's work on the sector and cross-staff in 1623.

William Purefoy.basis: Caldecote Hall was that William Purefoy's seat, but the identification with the regicide is not certain.
William Purefoy.who: William Purefoy of Caldecote, Warwickshire, later a Parliamentarian and regicide.

Windsor.who: Windsor, the Berkshire town on the Thames.

Winifred.who: St Winifred (Gwenfrewi), 7th-century Welsh virgin martyr, said to have been restored to life, venerated at Holywell.

Wisdom.who: Not a name: wisdom, a personification in a fable in one passage and a faculty of the understanding in the other.

Wit.who: Not a name: wit, the agent understanding.

Wither’s Sat.basis: 'Sat.' abbreviates satires; Wither's satires are the obvious source, but the exact work is not settled.
Wither’s Sat.who: The satires of George Wither (1588–1667), English poet, chiefly Abuses Stript and Whipt (1613).

Wittenberg.who: Wittenberg in Saxony, Germany, seat of the Lutheran university.

Wolfgangus.who: Wolfgang Heider (1558–1626), professor of ethics at Jena, author of a Systema philosophiae moralis.

Wolfius.basis: The first passage's citation fits Hieronymus Wolf; the Brunsellius anecdote may come from a different author.
Wolfius.who: In the first passage, Hieronymus Wolf (1516–1580), German humanist, author of the dialogue prefixed to Leovitius's collection of nativities; the second may be another Wolf.

Wollerton.who: Wollaton Hall near Nottingham, the Elizabethan mansion built in the 1580s by Sir Francis Willoughby.

Woodstock.who: Woodstock in Oxfordshire, site of a royal manor where Henry II is said to have kept Rosamond Clifford.

Worcester.who: Worcester, cathedral city on the Severn in the west Midlands of England.

Wye.who: The River Wye, flowing from mid-Wales through Herefordshire to the Severn estuary.

Xanthippe.who: Xanthippe, wife of Socrates, proverbial in ancient anecdote as a shrew.

Xanthus.who: Xanthus of Miletus, in Parthenius's love stories, who travelled through Europe to ransom his wife Herippe, carried off by the Gauls.

Xenocles.who: Xenocles, Athenian architect under Pericles who completed the lantern of the Hall of Initiation at Eleusis (Plutarch, Pericles 13).

Xenocrates.who: Xenocrates of Chalcedon (c.396–314 BC), pupil of Plato and head of the Academy, who defined the soul as a self-moving number.

Xenophanes.who: Xenophanes of Colophon (c.570–c.475 BC), Greek philosopher-poet who explained the lights seen on ships' masts as small glowing clouds.

Xenophilus.who: Xenophilus, Pythagorean musician of Chalcidice, recorded by Pliny as living 105 years without illness.

Xenophon Cliniam.who: Xenophon (c.430–c.354 BC), Athenian historian and pupil of Socrates; Clinias is the beautiful youth praised in his Symposium.

Xenophon Cyrus.who: Xenophon (c.430–c.354 BC), Athenian historian, whose Cyropaedia portrays Cyrus the Great as the ideal ruler.

Xenophon’s Tyrannus.who: Xenophon's Hiero (also called Tyrannicus), a dialogue in which the tyrant Hiero of Syracuse tells Simonides the miseries of a ruler's life.

Xenopithes.who: Xenopithes, a fictional woman-hating philosopher in one of the love letters of Aristaenetus (c. 5th century AD).

Xerxes.who: Xerxes I (r. 486–465 BC), Persian king who invaded Greece, famous for having the Hellespont whipped.

Ximenius.who: Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros (1436–1517), Archbishop of Toledo and regent of Castile, founder of the University of Alcalá.

Xuntain.basis: Burton cites Ricci on Peking; Ricci/Trigault spell Shuntian 'Xuntien'.
Xuntain.who: Shuntian, the prefecture of Peking (Beijing), as named in the Jesuit accounts of China.

Xylander.who: Wilhelm Holtzmann, called Xylander (1532–1576), German classical scholar of Heidelberg, Latin translator of Plutarch.

Ybouyapab.who: The Serra da Ibiapaba, a flat-topped plateau in Ceará, northeastern Brazil, described by Joannes de Laet.

York.who: The House of York, the royal dynasty that fought the House of Lancaster in the Wars of the Roses.

Yorkshire.who: Yorkshire, county of northern England; St Wilfrid's Needle was a narrow passage in the crypt of Ripon Minster.

Zabarel.who: Jacopo Zabarella (1533–1589), Paduan Aristotelian philosopher and logician who wrote on the soul.

Zacharias.who: Zacharias Scholasticus (6th century), bishop of Mytilene, whose dialogue Ammonius refutes the Neoplatonist Ammonius on the eternity of the world.

Zachary.who: Zechariah, Hebrew prophet (late 6th century BC), author of the biblical Book of Zechariah.

Zacynthus.who: Zakynthos (Zante), Ionian island off the western Peloponnese, then under Venice.

Zamzummims.who: The Zamzummim, a race of giants said in Deuteronomy 2:20 to have lived in the land of the Ammonites.

Zanchy.who: Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), Italian Reformed theologian who taught at Strasbourg and Heidelberg.

Zante.who: Zakynthos (Zante), Ionian island off the western Peloponnese, then a Venetian possession.

Zebedee.who: Zebedee, Galilean fisherman, father of the apostles James and John.

Zeeland.who: Zeeland, the low-lying island province of the southwestern Netherlands, much of it reclaimed from the sea.

Zeno.basis: The 'scurra Atticus' jibe is Zeno the Epicurean's (Cicero); the soul-as-fire view and the suicide are Zeno of Citium's.

Zephyrus.who: Zephyrus, Greek god of the west wind, who killed Hyacinthus out of jealousy of Apollo.

Zerbino.who: Zerbino, prince of Scotland in Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, who dies thinking of his beloved Isabella.

Zerubbabel.who: Zerubbabel, governor of Judah after the Exile, who in 1 Esdras wins Darius's contest by arguing that women and truth are strongest.

Zetes.who: Zetes, winged son of Boreas and Orithyia, who sailed with his brother Calais among the Argonauts.

Zeuxis.who: Zeuxis of Heraclea (fl. late 5th century BC), Greek painter famed for his Helen.

Ziim.who: Hebrew ziyyim, the wild desert creatures of Isaiah 13:21, read by some commentators as demons or spirits.

Zion.who: Zion, the hill of Jerusalem, used here figuratively for the Church.

Zisca.who: Jan Žižka (c. 1360–1424), blind Hussite general of Bohemia, said to have ordered that a drum be made of his skin after his death.

Zocotora.who: Socotra, an island in the Arabian Sea off the Horn of Africa, famous for 'Socotrine' aloes.

Zoilus.who: Zoilus of Amphipolis (4th century BC), Greek critic notorious for his attacks on Homer; his name became proverbial for a carping critic.

Zona Torrida.who: The torrid zone, the band of the earth between the tropics.

Zonarus.who: John Zonaras (12th century), Byzantine historian, author of the *Epitome historiarum*, a world chronicle.

Zopyrus.who: Zopyrus (5th century BC), Greek physiognomist who read vicious traits in Socrates' face, as reported by Cicero.

Zoroastes.who: Zoroaster (Zarathustra), the ancient Iranian prophet, whom Renaissance writers treated as a source of ancient wisdom.

Zubeda.basis: Augustine, City of God 22.8, names Hesperius's farm 'Zubedi'
Zubeda.who: Zubedi, an estate of the tribune Hesperius in the district of Fussala near Hippo Regius (modern Annaba, Algeria).

Zur.who: The South Sea (Spanish 'Mar del Sur'), i.e. the Pacific Ocean.

Zurich.who: Zurich, city in Switzerland, home of Conrad Gessner.

Zwinger.who: Theodor Zwinger (1533–1588), Basel physician and encyclopedist, author of the *Theatrum vitae humanae* and a treatise on travel.
